rationale: Tax legislation is traditionally scored by the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT), not primarily by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO). While CBO often prepares accompanying budgetary analyses and sometimes issues its own estimates, it is normal for the JCT to provide the official revenue scoring for tax bills, so saying the bill is "not being scored by the CBO, as it is traditionally" misstates the usual practice.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: The statement overstates and mischaracterizes the evidence. While many studies report a substantial proportion of hospitalized older adults are malnourished or at risk (estimates vary widely, often ~20–50% depending on setting and criteria), the claim that half have malnutrition 'so severe' that it caused their illness or prevents recovery is unsubstantiated and conflates association with causation.

claim: In the 2012 election, there were more votes cast than registered voters in St. Lucie County, and Palm Beach County had 141 percent turnout.
rationale: The claim is inconsistent with certified 2012 Florida election returns and basic arithmetic: a county cannot legitimately have more votes cast than registered voters in the same election without errors or a mismatched denominator. Official county tallies for St. Lucie and Palm Beach in the 2012 general election show turnout well below 100%, so the reported figures of >100% (and 141% for Palm Beach) are incorrect or a misinterpretation.

claim: "Medicaid expansion isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street."
rationale: Numerous national and state polls over the last decade have shown consistent majority support for Medicaid expansion, and several states have approved expansion at the ballot box, indicating it is generally popular with the public. While intensity and salience can vary by locality and how the question is framed, the broad pattern contradicts the claim that expansion is not a popular issue 'on the street.'

claim: Says "I have been through the gauntlet, when we had riots in that Capitol."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted statement but gives no speaker, date, or source to verify it. Without attribution or corroborating reporting, there is insufficient evidence to confirm the person actually said this about having "been through the gauntlet" during riots at a Capitol.

claim: "When you look at the nearly 150 men and women who have served us on the Texas Supreme Court, more than half of them had zero prior judicial experience."
rationale: The claim is a specific numerical assertion but I am not aware of any compiled historical count showing that a majority of roughly 150 Texas Supreme Court justices had no prior judicial experience. Historical patterns in Texas show many justices previously served as district or county judges or in other judicial roles, so the blanket statement that more than half had zero prior judicial experience is unlikely and unsubstantiated without a detailed roll-call analysis.

claim: "While all COVID-19 news has been going on, the U.S. Government has been sneakily trying to remove end-to-end encryption" which means "the government will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls."
rationale: It is true U.S. law enforcement and some legislators have publicly pushed for ways to limit or obtain access around end-to-end encryption, but these efforts have been debated openly rather than being a secret ‘sneaky’ removal during COVID. Moreover, even if E2EE were weakened or removed, that would not automatically mean the government can instantly read and listen to all communications—access would still depend on service-provider implementation, legal process, and technical constraints.

claim: "I have given $30,000 of my unused travel expenses over the years to supplement the school system's general budget."
rationale: There is no verifiable public evidence provided to substantiate a specific $30,000 figure or that unused travel reimbursements were redirected to a school system's general budget. Specific claims about personal financial transfers require supporting documentation (expense reports, donation or accounting records); absent that, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because there is no accessible, specific fiscal analysis tying measures labeled 3-386 and 3-388 to definitive cost outcomes. Costs of ballot measures depend on their exact text, implementation details, and official fiscal notes; without that jurisdictional and textual context, the assertion that 3-386 will “cost a fortune” while 3-388 will cost less is unsubstantiated.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: Richmond (no NFL franchise) did not build a $14 million stadium for an NFL team, and modern NFL stadiums cost hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars. There is no evidence an NFL team — let alone the 'second richest' — was given a $14M stadium by the city of Richmond.

claim: "CNN-NPR photojournalist Jade Sacker was embedded with antifa leader" during the U.S. Capitol attack.
rationale: There is no evidence that a CNN or NPR photojournalist named Jade Sacker existed or was embedded with an “antifa leader” at the U.S. Capitol. Both outlets and independent fact-checkers have found the social‑media claims to be misattributions or fabrications, and law-enforcement investigations into Jan. 6 found no credible evidence of organized antifa infiltration as described.

claim: David Dewhurst "has never once cut one penny from the state budget."
rationale: David Dewhurst served as Texas lieutenant governor during multiple legislative sessions in which the state budget was reduced; as presiding officer and a member of Republican leadership he was part of the budget process that produced spending cuts. Therefore the absolute statement that he "has never once cut one penny from the state budget" is incorrect.

claim: Says Christopher Little has "a history of working against environmental protection by defending the worst types of corporate polluters"
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated: there is no widely known public record tying a prominent Christopher Little (such as the literary agent) to a sustained pattern of defending major corporate polluters or opposing environmental protection. The name is ambiguous and searches of major biographical and news sources do not corroborate allegations of a documented history of environmental defense for corporate polluters.

claim: "State Rep. Kathleen Peters has a 100 percent pro-abortion voting record – even voting against a ban on sex-selection abortions."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that she has a "100 percent" pro-abortion voting record and cites a specific vote; public roll-call records and interest-group scorecards do not support such an unqualified assertion. While Peters has taken some votes at odds with her party on reproductive issues in particular sessions, there is no clear evidence she has a perfect, across-the-board pro-abortion record, and the specific sex-selection ban vote cited is not verifiably linked to her without a bill number and session.

claim: "Now, I also support the Bush tax cuts. Sen. McCain voted against them originally. He now believes they should be made permanent. I'm glad he agrees they should be made permanent."
rationale: The claim that 'Sen. McCain voted against them originally' is incorrect as stated — McCain’s Senate voting record shows he supported the major Bush-era tax cut packages and later publicly supported making large portions of those cuts permanent. Therefore the assertion that he originally voted against them but now agrees to make them permanent misstates his earlier position.

claim: Says a Bureau of Labor Statistics report attributed a sharp increase in work-related fatalities to "increasing numbers of employees and drivers could not read or understand warning signs in English."
rationale: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' fatality reports (CFOI) do not include language blaming 'increasing numbers of employees and drivers could not read or understand warning signs in English' as the cause of a sharp increase in work-related fatalities. BLS releases attribute year-to-year changes to factors like more hours worked, changes in industry composition, motor-vehicle incidents, and COVID-19, and do not make blanket claims about workers' English comprehension.

claim: Congressman Scott DesJarlais "is spending his one year anniversary on vacation -- only working 6 days in all of January."
rationale: The statement provides no year or source and I could not corroborate that Rep. Scott DesJarlais worked only six days in a given January or was on vacation for a "one year anniversary." Congressional schedules, travel and roll-call records are public and would be needed to substantiate such a specific claim; without a verifiable date and supporting evidence it should be treated as unverified and therefore false.

claim: Elena Kagan "has published five scholarly review articles, mostly on administrative law and the First Amendment. These articles were mostly on technical and procedural issues."
rationale: Contemporary sources and Kagan's nomination materials record that she had authored five law-review/scholarly pieces prior to her Supreme Court appointment, with most addressing administrative law and First Amendment topics. Those writings were generally focused on technical and procedural aspects rather than sweeping doctrinal manifestos.

claim: Says Joe Biden "helps build Afghanistan’s pipeline."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden personally helped build any pipeline in Afghanistan. Major proposed projects (notably the Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India, TAPI, pipeline) have been regional initiatives involving Turkmenistan and private firms and remain largely unbuilt; the United States did not directly construct Afghan pipelines or credit Biden with doing so.

claim: Says Chuck Todd said the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated."
rationale: There is no reliable record or transcript showing Chuck Todd saying the Roy Moore story 'felt completely orchestrated.' Major broadcast transcripts and contemporaneous coverage of the Moore allegations show Todd discussed the story as newsworthy and politically consequential, but fact-checkers and archives do not support that exact quoted phrase being uttered by him.

claim: "I’ve already traveled to Washington, D.C., and secured a historic commitment from the Trump administration to provide assistance to the communities that Michael battered."
rationale: The claim as phrased is not verifiable. Although the Trump administration did approve federal disaster declarations and provide aid after Hurricane Michael in October 2018, there is no clear, public evidence that a specific individual ‘‘traveled to Washington, D.C., and secured a historic commitment’’ from the administration; the wording appears to overstate routine federal disaster-assistance actions. Without named actors, dates, or documentary proof, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says he authored legislation "to guarantee coverage to people with pre-existing conditions -- no matter what happens to Obamacare."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it names no person or specific bill and federal guarantees of pre-existing condition coverage require explicit statutory language. Many repeal-and-replace proposals have claimed to protect people with pre-existing conditions but either relied on the Affordable Care Act's framework or used limited mechanisms (state waivers, high-risk pools) rather than an unconditional, independent federal guarantee. Without a named author and bill text showing an enforceable guarantee 'no matter what happens to Obamacare,' the assertion is misleading.

claim: "We've had 11,000 attempts to amend the Constitution since 1789."
rationale: Congressional records and multiple fact-checkers report that well over 11,000 proposed constitutional amendments have been introduced in Congress since 1789, though the vast majority never advanced. The exact tally can vary by source because identical proposals introduced in different sessions are often counted separately.

claim: Says Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie made a late-night visit to Kinko’s to forge President Barack Obama’s birth certificate two days before Obama unveiled it to the media.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Neil Abercrombie made a late-night trip to a Kinko's to forge President Obama's birth certificate. Contemporary reporting and fact-checks show the claim originated in birther conspiracy writings and was not substantiated; Abercrombie did say he had seen the state's birth record but never admitted any forgery or Kinko's involvement.

claim: Says for otherwise healthy people "experiencing mild to moderate respiratory symptoms with or without a COVID-19 diagnosis … only high temperatures kill a virus, so let your fever run high," but not over 103 or 104 degrees.
rationale: The claim that "only high temperatures kill a virus, so let your fever run high" is incorrect and potentially dangerous. While fever is part of the immune response and can make the body less hospitable to some pathogens, the temperatures required to reliably inactivate respiratory viruses in vitro are far higher than safe human body temperatures; deliberately allowing fevers to reach 103–104°F risks harm without proven antiviral benefit. Medical guidance is to treat fevers for comfort and to seek care at established warning thresholds, especially for infants, elderly, or those with comorbidities.

claim: Says Sidney Blumenthal wrote that the Benghazi attack was "almost certainly preventable. Clinton was in charge of the State Department, and it failed to protect U.S. personnel and an American consulate in Libya."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence that Sidney Blumenthal wrote or published the quoted sentence. Blumenthal, a longtime Clinton adviser and commentator, has written about Libya and Benghazi but is not documented as having authored that specific critique attributing failure to Hillary Clinton and the State Department in those exact words. The quote appears to be either misattributed or paraphrased from other critics rather than a verified Blumenthal statement.

claim: Republicans "nominated the 1st Black woman to the SCOTUS & she was BLOCKED & filibustered by… Joe Biden."
rationale: The President, not a party, nominates Supreme Court justices; the first Black woman nominated to the Court was Ketanji Brown Jackson and she was nominated by President Joe Biden in 2022 and subsequently confirmed. There is no record of Republicans having 'nominated' that Black woman, nor of Joe Biden filibustering or blocking a Black woman's Supreme Court nomination. The claim conflates roles and misstates the facts.

claim: Austin was the "site of the first mass shooting in the country."
rationale: The statement is false because Austin was not the site of the first mass shooting in the country. While the 1966 University of Texas tower attack in Austin is often described as the first modern mass shooting to receive national attention, there were earlier mass killings involving firearms in the United States, notably the Bath School massacre in Michigan in 1927, among others.

claim: "But for immigrants, we would have a contracting population..."
rationale: The statement is overly general and cannot be treated as true for all places and times. While many high-income countries have fertility below replacement rates and therefore rely on immigration to avoid population decline, other countries still have natural population growth and would not contract without immigrants. Whether the population would contract 'but for immigrants' depends on the specific country and timeframe.

claim: "Today, the five largest financial institutions are 38 percent bigger than they were back in 2008, when they were too big to fail."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and cannot be verified as stated: it gives no date for "today," does not specify which five institutions, nor the metric (assets, market value, or deposits). While the largest banks in the U.S. and globally have generally grown since 2008, the percent change varies by institution and by measure, and a blanket 38% figure is not reliably supported without those details.

claim: Says the Obama administration approved a major disaster declaration for Oklahoma in 2009, when nine of the state’s 77 counties burned for "about three days," while Texas wildfires have been burning for longer without such a declaration.
rationale: The Obama administration did approve a major disaster declaration for Oklahoma wildfires in February 2009 covering multiple counties that burned over a short period, so that part is accurate. However the implication that Texas wildfires were burning longer without any comparable federal declaration is misleading: Texas wildfire events (notably in 2011) later received federal disaster declarations and assistance, and declarations depend on state requests and assessed damage rather than simple duration.

claim: A recall election for Wisconsin governor would cost "$7.7 million -- $7.7 million that may already be allocated to merit raises for teachers or health care for the poor or school books for your kids."
rationale: State officials and contemporaneous reporting did estimate a Wisconsin gubernatorial recall could cost roughly $7–8 million (often cited as $7.7 million), but the claim that those dollars 'may already be allocated' to teacher raises, health care for the poor, or school books is misleading. Recall costs are paid from election/administrative budgets or the general fund and are not necessarily pre-committed line-item allocations that would automatically displace those specific programs.

claim: "KXL Radio in Portland reported today that Firefighters are now being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members."
rationale: There is no corroborated evidence that KXL (Portland) posted or broadcast a verified report today saying firefighters are being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members. Major local and regional news outlets and available summaries of KXL reporting do not support this claim, and similar accusations have circulated as unverified social-media disinformation in the past.

claim: The media "never show crowds."
rationale: The absolute claim that the media "never show crowds" is contradicted by abundant evidence: news broadcasts, print and online outlets, and social media routinely publish photos and footage of crowds at protests, rallies, sporting events, concerts, parades and other gatherings. While individual outlets may sometimes omit or downplay particular crowd images for editorial reasons, the blanket statement "never" is demonstrably false.

claim: Members of Congress "have not reduced their salaries ... since the Great Depression," meaning they've gone "eight decades without a pay cut."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Congressional pay is set by statute and has been adjusted, frozen, and in some instances effectively reduced since the 1930s; moreover real (inflation-adjusted) pay has fallen in many years even when nominal pay did not. Saying members have gone “eight decades without a pay cut” ignores these freezes, statutory changes, and the nominal vs. real-pay distinction.

claim: A photo shows "brave women of the Red Cross" arriving in Normandy on D-Day to help injured troops.
rationale: It is very unlikely the pictured women were Red Cross workers landing on Normandy on D‑Day. Allied humanitarian volunteers and many civilian aid organizations were not deployed ashore during the initial June 6, 1944 assault; the beaches were tightly controlled combat zones and early medical care was provided by military surgeons and medics. Many widely shared images claiming to show 'Red Cross girls on D‑Day' have been miscaptioned or actually date from other times or locations.

claim: "Biden confirms agenda to microchip the masses"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden or his administration has 'confirmed' any plan to microchip the general population; this claim arises from online conspiracy theories and misinterpretations of unrelated statements. U.S. public-health and technology policies do not include mass microchipping, and such a program would require explicit legal authorization and widespread, verifiable reporting which does not exist.

claim: "When Abraham Lincoln made the Gettysburg Address speech, the great speech, do you know he was ridiculed? He was ridiculed."
rationale: Contemporary reaction to the Gettysburg Address was mixed: while many praised its eloquence, several newspapers and commentators at the time mocked or criticized Lincoln’s brief remarks and choice of wording. Historical accounts record both praise (including comparisons to Edward Everett’s oration) and ridicule in the press and public commentary.

claim: "President Obama will now own 60 percent of GM, and his union buddies will own almost 20 percent."
rationale: The claim mixes a roughly accurate post‑2009 GM ownership split with a false personal attribution. After GM’s government‑backed restructuring the U.S. Treasury owned about 60% of the reorganized company and the UAW retiree trust (VEBA) received about 17–18%, but those stakes were held by government entities/trusts — not personally by President Obama or his associates.

claim: Says Texas unemployment is dire in various ways such as a doubling in the jobless rate during Rick Perry's governorship. Also, the Texas rate has increased faster than the national rate during Barack Obama's presidency.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Texas unemployment did rise during the 2008–2009 recession while Rick Perry was governor, but it did not sustain a doubling over his entire 2000–2015 tenure (state unemployment peaked in the high single digits versus mid-single digits earlier, not a sustained 2x increase). Similarly, during Barack Obama’s presidency the national unemployment rate rose sharply in 2008–2009 and fell thereafter; the Texas increase did not uniformly outpace the national increase over the Obama years.

claim: Says Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or documented evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott offered money to an uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim to say 'we don’t need stronger gun laws.' Major news outlets covering the Uvalde aftermath reported on Abbott's meetings and public statements but did not report any payment-for-endorsement, and the claim appears to originate from social-media rumor rather than verified reporting.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: This wording is not an accurate summary of Hillary Clinton’s publicly stated position. Across her Senate and campaign record and as Secretary of State she consistently argued against unconditional surrender and generally supported conditions-based drawdowns rather than declaring a fixed withdrawal date or 'waving the white flag'; the quoted language is characteristic of opponents' attacks, not a direct reflection of her policy statements.

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: I cannot find reliable, corroborated evidence that Rick Scott skipped an official "education summit" and instead attended a Tea Party convention in the same week. Such scheduling and attendance by a high-profile politician would be reported in news coverage and official calendars; no clear records or multiple credible reports support the specific claim as stated. Given the lack of verifiable specifics (which summit, which week) the claim as presented is unverified and treated as false.

claim: Sarah Huckabee Sanders dressed up as KKK member on Halloween in 1993.
rationale: There is no credible, contemporaneous evidence that Sarah Huckabee Sanders dressed as a Ku Klux Klan member in 1993. Reputable fact-checkers and public records show the claim originated on social media and has not been substantiated; Sanders would have been about 11 years old in 1993, and no verified photo or reliable reporting supports the allegation.

claim: "There have been 30 published polls in this election cycle and Harry Reid's been trailing in every single one."
rationale: The statement is a blanket claim with no time frame or sources and is implausible given typical poll variation; it is unlikely that in an entire election cycle 30 published polls all showed Harry Reid trailing. Historical polling around Reid's Senate races has shown mixed outcomes (some polls had him leading or tied), so the assertion that every single one showed him behind is unsupported. Without a specific cycle and poll list the claim cannot be verified and is almost certainly false.

claim: "9,871,525 is the number of registered voters in AZ according to FB. AZ population is 7,270,000."
rationale: The claimed 9,871,525 registered voters exceeds Arizona's total population (~7.27 million), which is implausible; official Arizona voter registration totals are roughly in the 4–5 million range, not nearly 10 million. Therefore the statement that AZ has 9,871,525 registered voters is false, while the population figure ~7,270,000 is roughly correct as a state estimate.

claim: Says "Rick Perry doubled spending in a decade."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and misleading: while Texas state spending rose during Rick Perry’s tenure, independent fact-checkers and budget data show the result depends on which spending measure, whether federal funds are included, and whether figures are inflation-adjusted. Under common measures (state-funded General Revenue or inflation-adjusted totals) spending did not literally double over a single ten-year span attributable solely to Perry’s actions. Thus the blanket statement that “Rick Perry doubled spending in a decade” is not supported without much more context.

claim: "As chair of the Senate Education Committee, I led the charge to restore most of the education cuts from last session."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits crucial specifics (which Senate, which legislative session, which cuts, and what 'most' means). Without named jurisdiction, dates, bill numbers, or public legislative records showing the chair's sponsorship and vote outcomes restoring the cuts, the assertion cannot be confirmed. It might be true in a specific context, but the available statement lacks the verifiable detail required to treat it as a factual claim.

claim: "Since Newtown, more people have died at the end of a gun than we have lost in Afghanistan."
rationale: Sandy Hook occurred on December 14, 2012. The United States records tens of thousands of firearm deaths per year (including suicides and homicides), so the cumulative number of people killed by firearms in the U.S. since Newtown far exceeds the roughly 2,400 or so U.S. service members who died in the Afghanistan war. Even using conservative counts (only homicides) the total since 2012 is still much larger than U.S. combat fatalities in Afghanistan.

claim: Says there’s "no wait list" for private school vouchers
rationale: The statement as presented is unverified and implausible as a universal claim: private school voucher programs vary by jurisdiction and many are limited by annual funding or capped slots, which commonly produces wait lists. Without specifying the particular program, time period, or location, the blanket assertion that there is "no wait list" cannot be supported.

claim: Says CNN deleted an online poll showing Bernie Sanders won the first Democratic presidential debate to help out Hillary Clinton.
rationale: There is no evidence that CNN deleted an online debate poll specifically to help Hillary Clinton; independent fact-checkers investigated similar claims and found them unsubstantiated. CNN does sometimes remove or reset user-voted polls for technical reasons or suspected manipulation, but that is not the same as deliberately deleting a poll to favor a candidate.

claim: Says "Rep. Ann Wagner, a three-term incumbent, has never held a town hall in the Second District."
rationale: The claim is unlikely: Ann Wagner, who has served multiple terms representing Missouri's 2nd District, has held constituent events (including district meetings and tele-town-hall style events) rather than never holding any town halls. Incumbent members typically hold such meetings and news coverage of Wagner has described constituent outreach in the district.

claim: Says he banned texting while driving in Austin.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and implausible as written because traffic bans are enacted by legislatures, city councils, or governors — not unilaterally by a single individual. If the intended meaning is that a named official personally "banned" texting while driving in Austin, that would be incorrect: any ban would have been passed by the Austin City Council or enacted by state law and/or signed by a governor. Without a clear subject, the statement is unsupported.

claim: "Trump revokes Barack Obama’s security clearance."
rationale: This is false. In August 2018 the Trump administration revoked or suspended clearances for several former intelligence officials (e.g., Brennan, Clapper, Hayden), but fact-checkers and White House statements noted that Barack Obama, as a former president, did not hold a routine security clearance that could be revoked.

claim: Says "Morgan Carroll opposed requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles, making it harder to track online sex offenders and child predators."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Morgan Carroll broadly opposed a requirement that convicted sex offenders register their online profiles. Allegations like this often stem from opposition to a specific bill or language (e.g., on constitutional or privacy grounds) rather than a blanket refusal to support online-registration requirements, so the claim as stated is misleading and unsubstantiated without citation of a specific vote or reputable fact-check.

claim: "Dark money is paying for over 80 percent of (Kavanaugh’s) ads."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and ambiguous — it does not specify which 'Kavanaugh' or what time period, and reputable ad‑spending trackers and reporting do not show that over 80% of ads for Brett Kavanaugh (or any similarly prominent Kavanaugh-related fight) were paid by undisclosed 'dark money.' While some outside groups with undisclosed donors spent heavily in related fights, there is no evidence that such spending comprised more than 80% of the ads overall.

claim: Says the state’s pension and health benefits reform includes "the destruction of public sector collective bargaining rights."
rationale: The statement asserts that a state's pension and health benefits reform includes “the destruction of public sector collective bargaining rights,” but no specific state or bill is identified and the claim is thus not verifiable as stated. In practice, pension and health benefit reforms commonly change contribution rates, benefit formulas, or limit bargaining over certain financial subjects, but do not typically abolish collective bargaining rights outright without explicit statutory language or court action.

claim: "California Democrat Maxine Waters charged on 3 counts."
rationale: There is no record or credible reporting of Representative Maxine Waters being criminally charged on three counts. As of mid-2024, she has been the subject of political controversy and criticism but has not faced any DOJ indictments listing three charges.

claim: "If you give guns to gangs, you can get out of jail free, if (California’s Proposition 57) passes. If you do a drive-by shooting, you can get out of jail free, if Proposition 57 passes. If you discharge guns on a school yard, you can get out of jail free."
rationale: California Proposition 57 (2016) only created parole consideration for people convicted of nonviolent felonies and expanded judicial review for juvenile transfers; it explicitly excluded violent and serious sex offenses. Crimes like supplying guns to gang members, drive-by shootings, or discharging a firearm at a school would typically be charged as violent felonies or carry firearm enhancements and are not covered by automatic release under Prop 57.

claim: "92 percent" of President Barack Obama's administration has "never worked outside government."
rationale: The 92% figure is a mischaracterization. Publicly available rosters and contemporary fact-checks show many Obama appointees and staff had prior private‑sector, nonprofit, academic or law‑firm experience, so it is not true that 92% had never worked outside government. The claim appears to conflate different statistics or misinterpret the data about prior government experience rather than exclusive career history.

claim: "Fox News uses photo of a married couple promoting ‘traditional marriage’ and the photo is actually of a same-sex couple."
rationale: The claim is presented without a specific incident, date, or image to verify, and there is no clear, widely reported documented example that Fox News systematically used a same-sex couple's photo while promoting ‘traditional marriage.’ While media outlets occasionally misidentify or miscaption images, I cannot substantiate this specific assertion as a verified fact.

claim: Says in Chicago, "we take more guns off the streets than New York or L.A."
rationale: The statement is an unqualified, timeless comparison but public gun-recovery totals vary by year and by metric (total recoveries, traces, or per-capita). Available reporting and police data show that NYPD and LAPD often recover comparable or larger numbers of firearms in many years, so a blanket claim that Chicago takes more guns off the streets than New York or L.A. is not consistently supported.

claim: Rhode Island is the last state still using the Optech III P voting machines and they don’t meet suggested federal standards.
rationale: Reporting and state election inventories identified Rhode Island as the last state relying statewide on legacy Optech III-P precinct optical scanners, and those machines are older models that do not meet more recent voluntary federal guidelines (EAC/VVSG updates) and contemporary accessibility and security recommendations. The statement is time-sensitive—Rhode Island has been cited as the final holdout and the machines have been judged noncompliant with suggested modern standards.

claim: Says Allen West violated federal law by scuba diving with U.S. flag.
rationale: Even if Allen West was photographed or reported scuba diving with a U.S. flag, that does not constitute a violation of federal law. The U.S. Flag Code (Title 4) is largely advisory and does not prescribe criminal penalties, and flag treatment issues are generally protected by the First Amendment unless other specific statutes apply. No credible evidence shows a federal criminal statute was violated in this situation.

claim: Says Bubba Watson wrote a viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Bubba Watson authored a specific widely viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter; while he has made political comments on social media at times, claims that he wrote a particular viral BLM post circulated online are unsubstantiated and appear to be misattributed. Reliable news sources do not document a single viral Facebook post by Watson on BLM that matches the claim.

claim: A bill backed by Sean Duffy and other House Republicans "could actually require the Internal Revenue Service to conduct audits of rape victims" who get an abortion.
rationale: No credible text of a House bill would directly instruct the Internal Revenue Service to single out and audit rape victims who obtain abortions. IRS audits are triggered by tax filings and enforcement priorities, while statutes regulating abortion exceptions or medical-record requirements are typically implemented through health or criminal law, not by ordering tax audits. The claim appears to conflate possible paperwork or reporting changes with a direct statutory mandate for IRS to audit victims.

claim: Compared to President Obama, "President Reagan rushed home from Santa Barbara vacation, from the Reagan ranch when the Korean jetliner was shot out of the air by the Russians."
rationale: President Reagan was at his Rancho del Cielo ranch near Santa Barbara when Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down by a Soviet fighter on September 1, 1983, and he cut short his vacation to return to Washington and deal with the crisis. Contemporary accounts describe him leaving the ranch and convening his national security team promptly, so saying he 'rushed home' is broadly accurate.

claim: "All of the records, as far as I know, about what we did with health care, those are already available."
rationale: The categorical claim that "all" records about what was done with health care are already available is implausible. Patient-level medical records are protected by privacy laws and many internal government or organizational documents are routinely withheld or redacted under privacy, security, and deliberative-process exemptions.

claim: "The president gave the (auto) companies to the UAW."
rationale: No U.S. president has transferred ownership of major auto companies to the United Auto Workers. Auto manufacturers (Ford, GM, Stellantis) are privately or publicly owned and remain under corporate/stockholder control; while the federal government has at times provided bailouts or negotiated settlements that affected workers (e.g., 2009 GM/Chrysler bailout and creation of a UAW VEBA for retiree health), that did not equal giving the companies to the UAW.

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: If the claim refers to Queen Elizabeth II, she died on 8 September 2022 and was born 21 April 1926, which means she was 96 at death, not 95. The statement is therefore incorrect as stated.

claim: Sen. Jeff Merkley "voted six times for more debt."
rationale: The statement is vague and presents a specific numeric count without context or a source. Senator Merkley has voted multiple times on debt-limit increases, continuing resolutions, and spending measures that affect federal debt over his long Senate tenure, but there is no clear, verifiable record that he specifically "voted six times for more debt" as an accurate, standalone fact.

claim: Says Democratic Senate candidate "Bruce Braley voted to cut $700 billion from Medicare to support Obamacare."
rationale: Bruce Braley, then a U.S. Representative, voted for the Affordable Care Act, which the Congressional Budget Office and other analysts estimated included roughly $700–716 billion in Medicare savings over a ten-year window. Those savings were used in part to help finance the law and reduce the federal deficit. The phrasing "cut $700 billion from Medicare" is misleading, however, because most of the savings came from lower payment rates to providers and Medicare Advantage plans rather than direct benefit cuts to traditional Medicare enrollees.

claim: "If you are a hard-working law-abiding citizen who earns $80,000, you don’t get a stimulus check. But if you are a convicted murderer or rapist sitting in jail, you do."
rationale: The claim is false. Eligibility for stimulus payments was based on adjusted gross income, filing status, and dependency status, not whether someone is a convicted criminal; taxpayers with roughly $80,000 of income would generally have qualified for at least a partial payment in 2020 and for a full payment in the 2021 round depending on filing status. While some incarcerated people were eligible in principle, many did not receive payments for administrative or dependency-related reasons, so it is incorrect to state categorically that prisoners received checks while a law‑abiding $80k earner did not.

claim: "28.2 million Americans are still waiting under Obamacare and remain uninsured!"
rationale: The claim mixes a historical uninsured estimate with an inaccurate characterization: while roughly 28 million Americans were uninsured in some past years (Census estimates around 28.2 million in certain years), there is no evidence that 28.2 million people are on an official ‘waiting under Obamacare’ list. The uninsured count varies by year and includes many people who are ineligible for marketplace coverage or who chose not to enroll, not a cohort actively waiting to be covered.

claim: Claims that Obama said, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away."
rationale: There is no credible record or transcript of President Obama saying 'For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away.' Reputable fact‑checking organizations and searchable presidential speech archives do not support this quote, which appears to be a fabricated or misattributed statement.

claim: "Bill Gates calls for the withdrawal of all Covid-19 Vaccines; ‘The vaccines are far more dangerous than anyone imagined.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates called for the withdrawal of all COVID-19 vaccines or said they are "far more dangerous than anyone imagined." Gates and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation have consistently supported COVID-19 vaccination efforts and public health measures, and reputable fact-checkers have debunked similar fabricated attributions. The quoted line does not appear in any verifiable public statement, interview, or transcript from Gates.

claim: "Californians are overwhelmingly against this concept of the illegal sanctuary state."
rationale: The statement that "Californians are overwhelmingly against" an "illegal sanctuary state" is not supported by available evidence. California is a sanctuary-state jurisdiction and public-opinion polling and electoral results in the state generally show significant support for immigrant-protective policies rather than overwhelming opposition. While opinions vary across subgroups and wording of questions affects responses, describing Californians as overwhelmingly against such a concept overstates the case.

claim: Says that under order from Gov. Tony Evers, he and his eight children can’t legally have dinner together anymore.
rationale: The claim is false. Tony Evers does not have eight children (public biographies list three), and Wisconsin public-health orders limited large or non-household gatherings during the pandemic but did not prohibit a parent from having dinner with members of their own household. Limits applied mainly to non-household gatherings and specific capacity rules that varied over time.

claim: "There’s no wildlife" in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
rationale: This claim is false. The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is explicitly designated to protect wildlife and supports abundant species—most notably the Porcupine caribou herd—along with polar bears, migratory birds, muskoxen, wolves, Arctic foxes, fish, and coastal marine mammals; many species undertake seasonal migrations through the refuge.

claim: "There is no reason for these massive, deadly and costly forest fires in California except that forest management is so poor."
rationale: The claim is false because many well-documented factors besides forest management drive California's massive, deadly, costly wildfires. Climate change (warmer, drier conditions and more extreme fire weather), prolonged droughts, insect outbreaks and fuel buildup from past suppression, expansion of the wildland–urban interface, and human ignitions including failing utility equipment all contribute. Forest management (thinning, prescribed burns) can reduce risk in some areas but is not the sole cause.

claim: "Voted the ‘best specialty plate in America’"
rationale: The claim as stated is unsubstantiated because it provides no name of the plate, awarding organization, or date, and there is no well-known, universally recognized national award that names a single 'best specialty plate in America.' Without a cited source or specific contest, the assertion cannot be verified and should be treated as false.
cited_knowledge: General fact-checking standards: awards and recognitions require a named awarding body and source; no widely recognized national accolade matching this exact phrase is known.
safety_notes: Ambiguous: could be true for a specific plate in a particular contest or readers' poll—need the plate name, the organization that voted, and date/source to verify.

claim: "The Biden administration is engaging in human trafficking because they are enabling this to happen" at the southern border.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Biden administration itself is committing or directing human trafficking. Public reporting and law-enforcement investigations attribute human trafficking and smuggling at the southern border to criminal networks and smugglers, not to federal officials or policies. While some critics argue certain border policies may have unintended effects on migration flows, that is different from the government 'engaging in' trafficking.

claim: "Only 536 Georgians are signed up for Obamacare while 400,000 in the state lost their health insurance."
rationale: The claim mixes inconsistent metrics and gives implausibly low enrollment numbers. Actual ACA marketplace enrollments in Georgia were in the tens or hundreds of thousands during open enrollment periods, not 536, and the '400,000 lost their health insurance' figure is either misattributed or refers to a different metric (eg. potential Medicaid expansion eligibles or changes over time) rather than documented simultaneous losses tied to Obamacare. Therefore the paired assertion as stated is inaccurate.

claim: Through the Clinton Foundation, "the Clintons are now worth in excess of $100 million."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation is a nonprofit charitable organization whose funds are legally distinct from the Clintons' personal assets, so it did not make them personally "worth" over $100 million. The Clintons' personal wealth has come mainly from book advances, speaking fees, and investments, and estimates of their combined net worth vary by source and year but are separate from Foundation assets.

claim: Says President Barack Obama failed "to stand up for the bipartisan debt solutions of the Simpson-Bowles Commission."
rationale: President Obama convened and praised the bipartisan Simpson-Bowles commission in 2010 but did not champion or secure adoption of its comprehensive deficit-reduction package. He endorsed some ideas from the report but publicly rejected or did not press for several key recommendations, and Congress never enacted the commission's full plan.

claim: Says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Tammy Baldwin ranks "as the most liberal member of the House."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and therefore false as stated: Tammy Baldwin was frequently ranked among the most liberal House members by some measures, but she was not unambiguously "the most liberal member of the House" across all widely used rankings or time periods. Ideological placement depends on the metric and Congress studied, and no single consistent source shows her as the sole top liberal for the entire period in question.

claim: In 2011, "the average annual compensation for a teacher in the Milwaukee Public Schools system will exceed $100,000."
rationale: Contemporary public data and typical teacher salary scales indicate that the average MPS teacher annual pay in 2011 was well below $100,000; most public school teacher salaries nationwide in that period were in the $40,000–$60,000 range, and adding benefits would not normally double that to exceed $100,000 on average. No credible reports or district payroll records show an average teacher compensation in Milwaukee above $100k for 2011.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees, including the Intelligence Committee chaired by Rep. Adam Schiff, have longstanding authority under House and committee rules to conduct investigations and hold closed-door depositions. Legal scholars and historical precedent show that a separate full House floor vote is not strictly required to start or carry out committee-led impeachment inquiry depositions. Some members disputed the political propriety of the process, but the committee actions were within parliamentary rules.

claim: Says a New York physician and his wife jumped to their deaths because they "can’t afford" Obamacare.
rationale: The viral claim tying a New York physician and his wife's deaths to being unable to 'afford Obamacare' is not supported by reliable reporting. Local news and police statements did not identify the Affordable Care Act or insurance costs as the motive, and fact‑checking organizations found no evidence linking the deaths to Obamacare.

claim: "If you stop testing (for COVID-19) it all goes away and people just have colds like before."
rationale: Stopping testing would reduce reported case counts but would not stop infections or eliminate COVID-19; testing and surveillance are how public health systems detect ongoing transmission and new variants. SARS-CoV-2 causes higher rates of severe disease, hospitalizations, death, and long COVID in a portion of infections compared with common cold viruses, so it does not simply 'go away' if testing stops. Therefore the claim that stopping testing makes COVID-19 vanish and become just colds is incorrect.

claim: President Barack Obama supports immigration amnesty.
rationale: President Obama publicly supported comprehensive immigration reform that included a pathway to legal status and eventual citizenship for many undocumented immigrants, and implemented deferred-action policies (e.g., DACA/DAPA) to protect certain groups from deportation. While he often rejected the pejorative label "amnesty," his policy positions and actions clearly favored legalization for many undocumented immigrants rather than strict mass deportation.

claim: "Right now, in every major poll, national poll and statewide poll done in the last month, six weeks, we are defeating Trump, often by big numbers and always at a larger margin than Secretary Clinton is."
rationale: The claim's absolute wording (“every,” “always”) is contradicted by publicly available polling: major national and statewide polls in any recent 4–6 week window routinely show variation, with some polls showing closer margins or different leaders. Aggregated polling (and individual reputable polls) do not uniformly show a single candidate beating Trump by consistently larger margins than Hillary Clinton or another named rival.

claim: Abigail Spanberger "wants a tax increase of $32 trillion - that’s with a `T,’ to pay for her socialist health care plan."
rationale: Abigail Spanberger has not proposed a $32 trillion tax increase nor advocated for 'socialist' Medicare-for-All; she has described herself as opposing single-payer plans and has supported more moderate, market-based or incremental health reforms. The $32 trillion figure is a number that has been used in estimates of some Medicare-for-All proposals, but it is not a price tag linked to any Spanberger proposal or public plan she has endorsed.

claim: Under President Barack Obama, "We’ve got the lowest labor force participation in over three decades, since 1978."
rationale: The U.S. civilian labor force participation rate fell during and after the Great Recession and by 2014–2015 reached roughly 62.4–62.7%, levels not seen since the late 1970s (around 1978) according to the standard BLS series. Thus saying it was the lowest participation in over three decades (since 1978) during President Obama is consistent with official labor-force data.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan promised to "end health care for our seniors."
rationale: Paul Ryan did not literally promise to 'end health care for our seniors.' He advocated restructuring Medicare (notably proposing a shift to a premium‑support/voucher-style approach and slower growth in benefits) and supported repealing parts of the Affordable Care Act, but his public proposals were framed as reforms to control costs rather than an explicit pledge to terminate seniors' health care. Political opponents frequently summarized those reforms as 'ending Medicare as we know it,' which is a rhetorical characterization rather than a word-for-word promise to end senior health care.

claim: "Governor Carcieri has not been campaigning with me."
rationale: The claim is unverified because it lacks critical context (who is 'me' and what time period is meant). Without a specific speaker, date, or public event, the blanket negative cannot be confirmed; moreover, political figures like Governor Carcieri have made campaign appearances for allies at various times, so the universal statement is likely false or at least unprovable as written.

claim: "Trump bailed out Wall Street, but not Main Street."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the Trump administration oversaw large Wall Street and corporate supports during the 2020 COVID crisis, but it also enacted substantial relief for 'Main Street' including the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) and a Main Street Lending Program intended for small and mid‑size businesses. Critics rightly note that corporate facilities were larger and sometimes easier to access, but it is incorrect to say Trump bailed out Wall Street while providing no bailout for Main Street.

claim: "When I become the nominee, the Democratic nominee, I will be the only pro-choice candidate on the ballot."
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be true because general election ballots typically include candidates from multiple parties and independents, several of whom may hold pro-choice positions. Parties such as the Libertarian and Green parties, and various independent or third-party candidates, frequently support abortion rights, so the Democratic nominee would not reliably be the only pro-choice candidate on the ballot.

claim: A photo of Pete Buttigieg in a military uniform without visible patches shows that "he is a fraud."
rationale: A single photo lacking visible patches is insufficient evidence to prove someone is a fraud. Pete Buttigieg has a documented record as a U.S. Navy Reserve officer (including a deployment), and uniforms, photography angles, cropping, and image edits can obscure insignia or patches without indicating deceit.

claim: "FOX Network Picks Up ‘Roseanne,’ Saying It Has No Problem With Occasional Racism"
rationale: ABC cancelled Roseanne in May 2018 after creator/lead Roseanne Barr posted a racially offensive tweet; there is no reliable record that FOX picked up the show afterward, nor any credible statement from FOX saying it had "no problem with occasional racism." Reports at the time discussed rumors and speculation about other outlets, but nothing supports the specific claim as stated.

claim: Says "Bruce Starr voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment."
rationale: I cannot verify a specific vote by Bruce Starr that directly 'threw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment.' Such phrasing is typical of political advertising and likely compresses or exaggerates the effect of a particular legislative vote; without a cited bill and official estimate the precise numeric claim is unsupported. It is possible he voted for legislation that reduced benefits or eligibility affecting some people, but the statement overstates causation and certainty.

claim: "Before 1973 it was illegal in the U.S. to profit off of health care."
rationale: This is false. For-profit hospitals, private physician practices, and for-profit health insurers were operating in the United States long before 1973, and there was no federal ban making it illegal to profit from providing health care. While 1973 saw policy activity related to managed care (the HMO Act), that did not create or remove a blanket prohibition on profiting from health services.

claim: "The bill also provides full federal funding for abortions…"
rationale: The claim is vague and cannot be confirmed as stated: U.S. federal law has long restricted most funding for abortions (e.g., the Hyde Amendment), and no widely enacted federal bill currently provides blanket "full federal funding" for abortions. Without a specific bill identified, the statement is misleading and likely false in the U.S. context.

claim: Since 2009, "millions of Americans have lost their health care plans."
rationale: Multiple official estimates and contemporaneous news reports found that several million Americans lost individual-market health plans as Affordable Care Act rules took effect. For example, the Congressional Budget Office estimated about 3.8 million would lose noncompliant individual policies by 2016, and insurers sent cancellation notices to several million customers in 2013–2014. Thus the plain claim that "millions" lost plans is supported, though the details vary by type of plan and reason.

claim: "During three and a half years of campaigning," Lamar Smith "has never once appeared at a moderated debate to defend his positions on the issues."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that Smith 'never once' appeared at a moderated debate over a multi-year span; such absolute claims are unlikely and inconsistent with the public record showing incumbents like Lamar Smith have participated in debates and moderated forums at various points in their long careers. Without a specific start and end date or definition of 'moderated debate,' the claim cannot be substantiated. Press coverage and campaign calendars historically show Smith attended some public forums and media events where questions were moderated.

claim: Says that in polls about 2016 candidate leadership skills, he comes out "two and three and four times higher than anybody else."
rationale: There is no evidence from mainstream 2016 candidate polling that any candidate’s leadership-skill rating was two, three, or four times higher than all others; most national and primary polls show differences measured in percentage points or modest rating gaps, not multi-fold multiples. The claim is vague about which polls and what exact metric is being compared and is not supported by published polling aggregates from 2015–2016.

claim: The United States gives $8 million a day to Israel and gives that country a blank check.
rationale: The claim is misleading. U.S. aid to Israel varies by year and program — the 2016 U.S.-Israel Memorandum of Understanding pledged $38 billion over 10 years (about $10.4 million per day on average), and more recent emergency supplements have changed annual totals; it is not a fixed $8 million/day. Additionally, U.S. aid is approved and overseen by Congress and includes conditions and expenditure rules, so describing it as an unconditional 'blank check' is inaccurate.

claim: "While states used to have regulatory power over fishing, federal law now regulates down to the tenth of the inch the minimum size of fish that anglers can keep."
rationale: The claim overstates federal reach and precision. In the U.S. states still regulate many inland and state-water fisheries and federal law (e.g., Magnuson‑Stevens) applies mainly in federal waters and typically sets species‑ and area‑specific limits; regulations commonly use whole inches or conventional length measures rather than a universal tenth‑of‑an‑inch standard. While some specific federal rules may specify precise measurements for particular fisheries, it is not true that federal law uniformly regulates minimum keep sizes down to the tenth of an inch.

claim: "Even today part of Romney’s fortune is invested in China."
rationale: There is no clear public evidence that Mitt Romney currently holds direct, identifiable personal investments specifically in China. His wealth stems from Bain Capital and diversified funds, and public financial disclosures list broad mutual funds, trusts and private equity stakes rather than named, current China holdings. Some Bain investments historically involved overseas manufacturing, but that does not verify the specific, ongoing claim as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott is "spending a quarter of a million of our tax dollars to robocall people."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific, concrete expenditure ($250,000 of tax dollars) by Gov. Rick Scott for robocalls but provides no time frame or source. Public officials’ use of taxpayer funds is typically documented and there is no widely reported, verifiable record that Scott authorized exactly that payment for robocalls; many robocalls are paid by campaigns or party committees rather than by state coffers. Given the lack of corroborating evidence and the ambiguity about which “tax dollars” are meant, the specific allegation is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Since December 2010 Florida has created 540,000 new jobs."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives no end date and the number does not match official employment series. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics state nonfarm payroll and household employment data show Florida added substantially more (or, depending on the end date, a different amount) than exactly 540,000 jobs since December 2010, so the claim as phrased is inaccurate. Without a specified cutoff the raw number cannot be verified as correct.

claim: Says Emma Gonzalez, a survivor of the Parkland school shooting, ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Emma González ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution; multiple contemporary news outlets and fact-checkers reviewed video and photo coverage of her March 2018 appearances and found no instance of her tearing the Constitution. The claim appears to be a misattribution or a circulation of doctored images and false social-media posts.

claim: Says crime is ‘rising’ in Manchester and has gone up 19 percent under Mayor Ted Gatsas.
rationale: The claim presents a precise 19% rise in crime under 'Mayor Ted Gatsas' without specifying the city variant, time frame, or which crime measure. Ted Gatsas is the former mayor of Manchester, New Hampshire, and publicly available police and FBI crime reports for Manchester and the surrounding period show mixed year-to-year changes across crime categories rather than a clear, uniform 19% increase attributable to his tenure. Without a specified metric and corroborating official statistics, the blanket assertion is not supported.

claim: "I'm the only candidate in the Democratic primary, or actually on either side, who Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers are actually running ads against."
rationale: The claim that one candidate is uniquely the only person in either party being targeted by ads from Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers is implausible and contradicted by common campaign finance patterns. Wealthy financial-sector donors and affiliated groups have funded independent expenditures and attack ads against multiple candidates across both parties, not a single individual alone.

claim: The U.S. spends "57 cents on the dollar on defense."
rationale: As stated, the claim that the U.S. spends "57 cents on the dollar on defense" is misleading. Defense does not consume 57% of total federal outlays (it is roughly in the mid-teens percentage of total federal spending in recent years); defense does account for a large share of discretionary spending (around half, varying by year) but not 57 cents of every federal dollar overall.

claim: Facebook video shows "counting Biden’s votes at 2 a.m."
rationale: The claim that a Facebook video shows "counting Biden’s votes at 2 a.m." is not verifiable from the assertion alone; social media posts often label or narrate footage in misleading ways and a caption does not prove who the votes were for or the exact time. Without verifiable metadata (timestamp, chain of custody, or official election logs) the video cannot be reliably identified as showing votes specifically for Biden being counted at 2 a.m.

claim: UW-Madison "spent down reserves" as it was told to do two years ago and, facing new state budget cuts, has "no more reserves to spend down."
rationale: UW–Madison was directed to use one-time balances in prior budget cycles and did reduce some unrestricted reserves, but public financial statements and university communications indicate it still retains other reserve balances and restricted carryforwards. Saying it has “no more reserves to spend down” overstates the situation because universities maintain multiple categories of funds (some restricted) and the campus did not report zero reserves.

claim: "Washington, D.C., now has greater population than Wyoming and Vermont, more active duty military than 29 states, more tax revenue than 29 states (and) a larger domestic product than 27 states."
rationale: The population portion is accurate — Washington, D.C. has more residents than Wyoming and Vermont by recent Census estimates. However the assertions about having more active-duty military than 29 states, more tax revenue than 29 states, and a larger domestic product than 27 states are either unsupported or depend heavily on the year and exact definitions used (e.g., active-duty assigned vs. total personnel, which revenue measure, nominal GDP vs. metropolitan GDP). Available DoD, state revenue and BEA GDP data do not robustly confirm all three ranking claims as stated and such rankings change with different data years and metrics.

claim: "In New York State, Democrats blocked a Bill expanding College Tuition for Gold Star families after approving aid for illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that New York Democrats deliberately blocked a bill to expand college tuition benefits for Gold Star families immediately after approving aid for undocumented immigrants. Reporting and legislative records show separate actions: the state budget and immigrant assistance discussions were distinct from proposals affecting Gold Star tuition, and claims tying a Democratic 'block' to those approvals appear to conflate unrelated measures or misstate procedural history.

claim: "You take Pulse nightclub. If you had one person in that room that could carry a gun and knew how to use it, it wouldn’t have happened, or certainly to the extent that it did."
rationale: The statement is a speculative counterfactual that cannot be proven and treats a complex, variable event as if a single factor (one armed person) would deterministically prevent it. Empirical evidence on whether armed civilians stop mass shootings is mixed and context-dependent; some incidents have been ended by armed intervenors but these are a minority and outcomes depend on training, positioning, confusion, and the shooter's actions. It is therefore incorrect to assert as a fact that the Pulse massacre 'wouldn’t have happened' or would have been substantially reduced solely because one patron was armed.

claim: If the General Assembly does not address the state's structural deficit, "more than 23,000 education professionals will be immediately yanked out of Pennsylvania schools."
rationale: The statement is misleading: there is no authoritative evidence that more than 23,000 education professionals would be 'immediately yanked out' of Pennsylvania schools solely because the General Assembly fails to address a structural deficit. Estimates of potential job impacts are typically modelled under worst‑case funding scenarios and depend on definitions of "education professionals," district reserves, federal relief, and local decisions; layoffs would not be automatic or uniformly immediate across the commonwealth.

claim: Says under his leadership "Wisconsin median household income" is up 2.7%, while it is down 1.3% nationally under President Obama.
rationale: The statement is misleading: it omits the timeframe and presents cherry-picked percentage changes. U.S. Census Bureau data show national median household income fell early in the recession but recovered and rose during much of President Obama’s terms, so a blanket "down 1.3% under President Obama" is not correct without specific start/end years. Similarly, Wisconsin’s change depends on the chosen endpoints and can differ from the quoted 2.7%.

claim: Says Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS."
rationale: The claim is a blanket statement that Thom Tillis "refuses to say" what to do about ISIS but provides no time or context. Publicly Tillis has repeatedly commented on policies to combat ISIS (supporting military options, coalition efforts, and legislative measures), so a universal refusal is inaccurate or misleading without a specific instance. Absent a cited interview where he explicitly refused to answer, the broad claim cannot be verified.

claim: Speedway is offering $500 fuel cards for $1.95 to help customers with rising fuel costs.
rationale: No credible reports or official announcements from Speedway (or its parent company) corroborate an offer to sell $500 fuel cards for $1.95; such claims match common social-media gift-card scams. It is highly unlikely a major fuel retailer would legally sell $500 cards for a nominal fee without verification or press coverage, and past similar claims have been debunked.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of recurring social-media gift-card scams, typical corporate promotional practices, and prior fact-checks debunking similar false offers from fuel retailers.
safety_notes: Offers like this often lead to phishing sites that request payment or personal data; verify promotions only via Speedway's official website, app, or verified social media accounts before providing information or money.

claim: Says Michael Screnock "let a child predator walk without time and let a rapist who preyed on an underage girl go free after only an eight-month sentence."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence that Michael Screnock himself uttered that exact line. Similar wording appeared in partisan attack ads and third‑party campaign materials in Wisconsin Supreme Court contests, but those were produced by outside groups or opponents rather than documented direct quotes from Screnock. Without a primary source (audio/video or contemporaneous reporting) attributing the statement to him, the claim that he said it is unverified and likely false.

claim: "$1.8 billion Of Soros’ money just intercepted – he could officially go to prison for years"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that $1.8 billion of George Soros's funds were intercepted or that he faces prison time; major news organizations and official records do not report any such seizure or criminal charges. The claim matches patterns of sensational misinformation circulated about Soros without supporting facts.

claim: Says in 2000, Fox News broke the story of George W. Bush’s drunk driving arrest. "Who broke it? Fox News."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and later fact-checks show the 2000 DUI allegation about George W. Bush circulated via the Drudge Report, gossip sites and talk radio rather than being 'broken' by Fox News. Major news organizations and local law-enforcement records found no evidence of a 1976 arrest, and Fox News did not originate the claim.

claim: Says the Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted "Happy International Women's Day! You ladies should get paid less and not be able to make health care decisions."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the official Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted that message; similar inflammatory screenshots have circulated as doctored or parody posts. Reputable news outlets and fact-checkers have not substantiated such a tweet from the party's verified account up to my knowledge cutoff.

claim: "Australia Closing Borders in a few hours for 6-months"
rationale: There is no evidence that the Australian government announced an imminent closure of its borders “in a few hours” for a six-month period. Major, multi-month border closures are publicized by federal authorities and widely reported in mainstream media; no such announcement exists in current public records. While Australia did impose COVID-era border restrictions in 2020, that historical event does not validate this present claim.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official announcements that President Joe Biden resigned or that former Speaker Nancy Pelosi was detained. Such major developments would be widely reported by the White House, Congress, and mainstream news outlets, and no reliable sources up to mid-2024 support those claims.

claim: "ALERT: Massive Easter Egg Recall Leaves MILLIONS Of Children In Danger- THROW THEM AWAY- They WILL Kill Your Kids."
rationale: The message is a vague, sensational alarm with no specific brand, batch, date, or regulatory source. Major product recalls—especially those affecting millions and posing lethal risks—are publicly documented by regulators and mainstream outlets; there is no credible evidence of a nationwide Easter-egg recall that 'will kill' children. While individual toys or eggs have occasionally been recalled for choking or contamination hazards, the extreme claim here is unsupported.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi bought $1.25 million in Tesla stock the day before Joe Biden signed an order "for all federal vehicles" to be electric.
rationale: There is no credible record that Nancy Pelosi bought $1.25 million in Tesla stock the day before a Biden order; public disclosures for members of Congress and their spouses do not show such a purchase tied to an executive order. In addition, the Biden executive actions on federal vehicles set procurement timelines and targets for zero-emission vehicles rather than an immediate order making all federal vehicles electric, so the claim misstates both the trading allegation and the scope/timing of the policy.

claim: "There's nothing in the voting instructions that we've been getting in the last several elections that lets you know" about the limitations of the master lever.
rationale: The claim asserts a universal absence of information in recent voting instructions about 'limitations of the master lever,' which is not verifiable and unlikely to be true everywhere. Election instructions and notices vary by state and county; some jurisdictions and voting-machine vendors do include warnings or explanations about equipment limitations, so a blanket statement that 'there's nothing' is unsupported.

claim: Says Stacey Evans "voted for (school) vouchers...in the beginning."
rationale: I cannot find clear, well-documented evidence that Stacey Evans cast a vote explicitly authorizing a traditional school voucher program; she has publicly positioned herself as a supporter of public schools and opponents have sometimes characterized isolated or early votes on narrow tax-credit scholarship measures as 'vouchers.' Without a specific bill and roll-call showing she voted for a voucher law, the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Says the new coronavirus vaccines contain toxic ingredients and are more dangerous than getting COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is false: authorized COVID-19 vaccines have publicly available ingredient lists (mRNA or viral vector, lipids, buffers, salts, and stabilizers), none of which are 'toxic' at the doses used, and they underwent large clinical trials and ongoing safety monitoring. While rare serious adverse events (e.g., myocarditis, thrombosis with thrombocytopenia) have been identified for some vaccines, the overall risk of severe illness, hospitalization, long COVID, and death from SARS-CoV-2 infection is substantially higher than the risk of serious vaccine side effects for most people.

claim: "It’s estimated that in 2018 alone, dead people received $1 billion in benefits from Medicare, Medicaid, social security payments, and federal pensions."
rationale: I could not find an authoritative source that the four programs together paid $1 billion to deceased people in 2018; official improper-payment and recovery reports show large overall improper-payment estimates for programs like Medicare and Medicaid but do not support a consolidated $1 billion figure specifically paid to dead beneficiaries in that single year. Some payments are mistakenly made after death but are often recovered, and agencies report different metrics, so the precise $1 billion claim is unsupported or misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Alec Baldwin, a total loser, has taken his impression of me to a new low by testing out this theory" by shooting someone.
rationale: There is no reliable record in contemporary news coverage or compiled public statements showing Donald Trump saying that exact line about Alec Baldwin shooting someone. The wording appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote tied to the Rust shooting incident rather than a verifiable Trump statement.

claim: "Texas has launched ‘Operation Lone Star’ to finish the border wall themselves."
rationale: Operation Lone Star was launched by Texas in March 2021 as a state law-enforcement and border-security initiative to deploy DPS, National Guard, and other resources to deter illegal crossings and drug smuggling, not specifically to 'finish' the federal border wall. Although Texas later funded and contracted construction of some barrier segments under related efforts, saying OLS was launched to finish the border wall is misleading.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: This sentence is widely attributed to Ayn Rand online but there is no clear primary-source citation in her published works or documented speeches supporting the attribution. Reliable quote researchers and bibliographies of Rand’s writings do not locate the exact wording in her corpus, so the attribution is likely incorrect or unverified.

claim: "We need to also recognize that we just had two of the coldest years, biggest drop in global temperatures that we have had since the 1980s, the biggest in the last 100 years. We don't talk about that."
rationale: Instrumental global temperature records do not show 'two of the coldest years' recently nor the largest drop since the 1980s; instead many of the last decade's years rank among the warmest on record. Short-term year-to-year variability (e.g., El Niño/La Niña) can cause temporary dips, but these do not constitute the claimed multi-decade cold anomaly or the biggest 100-year decline.

claim: "Overall we currently have $981 million, almost a billion dollars in active development projects right here in the City of Richmond."
rationale: The claim gives a precise $981 million figure for 'the City of Richmond' but provides no date or source and cannot be confirmed from general knowledge alone. Totals for active development projects vary by which Richmond is meant and change frequently, so without a current official city report this statement is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Eight in 10 people this year can find plans for $75 a month or less."
