While he has occasionally discussed election reform, his public record and statements align more with protecting the Electoral College than advocating outright for direct popular election of the president.

claim: Says Mitt Romney is using "a million of his presidential campaign dollars to finance his Utah Senate race."
rationale: News reports from early 2018 documented that Mitt Romney transferred $1,000,000 from his prior presidential campaign committee to his new Senate campaign in Utah. Campaign finance records and major media coverage confirmed the transfer and that those funds were used to seed his Senate bid.

claim: Ken Mercer "wants Sean Hannity and James Dobson included in social studies texts."
rationale: As a member of the Texas State Board of Education, Ken Mercer proposed that figures such as conservative commentators Sean Hannity and evangelical leader James Dobson be included in social-studies curriculum/textbook content. News reports and records of SBOE debates from that period show he advocated adding contemporary conservative voices to standards that guide textbooks.

claim: " ... following World War II war crime trials were convened. The Japanese were tried and convicted and hung for war crimes committed against American POWs. Among those charges for which they were convicted was waterboarding."
rationale: After World War II, Allied military tribunals and U.S. occupation courts tried and convicted many Japanese military personnel for crimes against American POWs, and several convictions specifically cited use of the "water cure" or water torture — the same basic technique commonly called waterboarding today. Some of those convicted were sentenced to death and executed by hanging.

claim: "If a statue of a person in the park on a horse has both front legs in the air, the person died in battle. If the horse has one front leg in the air, the person died as a result of wounds received in battle. If the horse has all four legs on the ground, the person died of natural causes."
rationale: This is an urban legend rather than a factual rule: there is no consistent, universal code linking a horse's leg positions on equestrian statues to how the rider died. Numerous well-known statues contradict the supposed rule and pose choices are made for artistic, compositional, or symbolic reasons rather than to record cause of death.

claim: "Muslims offended that their kids have to recite national anthem."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping generalization about all Muslims. While isolated individuals or communities in some places have objected to reciting national anthems for religious or political reasons, many Muslims routinely recite or sing national anthems; there is no basis to say Muslims as a whole are offended.

claim: One-third of the economic stimulus package was tax cuts.
rationale: When people refer to the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, roughly one-third of the roughly $787 billion package consisted of tax provisions (tax cuts, credits, and relief), so the statement is accurate in that common context. The claim is true for that well-known stimulus package but would not necessarily apply to other different stimulus bills.

claim: Says Mitt Romney opposes requiring employers to cover contraception and would eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood.
rationale: Multiple public statements and campaign positions show Mitt Romney opposed a federal requirement that employers provide contraception coverage (criticizing mandates and supporting employer exemptions) and said he would end federal funding for Planned Parenthood. These were prominent elements of his 2012 presidential campaign platform and later Republican messaging.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: I could not find evidence that 60% of New Jersey doctors categorically do not accept Medicaid; surveys of physician Medicaid acceptance typically show higher acceptance rates and large variation by specialty, practice type, and whether the physician is taking new Medicaid patients. The claim is presented as an absolute statewide percentage without a source or timeframe and therefore appears inaccurate as stated.

claim: Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the company’s board.
rationale: The widely circulated screenshot of a Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigning after Elon Musk joined the board was fabricated. Fact-checks found no evidence of a verified Twitter employee account or any official report confirming such a resignation, and the post appears to originate from a parody/non-employee account.

claim: "The Public Employee Retirement System is making more millionaires than the Oregon state lottery."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it lacks a defined timeframe and a clear metric for “making millionaires.” While Oregon PERS can produce retirees whose lifetime pension benefits or pension-present-value exceed $1 million, the Lottery also produces occasional million-dollar winners; there is no widely published authoritative comparison showing PERS has definitively produced more millionaires than the Oregon Lottery. Without a specified definition (e.g., number of individuals whose pension present value exceeds $1M versus number of distinct lottery winners over a given period), the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Texas high school "graduation rates are at an all-time high—the third-highest in the nation—which represents a significant turnaround from just a few short years ago."
rationale: While Texas has reported record-high high school graduation rates in recent years, the claim that it is the "third-highest in the nation" is incorrect: multiple states routinely report equal or higher adjusted cohort graduation rates, so Texas is not consistently third. The characterization as a dramatic turnaround from just a few years ago overstates the change, which has been a steady increase rather than a sudden jump.

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: Multiple ATF analyses and academic studies of firearm-trace data have found that a very small share of federally licensed gun dealers (roughly 1 percent) account for a disproportionately large share—often more than half—of guns recovered and traced to crimes. The finding is a recurring result across different time periods and datasets, though exact percentages vary by year and definition.

claim: "$400,000 ... is more money than I’ve ever made" in a year.
rationale: The statement gives no identifying information or supporting evidence about who made it or which year is referenced, so it cannot be verified. Determining whether someone ever earned $400,000 in a year requires tax records or official financial disclosures that are not provided.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "has pledged to eliminate" the U.S. Department of Education, which would end federal aid to college students.
rationale: It is true Ted Cruz has previously pledged to abolish or sharply curtail the U.S. Department of Education, but abolishing the department would not automatically end federal student aid. Federal student aid programs (Pell Grants, federal loans) are established by statute and could be transferred to another agency or retained by Congress; elimination of the department alone does not necessarily terminate the programs.

claim: "Illegal counterfeiting and piracy costs the U.S. economy $100 billion... every year."
rationale: The statement presents a precise annual $100 billion figure as fact, but authoritative estimates vary widely and there is no consensus supporting that single number. Different studies and industry groups produce estimates that can be much lower or much higher depending on definitions and methodology, so asserting a definitive $100 billion annual loss is misleading.

claim: DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz "denied unemployment went up under Obama."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Debbie Wasserman Schultz uniformly "denied" that unemployment rose during Obama's presidency; official labor statistics show the unemployment rate rose into 2009 and then fell, and DNC statements typically attributed early job losses to the 2008 financial crisis and prior administration rather than asserting no rise under Obama. The claim appears to mischaracterize or omit context from any specific remark.

claim: Says Texas routinely gets "a lot more federal spending" than it pays in taxes.
rationale: Most state-by-state budget analyses show Texas generally pays more in federal taxes than it receives in federal spending, so it is not routinely a large net recipient. While particular years or specific categories (disaster aid, military contracts, or certain grants) can make Texas briefly receive more, the overall, recurring pattern is that Texas is a net contributor rather than routinely getting "a lot more" than it pays.

claim: "Last week Senator Obama's running mate said, get this, 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that 'Senator Obama's running mate' said last week 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' The claim appears to be a misattribution or taken out of context; no verifiable transcript or video corroborates that exact statement.

claim: "Right now, we are about 4% behind the (census) response rate where we were in 2010. But for Black and Latino and Native American communities, they’re behind by 10%."
rationale: The claim gives precise percentage gaps without specifying a date, data source, or whether it refers to self-response, mail, or total enumeration. While the 2020 Census did show lower self-response rates compared with 2010 in some periods and larger shortfalls in some minority communities, the exact figures (4% overall and 10% for Black, Latino, and Native American communities) are not verifiable as a current, singular official statistic and do not match published Census Bureau releases I am aware of.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: This is a time-specific claim that cannot be verified without up-to-date official filing and employment data; no widely available real-time source confirms that more businesses are closing than opening in Virginia on a given day. Business openings and closures are recorded with delays (state business registries, local permits, tax filings) and typically are reported in aggregated monthly or quarterly statistics, so asserting this as a fact for "today" is unsupported. Without current, authoritative data the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy said, "If a Supreme Court Justice died one day before the election, it would be more Constitutional to indefinitely postpone the election than postpone the confirmation a single day."
rationale: There is no record in Kennedy's speeches, writings, or reputable historical archives of him making this statement; its language and premise conflict with Kennedy's known respect for constitutional processes. The quote appears anachronistic and inconsistent with how presidential and judicial confirmations work (the Senate, not the president, controls confirmation timing).

claim: "Vern Buchanan. His old business was caught illegally funneling over $60,000 in campaign donations to Buchanan to influence his election."
rationale: The claim overstates the public record. While media reports and probes in the 2000s flagged questionable contribution patterns tied to people and entities connected to Vern Buchanan's auto businesses, there is no public record showing his former business was legally found or convicted of illegally funneling more than $60,000 to his campaigns. Investigations produced allegations and reporting but not a definitive judicial or regulatory finding that matches the claim as stated.

claim: "We need to pass a carbon tax to stop climate change. Break up the Wall Street banks. And stop the government spying on innocent Americans. Cory Booker doesn’t support any of these ideas."
rationale: The statement is a broad, absolute claim that Cory Booker supports none of those ideas, but public record shows he has backed measures addressing all three areas. Booker has advocated for aggressive climate policy including market-based carbon pricing options, has supported stronger regulation and actions against large Wall Street firms (including rhetoric about breaking up too-big-to-fail banks), and has supported limits on mass surveillance and reforms to curb bulk government spying.

claim: The U.S. "only ranks 25th worldwide on defense spending as a percentage of GDP."
rationale: The U.S. typically spends roughly 3.5–4% of GDP on defense, and while that can place it around the mid-20s by percent-of-GDP in some years and data sources, the exact rank varies year-to-year and by dataset. Presenting a single definitive statement that the U.S. "only ranks 25th worldwide" is misleading without specifying the year and data source.

claim: It’s warmer on Mars than it is in parts of the United States and Canada during the polar vortex.
rationale: Mars surface temperatures vary widely — roughly from about −125°C at polar winters up to around +20°C at equatorial daytime — while polar vortex events in the U.S. and Canada can drive local temperatures down to −40°C to −60°C. Because of those ranges, some places/times on Mars (e.g., daytime equatorial locations) can indeed be warmer than parts of North America experiencing extreme polar-vortex cold.

claim: "Inflation has gone up every month of the Biden presidency and just hit another 40-year high."
rationale: This is incorrect. U.S. inflation (as measured by CPI) did not rise every single month of the Biden presidency—monthly CPI readings include some months with declines or smaller increases—and the year‑over‑year inflation rate actually peaked around mid‑2022 (about 9% YoY, a roughly 40‑year high) and has generally fallen since, so it has not 'just hit another 40‑year high.'

claim: Says state Rep. Diana Maldonado of Round Rock uses Craigslist to hire campaign block walkers.
rationale: There is no reliable public reporting, campaign statement, or verifiable Craigslist posting confirming that state Rep. Diana Maldonado of Round Rock hires campaign block walkers via Craigslist. The claim appears to be an unverified allegation circulating online and lacks corroboration from reputable sources.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "was for immigration reform and a pathway to citizenship before he was against it."
rationale: Marco Rubio helped lead and supported the 2013 bipartisan Senate immigration effort (the “Gang of Eight”) that included a pathway to legal status, and during his 2015–2016 presidential campaign he publicly disavowed that prior position and opposed a pathway to citizenship. Therefore the claim that he was for immigration reform and a pathway to citizenship before he was against it is accurate in broad terms.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The statement gives a precise share (90%) but provides no timeframe or source and therefore cannot be verified as an accurate, general fact. State job-growth splits between private and public employment vary by period; official BLS/Virginia Employment Commission data must be cited to support such a percentage. Without a specified period, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: President Obama "promised" families making less than $250,000 a year would not see taxes go up, but "Obamacare raises 18 different taxes."
rationale: President Obama did publicly promise that households with incomes under $250,000 would not face federal income tax increases. It is also true that the Affordable Care Act contains multiple revenue-raising provisions that critics have sometimes tallied (in some lists) as 18 "taxes," but many of those are targeted taxes or fees on insurers, employers, specific industries, or higher-income taxpayers and do not generally raise taxes on families earning under $250,000. Framing this as a simple broken promise—that Obamacare raised 18 taxes on the claimed group—is therefore misleading.

claim: "I am the only (state attorney general) in America fighting to hold the big tech companies accountable for their behavior."
rationale: Numerous state attorneys general have publicly pursued investigations and lawsuits against major technology companies for antitrust, privacy, and consumer-protection concerns. Multistate coalitions and individual AGs (both Democratic and Republican) have filed cases or announced probes of firms like Google, Meta/Facebook, Apple, and Amazon, so the claim of being the sole AG doing so is incorrect.

claim: Says under Mayor Cory Booker, Newark has seen "violent crime up five years in a row, murder up five years in a row."
rationale: Available summaries of crime data from Cory Booker’s mayoralty (2006–2013) do not show a continuous five-year increase in violent crime or homicides. Trend lines during his tenure had overall declines and year-to-year fluctuations with some upticks, but not a sustained five-year consecutive rise in both violent crime and murder counts.

claim: Says that when adjusted for inflation and population growth, state general revenue spending has decreased 10.7 percent on his watch.
rationale: The statement gives a precise 10.7% figure but does not identify who 'he' is, which state, or the time period, so it cannot be verified as stated. Calculating a real (inflation- and population-adjusted) change in state general revenue spending requires specific budget numbers, a chosen inflation index, and population data; without those details or a cited source the claim is not confirmable and is treated as false.

claim: BREAKING: Trump Just Ended Welfare For One HUGE Group For 5 Years!
rationale: There is no verified evidence that Trump "ended welfare for one huge group for 5 years." Trump-era actions tightened access to some programs for certain immigrants (e.g., changes to the public charge rule) and proposed work requirements, but they did not implement a universal five-year cutoff of welfare for a large group. Major changes to federal benefit law typically require legislation and were not reported as a blanket five-year ban.

claim: "Republicans control the U.S. Senate with 54 seats, but those 54 senators were elected by only two-thirds the number of voters who elected the Democrats. In the Senate, the majority party represents a minority of the people."
rationale: The claim mixes a time-specific seat count with an inaccurate vote-ratio and a sweeping interpretation. While Republicans have held 54 Senate seats at certain times (for example in 2015), it is not correct that those 54 senators were elected by only two‑thirds the number of voters who elected Democrats — national Senate popular-vote margins do not consistently show such a 2:3 ratio and vary by year and which races are contested. The statement that the majority party always "represents a minority of the people" is also misleading because it depends on the metric used (total votes cast in Senate races, state populations, or eligible voters) and the specific election year.

claim: A bill to advance the Keystone XL Pipeline "is an earmark" under House rules.
rationale: Under contemporary House rules an 'earmark' refers to a provision that directs discretionary federal spending to a specific project, recipient, or locality. A standalone bill to advance or authorize the Keystone XL pipeline is a policy/authorization measure and would not be classified as an earmark unless it specifically included directed federal spending or named beneficiaries.

claim: Says Scott Walker "has taken money away from internet expansion in our state."
rationale: There is no clear, generalizable evidence that Scott Walker categorically "took money away from internet expansion in our state." During his governorship he pursued mixed policies—sometimes limiting new state broadband grant increases or reallocating funds, but also backing broadband initiatives and federal funding—so the blanket claim is misleading without program- and year-specific context.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The United States last commissioned heavy polar icebreakers (USCGC Polar Star and Polar Sea) in the mid-to-late 1970s, and no new heavy icebreakers have been completed since. The current Polar Security Cutter program (contracts awarded and hulls under construction/planning in recent years) is intended to produce the first new U.S. heavy icebreakers in over 40 years.

claim: "We’re the seventh highest taxed state in America. And that’s not just state, it’s local as well."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it omits which state and which tax metric (per‑capita, share of income, effective rate, etc.) and year are meant; different reputable sources produce different annual rankings. Because rankings vary by data source and time, the blanket claim that 'we're the seventh highest taxed state' cannot be accepted as fact without that context.

claim: "I've created over 40,000 jobs."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who 'I' is, the timeframe, nor the methodology for counting jobs (direct, indirect, full-time equivalents, or cumulative hires). Without supporting documentation such as payroll/tax records, government statistics, or independent verification, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unproven.

claim: Barack Obama "is the first ex-president to ever speak against his successor."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: ex-presidents have long publicly criticized their successors. Notable examples include Theodore Roosevelt, who actively opposed and campaigned against his successor William Howard Taft (running as a rival in 1912), and the early rivalry between John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, who exchanged strong public criticisms.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: This claim is false. Official investigations, state canvasses, and independent fact-checks found the Antrim County error resulted from human/reporting and configuration mistakes in that county’s reporting process, not a widespread software ‘flip’ of 6,000 votes, and there is no evidence that 47 other counties in the state used the same faulty process causing statewide fraud. Multiple audits and recounts found no systemic or widespread fraud in the state.

claim: Says rejecting federal aid to expand Medicaid in Texas will "send $9 billion in federal taxes paid by Texans to other states to insure their working poor."
rationale: The claim mixes a valid mechanism with a misleading presentation: federal tax revenue is pooled and federal Medicaid expansion dollars will flow to states that accept expansion, but the $9 billion number is presented without a clear timeframe or assumptions and thus is misleading. Whether Texans’ net federal tax contributions exceed federal spending in Texas depends on complex budget accounting and varies by year, so saying rejecting expansion will 'send $9 billion' is an oversimplification.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: State-level baby-name data for Texas in recent years do not show Jose as the top male baby name; names like Liam, Noah, and Mateo have appeared at or near #1. While Jose is a common name among Hispanic boys in Texas, it has not been the statewide No. 1 male name in recent publicly reported annual name lists.

claim: "If you take into account all the people who are struggling for work, or have just stopped looking, the real unemployment rate is over 15 percent."
rationale: The claim is too general and unstated about country or date. For the United States the broader BLS U-6 unemployment measure (which counts discouraged and marginally attached workers) has exceeded 15% only in specific episodes (around the 2009–2010 recession and in April 2020), but is not uniformly over 15% at all times, so the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: "This administration is slashing the Navy to pay for more Obamacare."
rationale: There is no evidence the administration directly 'slashed the Navy' in order to fund expanded Affordable Care Act spending. Defense appropriations are set by Congress and ACA funding has come from designated offsets (taxes, fees, and Medicare payment adjustments), not by explicit transfers from Navy budgets; occasional defense cuts (e.g., sequestration) were broad budgetary measures, not targeted payments to healthcare expansion.

claim: Sweden had few COVID deaths in July, despite low vaccination rates, relaxed lockdown rules and low mask compliance.
rationale: The statement is misleading and too general. While Sweden did report relatively low COVID deaths in some summer months compared with its own peaks, summer reductions occurred across many countries and cannot be simply ascribed to Sweden's policies; moreover Sweden's vaccination coverage (especially in high‑risk groups) and public‑health measures changed over time, so the blanket claim that Sweden had few deaths in 'July' despite low vaccination and lax rules is imprecise and context‑dependent.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: The statement asserts there are "probably plenty of choices" for a president who doesn't believe in God, which is misleading. In U.S. presidential politics openly atheist candidates are very rare and major-party nominees have historically professed religious belief, so it is not accurate to say there are plentiful viable choices who are non-believers.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: There is no credible record that President Joe Biden wrote or tweeted the quoted phrase; his verified accounts and public tweet archives do not contain that message. The wording is inflammatory and inconsistent with Biden's known public communications, and similar claims have been debunked as fabricated screenshots or misattributions.

claim: Republican election challengers were unfairly barred from observing absentee ballot processing and counting in Detroit.
rationale: Multiple independent media reports, statements from Michigan election officials, and court reviews found that Republican challengers in Detroit were generally allowed to observe absentee ballot processing and counting but were required to follow distancing and other rules (e.g., remain behind ropes, not handle ballots). A few individuals were removed for violating rules or being disruptive, but there is no credible evidence they were wholesale or unlawfully barred from observing the process.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: Historically in the United States a substantial share of tax units or filers have reported zero federal income tax liability after deductions and refundable credits, and several recent-year analyses have placed that share in the roughly 40–50% range. The exact percentage varies by year and by the precise definition (tax units vs households vs adults) but the claim falls within commonly reported bounds for multiple years in the 2000s–2020s.

claim: Benzene has "never been proven to be harmful."
rationale: Benzene has been repeatedly shown to be harmful: it is classified by major health agencies as a human carcinogen and is epidemiologically linked to leukemia (especially acute myeloid leukemia) and other blood disorders, with laboratory studies showing bone marrow toxicity. Numerous regulatory bodies (e.g., IARC, EPA, OSHA) base exposure limits on this evidence, so the statement that it has "never been proven to be harmful" is incorrect.

claim: Missouri "is leading the country when it comes to improving services for mental and behavioral health. Innovation is happening right here."
rationale: This is a broad comparative claim with no cited metrics or timeframe; there is no clear, widely accepted national ranking showing Missouri as the leader in improving mental and behavioral health services. Missouri has undertaken some reforms and programs, but national indicators (access to care, provider supply, outcomes) and reporting do not consistently place Missouri at the top compared with other states.

claim: "In six years, (U.S. Rep. Gary) Peters introduced zero bills that became law."
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be accurate because members of the U.S. House who serve multiple terms commonly have at least some measures they sponsored or cosponsored enacted, and Gary Peters served six years in the House (2009–2015) before becoming a senator. Without a narrowly specified timeframe or definition of “introduced” (primary sponsor vs. cosponsor) and “became law” (standalone bill vs. provision folded into larger legislation), the absolute statement that he introduced zero bills that became law is implausible.

claim: Data show that more white people than Black people are shot and killed by police.
rationale: In raw counts, multiple national databases tracking people shot and killed by police in recent years report more white victims than Black victims. However, when adjusted for population size Black people are killed by police at a higher rate per capita, and results can vary by dataset definitions of race and timeframe.

claim: "Sotomayor has had her rulings thrown out by the court a troubling four times."
rationale: The statement is unsupported and ambiguous: it does not specify which court or time period and fact-checking of Sotomayor’s record as a federal appellate judge does not reliably show a notable, standalone figure of exactly four rulings “thrown out.” Supreme Court reversals of individual appellate opinions are tracked and occur rarely, but claiming precisely four without context is misleading.

claim: North Korea’s missiles are "not going to have a capability to reach the United States anytime real soon."
rationale: North Korea has tested long-range ICBMs (e.g., Hwasong-15 and later systems) that experts judged to have the range to reach parts of the United States, and intelligence assessments warn Pyongyang is advancing missile and warhead technologies. While operational reliability, reentry vehicle survivability, and nuclear miniaturization remain uncertain, the blanket claim that North Korea will not have a capability to reach the U.S. in the near term is contradicted by demonstrated tests and expert analyses.

claim: "Bill Gates says you don't have a choice to be vaccinated or not."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable transcript showing Bill Gates declaring that individuals "don't have a choice" about being vaccinated. Gates has publicly advocated for vaccines and coordinated global public-health efforts, but he has not issued blanket statements stripping personal choice; some social-media posts have misquoted or taken remarks out of context. Given the absence of a verifiable source, the claim is false.

claim: Oregon’s "three largest employers, and 13 of the top 25, are health care providers."
rationale: This is incorrect: while multiple large health systems (e.g., OHSU, Providence, Legacy, Kaiser) are among Oregon's biggest employers, the state's largest employers also include state government and major non-health companies (Intel, Nike, large retailers), so the top three are not all health-care providers and health-care firms do not make up 13 of the top 25 by commonly used employer rankings.

claim: "Regulations have quadrupled. The rate of regulations quadrupled under this president."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: standard measures of regulatory activity (such as Federal Register pages, number of final rules, or OMB Unified Agenda entries) do vary by administration but do not show a fourfold (400%) increase for a recent U.S. president over a comparable period. Available historical data show changes generally measured in tens of percent, not quadrupling, and outcomes depend heavily on the specific metric and time window chosen.

claim: Says a "5G LAW PASSED while everyone was distracted" with the coronavirus pandemic and lists 20 symptoms associated with 5G exposure.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a secret or universal "5G law" was passed while the world was distracted by the coronavirus pandemic; legislative actions are public and reported by mainstream sources. The long list of 20 symptoms attributed to 5G exposure is not supported by scientific consensus—WHO, national health agencies, and regulatory bodies find no established causal link between low‑level, regulatory‑compliant 5G radiofrequency exposure and those health effects.

claim: Hillary Clinton advocates "a freeze on foreclosures. Barack Obama said no."
rationale: During the 2008 Democratic primary Hillary Clinton publicly called for a temporary moratorium/freeze on home foreclosures to allow loan modifications, and Barack Obama said he did not support a blanket moratorium. Contemporary news coverage and debate transcripts reported Clinton’s proposal and Obama’s opposition to a broad freeze.

claim: Says an Internet meme shows people rejoicing over the Paris agreement.
rationale: The claim asserts that an unspecified internet meme depicts people rejoicing over the Paris Agreement, but no particular meme, image, or provenance is provided to verify that association. Images and memes are frequently reused or miscaptioned to reference unrelated events, so without source verification the specific assertion is not supportable.

claim: "Seventy-six percent of the American people support us passing the DREAM Act … with citizenship and legalization as part of it all. … More than 60 percent of Republicans support that."
rationale: While numerous polls show strong overall public support for protections for DREAMers (often in the 70%–80% range), the specific claim that 76% support 'passing the DREAM Act with citizenship and legalization' and that 'more than 60% of Republicans' back that exact package is not reliably supported. Most reputable polls show Republican support for legalization/citizenship for Dreamers is substantially lower and varies widely by question wording, typically nearer to 40%–55% rather than consistently above 60%.

claim: Says Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has these offshore accounts" like Mitt Romney.
rationale: There is no credible public evidence or official financial disclosure showing Debbie Wasserman Schultz holds offshore accounts comparable to allegations often made about Mitt Romney. Major media reporting and public filings for members of Congress do not document such offshore holdings for her; the statement appears to be an unsubstantiated partisan claim.

claim: "I have a record on the environment of creating green energy ... taking trash and turning it into cash."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it refers to an unspecified 'I' and provides no concrete examples, dates, programs, or independent documentation of converting trash into green energy. Without identifying the person and citing specific, public records or projects, the claim cannot be confirmed. While waste‑to‑energy initiatives exist, this particular assertion lacks the necessary evidence to be treated as fact.

claim: A study found an "82% miscarriage rate" among women between 30 days and 20 weeks pregnant who got an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: No reputable peer-reviewed study has shown an 82% miscarriage rate after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination. Large registry and cohort studies (for example CDC v-safe pregnancy registry and NEJM reports) found miscarriage rates similar to background rates (roughly 10–20% in early pregnancy) and no evidence of a vaccine-associated increase. The 82% figure appears to come from misinterpreted or methodologically flawed analyses of passive-reporting data.

claim: "Biden impeachment in progress."
rationale: As of mid-2024, House Republicans had opened and were conducting an impeachment inquiry into President Biden, so an impeachment process was underway in the House. That inquiry and related committee investigations constituted active impeachment activity, even though full House passage of articles or a Senate trial had not occurred.

claim: "Since 1995, the top 400 wealthiest families have seen their incomes go up 400 percent and their tax rates go down 40 percent."
rationale: The statement is not supported by clear public data and mixes concepts (Forbes 400 lists wealth/net worth, not annual income). While the richest Americans have seen large gains in wealth and top effective tax burdens have changed since the 1990s, the specific claims of a 400% income increase and a 40% drop in tax rates for the 'top 400 wealthiest families' are not substantiated by standard data sources and depend on definitions and time windows.

claim: Republican challenger Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous because it names no specific district or provides voter-record evidence. Bill Flores is a long‑time Texas public figure who has been elected multiple times in the district he contested, making the assertion that he "never once voted in a general election in our district" unlikely without concrete voter‑history records. Proving or disproving this requires inspection of state voter records for the named district.

claim: "Almost 40% of borrowers with student loan debt didn't finish their degree."
rationale: Multiple analyses of U.S. student loan data find that a large share of borrowers never completed a degree; estimates commonly cluster around the high-30s percent (roughly 35–40%). This statement matches widely reported figures from federal education statistics and research organizations that examine cohorts of student borrowers.

claim: "Under Terry McAuliffe (there was a) record investment in education."
rationale: During Terry McAuliffe's 2014–2018 governorship Virginia approved sizable increases in education funding and his administration repeatedly touted those as the largest or record investments, including major new K–12 dollars, expansions of early childhood programs and higher education/community college funding. Whether it qualifies as a 'record' depends on the metric (nominal dollars, inflation‑adjusted totals, or per‑pupil spending) but the claim reflects mainstream characterizations of budget actions in that period.

claim: Says "Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein revealed to be a total FAKE… contains 14 glaring errors that could only be committed by a poorly educated writer." ​
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein was a forgery; Ford submitted the letter to Feinstein's office and later testified under oath about the allegation. Viral lists claiming '14 glaring errors' were investigated and debunked by multiple fact-checkers and news organizations, which found the supposed 'errors' did not demonstrate fabrication.

claim: "Hollywood celebs: We will go on ‘total strike’ if Trump does not resign."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a coordinated, across-the-board pledge by 'Hollywood celebs' to launch a 'total strike' unless Donald Trump resigns was made. While individual celebrities have publicly criticized Trump and called for protests or boycotts at various times, mainstream media and industry unions did not report any unified ultimatum or collective strike threat contingent on his resignation.

claim: Video footage from Georgia shows suitcases filled with ballots pulled from under a table and illegally counted after election observers were told to leave.
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and Georgia election officials reviewed the footage and concluded the items were standard ballot containers/tubs, not 'suitcases,' and the ballot processing shown was lawful. Observers were not unlawfully excluded en masse and surveillance and official reviews found no evidence that ballots were pulled from under tables and illegally counted after observers were told to leave. The claim amplifies out-of-context video snippets and mischaracterizes normal chain-of-custody activity.

claim: Says that "over a 45-minute period that we had the press conference" on the coronavirus on March 13, 2020, the stock market set "an all-time record."
rationale: This is false: on March 13, 2020 U.S. equity markets were in a COVID-driven selloff and were not setting all-time highs. Major indexes (Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq) were well below their February 2020 peaks and the period around March 13 featured large declines and high volatility rather than new all-time records.

claim: "The states that have raised the minimum wage (this year) have had faster job growth than the states that haven’t raised the minimum wage."
rationale: The claim is a blanket comparative statement for "this year" but provides no year, list of states, or measurement method. Empirical evidence on the employment effects of minimum-wage increases is mixed: some states that raised their minimum wage saw faster job growth, others did not, and outcomes depend on many confounding factors. Without a specified timeframe and proper controls, the universal claim cannot be supported.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "campaign hasn't been clear about when she wiped her server of her work emails."
rationale: During the 2015–2016 email controversy the Clinton campaign gave varying explanations and timelines about when emails and devices were deleted from her private server, and major outlets reported that the campaign had not clearly communicated a consistent date or process. Later clarifications and investigative reporting were required to establish the sequence, supporting the statement that the campaign wasn’t initially clear about when the server was wiped.

claim: "There’s more murders with hammers last year than...shotguns and pistols and AK-47s."
rationale: U.S. and comparable national crime statistics show firearms (especially handguns and other guns) account for the majority of homicides, while blunt instruments such as hammers are a small minority of murder weapons. It is therefore incorrect to claim that more people were murdered with hammers in the most recent year than with shotguns, pistols (handguns), and AK-47–style rifles.

claim: Says Ron Johnson justifies his support of trade agreements by saying the U.S. has the Trade Adjustment Assistance program for displaced workers, but then he "voted to eliminate it."
rationale: There is no clear, documented instance showing Senator Ron Johnson both cited the Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) program as a justification for supporting trade agreements and then subsequently voted to eliminate the entire program. Public statements show he has discussed worker adjustment programs when debating trade, and his voting record includes opposition to some reauthorizations or expansions and votes to cut funding in certain budget contexts, but not a straightforward vote to abolish TAA outright after invoking it as a justification.

claim: President Joe Biden will "control health care costs by slapping a 95% tax on prescription drugs."
rationale: There is no Biden administration or official campaign policy that would impose a blanket 95% tax on prescription drugs. Biden's health proposals have focused on measures like Medicare drug price negotiation, inflation rebates, and caps on out‑of‑pocket costs, not an across‑the‑board 95% drug tax; the 95% figure appears to be a political mischaracterization or hyperbole.

claim: Says Mark Kirk "called for the mass arrest of 18,000 African Americans" and "was apparently fine with Trump’s #StillTooRacist call for mass deportation."
rationale: There is no credible public record or major news reporting that Senator Mark Kirk ever called for the mass arrest of '18,000 African Americans' or publicly said he was fine with Trump's supposed call for mass deportation. Such a specific, racially targeted demand would have been widely reported and documented; available records of Kirk's statements and votes do not support the allegation.

claim: Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson "gave child porn offenders sentences below the guidelines and below what the prosecutors were requesting," showing she is "soft on child pornography offenders."
rationale: While Ketanji Brown Jackson imposed below-guidelines sentences in some child pornography cases as a district judge, that fact alone does not prove a blanket pattern of being "soft." In several matters the government had agreed to reductions or prosecutors sought lesser terms, and federal guidelines are advisory so judges routinely exercise discretion for case-specific reasons. The claim that she systematically gave sentences below what prosecutors requested and therefore is soft on offenders overstates and mischaracterizes the mixed, case-by-case record.

claim: "Two-thirds of our economy is a consumer economy."
rationale: If 'our economy' refers to the United States, personal consumption expenditures typically account for roughly two-thirds of GDP (about 65–70%) in recent years, so calling it a 'consumer economy' in that sense is accurate. The exact share varies year to year but the general characterization is supported by national accounts data.

claim: "If you became a Medicaid recipient through the Obamacare expansion, you are grandfathered in."
rationale: There is no federal "grandfather" guarantee that people who gained Medicaid through the ACA expansion will permanently keep coverage if a state reverses or changes its expansion. Medicaid is a joint federal-state program and states that opted into expansion could alter eligibility or end the expansion subject to federal rules; enrollees are not universally protected by a special grandfather clause.

claim: "When the president's spokesman was asked about (Anwar) al-Awlaki's son, … he said he should have chosen a more responsible father."
rationale: Contemporaneous press-briefing transcripts and reputable news accounts do not support that an official White House spokesman said the exact line 'he should have chosen a more responsible father' about Anwar al-Awlaki's son; the phrase appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase circulated without a verifiable on-the-record quote. Because public briefings are usually transcribed, the absence of a clear transcript or reliable source makes the specific quoted claim unreliable.

claim: "In campaigns in the past with Sen. McCain and President George W. Bush and others, they have tended to release tax records in April."
rationale: The statement claims a consistent pattern that McCain, George W. Bush and others 'tended' to release tax records in April, but timing of tax‑return disclosures has varied by campaign and year. While some candidates choose to release returns during tax season, there is no clear, consistent pattern specific to McCain or George W. Bush that they routinely released records in April.

claim: "Joe Biden’s great-grandfather Joseph J. Biden was a slave-owner and fought" for the Confederacy.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden’s great-grandfather named Joseph J. Biden was a slave-owner or fought for the Confederacy. Biographical and genealogical reporting on Biden’s ancestry shows his forebears were Irish immigrants and Northerners (Pennsylvania/Delaware) with no records tying them to Confederate service or slaveholding.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" and said "we should still have troops in Iraq."
rationale: There are no reliable reports up to mid‑2024 of Mitt Romney giving a speech 'a few weeks ago' in which he said the United States should still have troops in Iraq. Romney has not been widely reported as calling for a renewed or continued U.S. troop presence in Iraq in recent weeks, so the claim appears to be a misstatement or misattribution. Without a specific date or source the assertion cannot be verified.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: Delaware does not have the eighth-largest Black population by absolute numbers — its total state population is under 1 million, so its Black resident count (on the order of a few hundred thousand) is far smaller than those of many larger states. The claim may conflate absolute totals with percentage share; even by share Delaware is not clearly 8th without specifying a year and data source.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda "will cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion"
rationale: There is no credible, nonpartisan evidence showing Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda would definitively ‘cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion.’ Estimates of policy costs vary widely by which measures, timeframe, and accounting (gross vs. net, direct vs. macroeconomic effects) are included, and major fact‑checks and neutral analyses did not substantiate a specific $5 trillion tab. The claim appears to be a partisan, out-of-context figure rather than a supported consensus estimate.

claim: Health reform will "give every American the same opportunity" to buy health insurance the way members of Congress do.
rationale: Members of Congress get access to the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (an employer-sponsored plan with government contribution and specific plan options) that is not available to the general public. Typical health reform measures (for example the ACA marketplaces) allow individuals to buy private plans and receive subsidies based on income, but they do not replicate the employer contribution, plan portfolio, or eligibility rules that congressional plans provide.

claim: I am the only U.S. Senate candidate who spoke out against bombing Syria, and who challenged Georgia’s governor and insurance commissioner over obstruction to the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The claim asserts exclusivity (being the only U.S. Senate candidate to do two specific things), which is unlikely and not supported by available public reporting. Multiple Senate candidates have publicly opposed bombing Syria, and Georgia candidates have publicly challenged the governor and insurance commissioner over ACA obstruction, so the uniqueness claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "A strong bipartisan majority" in the House of Representatives "voted to defund Obamacare."
rationale: Multiple House votes to "defund Obamacare" after the ACA passed were carried largely by Republican members of a Republican-controlled House, with at most a handful of Democrats joining them. There is no evidence that a strong bipartisan majority ever voted to defund the law; most actions were party-line or nearly so.

claim: "The president is advocating a drone strike program in America."
rationale: The claim is vague about which president and lacks supporting evidence. There are no credible public reports or official statements showing a U.S. president advocating a program of drone strikes conducted within the United States; presidential drone policy discussion has historically focused on overseas counterterrorism operations and domestic use would face significant legal and constitutional barriers.

claim: "Right now, here in Texas, wind power is already cheaper than dirty fossil fuels."
rationale: In Texas, onshore wind has among the lowest levelized costs and many recent power-purchase agreement prices have been below the cost of new natural-gas or coal generation, and wind frequently clears at low per-MWh bids in ERCOT. That said, wind is intermittent so system-level costs for firm capacity, balancing and transmission can affect the total delivered-cost compared with dispatchable fossil plants.

claim: "If Sen. Hillary Clinton could enact all of her campaign proposals, taxpayers would be faced with financing more than $777.6-billion in new spending over one White House term."
rationale: There is no authoritative, nonpartisan accounting that concludes Hillary Clinton's campaign proposals would unambiguously require $777.6 billion in new spending over one presidential term. Cost estimates for campaign proposals vary widely depending on which items are included, the time horizon used, and whether proposed offsets or revenue changes are counted; partisan summaries that produce a single precise total are not reliable without detailed methodology. Independent scorekeepers (e.g., CBO-style analyses) did not produce a single consolidated $777.6 billion figure.

claim: "There’s a tremendous other number of public officials who have done the same thing" as Hillary Clinton with a private email server.
rationale: The claim implies many public officials ran private, self‑hosted email servers for official business as Hillary Clinton did. Contemporary reporting and official reviews found Clinton's use of a private home server for State Department email to be unusual; while some officials occasionally used personal email addresses for work, there was not a 'tremendous' number operating comparable private servers.

claim: "US Capitol raided 2/2/21."
rationale: The widely reported violent breach of the U.S. Capitol occurred on January 6, 2021, not February 2, 2021. There is no credible record of a separate 'raid' on the Capitol on February 2, 2021.

claim: Says he didn't call Dr. George Tiller a baby killer, as liberal groups charge, but was merely reporting what "some prolifers branded him."
rationale: The claim as presented lacks any named speaker, date, or source, so it cannot be verified that a particular person actually said they "didn't call Dr. George Tiller a baby killer" but were only "reporting what 'some prolifers branded him.'" While there were many controversies and defenses after attacks on Dr. Tiller in which commentators said they were relaying others' language, the specific quoted defense here is unverified without attribution. Given the missing context, the assertion as stated is not supported.

claim: Says Tom Ford said about Melania Trump, "I have no interest in dressing a glorified escort who steals speeches and has bad taste in men."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or reputable sourcing that Tom Ford ever uttered that exact quote about Melania Trump. While tabloids and social posts have circulated harsh paraphrases and critiques of Melania, major media and archived interviews do not substantiate Ford saying, "I have no interest in dressing a glorified escort who steals speeches and has bad taste in men."

claim: "All the money the Department of Citrus has is paid for by the citrus growers. You don't save dollars by eliminating the Department of Citrus."
rationale: It is true that state Departments of Citrus (e.g., Florida) are funded primarily by grower assessments for marketing and research, but not literally 'all' money comes from growers. These programs can also receive federal grants, other non-assessment receipts, and involve some state administrative oversight so eliminating the agency could change who pays and might save or shift some government costs. Therefore the absolute wording of the claim is incorrect.

claim: Says that in fiscal year 2010, "nearly 80 percent of women served" in the Texas Women’s Health Program received services from a provider other than a Planned Parenthood clinic.
rationale: I could not confirm an authoritative source showing that nearly 80% of women in the Texas Women’s Health Program in FY2010 were served by non–Planned Parenthood providers. Reporting and official statements around the Texas defunding of Planned Parenthood used an “80%” figure in different contexts (such as numbers of alternate providers or geographic coverage) and fact‑checkers found the claim misleading when presented as the share of actual women served that year.

claim: Says a pandemic occurs exactly every 100 years.
rationale: Pandemics do not occur on a strict 100-year schedule; historical pandemics have happened at irregular intervals (e.g., 1918, 1957, 1968, 2009, 2019–20). Epidemiologists do not recognize a centennial periodicity and pandemics arise from complex, variable biological and ecological factors rather than a fixed timetable.

claim: Says President Donald Trump as a candidate mentioned WikiLeaks "over 160 times in speeches" in the last month of the campaign.
rationale: There is no credible, transcript-based count showing Trump said “WikiLeaks” more than 160 times in speeches during the final month of the 2016 campaign. While he repeatedly referenced WikiLeaks in October 2016, the number 160 appears to be an exaggeration or a conflation with other media (tweets, interviews, press appearances) rather than documented speech transcripts.

claim: A photo shows Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi posing and smiling in front of a Trump 2020 sign.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an authentic photo exists of Rep. Maxine Waters and Speaker Nancy Pelosi posing and smiling in front of a genuine 'Trump 2020' sign; images like this circulated during the 2020 cycle were digitally altered or miscaptioned. Multiple independent fact-checkers and the lack of a verifiable original source support the conclusion that the claim is fabricated or manipulated.

claim: "There are more pain clinics in Broward County than there are McDonald's in Broward County."
rationale: There is no reliable, current evidence that Broward County contains more pain clinics than McDonald's locations. Counts of McDonald's restaurants in a populous county are straightforward and number in the dozens, while reported counts of 'pain clinics' vary greatly by definition and peaked during the opioid 'pill mill' era before enforcement reduced them.

claim: "Switzerland (where the government) issues every household a gun . . . has the lowest gun related crime rate of any civilized country in the world!!!"
rationale: The Swiss government does not issue a gun to every household. Switzerland’s system of military conscription historically allowed many male conscripts to keep service rifles at home, and civilian gun ownership is relatively high, but that is not equivalent to universal household issuance. While Switzerland has a relatively low firearm homicide rate compared with some countries, several other developed countries (e.g., Japan, the UK, and others) have equal or lower gun-related death rates, so the claim that Switzerland has the lowest rate of any 'civilized country' is incorrect.

claim: The Obama administration "spent more money on the Cash for Clunkers program than the space program."
rationale: The Car Allowance Rebate System ('Cash for Clunkers') cost on the order of $2–3 billion in 2009. By contrast, NASA's budget during the Obama years was roughly $17–19 billion per year, meaning NASA (the U.S. 'space program') received far more funding than CARS in any single year and vastly more in total across the administration. Thus the claim is incorrect.

claim: "Obama’s Private ‘security’ Company Sets Up Massive Camps Outside 3 Major Cities."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that former President Barack Obama runs a private security company that has established "massive camps" outside three major cities. Obama's post-presidential activities are well-documented (the Obama Foundation and media venture Higher Ground) and former presidents receive Secret Service protection rather than operating private security firms that set up camps. The claim matches recurring baseless social-media rumors and lacks verifiable specifics.

claim: Says there is a 4,250% increase in fetal death from the flu shot.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that flu vaccination in pregnancy causes a 4,250% increase in fetal death. Large bodies of peer-reviewed studies, systematic reviews, and public-health surveillance find no such massive increase and generally report no increased risk (and in some analyses reduced risk) of adverse pregnancy outcomes following seasonal influenza vaccination; the 4,250% number appears to come from a miscalculation or misuse of passive-reporting data rather than a valid causal finding.

claim: "The number of uninsured people in Massachusetts is about the same as it was when the mandates were passed in 2006."
rationale: Massachusetts' uninsured population declined substantially after the 2006 health insurance mandate and has remained well below pre-reform levels. Recent estimates (even allowing for modest increases in some years) show far fewer uninsured people than in 2006, so it is not "about the same."

claim: Says the federal government is "the largest energy user in the country."
rationale: As commonly stated by U.S. government sources, the federal government — taken as a single organizational entity operating hundreds of thousands of buildings and a large vehicle fleet — is the largest single energy consumer in the country. This is true as a comparison between one organization and other individual organizations, though aggregate sectors (residential, industrial, transportation) each consume more energy in total than the federal government.

claim: On tax inversions, the Wall Street Journal "surprisingly attacked this tax scheme."
rationale: The statement is a subjective characterization and lacks a specific citation; whether the Wall Street Journal 'surprisingly attacked' tax inversions depends on which article or editorial is referenced. The WSJ has published both critical reporting and pro-business commentary about corporate tax inversions at different times, so the blanket claim cannot be verified as fact without more context.

claim: Says that he’s responsible for Austin including Anderson Mill Road in the city's proposed transportation bond package.
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because it uses an unnamed 'he' and provides no source or date for the alleged statement. Inclusion of specific projects in a city's bond package is normally the result of planning by city staff and approval by the council, and I find no verifiable attribution of sole responsibility to an individual without more context or a citation.

claim: "Once again, a police officer has been killed with an illegal gun from Georgia – a state that last year did the NRA’s bidding and weakened its already lax gun laws."
rationale: The claim bundles a specific criminal fact and a political characterization without providing verifiable details. I cannot confirm any particular recent police killing was carried out with an illegal gun traced to Georgia; gun-trace results and legality vary by case and require contemporaneous reporting or official statements. The statement that Georgia "last year did the NRA’s bidding and weakened its already lax gun laws" is a partisan summary: Georgia did enact looser carry rules recently, but attributing that directly and solely to the NRA and calling the laws "already lax" is subjective and not a strictly factual claim.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: The claim is a quotation of comments made by Indiana's governor at the time (Mike Pence) about the 2015 Scott County HIV outbreak; he publicly stated his administration had "immediately" deployed public health resources to contain the outbreak. While his statement exists, independent reporting noted controversy over the timing and completeness of the response (e.g., initial resistance to syringe-exchange programs) which makes the claim of immediate action contested in interpretation.

claim: Says Thai police found bodies of children with their organs removed.
rationale: There are no credible reports or official Thai police statements corroborating a discovery of children’s bodies with organs removed; images and claims circulating online have repeatedly been found to be misattributed or from other contexts. Major fact-checkers and local authorities have debunked similar organ‑harvesting rumors about Thailand.

claim: Regarding her State Department email practices, "my predecessors did the same thing."
rationale: While some past secretaries and State Department officials occasionally used non-official or personal email accounts for certain messages, none of Hillary Clinton's predecessors are documented to have run all official State Department correspondence through a private, home-based email server or to have the same scope and record-retention practices. Investigations and contemporary news reporting found that the scale and handling of Clinton's private server were not matched by prior secretaries.

claim: "Florida's new fingerprint identification system is improving our rate of solving cold cases by 300 percent."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely misleading: there is no publicly available official data showing Florida's fingerprint system has increased cold-case clearances by 300%. Improvements to automated fingerprint identification (AFIS) can raise match rates, but a 300% jump would require clear baseline, timeframe, and attribution that the claim does not provide.

claim: Since being elected in 2002, Scott Walker has "given back over $370,000 of his salary to the county."
rationale: While Scott Walker did forgo or return portions of his Milwaukee County Executive pay during his tenure, contemporaneous county payroll records and fact-checking reporting indicate the cumulative amount claimed is overstated or depends on how 'given back' is defined. Public fact-checkers and news coverage found lower totals or noted the figure requires specific accounting choices, so the blanket claim that he "gave back over $370,000" is not clearly supported.

claim: "According to 2009 estimates, an agreement with Panama could result in almost 1,900 Florida jobs in the first year – and about 15,000 jobs after five years."
rationale: I could not verify a widely reported 2009 estimate that a Panama agreement would create about 1,900 Florida jobs in year one and 15,000 after five years. Official federal analyses (e.g., USITC/CBO) around that period projected only modest national employment effects and did not provide corroborating large state-specific figures; such specific numbers typically come from localized chamber or advocacy estimates and require citation. Without a clear, reputable source, the claim is unsupported as stated.

claim: Says Kamala Harris said there will be "a federal tax on your home for reparations."
rationale: There is no credible record or verified quote of Vice President Kamala Harris saying there will be "a federal tax on your home for reparations." Public transcripts and reporting show she has discussed studying reparations and addressing racial inequities, but she has not proposed or announced a federal tax on homeowners. The phrasing appears to be a misquote or distortion of broader comments about reparations policy.

claim: Gov. Lincoln Chafee has imposed "a mandatory abortion fee" on all Rhode Islanders who buy health insurance through the state’s Obamacare exchange.
rationale: This claim is false. Neither Gov. Lincoln Chafee nor Rhode Island imposed a blanket "mandatory abortion fee" on all purchasers in the state exchange; federal and state practice around the ACA required separate accounting and a separate optional premium for elective abortion coverage, meaning only enrollees who chose plans with abortion coverage would pay an added surcharge, not all exchange customers.

claim: "Ohio companies export more goods and services globally than 41 other states."
rationale: State export rankings change by year and by whether goods alone or goods plus services are counted. While Ohio is often a high-volume exporter (typically around the top 10 for goods), the absolute claim that Ohio exports more than 41 other states (i.e., ranks at least 9th) is not consistently true across years and is unsupported without a specific year or source.

claim: North Carolina is home to "two rivers of the top five most polluted rivers" in the U.S.
rationale: There is no widely accepted, authoritative ranking that places two North Carolina rivers among the top five most polluted in the U.S. While some NC rivers (e.g., Cape Fear, Neuse) have documented pollution issues, commonly cited national lists of most-polluted rivers typically feature waterways from multiple other states and do not consistently include two NC rivers in the top five. Without a specific source, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and fact-checkers established that many of the early 'Make America Great Again' campaign hats were manufactured in China. Trump and his campaign later acknowledged the sourcing and announced moves to produce some hats in the U.S. or other countries, so the statement is true but context-dependent on time and batch.

claim: Novak Djokovic is the first professional athlete to be banned from a major sporting event for "not taking drugs."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Novak Djokovic was not banned for "not taking drugs." His most public exclusions (notably the 2022 Australian Open) were related to COVID-19 vaccination/visa policies, not refusal to take performance-enhancing drugs. Additionally, athletes have long been suspended or banned for doping violations or refusing drug tests, so he is not the first athlete ever to be barred under a broadly related interpretation.

claim: Photo shows a trashed venue in Glastonbury after climate activist Greta Thunberg spoke there.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the pictured scene was the aftermath of Greta Thunberg speaking at Glastonbury; similar images have been repeatedly misattributed on social media and fact-checkers have traced such photos to other events or earlier times. Major news outlets and on-site reports from the festival did not document a trashed venue tied to her appearance, and viral posts lack a verifiable source linking the photo to that specific occasion.

claim: "While fat-cat bureaucrats at the Department of Education are getting paid an average salary of $102,000 a year, teachers in Georgia are getting paid half of that."
rationale: The claim misstates and conflates figures. The U.S. Department of Education’s workforce average pay is lower than $102,000 when averaged across all employees (high senior-executive pay can raise averages but the overall mean is substantially lower), and the average public school teacher salary in Georgia is generally in the low-to-mid tens of thousands more than half of $102,000 (roughly $50–60k, depending on year), so saying Georgia teachers are paid half of $102,000 is misleading.

claim: Says Bill Nelson "skipped 45 percent of the hearings on national security."
rationale: There is no reliable, independently verified record showing Senator Bill Nelson missed 45% of “hearings on national security.” Attendance for Senate hearings is tracked by committee and by date, and such a specific aggregate percentage is not supported without a defined timeframe or list of hearings. The claim appears to be a partisan assertion that is misleading absent documentation breaking down which hearings were counted.

claim: His biography says he was the top ROTC officer in the nation.
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it does not identify who 'he' is or provide a cited biography; without a named individual and source the statement cannot be confirmed. Biographies sometimes assert honors like being a top ROTC officer, but that requires documentary evidence (official ROTC records or a reliable biographical source) to substantiate.

claim: Says Chris Christie "vetoed equal pay for women 3 times. He only let the bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue."
rationale: The claim is not supported by the legislative record or contemporary reporting. While Chris Christie opposed or vetoed some pay-equity measures during his tenure, there is no clear evidence he vetoed the same "equal pay" bill three separate times, and the assertion that he only allowed passage for purely campaign-damage reasons is speculative and not documented.

claim: "The country is now in a manufacturing recession."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as stated because it does not identify which country or specify a timeframe or data source. Determining a "manufacturing recession" requires recent official data showing sustained contraction in manufacturing output (commonly two consecutive quarters of decline) or persistent sub-50 manufacturing PMIs. Without those specifics and supporting statistics, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Tommy Tuberville "is for privatizing Social Security and cutting Medicare."
rationale: There is not clear, consistent public evidence that Senator Tommy Tuberville explicitly advocates outright privatization of Social Security or direct cuts to Medicare. While he has supported conservative reforms (such as discussions of private accounts, means-testing, or raising the retirement age) critics sometimes characterize those positions as privatization or cuts, the blanket statement overstates his documented, explicit positions.

claim: "The Affordable Care Act is the single largest tax increase in my lifetime."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did include new taxes and revenue provisions but its net tax increases are smaller than several prior major tax increases in recent decades. Historical measures such as the 1993 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act and earlier payroll tax increases (e.g., 1983 Social Security reforms) raised comparable or larger amounts by common measures used by CBO and tax committees. Therefore the ACA is not accurately described as the single largest tax increase in a typical lifetime.

claim: Says the D.C. city council passed a law banning lethal rat trapping.
rationale: There is no record up to mid-2024 of the D.C. Council passing a law that broadly bans lethal rat trapping. Local debates and proposed measures have targeted specific methods (for example restrictions on certain rodenticides or glue traps) or sought increased use of nonlethal control, but not an outright prohibition on all lethal trapping. The claim appears to conflate proposed or limited restrictions with a total ban.

claim: Says as GOP was picking a convention city, "I recommended Ohio."
rationale: The assertion as presented is unverifiable because it gives no speaker, date, or supporting evidence; I could find no authoritative public record or contemporaneous reporting that someone explicitly said, while the GOP was choosing a convention city, 'I recommended Ohio.' Without attribution or corroboration, the claim cannot be confirmed. Because the statement could be true in a private or informal context but lacks evidence, it is treated as unproven and therefore rated false.

claim: "Terry (McAuliffe) calls in his friend Joe Biden to actually put the DOJ on Virginia parents."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Terry McAuliffe actually called President Joe Biden and had the Department of Justice formally target Virginia parents. McAuliffe did make controversial remarks in the 2021 campaign criticizing some parents' actions at school board meetings, but reports and official records do not show a direct Biden/DOJ intervention at McAuliffe's behest.

claim: The "Buffett rule" "raises virtually no money, maybe a day and a half of our borrowing per year."
rationale: Estimates for the Obama-era "Buffett rule" (a minimum 30% tax on very high incomes) put its revenue at roughly $47 billion over 10 years, i.e. about $4–5 billion per year. With annual federal borrowing on the order of $1–1.2 trillion at the time, that annual revenue is indeed on the order of a day or two of U.S. borrowing, so the claim about its very small revenue impact is essentially correct in scale.

claim: "Our (Texas) graduation rate ranks 43rd out of 50 states."
rationale: The claim gives no year or data source and is inconsistent with recent national data: Texas' four‑year adjusted cohort high‑school graduation rate in recent years has been near or above the national average (high‑80s to low‑90s percent), which would not place Texas as low as 43rd among the 50 states. Without a specific year or metric the statement is unsupported and likely incorrect for contemporary figures.

claim: "I finished" the controversy about where President Barack Obama was born.
rationale: The claim asserts a specific individual personally 'finished' the controversy over Obama's birthplace, but the widely documented resolution came when President Barack Obama released his long-form birth certificate in April 2011 and Hawaiian officials verified his Hawaii birth. No independent evidence shows a third party single-handedly ended the dispute; some fringe skepticism persisted afterward. Because the speaker is unidentified and the factual resolution was an official action by Obama and Hawaiian authorities, the claim is not supported.

claim: There are about 120,000 solar energy jobs in the United States, but only 1,700 of them are in Georgia.
rationale: Contemporary industry tallies put U.S. solar employment well above 120,000 — typically in the low-to-mid hundreds of thousands (e.g., ~200,000–250,000 in recent years) — and Georgia's solar workforce is reported at several thousand rather than only 1,700. The claim understates national totals and likely misreports or uses an atypical subset or an out-of-date year.

claim: Republicans "created a trillion dollar prescription drug entitlement program without paying for it."
rationale: The statement refers to the 2003 Medicare Part D prescription drug benefit, enacted under Republican congressional leadership and President George W. Bush; Congressional Budget Office analyses at the time and afterward showed the benefit was not fully offset and added substantially to federal deficits. Over the ensuing decades Medicare Part D spending has exceeded a trillion dollars in cumulative outlays. While some limited offsets and provider-payment changes were included, the program was not paid for in a way that prevented large net federal spending increases.

claim: "Business spirit is the highest it's ever been, according to polls."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated because it lacks any specification of country, time period, or which polls are meant. Business sentiment indicators (PMI, consumer/business confidence indices, NFIB, Ifo, etc.) vary by country and over time and do not collectively show a universal "highest ever" reading. Without a named poll and timeframe the claim cannot be verified and is misleading.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tweeted, "Let’s begin ‘The Purge’ to roundup all Conservative traitors."
rationale: There is no credible record that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez posted that tweet; the phrasing is an extreme, violent call that would be highly notable and has been circulated as a fabricated quote. Public archives of her verified social media and routine fact-checking of viral screenshots show no evidence the tweet was authored by her, so the claim is a misattribution.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers "tried to make us pay even more at the pump by hiking the gas tax."
