A Cornell researcher (David Pimentel) did publish analyses asserting roughly a 29% net energy loss for corn ethanol, but that conclusion is controversial and not endorsed as a Cornell consensus; most peer-reviewed lifecycle studies and government analyses find corn ethanol yields a modest positive net energy balance. The statement also misleadingly equates the percentage to literal gallons of gasoline, while the original analyses refer to fossil energy inputs and accounting choices, not a simple volume-for-volume gasoline equivalence.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Small, bird-sized and even smaller micro/nano drones with onboard cameras exist and can operate indoors; many models can stream or upload live video via Wi‑Fi or cellular links, so the technical capability to record an individual in their home and immediately upload footage to the internet is real. Practical limits (battery life, image/audio quality, navigation and obstacle avoidance) and legal/privacy restrictions affect how feasible and common this is in practice.

claim: "In 1935, more than 50% of the elderly population lived in poverty. Today that poverty rate stands officially at 9.4%."
rationale: Historical data and summaries of the pre–Social Security era show that more than half of Americans aged 65 and older were in poverty around 1935. Contemporary official U.S. Census Bureau poverty rates for people 65+ are on the order of about 9–10% (commonly cited as ~9.4% for a recent year), reflecting the large long-term decline.

claim: Before "our last three presidents, you have to go back to the 1800s, early 1800s to find three presidents in a row being consecutively re-elected."
rationale: This claim is incorrect because there are later examples than the early 1800s of three consecutive U.S. presidents who were each re-elected. For example, Franklin D. Roosevelt (re-elected multiple times), Harry S. Truman (won election in 1948), and Dwight D. Eisenhower (re-elected in 1956) are three consecutive presidents in the mid-20th century who were re-elected. Therefore you do not have to go back to the early 1800s.

claim: "In the 2020 election, President Trump voted from behind the desk in the White House in Florida."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because the White House is in Washington, D.C., not in Florida. President Trump was a registered voter in Florida in 2020 and cast an absentee ballot for that election, but saying he 'voted from behind the desk in the White House in Florida' conflates his Florida residency with the actual location of the White House.

claim: "There's no such thing as a lone wolf. ... That was a phrase invented by the last administration to make Americans stupid."
rationale: The phrase and concept of a 'lone wolf' (or lone-actor) have been used by law enforcement, scholars, and media for decades to describe individuals acting without formal organizational ties. Claiming it was 'invented by the last administration to make Americans stupid' is factually unsupported and imputes an intentional motive that cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: Claims that a particular viral video shows a “gay party in Italy a few weeks before COVID-19” are not verifiable and have frequently been debunked: similar videos circulating on social media have often been older footage or from other countries and events, not Italy in early 2020. Without geolocation, date metadata, or credible sourcing, the assertion that the clip depicts that specific time and place is unsupported.

claim: Paul Ryan’s budget "keeps the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare, but then cuts all of the benefits."
rationale: This overstates and mischaracterizes Ryan’s proposals. Paul Ryan’s budgets generally sought to repeal or roll back many ACA taxes and to reshape/scale back Medicaid and other federal health spending, not to keep all of the ACA’s funding streams intact while eliminating only benefits. The plans varied by year, but they did not consistently ‘keep the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare, but then cut all of the benefits’ as a single, accurate description.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is false because many countries reached and exceeded 50% of their populations fully vaccinated; the United States did hit ~50% in 2021, but it was not uniquely highest. Nations such as the United Arab Emirates, Portugal, Chile and others had higher fully vaccinated shares, so 50% is not "more than any other country."

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: Both Luke Messer and Todd Rokita voted in favor of the 2015 Trade Promotion Authority (TPA) / 'fast-track' measure that enabled the Obama administration to negotiate trade agreements like the TPP under expedited congressional consideration. TPA is commonly described as 'fast-tracking' trade deals because it limits amendments and requires an up-or-down vote.

claim: More than one-quarter of America’s young adults are too fat to serve in the U.S. military
rationale: Multiple government analyses and public-health studies have found that roughly a quarter to a third of 17–24-year-old Americans exceed military weight/body-fat standards or meet obesity thresholds that typically disqualify them from service. Obesity is routinely cited by the Department of Defense and researchers as a leading single medical reason many young adults are ineligible to enlist.

claim: Quotes show Joseph Stalin and Joe Biden expressed similar views about counting votes.
rationale: The line attributed to Joseph Stalin ('Those who count the votes decide everything') implies manipulating counts to determine outcomes, while Joe Biden's public statements (especially during the 2020 election) repeatedly urged that every vote be counted and legal processes respected. The two quotes express opposite principles—Stalin’s is about controlling the count, Biden’s about ensuring all ballots are counted—so they are not similar.

claim: "In Ohio, more than half the providers of safe and legal abortion have had to shut down" since Gov. John Kasich took office in 2011.
rationale: Ohio did experience a substantial reduction in clinics and providers offering abortion care after 2011, but authoritative counts and reporting do not consistently support the assertion that more than half of all ‘safe and legal’ providers statewide have shut down. Different data sources (state health reports, reproductive health research groups, and local reporting) show a large decline but yield smaller proportions once definitions and counting methods are reconciled.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: Al Sharpton traveled to Ferguson after the 2014 Michael Brown shooting and in public remarks and rallies publicly argued that Brown was unarmed and did not pose a deadly threat, citing witness accounts and challenging the police narrative. Although the claim's quoted phrasing ('declaring as a matter of fact') is slightly stronger than some of his exact words, the substantive assertion that he publicly maintained Brown did not use deadly force is accurate.

claim: Georgia spends fewer tourism advertising dollars than any other state in the South.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Georgia consistently spends the least on tourism advertising of any Southern state; Georgia runs a sizable tourism marketing program and many smaller Southern states have smaller advertising budgets. State tourism advertising spending varies year-to-year and by how spending is counted, so the blanket claim is unlikely to be accurate without a specific year and definition.

claim: Says each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks a timeframe; it is not generally true that the most recent three years in a row were each the hottest on record. While there have been stretches when three consecutive years successively set new global temperature records (for example 2014, 2015, 2016), recent global datasets (NOAA/NASA) show 2023 was the warmest year on record but 2021 and 2022 were not, so the blanket claim is false without a specified period.

claim: "To give a sense of how families are struggling, a record four out of every 10 school kids in Ohio now qualifies for subsidized lunch."
rationale: The statement is a specific, time‑bound statistical claim without a cited source and is likely inaccurate as written. Eligibility for free/reduced-price school meals is reported annually by state education agencies and the USDA, and Ohio's percentage has varied year to year (including pandemic-related rises) but the claim’s precise 'record four out of every 10' figure and 'record' qualifier cannot be verified from general knowledge alone.

claim: In Ohio, "each year an estimated 1,000 children become victims of human trafficking, and over 3,000 more are at risk."
rationale: There is no authoritative, transparent source that documents an annual, validated count of exactly 1,000 child victims and 3,000 children at risk in Ohio; the figures appear to be estimates cited by advocacy or government communications that rely on extrapolation methods rather than direct measurement. State- and national-level human trafficking numbers are widely acknowledged to be undercounted and estimates vary substantially depending on methodology, so the precise claim is not supported as a verified fact.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: The absolute claim that Wisconsin's unemployment rate has "never been this low before, ever" is not supported. Historical state unemployment series (from sources such as the BLS and Wisconsin Dept. of Workforce Development) show similarly low or lower readings in prior periods depending on the exact measure and seasonal adjustment, so the blanket "never before" statement is inaccurate.

claim: Says former NBA player Rick Fox was also on board with Kobe Bryant
rationale: The widely reported January 26, 2020 helicopter crash that killed Kobe Bryant included a specific list of nine victims (Kobe Bryant, his daughter Gianna, the pilot, and seven others). Rick Fox was not listed among the passengers and was not on board. Multiple contemporaneous news reports and official victim lists do not include Rick Fox.

claim: "The very first Republican convention after the Civil War was held in Virginia in a Black church."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: the first post–Civil War Republican National Convention was not held in Virginia or in a Black church. Republican National Conventions around Reconstruction (for example 1868) met in major northern cities such as Chicago; while Reconstruction-era state GOP meetings and constitutional conventions in Southern states sometimes met in Black churches, there is no clear evidence that the "very first" Republican convention after the war occurred in Virginia in a Black church.

claim: "The  firefighters, the policemen and others who supported (Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker) in his election bid ... don't have to worry about their collective bargaining rights."
rationale: This claim is misleading. In 2011 Wisconsin Act 10 substantially curtailed collective bargaining for most public employees, so supporters were not categorically spared. While certain public safety bargaining rights (police and firefighters) had limited protections or exemptions in some respects, overall bargaining power for many public employees was sharply reduced, so it is incorrect to say they “don't have to worry.”

claim: Says state budget deal between Texas House and Senate leaders "funds nursing homes, our public schools and universities and provides financial aid for college students."
rationale: State budget agreements between the Texas House and Senate routinely allocate money to long-standing state priorities such as Medicaid-funded nursing homes, K–12 public schools, and public universities, and they typically include line items or programs that provide financial aid to college students. The recent budget deal negotiated by House and Senate leaders did contain appropriations for long-term care, public education and higher education, and funding for student financial aid programs.
cited_knowledge: General understanding of how Texas biennial budgets allocate funds to Medicaid/nursing homes, the Foundation School Program for K–12, higher education formulas, and state financial aid programs; reporting on the recent House–Senate budget agreement.
safety_notes: The claim does not specify which year's budget deal; while the described categories are commonly funded, exact amounts, scope of increases, or program details vary by biennial budget.

claim: Says Ken Cuccinelli "attacked churches for helping the poor."
rationale: There is no clear, credible public record showing Ken Cuccinelli explicitly 'attacked churches for helping the poor.' His public controversies have centered on immigration, healthcare, and conservative legal positions, not documented assaults on charitable church activity. Without a specific incident or reliable reporting, the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: In-N-Out cups say "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no evidence that In-N-Out prints the political slogan "Let’s go Brandon" on its official cups; their standard packaging only features the company logo and menu/branding elements. Viral images showing that phrase have typically been user-altered or involve customers writing on cups by hand rather than factory-printed messaging.

claim: Says President Trump "has ended up attracting larger numbers of people coming to the United States presenting themselves for asylum status at our border than we’ve ever seen."
rationale: While there were notable surges in migrants and asylum-seekers at the U.S. southern border during 2018–2019, official statistics and historical records use different metrics (CBP encounters, asylum applications, credible-fear claims) and do not unambiguously show that more people presented for asylum during the Trump years than in every prior period. Moreover, attributing those flows to President Trump as the cause is speculative—migration trends reflect many push and pull factors beyond a single administration.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported as a blanket fact — aggregated insurer profits vary by line (life, health, property‑casualty), by metric (net income, underwriting profit, profit margin), and by country. Public industry data and regulator reports show large swings (including steep losses around 2001–2002 and during major catastrophes) and while some insurers or segments saw large percentage gains over some periods, there is no clear, industry‑wide >400% increase since 2001 once you account for the choice of metric and inflation.

claim: "Throughout his time in elected office, Barack Obama has taken multiple positions on banning handguns and the D.C. handgun ban."
rationale: Over his career Obama made different public statements about handguns and the District of Columbia's handgun restrictions. As an Illinois state legislator and early candidate he voiced support for strict local handgun limits and regulatory approaches, while during the 2008 campaign and his presidency he took more nuanced positions after the Supreme Court's D.C. v. Heller decision, emphasizing enforcement of laws and broader gun-control measures rather than an absolute federal handgun ban.

claim: "I’m running the second-largest county district attorney’s office … at 1985 staffing levels."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it omits which county and the specific staffing numbers or metric for 'second-largest.' Moreover, general historical trends show most large county district attorney offices have grown in staff and specialized units since 1985, making it unlikely the office is operating at 1985 staffing levels today.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate "is proposing the universal registration of all firearms and their owners."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as phrased because no specific Senate bill is identified and there is no general evidence that a current federal gun bill mandates a universal registry of all firearms and owners. Recent federal proposals have typically focused on background checks, licensing, reporting lost or stolen guns, or restrictions on certain sales rather than explicit universal registration. Without the exact bill text, the claim appears to be misleading or inaccurate.

claim: "On the pace that we're on with job creation in the last four months ... we will have created more jobs in this year than in the entire Bush Presidency."
rationale: The claim is not supported by labor-market data. The Bush presidency (2001–2009) saw a cumulative net change of multiple millions of jobs by standard BLS measures, and the observed four‑month job‑creation pace cited would not reasonably scale to exceed that entire eight‑year total by year‑end. Contemporary fact‑checks found similar assertions to be misleading or false because they depended on cherry‑picked time windows and ambiguous job metrics.

claim: "Barron Trump was born in March 2006 and Melania wasn’t a legal citizen until July 2006. So under this executive order, his own son wouldn’t be an American citizen."
rationale: Barron Trump was born in the U.S. in March 2006 and Melania did not become a naturalized U.S. citizen until later in 2006, but an executive order cannot override the Fourteenth Amendment. Birthright citizenship for anyone born on U.S. soil is constitutional law, so a unilateral executive order could not legitimately strip his citizenship and would face immediate judicial challenge.

claim: If sea levels rise six feet due to climate change, Waterplace Park in Providence and Wickford village would be swamped
rationale: Both Waterplace Park in downtown Providence and Wickford village lie at very low elevations adjacent to tidal rivers and Narragansett Bay. A 6-foot (≈1.8 m) mean sea-level rise would inundate large portions of low-lying waterfront areas in Providence and the coastal village of Wickford, causing them to be swamped absent major protections.

claim: "During my administration, funding for education has increased by over $930 million."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no details about who 'my' refers to, what jurisdiction or time period is meant, or how 'funding for education' is defined (annual vs. cumulative, appropriations vs. spending, adjusted for inflation). Without those specifics and without cited budget documents or official figures, the statement cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unproven.

claim: Says Donald Trump "cashed in" on Sept. 11,  "collecting $150,000 in federal funds intended to help small businesses recover — even though days after the attack Trump said his properties were not affected."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that Donald Trump personally "collected $150,000" in federal small-business recovery funds after Sept. 11, 2001, nor credible reporting showing he said his properties were unaffected days later and then accepted that specific payment. Public records and contemporary reporting do not clearly document a $150,000 federal payment to Trump from 9/11 recovery programs, so the precise claim as stated is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Not a single person in the crowd on January 6 was found to be carrying a firearm. Not one."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reporting and Department of Justice charging documents show that some people associated with the January 6 events were found in possession of firearms or charged with weapons offenses. The absolute claim that not a single person was found carrying a firearm contradicts those documented instances.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: The U.S. federal government did not "run out of money" about halfway through fiscal year 2009 (FY2009 ran Oct 1, 2008–Sept 30, 2009); the government continued operations using appropriated funds and Treasury borrowing and there was no documented cessation of federal payments mid‑FY2009. While some state and local governments faced budget shortfalls during the 2008–2009 recession, that is a different situation and does not support the blanket claim that "Washington has run out of money."

claim: "Americans not vaccinated before 2022 will be put in camps"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official policy that the U.S. government planned or announced placing unvaccinated Americans into 'camps' for refusing COVID-19 vaccination before 2022. Such an action would conflict with U.S. constitutional protections and public-health practice, and reputable fact-checkers and officials have repeatedly denied any such policy. Claims of planned internment are tied to conspiracy theories rather than verifiable government action.

claim: Says Steve Jobs said, "I realize that all my recognition and wealth that I have is meaningless in the face of imminent death."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Steve Jobs having said that exact sentence. Jobs did make widely documented remarks (e.g., his 2005 Stanford commencement speech and interviews covered in his biography) expressing that death puts fame and wealth in perspective, but the precise quoted wording does not appear in primary sources and seems to be a paraphrase or misattribution.

claim: "More than 9,000 Rhode Island voters used the Moderate Party master lever mechanism and they didn't have a single Moderate on their ballot."
rationale: The claim is implausible given how Rhode Island's master-lever (party-line) mechanism works and common ballot-access rules: a party line is only shown if the party qualified candidates for that election, so voters cannot validly use a 'Moderate' master lever if no Moderate candidates were on the ballot. Reports and official results would be required to support a specific 9,000+ figure, and without a cited election year this precise number is unsupported.

claim: "In Florida, for eight years we cut taxes every year, totaling $19 billion."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported by available public budget records: Florida has enacted various tax relief measures over different years, but there is no clear, verifiable record that the state cut taxes in eight straight years totaling exactly $19 billion. Public claims by officials often aggregate different kinds of relief (one‑time rebates, rate changes, exemptions) and different time periods, making the precise consecutive eight‑year, $19 billion assertion unsupported without additional context.

claim: "On issue after issue that really were hard to explain or understand, you voted present . . . And anytime anyone raises that, there's always some kind of explanation."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific and repeated voting pattern by an unnamed individual but provides no identity, timeframe, or supporting evidence. Without identifying who “you” refers to and consulting official roll-call records or contemporaneous reporting, the pattern cannot be verified and thus should not be accepted as fact.

claim: "FBI uncovers evidence that 62 million Trump voters are all Russian agents!"
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public statement from the FBI that it has uncovered evidence labeling 62 million Trump voters as Russian agents. The claim is extraordinary and implausible—62 million roughly matches a national vote total and would have produced widespread, verifiable announcements and legal actions if true.

claim: Says Joe Biden stayed silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests.
rationale: This is inaccurate: Joe Biden did not stay silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests. During the 2020 protest period and afterward he issued multiple public statements, interviews, and speeches denouncing violence and looting, urging peaceful protest and de‑escalation while expressing support for protesters' grievances.

claim: "Bad math (is) driving Wisconsin’s exploding positive test rate."
rationale: The claim overstates the case: while reporting errors, changes in the mix of tests reported, or denominator/counting issues can temporarily distort percent-positive figures, they are unlikely to be the sole explanation for a sustained or large ‘explosion’ in positive test rates. In Wisconsin’s observed surges, increased community transmission and changes in who was being tested (more symptomatic people, outbreak-driven testing) were major contributors alongside occasional reporting artifacts. Therefore saying 'bad math is driving' the spike is misleading without specific evidence that a persistent calculation error caused the increase.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: U.S. data show taxpayers with about $1 million pay substantially higher effective federal tax rates than those earning about $100,000, but the difference is on the order of twofold, not fourfold. Typical effective federal income tax rates for million-dollar filers are often in the ~20–30% range versus roughly ~10–15% for $100k filers, so the claim greatly overstates the gap.

claim: Says video shows "Ukrainian forces shoot down Russian plane carrying hundreds (of) troops on Kyiv airport."
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified reporting that Ukrainian forces shot down a Russian plane carrying 'hundreds' of troops at Kyiv airport. Videos making such claims circulating online have been uncorroborated or misattributed, and aircraft capable of carrying 'hundreds' of troops are rare, making the claim implausible without strong evidence.

claim: The Mack Penny Plan for the federal budget  "would balance our budget by 2019" and "continues to gain support."
rationale: The United States federal budget was not balanced in 2019 (the 2019 fiscal year ran a large deficit of roughly $1 trillion), so any claim that the Mack Penny Plan "would balance our budget by 2019" is inconsistent with outcomes. Additionally, there is no clear evidence that an obscure plan called the "Mack Penny Plan" achieved growing mainstream or legislative support after its proposal.

claim: "We have to recognize that our salaries for faculty are the lowest in New England with the exception of the University of Maine."
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely inaccurate as presented because it names no specific institution or year and asserts a blanket regional ranking. Faculty salaries vary by institution, rank, discipline and year, so a definitive claim that "our salaries are the lowest in New England except University of Maine" requires a cited, current comparative salary survey.

claim: "Youth unemployment in minority communities is about 40 to 45 percent."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unqualified statement and is inconsistent with mainstream labor statistics: youth unemployment rates for racial and ethnic minority groups in countries like the United States have been substantially elevated compared with whites but typically fall well below 40–45% when measured nationally. While some localities, specific subgroups, or short periods (e.g., early COVID lockdowns) have seen very high youth joblessness, a blanket figure of 40–45% for "minority communities" is misleading and unsupported as a general statement.

claim: Says Gov Tony Evers’ administration deemed dentists non-essential
rationale: The Evers administration did restrict elective medical and dental procedures early in the COVID-19 pandemic to conserve PPE, but it did not categorically declare dentists as non-essential. Emergency and urgent dental care continued to be permitted, so saying the administration 'deemed dentists non-essential' is misleading.

claim: Says under his utility rate plan, "An estimated 50 percent of our residential households will see a decrease in their water and wastewater bills."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because the claimant and the specific utility rate plan are not identified and no supporting rate study or public data is provided. Claims that a precise share of households will see bill decreases require jurisdiction-specific modeling and baseline assumptions; without that evidence the quoted 50% figure is unsubstantiated.

claim: "I have more military experience than anybody who’s arrived behind that desk since George H.W. Bush."
rationale: The claimant (Donald Trump) did not serve in the U.S. armed forces beyond attending the New York Military Academy as a youth and receiving draft deferments during Vietnam, while George W. Bush served in the Texas Air National Guard. Presidents since George H.W. Bush include Bill Clinton (no military service), George W. Bush (military service), and Barack Obama (no military service); Bush's documented service means the claimant does not have more military experience than everyone who has occupied the Oval Office since H.W. Bush.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: Under ordinary rules members of both chambers are expected to be physically present to participate in floor debates and to cast votes; the House and Senate require a quorum of members present for business. The House did temporarily authorize proxy voting during the COVID-19 pandemic (a limited exception), but the Senate continued to require in-person participation and the proxy rule in the House was not a permanent change.

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP does not automatically send a portion of every payment or membership fee directly to the Democratic Party. AARP is a nonprofit that says it is nonpartisan; it operates a separate PAC that accepts voluntary contributions and that PAC's spending and candidate contributions (publicly reported) have gone to candidates of both parties. Membership dues primarily fund member services and advocacy, not direct transfers to a political party.

claim: Says "Eric Holder and his group came in and made" the Wisconsin Supreme Court race "highly partisan."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Eric Holder personally or a single "group" he led was solely responsible for making a Wisconsin Supreme Court race highly partisan. Wisconsin high-court contests have been polarized for years and recent races attracted large outside spending from multiple national Republican and Democratic organizations, not just one actor. Saying Holder and his group "made" the race highly partisan overstates their singular causal role.

claim: "For four years, we balanced the budget and paid off $405 billion in debt."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported as written. While the U.S. experienced consecutive budget surpluses in the late 1990s (roughly 1998–2001), whether exactly $405 billion was “paid off” depends on which debt measure is used (gross debt vs. debt held by the public) and the chosen timeframe; commonly reported reductions in debt during that period differ from a clean $405 billion figure. Without a clear subject, dates, and debt definition, the claim is misleading.

claim: Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and his wife Ginni posted a photo of themselves enjoying a $5,135 bottle of wine "as American women despair about abortion rights being taken away from them."
rationale: The viral claim misstates context and adds a price/caption that are not supported by available evidence. While a photo of Justice Clarence Thomas and his wife Ginni circulated online, independent fact-checkers found no proof they posted the quoted caption nor that the bottle pictured was identified or sold for $5,135; the price and wording appear to have been fabricated or falsely attached to the image.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "opposed Obamacare, didn't like the fact we didn't push a single-payer option."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has publicly said he opposed the Affordable Care Act because it did not go far enough and repeatedly criticized that Democrats did not push for a single-payer (Medicare-for-All) solution. His long-standing advocacy for single-payer and his statements during and after the ACA debates support this characterization.

claim: Says Congressmen Paul Ryan and Todd Akin co-sponsored legislation "to limit federal funding for abortion to victims of ‘forcible rape.’"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Paul Ryan and Todd Akin jointly sponsored a bill that specifically limited federal abortion funding only to victims of “forcible rape.” Both have supported restricting federal funding for abortion in various bills, and Akin’s well-known remarks about “legitimate” rape have caused confusion, but the precise claim that they co‑sponsored legislation using the phrase “forcible rape” or creating that sole exception is not supported by readily available legislative records.

claim: "There was no violence on the Senate side, in terms of the chamber."
rationale: During the January 6, 2021 U.S. Capitol breach rioters forced entry into and occupied the Senate chamber, damaged property, and law enforcement reported assaults and injuries in the Senate wing and surrounding areas. Therefore the categorical statement that there was "no violence on the Senate side" is incorrect given the documented events that day.

claim: "Since 2010, Republicans have won unaffiliated voters in every general election."
rationale: National exit polls and voter surveys show that Democrats won a majority of independent/unaffiliated voters in several general elections since 2010 (notably 2012 for Obama, 2018 midterms in many races, and 2020 for Biden). While Republicans carried independents in some cycles (e.g., 2010 and parts of 2014/2016), they did not win unaffiliated voters in every general election after 2010.

claim: "China has made enormous progress in its human rights. That is a fact recognized by all the people in the world."
rationale: While China has documented gains in economic and social indicators (large reductions in extreme poverty, expanded healthcare and education), its human-rights record on civil and political rights is widely criticized (e.g., treatment of Uyghurs, restrictions in Hong Kong, limits on free expression). The claim that such progress is "a fact recognized by all the people in the world" is false because governments, international organizations, and human-rights NGOs continue to dispute and condemn many aspects of China's human-rights practices.

claim: Will Hurd "tends to have a 96 percent straight Republican, straight party voting record."
rationale: The claim asserts Will Hurd consistently has a 96% party-line Republican voting record, but party unity scores fluctuate by session and Hurd was widely regarded as a more moderate Republican who broke with his party on notable votes. Public roll-call statistics and bipartisan rankings do not support a persistent, across-the-board 96% party-line rate for Hurd over his House tenure.

claim: "Smartmatic and Dominion systems ... were built to do this very thing, for changing the results of elections."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Smartmatic or Dominion systems were intentionally built to change election results. Multiple independent audits, recounts, bipartisan reviews, cybersecurity agencies, and court rulings after recent elections found no proof that these vendors designed their systems to alter vote totals; while software bugs or misconfiguration can occur, claims of deliberate build‑in fraud are unsubstantiated.

claim: Imitation dairy products often differ nutritionally from those they mimic, and labeling them "milk" or "cheese" or "yogurt" is "against the law."
rationale: It is true that many plant‑based or imitation dairy products differ nutritionally from the animal‑derived products they mimic (differences in protein, fat, micronutrients and fortification are common). However, the blanket claim that labeling them “milk,” “cheese,” or “yogurt” is “against the law” is false: some jurisdictions have rules or restrictions on dairy names, but there is no universal prohibition and practices vary by country and region.

claim: Says President Dwight Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country."
rationale: The Eisenhower administration did conduct large roundups and removals of Mexican nationals (notably the 1954 'Operation Wetback'), but mainstream historical estimates put removals in the roughly 1.0–1.3 million range and many were voluntary repatriations or included U.S. citizens; the commonly cited 1.5 million figure is higher than most reliable estimates and is therefore misleading. The total depends on counting methods and definitions, so saying he 'moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out' overstates and simplifies the historical record.

claim: Under the new Arizona immigration law, police can't stop someone to check their immigration status unless they think they see something illegal.
rationale: Arizona's immigration statute requires officers to have reasonable suspicion of unlawful presence before asking about immigration status; it does not permit stops solely to check status. In practice the law allows status checks during a lawful stop, detention, or arrest when an officer has reasonable suspicion someone is in the U.S. illegally, though courts have limited some provisions and wording like "see something illegal" is imprecise.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: The statement implies the decennial census has routinely asked “Are you a citizen…” for decades; that is misleading. The direct citizenship question appeared on early censuses (through 1950) and has been included for decades on sample surveys (the long form and later the American Community Survey), but it was not on the short-form decennial census questionnaires from 1960 through 2010.

claim: Georgia has the highest flu activity in the country.
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or data source and therefore cannot be verified; influenza activity fluctuates weekly and by region. Public health surveillance (e.g., CDC weekly influenza reports) shows state-level activity levels change over time and there is no basis to assert Georgia currently has the highest activity nationwide without a specific date and data.

claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics "supports banning guns."
rationale: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) advocates for evidence-based policies to reduce firearm injuries—such as universal background checks, safe storage laws, child access prevention, and in some statements restrictions on assault weapons or high-capacity magazines—but it does not call for a wholesale ban on all guns. Characterizing the AAP as supporting a blanket 'ban on guns' is an overbroad and misleading summary of its policy positions.

claim: "From 2000 to 2016, every major drug that was introduced came out of" National Institutes of Health funding.
rationale: The claim is overly broad: although NIH-funded basic research contributed to the scientific foundation of many drugs between 2000 and 2016, it is not true that every major drug introduced in that period directly 'came out of' NIH funding. Numerous drugs were discovered and developed primarily by pharmaceutical companies or private biotech without direct NIH funding. Therefore the absolute statement is incorrect.

claim: Starbucks executive "believes white men are the root of all evil."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that a named Starbucks executive publicly said 'white men are the root of all evil.' The claim appears to be a vague, unverified attribution common in viral misinformation; without a verifiable source (recording, reputable news outlet, or direct statement) the assertion is not supported. Absent such verification, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Says James Mattis said, "If you burn the American flag you’ll spend two years in the military. I promise you, you’ll be cured of the desire to burn a flag ever again."
rationale: The quoted wording is inaccurate. James Mattis did publicly say that people who burn the American flag should be made to serve in the military, but news reports attribute him as saying about a year of service (and used paraphrase), not the exact line claiming 'two years' and the verbatim promise quoted here.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: The claim is overstated: arena financing varies widely and many recent NBA/NHL arenas have been financed with a larger private share (and some largely privately financed), while others have received substantial public subsidies. Without a clear dataset or timeframe, it is incorrect to say a 50-50 split would be 'much better than most' because many projects have had lower public portions and others higher—so the comparative statement is ambiguous and unsupported as universal.

claim: The presence of gorillas calls into question the concept of evolution.
rationale: The existence of gorillas is fully consistent with evolutionary theory rather than contradicting it. Evolution predicts diversification of life into related species; gorillas are explained as part of the ape lineage with shared ancestry, genetic similarities, and fossil/ anatomical evidence that fit evolutionary models. Their presence supports, not undermines, the concept of evolution.

claim: "We've had two members engage in a Democrat-led persecution of ordinary citizens who engaged in legitimate political discourse."
rationale: The claim is a vague, unsubstantiated allegation that names no individuals, incidents, dates, or sources; without concrete evidence identifying the two members and documented actions it cannot be verified. Claims of a 'Democrat-led persecution' imply official or legal action against ordinary citizens and require corroborating reporting or records, which are not provided here.

claim: "As governor, Kasich delivered the largest tax cut in the nation."
rationale: John Kasich did sign multi-billion-dollar tax reductions for Ohio while governor, but the blanket statement that he "delivered the largest tax cut in the nation" is an unsupported superlative. Comparative state fiscal records show other states implemented larger or comparable tax-cut packages depending on the metric and timeframe, and the claim gives no qualifying definition.

claim: "Our country's got this huge debt, and (President Barack) Obama says raise taxes and keep spending more."
rationale: The statement is a misleading oversimplification. President Obama did advocate targeted tax increases (primarily on higher-income households and some business tax changes) and supported increased investment in areas like healthcare and infrastructure, but he did not broadly call for blanket tax hikes on everyone nor for unchecked perpetual spending; his budgets also included deficit-reduction proposals and some spending constraints negotiated with Congress.

claim: Oregon concealed gun applications include "home phone numbers, home address, Social Security numbers, what kinds of guns you have in the house … whether you were dishonorably discharged from the military, what controlled substances you are taking and  were you ever accused of -- accused, mind you -- of stalking."
rationale: Oregon concealed handgun license applications do request identifying contact information (address, phone) and a Social Security number for background checks, and they ask about disqualifying military discharge status and criminal convictions or protective orders. However, the form does not require applicants to inventory or list what kinds of guns are in their home, nor typically ask applicants to list specific controlled substances they are taking or whether they were merely "accused" of a crime (the questions focus on convictions, prohibiting conditions, or current unlawful use of controlled substances).

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because Tammy Baldwin, as a member of the U.S. Congress (House then Senate), did not have a vote on Wisconsin state budgets or state property-tax cuts; those were enacted by the Wisconsin Legislature. Moreover, reporting and roll-call patterns on Governor Scott Walker's budgets show that Democratic state lawmakers generally opposed his major budget and tax measures, so the statement that "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts is misleading.

claim: "For the second quarter in a row, my campaign has raised more money than any other challenger in the nation and brought our fundraising total to over $800,000."
rationale: The claim gives no candidate name or specific reporting period, and I cannot confirm a nationwide ranking or aggregate total from here. Statements about being the top fundraising challenger and exceeding $800,000 require checking FEC quarterly filings and independent fundraising trackers; without those data this specific assertion cannot be substantiated. Because the claim is unverifiable as presented, I classify it as false.

claim: "If every house in Florida had a solar-heated water tank, that would eliminate consumption by 17 percent."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated. While water heating is commonly cited as roughly 15–18% of a typical household's energy use, saying that installing solar-heated water tanks in every Florida house would 'eliminate consumption by 17 percent' improperly conflates a national/residential share with statewide total consumption and ignores real-world limits (system performance, backup heating, variability and adoption).

claim: "Piles of bricks are being staged in cities around the country, indicating riots are planned."
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a coordinated, nationwide effort to 'stage' piles of bricks for planned riots. Loose bricks and pavers are commonly present in cities for legitimate reasons (construction, landscaping, sidewalk/road repairs), and viral social-media posts often recycle or mislabel such images. Isolated instances of suspicious activity would not justify the broad claim.

claim: "More than a million Californians" do not have "clean water to bathe in or drink."
rationale: Estimates of Californians lacking safe drinking water vary and typically refer to people served by systems with water quality violations, not an absolute lack of any water to bathe or drink. State and expert estimates have often cited figures on the order of hundreds of thousands to around one million people affected by unsafe drinking water, but the precise claim that "more than a million" have no clean water to bathe or drink is an overstatement without clear definition or recent corroborating data.

claim: Says "John James supported Betsy DeVos’ agenda to cut public school funding and put it into wealthy private schools instead."
rationale: John James has publicly supported school choice policies similar to those promoted by Betsy DeVos (vouchers, education savings accounts), but there is no clear direct evidence that he explicitly said he favored cutting public school funding in order to transfer it specifically to wealthy private schools. The claim frames those policy positions as an intentional scheme to benefit wealthy private schools, which is an interpretive and politicized characterization rather than a documented factual statement by James.

claim: "Austin ISD has the highest graduation rate of every major city in Texas."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement without a year or definition of “major city.” Texas Education Agency district graduation-rate reports show variation year-to-year and several large-city districts have comparable or higher rates in some years, so it’s not accurate to assert Austin ISD is the highest across every major Texas city. Without a specific year and list of cities the claim cannot be supported.

claim: "Currently, 23 percent of our military's infrastructure is graded as 'poor' while 9 percent is 'failing.'"
rationale: The statement is presented as a current, DoD-wide fact but no single, up-to-date Department of Defense report universally reports exactly 23% of military infrastructure as "poor" and 9% as "failing." Official condition metrics (FCI and similar) vary by service, asset type, and reporting year; some past or service-specific reports have shown similar-but-not-identical figures, but the claim as stated is not verifiably true without a clear source and timeframe.

claim: Video shows Joe Biden saying "we can only re-elect Donald Trump."
rationale: No verified, unedited video shows Joe Biden saying the exact line "we can only re-elect Donald Trump." Viral clips that purport to show this phrase have been shown by fact-checkers to be edited, spliced, or taken out of context rather than showing Biden uttering those words in an original recording.

claim: "I've got five years of experience as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: There is no way to confirm this statement without the speaker's identity, dates, specific office, or supporting records. Congressional staff employment can typically be verified via official staff directories, office biographies, or employment records, and in the absence of such evidence the claim is unsubstantiated and treated as false pending verification.

claim: "(Mexican immigrants) are more law-abiding than U.S. citizens and that is a statistic."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and U.S. government data consistently find that immigrants from Mexico have lower rates of arrest, conviction, and incarceration than native-born U.S. residents, so the broad claim that Mexican immigrants are "more law-abiding" is supported as a statistical generalization. However, the pattern can vary by specific offense, legal status, and time period.

claim: "We’re now spending 42 percent of our economy on government."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it omits which country, year, and measure of "spending" is meant. Total government spending as a share of GDP varies by country and year; for the U.S. it has generally been in the mid-30s percent of GDP in recent non‑pandemic years and only temporarily climbed above 40% during the 2020 pandemic response depending on the measure used. Presenting a flat 42% as a current, unqualified fact is therefore incorrect.

claim: "Some of the things that (Megyn Kelly) said, I didn’t say."
rationale: The claim is a denial that certain words attributed to a speaker were actually spoken, but no context, transcript, audio/video, or attribution is provided to verify or falsify it. Without primary-source evidence (recordings or verbatim transcripts) one cannot confirm the denial, so the safe determination is that the claim cannot be verified as true. Given the lack of supporting evidence, I classify it as false-leaning.

claim: "Wendy Davis has already taken more $ from teacher unions than the past 3 Democrat gubernatorial candidates combined."
rationale: Public campaign finance reporting and contemporary fact-checks showed that while Wendy Davis received notable support from teachers' unions and related PACs in 2014, the amounts do not exceed the combined teacher-union-related receipts of the prior three Democratic gubernatorial nominees when counted on a comparable basis. The claim conflates different types of spending (direct contributions versus independent expenditures) and fails to specify which three prior candidates or which unions are included, making the categorical statement inaccurate.

claim: "After every major conflict ... what happened was that we ultimately hollowed out the force, largely by doing deep, across-the-board cuts."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. It is true that many post‑war periods (for example U.S. demobilizations after World War I and II, the Vietnam-era reductions and some 1990s drawdowns) produced capability gaps from across‑the‑board cuts, but it is not accurate to say this happened after every major conflict or that deep cuts are the sole cause. Outcomes vary by country, era, and political choices, and some wars led to sustained or expanded forces instead of wholesale hollowing.

claim: Says Mitch McConnell voted "two times against the Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: Senate roll-call history and contemporary fact-checks show Mitch McConnell opposed at least the 2013 VAWA reauthorization but he supported the original 1994 Violence Against Women Act and has not cast two plain ‘no’ votes on the core VAWA enactments. Saying he voted “two times against” the Act is misleading because it conflates different bills, amendments, or procedural votes rather than two distinct final opposing votes on the core law.

claim: "Every time the weight of that vehicle is reduced by a hundred pounds, your chances of dying are going to go up by about 5 percent. Peel three hundred pounds off – you’re 15 percent more likely to die in that car."
rationale: There is no universal rule that each 100‑pound reduction in vehicle weight increases a driver's chance of dying by about 5%; crash risk depends on many factors including crash type, relative mass of other vehicles, vehicle design, and safety features. While heavier vehicles tend to offer better protection to their own occupants in multi‑vehicle crashes, they also increase risk to occupants of other vehicles, and empirical studies show varying, context‑dependent effects rather than a simple linear 5% per 100 lb rule.

claim: The U.S. government spends less on energy innovation "than the pet food industry invests in its own products."
rationale: The claim is misleading and incorrect as stated. Federal spending on energy innovation (including DOE applied R&D, ARPA‑E, and related programs) runs into multiple billions of dollars annually, whereas the pet food industry’s spending on product R&D is much smaller (typically in the low hundreds of millions), so U.S. government energy innovation spending is not less than pet food product investment. The comparison also conflates different categories (public R&D vs. private product investment) making the claim unreliable.

claim: Since 2009, "after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it gives no country, end year, or definition of “after-tax incomes” (mean vs median, household vs individual, inflation-adjusted). U.S. data sources (Census, BEA, CBO) show different percentage changes since 2009 depending on those choices, and none uniformly support an unqualified “up nearly 14 percent” figure without additional context.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The claim cannot be evaluated as true because ‘our region’ is undefined and drought severity is region-specific. Although 2011 produced extreme drought in some areas (for example parts of the U.S.), many regions have earlier or later droughts that are worse by standard indices, so the blanket statement is unsupported without a specific location and data source.

claim: Says Oregon ranks 43rd in education.
rationale: The statement gives a single rank without citing a source, year, or metric; education rankings for states vary by methodology (test scores, funding, graduation rates, composite indexes) and change from year to year. Without a specific report and timeframe, the claim that Oregon "ranks 43rd in education" is unsupported.

claim: In 2021, "11,201 pounds of fentanyl were seized by Customs and Border Protection, which is enough to kill every American nearly seven times over."
rationale: CBP did report roughly 11,201 pounds of fentanyl seized in 2021, and a simplistic calculation using a 2 mg assumed lethal dose converts that mass into roughly 7–8 lethal doses per U.S. resident. However, that statement is misleading because it assumes all seized material is pure fentanyl and that a uniform 2 mg dose is universally lethal. In reality seized fentanyl is often adulterated or in mixtures and potency/lethality varies, so the "enough to kill every American nearly seven times over" claim overstates what the seizure data support.

claim: "40 percent of American households have female primary breadwinners."
rationale: National survey analyses show a lower share than 40%; Pew Research and Census-based studies report that roughly 28–30% of married‑couple households have wives as the primary earners, and overall shares of households with female primary breadwinners are not generally reported as high as 40%. Differences in definitions (primary vs sole earner, married‑couple vs all households) can change the figure, but 40% overstates commonly cited estimates.

claim: Says his "Act 10 reforms" have "saved the taxpayers some $3 billion."
rationale: The $3 billion claim is misleading because estimated savings from Wisconsin's 2011 Act 10 vary widely by timeframe and what is counted (state budget only vs. local governments, school districts, and employee benefit contributions). Independent analyses and the state fiscal office produced lower or inconsistent figures depending on assumptions, so presenting a single $3 billion figure without context overstates what can be reliably attributed to Act 10.

claim: It "is estimated that as many as 300,000 auto workers may be out of a job before the end of the year."
rationale: The claim presents a large numeric estimate without attribution or context; there is no widely cited, authoritative projection that 300,000 auto workers will be out of jobs before year-end. Such a large, near-term loss would be exceptional and widely reported by major labor and industry sources, but available public estimates of job impacts from industry shifts are much more varied and typically lower or longer-term.

claim: "We bailed out" Johnson Controls when "we saved the auto industry" and "now they want to avoid paying taxes."
rationale: The 2008–09 U.S. auto rescue primarily provided direct federal aid to the automakers (notably GM and Chrysler) and not a direct taxpayer 'bailout' of Johnson Controls. While large suppliers like Johnson Controls benefitted indirectly from stabilizing the auto market and later engaged in corporate tax strategies (including reorganizations and an Ireland incorporation after a merger) that critics call tax avoidance, the claim that the government specifically bailed out Johnson Controls is inaccurate or misleading.

claim: Tax rates were significantly higher "in the '40s, the '50s, and the '60s."
rationale: If referring to U.S. federal individual income tax rates (the common context for this claim), the top marginal rates were much higher in those decades: above 90% in much of the 1940s and 1950s and around 70% for much of the 1960s. Those top rates are substantially higher than typical top rates in later decades, so the claim is accurate in that common sense.

claim: "The reality is when you look at the Biden plan, it reads an awful lot like what President Trump and I and our task force have been doing every step of the way."
rationale: The claim that Biden's plan "reads an awful lot like" what Trump and his task force have done "every step of the way" overstates the similarity. While there are some overlaps (e.g., support for vaccine development and some testing efforts), Biden’s proposals emphasized different priorities and tools (stronger federal coordination, national mask emphasis, expanded testing and contact tracing, different messaging and use of authorities) and included measures the Trump task force did not pursue or implemented differently. Saying it mirrors Trump’s approach at "every step" is misleading.

claim: Says Rep. Martha McSally "has repeatedly tried to limit women’s access to birth control, and she even cosponsored a bill to make contraception more expensive for women."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While McSally has supported some Republican measures that limit reproductive-health funding and backed exemptions to the ACA contraceptive mandate, there is no clear record that she “repeatedly tried” in the sense claimed or that she cosponsored a specific bill whose purpose was explicitly to make contraception more expensive for women. The language overstates and conflates related votes and sponsorships into a narrower, more inflammatory assertion.

claim: "JFK Jr was declared the frontrunner for the NY Senate seat in 1999. Days later his plane crashed, making Hillary Clinton the newly elected senator."
rationale: This claim is false. John F. Kennedy Jr. died in a plane crash on July 16, 1999, but he was never an official candidate for the 2000 New York Senate race and was not formally declared the frontrunner; at most there was media speculation and favorable polling about a potential candidacy. Hillary Clinton ran in the 2000 election cycle and was elected U.S. Senator in November 2000, well over a year after JFK Jr.'s death, so she did not become senator 'days later.'

claim: "If you got rid of the income tax today you'd have about as much revenue as we had 10 years ago."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. In the United States the individual income tax is the single largest source of federal revenue (roughly 40–50% of receipts); eliminating it today would remove a large share of current receipts and leave far less revenue than the federal government collected a decade ago. Other sources (payroll taxes, corporate, excise) do not make up the gap to match total receipts from ten years earlier.

claim: "We’re already bombing seven countries."
rationale: While the U.S. has conducted air and drone strikes in several countries in recent years (notably Iraq, Syria, Somalia and Yemen), the specific claim that "we're already bombing seven countries" is not reliably supported without a precise timeframe and definition of "bombing." Public reporting up to mid‑2024 documents strikes in multiple places but does not consistently confirm active U.S. bombing in exactly seven countries right now.

claim: Ebola is "incredibly contagious," "very transmissible" and "easy to catch."
rationale: Ebola is not 'incredibly contagious' or 'easy to catch' in the way airborne diseases are. Transmission requires direct contact with the bodily fluids of symptomatic infected people or contaminated materials, so casual proximity or brief respiratory exposure typically does not spread the virus. However, without proper infection control (especially in healthcare or caregiving settings) it can spread readily and cause large outbreaks.

claim: "We have a fire marshal that said, 'Oh we can't allow more people’ ...  And the reason they won't let them in is because they don't know what the hell they're doing."
rationale: The claim attributes a direct quote and a judgment about a fire marshal's competence but provides no corroborating source, time, or location. Without verifiable audio, video, or reputable reporting confirming that a fire marshal said this and that the reason given was incompetence, the statement cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that the Chamber of Commerce itself publicly and unambiguously stated the precise figures "244,000 jobs a year" and "$1,200 a year" as a direct quote. Those numbers resemble results from industry-funded economic models that business groups (including the Chamber) sometimes cite, but attribution to the Chamber as having said those exact figures is unverified and likely imprecise.

claim: "We have counties where there have been one arrest under the SAFE Act. It indicates there's not a whole lot of interest in enforcing this in our upstate counties."
rationale: The claim combines a specific numeric assertion and an inference about local intent. Public reporting and records indicate SAFE Act enforcement and prosecutions in New York were uneven and relatively uncommon in many places, but there is no clear, verifiable evidence that multiple counties had exactly one arrest each nor that a single arrest reliably proves lack of interest in enforcement. The numeric claim and the causal inference are therefore not supported as stated.

claim: Planned Parenthood clinics are "closing down all over the country" because Roe v. Wade was overturned.
rationale: This is an overstatement. After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade (Dobbs), some Planned Parenthood centers in states that enacted near-total bans suspended abortion services or closed, but clinics were not shutting down nationwide. Many Planned Parenthood health centers remain open and the organization shifted resources to states where abortion remains legal.

claim: Says Tennessee has some of the lowest beer excise tax rates in the country.
rationale: Tennessee's beer excise tax has historically been well below the national average and is routinely listed among the lower-tier states in state-by-state comparisons, so characterizing it as 'some of the lowest' is accurate. Specific position can change year to year, but Tennessee consistently appears near the bottom for beer excise rates.

claim: Ron Johnson didn’t "show up" for a day of impeachment hearings.
rationale: The claim is presented without any date or specific hearing and therefore is unverifiable as stated. Senators' attendance at various impeachment-related proceedings has varied, and there is no widely reported, context-free incident establishing that Senator Ron Johnson emphatically 'didn't show up' for a particular day of impeachment hearings. Without a specific hearing and date, the blanket assertion is misleading.

claim: "We have one senator who’s a ‘yes’ vote ... but he’s in the hospital. And he’s a ‘yes’ vote. So we can’t do it by Friday. So we have the votes" to pass a health care bill.
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that this exact statement was made or that the factual situation described occurred as claimed. Major reporting and official Senate records around high-profile health-care votes do not corroborate a publicly documented quote asserting a hospitalized senator was a committed 'yes' and that the bill therefore could not be passed by a Friday deadline. Additionally, Senate procedure requires a senator be present (or otherwise accounted for under specific rules) for a vote, so such a claim would have been widely reported if accurate.

claim: The church Barack Obama belongs to only admits black people.
rationale: Barack Obama was a member of Trinity United Church of Christ, a predominantly African-American congregation, but there is no policy or practice that it admits only black people. The United Church of Christ denomination and Trinity's stated membership practices are open to people of all races, and media reporting and church records show members and leaders of diverse backgrounds. Claims of an explicit race-only admissions rule are unsupported.

claim: On immigration, what reports say President Barack Obama "plans to do is roughly on the same scale" as what President George H.W. Bush did.
rationale: The claim lacks support: contemporary reporting did not generally conclude that Obama's immigration plans were 'roughly on the same scale' as George H.W. Bush's actions. Obama's measures (administrative relief such as DACA and 2014 deferred-action proposals) were executive administrative steps affecting particular groups, whereas George H.W. Bush's record involved major legislative changes (the Immigration Act of 1990) and different shifts in legal immigration policy; the mechanisms and impacts are not directly comparable in scale as described.

claim: "The FBI just confirmed that it was ANTIFA, not Trump supporters, who breached the Capitol."
rationale: The FBI did not “confirm” that Antifa, rather than Trump supporters, breached the U.S. Capitol. Public FBI and DOJ investigations, arrests, charges, and prosecutions have documented that many participants were supporters of then-President Trump and included members of far-right groups; widespread social-media claims that Antifa was responsible were investigated and debunked.

claim: "The yearly cost of religious tax exemptions: $71 billion. If the church paid taxes, everyone would only have to pay 3% taxes."
rationale: The $71 billion figure is a disputed, headline estimate that often conflates tax expenditures for a broad set of nonprofits and uses debatable assumptions; it is not a settled annual shortfall attributable solely to churches. Even if $71 billion were collected, U.S. federal/state tax receipts and the taxable base are in the trillions, so that revenue would not plausibly reduce everyone's tax burden to a flat 3% — the arithmetic and the undefined term “everyone” in the claim make the conclusion unsupported.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s per-pupil education spending is "about $200 less" than what it was under Charlie Crist during the recession.
rationale: The statement is misleading because per‑pupil comparisons between the Crist recession years and the Scott years depend heavily on which years and which spending measure (state only vs. total, nominal vs. inflation‑adjusted) are used. Independent fact checks and budget data show that some nominal measures were similar or higher under Scott while inflation‑adjusted and state‑only measures can differ, so a blanket claim of "about $200 less" cannot be confirmed without specifying the metric. Because multiple legitimate ways to calculate per‑pupil spending produce different results, the simple assertion as stated is not reliably true.

claim: "A Florida judge ruled parts of Obamacare unconstitutional."
rationale: True — a federal judge in Florida (U.S. District Judge Roger Vinson of the Northern District of Florida) issued a ruling finding the ACA’s individual mandate unconstitutional and raising severability issues in a 2011 decision, effectively striking down parts of the law at that stage. That decision was appealed and later affected by appellate and Supreme Court rulings.

claim: "President Biden says he wants to ban handguns."
rationale: Public statements and policy proposals from President Biden have called for banning assault weapons, high-capacity magazines, ghost guns, and strengthening background checks, but he has not advocated for a blanket ban on all handguns. Claims that he said he wants to ban handguns misrepresent his stated gun-control priorities.

claim: "Teenage births cost Texas taxpayers $1.1 billion in health care, foster care and lost tax revenue in 2010 alone."
rationale: This specific $1.1 billion figure matches published estimates from studies (by the National Campaign to Prevent Teen and Unplanned Pregnancy/Power to Decide and similar analyses) that calculated the public costs of teen childbearing in Texas for 2010, including Medicaid/healthcare costs, child welfare/foster care expenses, and lost tax revenue from reduced earnings. The phrasing and categories align with those reports' methodology and headline figure for Texas in 2010.

claim: "The only time government employment has gone down during a recession has been under me."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: historical employment data show government payrolls have fallen in other recessions, not just under a single leader. For example, state and local government employment declined during the 2007–2009 Great Recession and other downturns, so a drop in government employment is not unique to one administration.

claim: Says six eradicated diseases such as whooping cough and the bubonic plague are making a comeback "thanks to refugees and illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: whooping cough (pertussis) has never been globally eradicated and periodically resurges mainly due to waning immunity and gaps in vaccination, while bubonic plague persists in animal reservoirs and causes rare, localized cases rather than a broad comeback. Public-health authorities and epidemiologists attribute resurgences to factors like vaccine coverage, waning immunity, surveillance, and ecological reservoirs, not to refugees or "illegal immigrants," and there is no credible evidence tying broad disease rebounds to migration as claimed.

claim: "Just about everyone everywhere is spending more hours on the job, less time with their families, bringing home smaller and smaller paychecks, while they're paying more and more at the gas pump and the grocery stores."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad universal statement that does not match available evidence: working hours, wages, and prices vary by country, time period, and household. While many workers in some countries have faced stagnant or declining real wages and recent spikes in fuel and food prices, average hours worked have not uniformly increased everywhere and some households have seen wage gains. The blanket phrase 'just about everyone everywhere' is therefore inaccurate.

claim: "Bill Nelson actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some conservative groups have produced tallies attributing hundreds of 'votes for higher taxes' to Bill Nelson, those counts rely on broad or arbitrary definitions (including procedural, budgetary, or spending votes) and omit context about what each vote actually did; independent fact‑checkers have flagged such claims as inaccurate or misleading without more precise definitions.

claim: "He's the only candidate who's balanced budgets and brought jobs to Providence."
rationale: The statement asserts a unique factual claim without identifying the candidate, timeframe, or criteria for 'balanced budgets' and 'brought jobs.' Fiscal and employment outcomes for a city are documented and typically involve multiple officeholders and external economic factors, so claiming one person is the only candidate to have achieved both is not supported as stated.

claim: "Roy Moore fought for pay increases for politicians while courts had to shut down because of lack of funding."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Roy Moore campaigned to raise politicians' pay while courts were forced to shut down from lack of funding. Moore, as Alabama's chief justice, was more often publicly at odds with the legislature and criticized court system funding, and contemporary reporting does not show him pushing raises for lawmakers contemporaneous with court closures. The claim appears to conflate separate budget disputes and misattribute advocacy to Moore.

claim: Australia is microchipping its public.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Australian government is implanting microchips in the general public as a policy. Reports of microchipping in Australia refer to routine pet microchipping, isolated voluntary RFID implants by some employees or individuals, and misinformation that has been debunked by fact-checkers and officials.

claim: Says that "along the southern border of the U.S.," the government apprehends "seven individuals a day who are either known or suspected terrorists."
rationale: Seven alleged 'known or suspected terrorists' apprehended per day along the southern border would equal roughly 2,500+ per year, a figure far larger than public DHS/CBP totals. Official CBP and DHS reporting and multiple fact-checks show only dozens to at most a few hundred such apprehensions over multi-year periods, not thousands annually, so the claim is not supported by available data.

claim: The Biden administration inherited gains of "50,000 jobs a month. We're now finally back to 500,000 jobs a month. We inherited a country where 4,000 people a day were dying from Covid. That's now down 75%."
rationale: The claim mixes and misstates metrics and timeframes. While the January 2021 payroll report showed roughly +49k jobs, that single-month figure does not represent a sustained '50,000 jobs a month' baseline; some later months under the Biden administration saw monthly gains near or above 500,000 but that was not a steady monthly rate. Similarly, COVID deaths in January 2021 peaked in the low thousands per day and later declined, but the exact 4,000/day starting point and a uniform 75% drop depend on which dates and averaging periods are used and are not accurate as stated.

claim: "Gene Green is the NRA’s favorite Democrat in Congress. ... "It’s no wonder the congressman has a lifetime A rating from the NRA."
rationale: The statement is overstated and partly subjective. While Gene Green was a pro-gun Texas Democrat who repeatedly received high NRA scores (A grades in multiple election cycles), there is no objective designation of "the NRA's favorite Democrat in Congress," and claims about an official "lifetime A" should be verified against NRA-PVF records because the organization typically issues cycle-by-cycle ratings rather than a single promotional label.

claim: Says Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak "has banned the use of an anti-malaria drug that might help cure coronavirus."
rationale: There is no evidence that Nevada Governor Steve Sisolak issued a statewide ban on the use of anti-malarial drugs such as hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19. While hospitals and health systems in various places adopted restrictions or guidelines limiting its use outside clinical trials, gubernatorial action in Nevada did not ban the drug statewide; prescribing decisions generally remained with physicians and federal regulators.

claim: "70 percent of the people who voted" on June 5, 2012, "just didn’t feel comfortable with the recall of the governor," weakening any idea that Wisconsin is "fully behind this Walker agenda."
rationale: The June 5, 2012 Wisconsin recall election results do not support a claim that 70% of voters opposed the recall; Scott Walker won the election with roughly 53% of the vote to Tom Barrett’s roughly 46%, so a 70% figure is inconsistent with the official vote split. I am not aware of any credible statewide poll or exit poll from that date showing 70% of actual voters expressed discomfort with the recall.

claim: "The Katy Freeway, or Interstate 10 west of Houston, is the widest freeway in the world, with up to 26 lanes, including frontage road lanes."
rationale: The Katy Freeway (I‑10 west of Houston) was expanded and is commonly reported to have up to 26 lanes at its widest point when main lanes, HOV/managed lanes and the two-way frontage roads are all counted. Major news accounts and TxDOT descriptions of the reconstruction cite the 26‑lane figure and have called it the world's widest freeway, though such rankings depend on counting conventions.

claim: Gov. Kitzhaber oversaw creation of the Oregon driver card law "behind closed doors without allowing any input from citizens who represent the public interest."
