Contemporary reporting, teammates' public statements, and medical accounts support that the sock showed real blood from an ankle injury, and allegations about painting stem from later third‑party speculation rather than a teammate's admission.

claim: "Forty years ago, a federal Pell Grant paid for nearly 80% of tuition, fees, room and board at a four-year college."
rationale: The claim is misleading on timing. The Pell Grant’s purchasing power peaked in the mid-1970s—around 1975—when the maximum grant covered roughly 75–80% of published costs (tuition, fees, room and board) at public four‑year institutions. By about 40 years ago (mid‑1980s) that share had fallen substantially due to rising tuition and flat grant levels, so the ‘nearly 80%’ figure does not accurately describe the situation 40 years ago.

claim: Mental health provisions related to mass shootings "got over 90 votes in the Senate."
rationale: The claim is too broad and misleading: while some bipartisan measures touching on reporting and mental-health records (for example the “Fix NICS” style reforms) have received overwhelming, near-unanimous support in the Senate, most high-profile mental-health or gun-control proposals tied to mass shootings did not receive more than 90 votes or were part of broader packages. Without a specific bill or vote identified, the blanket statement that mental-health provisions related to mass shootings “got over 90 votes” is inaccurate or at best misleading.

claim: Says most of Austin’s biggest parks have recycling though as "many as 293 out of 300" Austin city "parks have no recycling, including almost every neighborhood park."
rationale: The specific assertion that “as many as 293 out of 300” Austin parks have no recycling is not supported by available public information. The City of Austin and Austin Resource Recovery have established recycling services and placed recycling containers in many major parks, and there is no verified dataset confirming that nearly all ~300 parks entirely lack recycling. While some smaller neighborhood parks may not have bins, the blanket 293/300 figure appears unverified or misleading.

claim: ISIS sends out "90,000 social (media) messages a day."
rationale: The claim is presented as a steady, specific daily rate but there is no consistent evidence that ISIS continuously sent 90,000 social‑media messages per day. Some monitoring groups and media reports cited very high hourly or short‑term volumes (and counts that included retweets, automated posts, or multiple platforms) at certain peaks, but independent analyses and fact‑checks show the figure is often inflated or taken out of context.

claim: Says the man who rushed the stage at him in Dayton, Ohio, "had chatter about ISIS, or with ISIS" in his social media posts.
rationale: I am not aware of credible reporting or official statements confirming that the man who rushed the stage in Dayton posted "chatter about ISIS" on social media. Major news and law-enforcement coverage of the incident did not document ISIS-related posts, so the claim is unsupported by available evidence.

claim: Two photos show climate change "is a hoax."
rationale: Two photos cannot demonstrate that climate change is a hoax. Climate change is established from long-term, global observations and multiple lines of evidence (temperature records, ocean heat, glacier and ice-sheet mass loss, sea-level rise, and paleoclimate data); isolated images (which may show short-term weather, local variability, or be misleading/cherry-picked) do not refute this body of evidence.

claim: Says Donald Trump has written 10 checks to Hillary Clinton "and four of those checks were not to her Senate campaign. … It was to her presidential campaign."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and contemporaneous fact‑checks do not support the claim that Donald Trump wrote ten separate checks to Hillary Clinton, nor that four of them were to her presidential campaign. Trump's public donation history shows only occasional small contributions to various Democrats over many years, but not the specific tally or breakdown asserted.

claim: Says Mitt Romney wants to "get rid of Planned Parenthood."
rationale: Romney has repeatedly advocated cutting off federal funding to Planned Parenthood and during his 2012 campaign and afterward supported measures to defund the organization; opponents commonly paraphrase those positions as wanting to 'get rid of Planned Parenthood.' His public statements and votes have focused on eliminating government support and limiting the group's role rather than specifying a bureaucratic abolition process.

claim: Goldman Sachs was Barack Obama's "No. 1 private contributor."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and misleading: while Goldman Sachs and its employees were major donors to Obama-era campaigns, it is not demonstrably the single 'No. 1 private contributor' without specifying a year, contribution type (employees, PAC, or corporate), or source. Public campaign‑finance databases show large donations came from many firms, individuals, and unions, and different organizations top the lists depending on the metric used. Calling Goldman Sachs the undisputed top private contributor overstates the available evidence.

claim: "Education Secretary Betsy DeVos owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign finance violations and Mike DeWine's office refuses to collect the fine."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public record that Betsy DeVos owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign finance violations, nor that Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine's office has publicly refused to collect such a fine. The claim appears to conflate or invent a large dollar judgment and a refusal-to-enforce narrative that reputable reporting and official records do not support.

claim: "I have 2 and a half million more votes than he (Sanders) does."
rationale: The statement gives no time or speaker, and the most commonly compared Sanders contests do not match a 2.5 million vote gap. In the 2016 Democratic primaries Hillary Clinton led Sanders by roughly 3.5–3.6 million popular votes, while in the 2020 Democratic primaries Joe Biden led Sanders by about 2.0–2.2 million—neither is 2.5 million. Without a specific election or date the exact figure cannot be verified and the number stated is not consistent with the major known totals.

claim: Under President Barack Obama: 4 million jobs lost, unemployment rose from 7.8% to 9.9%, the S&P 500 was 1,115.1 and the GDP went down 2.8%.
rationale: The claim mixes and misstates statistics. While real GDP fell about 2.8% in 2009 (the recession year early in Obama’s term), Obama’s presidency overall saw net job gains (roughly +11 million payroll jobs from 2009–2017) rather than a 4 million-job loss, and the unemployment rate fell from about 7.8% in January 2009 to about 4.7% by January 2017 (it did peak near 10% in 2009). The cited S&P 500 figure (1,115.1) does not correspond to the typical benchmark points claimed and is misleading without a date.

claim: Says Texas voters are being asked to act this November on a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes.
rationale: The claim lacks a specific date or amendment reference, so it cannot be confirmed as stated. While Texas does put proposed constitutional amendments before voters during November general elections and such amendments sometimes affect property taxes, whether voters are being asked to act 'this November' depends on the particular year and whether the legislature referred a property-tax amendment to that ballot.

claim: "It has been estimated that only 12% of workers in businesses that are likely to stay open during this crisis are receiving paid sick leave benefits as a result of the second coronavirus relief package."
rationale: Analyses of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act (the emergency paid-leave measures enacted in spring 2020) concluded that because the law exempted large employers and certain worker categories, only a small share of workers in businesses likely to remain open would actually receive paid sick leave — estimates around 12% were published by nonpartisan analysts. The low figure stems from employer-size exemptions and exclusions for many essential-worker categories.

claim: "Bill Gates is behind the monkeypox outbreaks."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates engineered or is "behind" monkeypox outbreaks. Monkeypox is a zoonotic virus with established animal reservoirs and documented human-to-human transmission patterns studied by public health agencies; claims tying it to Gates originate from conspiracy theories linked to his public-health funding. Investigations and scientific literature do not support any role by Gates in creating or releasing the virus.

claim: Says Barack Obama said that "ordinary men and women are too small-minded to govern their own affairs" and that individuals should "surrender their rights to an all-powerful sovereign."
rationale: There is no credible record in Obama’s speeches, writings, or official transcripts of him saying that 'ordinary men and women are too small-minded to govern their own affairs' or urging people to 'surrender their rights to an all-powerful sovereign.' The phrasing is inconsistent with Obama’s known rhetoric and matches a widely circulated fabricated or misattributed internet quote.

claim: "COP26 luxury EVs to be recharged using diesel generators"
rationale: The claim is misleading. While COP26 organisers did use temporary diesel generators to supply some onsite power and there were electric vehicles present, there is no evidence of a formal policy or widespread program to specifically recharge 'luxury EVs' using diesel generators; most charging infrastructure was grid-connected and reports described isolated use of generators for temporary power needs, not a deliberate effort to run attendees' EVs on diesel.

claim: "Children don’t seem to be getting this virus"
rationale: The statement is too broad and unsupported: without specifying which virus, it is incorrect to claim children are not getting it. For many viruses (including SARS‑CoV‑2/COVID‑19), children can and do become infected—often with milder symptoms—but pediatric cases are documented in public health data. A blanket denial of pediatric infection is therefore inaccurate.

claim: "Because of #TaxReform, 4 million American workers have received raises and bonuses, and 90% of Americans are seeing bigger paychecks this month."
rationale: The claim combines two misleading assertions. The "4 million" figure came from administration and company announcements early after the tax law passed but mixed one-time bonuses, pre-planned pay actions, and unverifiable pledges rather than documented permanent raises for 4 million workers; independent fact-checkers found the total and its attribution to tax reform were exaggerated. The "90% of Americans are seeing bigger paychecks this month" overstates the impact of IRS withholding changes — while many taxpayers saw temporary withholding adjustments, not all Americans received larger net pay and timing/amounts varied by household, state, and employer.

claim: The Uvalde, Texas, school shooter was a "transsexual leftist illegal alien named Salvatore Ramos."
rationale: Contemporary law-enforcement statements and major news reporting identified the Uvalde school shooter as Salvador Ramos, an 18-year-old male from Uvalde, Texas, not someone named 'Salvatore Ramos.' There is no credible evidence he was a transsexual, a leftist political activist, or an illegal alien; those elements were part of fabricated or unverified online rumors.

claim: State pension fund staffers "lost billions. Then Sink gave them bonuses."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While investment staff overseeing state pensions experienced large market losses during the financial crisis, reporting and fact-checks indicate bonuses were governed by existing contracts or approved by the pension board and based on multi-year measures, and were not a simple case of Sink personally awarding bonuses after losses.

claim: "On my last trip to New Hampshire, I think I met the guy who founded the first and only bank since Dodd-Frank passed, since the financial crisis. One bank in the country."
rationale: Dodd-Frank raised regulatory burdens after the 2008 crisis but it did not stop new banks from being chartered. Numerous de novo FDIC‑insured banks, state‑chartered banks, and new online banking entities have been founded in the U.S. since the law passed, so the claim that only one bank was founded nationwide is incorrect.

claim: "Illegal immigration and the crime rate are as low as they’ve been in decades."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: measures of unauthorized border crossings and encounters were at historically high levels in recent years rather than at decades-long lows, and the undocumented population has not fallen to multi-decade lows. Likewise, U.S. violent crime rose notably in 2020–2021 and, while some categories have declined since, overall crime rates are not uniformly "as low as they’ve been in decades."

claim: In New York, "Average college debt - $30,000 per student."
rationale: The statement is too general and likely inaccurate as written. 'Average college debt' can mean several different measures (mean vs median, per borrower vs per enrolled student, undergraduate vs all borrowers) and state-level averages fluctuate by year; recent national averages are around $30,000 per borrower but New York’s borrower average is typically higher, and the average per enrolled student (including those with no debt) would be lower. Without a specified year and definition, the flat claim that New York average college debt is $30,000 per student is misleading.

claim: "Arizona and Georgia now have the proof," Joe Biden is "not our elected president!"
rationale: Multiple official recounts, audits, and certifications in Arizona and Georgia reaffirmed Joe Biden's victory and did not produce credible evidence that would overturn the results. Courts and election officials in both states rejected claims of widespread fraud, and independent reviews did not find proof that Biden was not the legitimately elected president.

claim: A map shows "all the cargo ships backed up by the Suez Canal. Get ready for shortages and prices to skyrocket."
rationale: The claim that a map shows "all" cargo ships backed up at the Suez is incorrect — public ship-tracking maps are incomplete and often omit vessels, and some ships were rerouting or anchored elsewhere. The warning that shortages and prices will necessarily "skyrocket" is speculative; while the Suez disruption caused delays and some localized effects, supply-chain impacts varied and did not universally produce immediate, catastrophic price spikes.

claim: Says Sen. Mitch McConnell's delay in seating Alabama Sen.-elect Doug Jones "is a flagrant violation of Senate policy, which requires Jones assume office the instant one of them wins the election."
rationale: There is no Senate rule or policy that automatically requires a senator-elect to assume office the instant votes are counted; the Constitution (and Senate precedent) gives each chamber authority to judge the elections, returns and qualifications of its members and seating normally awaits state certification and resolution of any contests. Therefore McConnell's delaying language would not by itself be a 'flagrant violation of Senate policy' requiring immediate seating upon election-night results.

claim: Says Hunter Biden "died of a crack overdose."
rationale: This claim is false: there are no credible reports or official announcements that Hunter Biden died of a crack overdose. Public records, media coverage, and his known public appearances and legal proceedings do not support any claim of his death; the statement appears to be fabricated or a piece of misinformation.

claim: "'Wrong precinct' rules exacerbate our provisional ballot problems (and) HB 194 does nothing to solve the wrong-precinct problem."
rationale: The first part (that wrong-precinct rules can worsen provisional-ballot issues) is plausible because many states reject or limit provisional ballots cast in the wrong precinct. However the blanket claim that “HB 194 does nothing” cannot be verified without the specific state and bill text; some bills titled HB 194 in various states have included provisions that affect provisional ballots and precinct handling. Therefore the statement as a whole is not reliably true as presented.

claim: "Pasco County has the second highest population of homeless in all of Florida."
rationale: Statewide homeless counts (HUD Point-in-Time counts and related state reports) consistently show large urban counties such as Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach, Hillsborough, and Orange having the highest total homeless populations. Pasco County is a smaller suburban/rural county and does not appear near the very top of total homeless population rankings for Florida, so the claim that it is second-highest is incorrect.

claim: "In many instances, (people's) health care costs are more than their mortgage costs or their rent, which, by the way, is a first in American history."
rationale: U.S. household spending data show housing is typically the largest expense category, while health care (out-of-pocket or even including insurance premiums) is generally smaller for most households. Although health-care costs have grown and some individuals with very high medical bills can pay more than their mortgage or rent, that is not true in “many” instances nor is it a unique first in American history.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because no speaker, timeframe, or supporting financial disclosure is provided. Determining whether someone has financial interests in Saudi Arabia requires review of personal financial disclosures, corporate records, investment accounts, or tax filings; without that evidence the claim cannot be confirmed and is judged false under uncertainty.

claim: "There are 63 million abortions a year in this country."
rationale: The claim is implausible: no individual country currently reports 63 million abortions per year. Global estimates from major public-health analyses put annual abortions worldwide at roughly 60–80 million, and the largest single-country estimates (for countries like India or historically China) are far below 63 million in recent years. The phrase "this country" is also unspecified, making the claim unsupported as stated.

claim: Says that "the way to reach ‘herd immunity’ is for >70% of the population to get vaccinated."
rationale: This statement is an oversimplification. Herd immunity threshold depends on the pathogen's basic reproductive number (R0), vaccine effectiveness against infection, and existing immunity from prior infection; while >70% vaccinated might suffice under certain assumptions (e.g., a lower R0 and near-perfect vaccine protection), more transmissible variants and imperfect/waning vaccine protection mean 70% vaccination is not a universal rule.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.
rationale: No reputable national statistics report a 59% unemployment rate for African‑American youth. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics series for Black teens and young adults historically show much lower unemployment rates (even at peaks they have been well under 59%), so 59% is inconsistent with standard BLS measures and likely stems from a misreading or a different metric.

claim: Federal money for Medicaid expansion "is guaranteed for a few years and then goes away."
rationale: This is incorrect: under the Affordable Care Act the federal government initially covered 100% of the costs for newly eligible expansion enrollees for a few years, then phased the match down to a permanent floor of 90%. Federal matching payments do not simply “go away” after a few years; they continue at the established FMAP rate.

claim: "I'm the only front-line prosecutor in this race that's actually used the resources of the Wisconsin Crime Lab in the prosecution of cases."
rationale: The claim is implausible and cannot be verified as stated because it lacks identification of the race and the other candidates. In Wisconsin, front-line prosecutors routinely submit evidence to and rely on the Wisconsin State Crime Laboratory for forensic testing, so it is unlikely one candidate would be uniquely the only user of those resources without detailed case-by-case records.

claim: Kasim Reed has kept every promise he made as a candidate.
rationale: The claim is absolute — that Kasim Reed kept every promise he made — and such all-or-nothing claims about politicians are almost never true. Public reporting and post‑term assessments of Reed’s mayoralty note accomplishments but also document unmet promises and controversies, so it is incorrect to state he fulfilled every pledge he made as a candidate.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Perry is "spending Texans’ hard-earned money to live like Louie XIV."
rationale: This is a rhetorical exaggeration rather than a factual statement. While governors incur official residence, travel, and security expenses, there is no evidence Rick Perry spent state funds to create an opulent, Louis XIV–style lifestyle or court on the scale implied by the claim.

claim: Sherrod Brown "failed to pay his own taxes three separate times."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Senator Sherrod Brown personally 'failed to pay his own taxes three separate times.' Brown has released public tax returns and reporters and independent fact-checkers have not documented multiple instances of personal tax nonpayment; attacks that allege this appear to mischaracterize isolated, minor issues or conflate different kinds of taxes or filings.

claim: "In my home state, nearly one in five Floridians live in poverty."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey estimates place Florida's overall poverty rate in the low teens (roughly 12–14% in recent years), substantially below 20%. While certain subgroups (for example children in some counties) and alternative measures can show higher rates, the statewide overall poverty rate is not "nearly one in five."

claim: "According to (Barack) Obama’s newest unconstitutionally enacted law, health care professionals are now required to violate HIPAA privacy laws and submit medical data to the government," which is "then used as justification for gun confiscation."
rationale: There is no federal law enacted by President Obama that required health care professionals to violate HIPAA and submit patient medical data to the government to justify gun confiscation. HIPAA remains the federal privacy standard with specific, limited exceptions for disclosures; reporting of mental-health adjudications or commitments to the federal NICS system is handled through state reporting systems and courts, not by a blanket Obama-era mandate forcing providers to hand over records for gun seizures. The claim conflates limited reporting exceptions and state-level reporting or 'red-flag' policies with a non‑existent federal requirement.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: State-reported data show Los Angeles Unified School District's four-year high-school graduation rate was roughly in the mid-40s when Villaraigosa became mayor (mid-2000s) and rose to about 72% by the early 2010s. The increase coincided with mayoral advocacy and district reforms during his tenure. While attribution of causation is complex, the numerical change cited is consistent with published state/district rates for that period.

claim: "Congress files charges against Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: There is no record of Congress as a body filing criminal charges or adopting articles of impeachment against Nancy Pelosi. While individual members have proposed investigations, referrals, or symbolic resolutions at various times, no formal congressional action charging Pelosi has been adopted.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "has been saying lately that she thinks that I am, 'not qualified to be president.' "
rationale: The claim asserts that Hillary Clinton has recently said an unnamed person is "not qualified to be president." Without a clear subject, date, or source, there is no verifiable public record of Clinton using that exact phrasing about an unspecified individual. Because the statement is ambiguous and uncorroborated, it cannot be treated as a factual quote.

claim: "Seismic airgun blasting (used for energy exploration) is ... 16,000 times louder than" a conventional airhorn.
rationale: The claim is misleading because it gives a single multiplicative factor without specifying the metric, reference level, medium (water vs air), or distance. Seismic airguns produce extremely high underwater source levels (commonly cited ~230–260 dB re 1 μPa at 1 m) while airhorns produce ~110–130 dB SPL in air; direct "times louder" comparisons across media or using dB differences require careful conversion and context, so the blanket statement that airgun blasting is "16,000 times louder" than an airhorn is unsupported. At best, particular conversions of a dB difference could yield large linear ratios, but the claim as stated is imprecise and therefore inaccurate.

claim: Bull sharks were released in an Arkansas river.
rationale: There are no verifiable reports or official confirmations that bull sharks were deliberately released into an Arkansas river. While bull sharks can survive in freshwater and have been documented far upriver in the Mississippi basin, claims of a release in Arkansas appear to be unsubstantiated or viral rumors without credible evidence.

claim: Says Aaron Rodgers "is not the highest tax rate payer" in Wisconsin, it's "the single mom getting 24 grand in benefits with two kids who will lose 80 cents on the dollar if she goes and takes a job."
rationale: I could not verify that Aaron Rodgers said the quoted lines verbatim. While the idea that low-income recipients face high effective marginal rates is a common political talking point and Rodgers has made public comments about taxation and fairness, there is no clear, reliable record of him uttering this specific statement as presented.

claim: "I have asked the Division of Emergency Management to report directly to me."
rationale: There is no supporting public evidence provided to confirm that such a request was made, and organizational changes for emergency management are normally documented by official orders or press releases. Without a named official, jurisdiction, date, or corroborating records, the claim cannot be verified and is treated as unproven.

claim: Mitt Romney "said it was 'tragic' to end the war in Iraq."
rationale: There is no well-documented, attributable quote in which Mitt Romney explicitly said it was "tragic" to end the war in Iraq. Romney frequently criticized the Obama administration’s withdrawal as a mistake or premature, but publicly available records and campaign statements show he framed the withdrawal as a strategic error rather than using that specific word to endorse ending the war as "tragic."

claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: U.S. law does provide a "credible fear" screening for people who express fear of persecution, and those who pass are referred into full asylum proceedings rather than immediately returned. However the claim's absolute wording — that people are simply brought in and "we don't send them back" — is incorrect: people who fail credible fear can be removed, and those who win or lose asylum claims may still be detained, paroled, returned, or expelled under other authorities or policies. The outcome depends on screening results, immigration court decisions, and changing administrative policies.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: The Department of Justice has not issued a general finding that consent decrees “don’t work” or that they typically cause crime to rise; DOJ has used consent decrees for decades as a remedy for unconstitutional policing and frequently reports progress and continued monitoring. Outcomes are mixed across jurisdictions and some critics or local officials have argued consent decrees coincide with short-term changes in crime, but that is not an authoritative, consistent DOJ conclusion.

claim: Says Ruben Kihuen "only managed in the minority to get one bill passed out of the eight to 10 he introduced" during the 2015 legislative session.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim that Kihuen introduced 'eight to 10' bills in the 2015 session and that only one passed; available summaries of legislative activity do not support that precise formulation. The statement is likely an oversimplification or miscount of bills sponsored versus co‑sponsored and of measures that advanced out of committee versus those enacted.

claim: "In the last year, Wisconsin ranked third in Midwest job growth."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim as stated because it lacks a specific 12‑month period and data source; Midwest job‑growth rankings change depending on the time window and whether one uses BLS payrolls, household employment, or state reports. Without a precise timeframe and metric, the statement is not verifiable and is likely inaccurate for at least some recent 12‑month spans.

claim: Georgia has recovered more than $60 million that was lost to Medicaid fraud
rationale: The statement is unqualified (no timeframe or source) and I cannot confirm from general knowledge that the U.S. state of Georgia or the country of Georgia has a documented recovery exceeding $60 million specifically labeled as ‘lost to Medicaid fraud.’ While state Medicaid fraud units often recover substantial sums, reported recoveries vary by year and program and I find no definitive, time-bound figure to support this exact claim.

claim: "BREAKING: Trump family donates $1 billion to wall fund."
rationale: There are no credible news reports, official filings, or charity disclosures showing the Trump family made a $1 billion donation to any 'wall fund.' A gift of that size would have been widely reported and require public documentation; no such evidence exists. Therefore the claim is false.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted for regime change with respect to Libya."
rationale: There is no clear congressional roll-call where Bernie Sanders explicitly voted for a policy described as "regime change" in Libya. Claims typically conflate his positions or votes on limited, UN/NATO-authorized actions or non-binding resolutions with an explicit vote to pursue regime change; Sanders has criticized open-ended military interventions and has not been recorded voting for a bill explicitly authorizing regime change in Libya.

claim: "Over the past 10 years, the number of people living in Lower Manhattan has nearly doubled. In fact, Lower Manhattan has added more people over the last 10 years than Atlanta, Dallas and Philadelphia combined."
rationale: City population data show Atlanta, Dallas and Philadelphia each added tens of thousands of residents in the last decade, and together their combined growth is on the order of a few hundred thousand. Lower Manhattan (even with significant residential conversions) did not nearly double in population over a single ten-year span nor add more residents than those three major cities combined. The claim therefore overstates Lower Manhattan's growth relative to whole-city growth in Atlanta, Dallas and Philadelphia.

claim: The Fair Tax proposal encourages innovation and investment "level the playing field" for American companies to compete globally.
rationale: The claim is promotional and not established fact: whether the Fair Tax would reliably 'encourage innovation and investment' and 'level the playing field' is contested and depends on many design details. Supporters argue removing income and corporate taxes could boost investment, but many economists say effects are ambiguous and hinge on issues like border adjustments, transitional incentives, and how a national retail sales tax affects demand and capital costs. There is no consensus empirical evidence that the Fair Tax as typically proposed would unambiguously produce those outcomes for American companies globally.

claim: Says "Joe Biden is absolutely on board with defunding the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has repeatedly said he does not support the 'defund the police' slogan and has advocated for police reform, accountability, and targeted investments (community policing, mental-health crisis response) rather than wholesale defunding. His 2020 campaign and subsequent administration proposals emphasized reforms and some reallocation of funds to social services in specific contexts, but not an outright elimination or broad defunding of police departments.

claim: "We in Indiana have . . . the highest credit rating in the nation."
rationale: The claim is misleading because no single U.S. state consistently holds a uniquely highest credit rating across all major rating agencies. Credit ratings are assigned by multiple agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) and several states often share top-tier ratings; Indiana has had strong ratings but is not uniquely the highest overall. Without a specific time and rating agency the assertion cannot be supported.

claim: Texas "could be very close to herd immunity."
rationale: Without a specific time or definition, the claim is misleading: achieving herd immunity requires a high population immune fraction (typically 60–90% depending on R0) and Texas’ combined vaccination and infection-induced immunity levels were generally below those thresholds and uneven across the state. The emergence of more transmissible variants raised the needed threshold, making it unlikely Texas was "very close" to herd immunity when such statements were commonly made.

claim: If COVID-19 was real, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge wouldn’t have been "allowed to join 50,000 other football fans inside a stadium."
rationale: The claim implies that a royal couple attending a large sporting event proves COVID-19 was not real. In reality, public-health rules, vaccination, testing, and phased reopenings meant large crowds were permitted at different times and places during the pandemic; attendance by public figures does not negate the existence of the virus. The fact that some events later operated at or near full capacity is consistent with evolving pandemic policy, not evidence that COVID-19 was fabricated.

claim: "Michigan prosecutor looks to release 90 convicted murderers serving life sentences."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that any Michigan prosecutor is unilaterally seeking to free 90 people convicted of murder serving life sentences. Prosecutors cannot simply release prisoners — releases require court action, parole board decisions, or gubernatorial clemency — and major reporting does not corroborate a claim that a prosecutor is attempting to free 90 life-sentenced murderers.

claim: Says proposal to boost teacher pension fund "puts no mandate on local government."
rationale: The statement that a proposal to boost a teacher pension fund "puts no mandate on local government" cannot be accepted as true without the specific proposal text and jurisdiction. In practice, many pension-boosting proposals either change employer contribution rates, shift costs to school districts or require local implementation, so a blanket claim of "no mandate" is likely incorrect absent evidence. Because the claim is categorical but lacks context, it should be treated as false until the actual legislative language and fiscal notes are reviewed.

claim: "AIG insures the pension trust of the United States Congress!"
rationale: There is no evidence that AIG insures the pension trust for the United States Congress. Congressional retirement benefits are provided under federal retirement systems (FERS/CSRS) and administered by government offices rather than being underwritten by a private insurer like AIG.

claim: "NASA will pay you $18,000 to stay in bed and smoke weed for 70 straight days."
rationale: NASA does sponsor bed-rest studies that pay volunteers to stay in bed for extended periods to simulate microgravity, but NASA would not fund or authorize participants to use illegal drugs as part of those studies. Cannabis remains a controlled substance under U.S. federal law, and institutional review boards and NASA safety policies prohibit using illicit substances in funded human research. The specific combination—being paid $18,000 to stay in bed and smoke weed for 70 days—is therefore false.

claim: Milwaukee’s problems include "52 percent black male unemployment."
rationale: The widely cited “52% black male unemployment” stat is a mischaracterization: it typically comes from a specific age cohort and from measures of men who are not employed (including those not in the labor force), not the official unemployment rate. Official unemployment-rate measures (people in the labor force who are unemployed) for black men in Milwaukee are substantially lower, and multiple fact-checks have flagged the 52% figure as misleading.

claim: "The administration raises revenue for nationalized health care through a series of new taxes, including a light switch tax that would cost every American household $3,128 a year."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any administration proposed or enacted a literal 'light switch tax' that would charge every American household $3,128 per year. Nonpartisan analyses of health-care funding proposals list specific tax and spending changes, none of which match this invented tax or the stated per-household figure, which is far larger than realistic estimates. The claim appears to be a fabricated or heavily distorted political attack line.

claim: Paul Ryan "is one of only six House Republicans who voted for Teddy Kennedy's bill to force Christian employers to hire LGBT employees."
rationale: The claim mixes misleading language and an unclear vote. There is no clear roll call of a single ‘Teddy Kennedy’ bill in the House where only six Republicans voted yes and included Paul Ryan; debates over Employment Non-Discrimination bills (often associated with Sen. Ted Kennedy in the Senate) produced multiple votes with varying Republican support and often included discussions of religious exemptions. The phrasing 'force Christian employers to hire LGBT employees' misstates typical bill language and exemptions.

claim: Says President John F. Kennedy released a star Green Bay Packer from military reserve duty so that he could play in the 1961 NFL Championship Game.
rationale: There is no credible historical evidence that President John F. Kennedy personally released a Green Bay Packer from military reserve duty to play in the 1961 NFL Championship. Military leaves and reserve status were handled through regular military channels, and notable Packers histories and biographies do not record a presidential intervention for that game. The claim appears to be a conflation or myth.

claim: Says the state tax burden per citizen in New York is twice as high as in Florida.
rationale: This categorical claim is not reliably true. While New York's per‑capita state and local tax burden is generally higher than Florida's, the gap varies by year and by whether one measures state-only or state+local taxes, and it is not typically a consistent 2:1 ratio.

claim: "One of the first nurses to receive the vaccine in AL is now dead."
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated reporting that one of the earliest nurses vaccinated in Alabama subsequently died as a result of the vaccine or that such a high-profile early recipient has been confirmed dead. Major local and national outlets and official health statements typically reported and investigated any early post-vaccination deaths, and no verified claim matching this statement emerged.

claim: In 1993, Newt Gingrich "first advocated for the individual mandate in health care. And as recently as May of this year, he was still advocating" for it.
rationale: The individual mandate concept predates and was promoted by conservative policy thinkers (e.g., Heritage Foundation staff) in the early 1990s, so Gingrich did not 'first' advocate it in 1993. While Gingrich has at times described the mandate as a conservative idea and made sympathetic comments later, the claim that he first advocated it in 1993 and was still actively advocating it as recently as 'May of this year' is misleading and lacks corroboration without a specific year or quotation.

claim: "In Cobb County, every meeting opened with a prayer. The ACLU objected. Sued ... [Sam] Olens took on the ACLU and won!"
rationale: The claim bundles several assertions (that every Cobb County meeting opened with a prayer, that the ACLU sued, and that Sam Olens personally ‘took on’ the ACLU and won). Public records and reporting do not support the sweeping phrasing that every meeting opened with prayer nor that Olens personally litigated and decisively 'won' a single ACLU suit in that form. Court outcomes on legislative prayer have varied and individual roles and case outcomes are more nuanced than the claim states.

claim: Says "Rep. Jim Weidner proposed a bill taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Jim Weidner introduced a bill explicitly "taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children." A proposal that would directly strip coverage from that many children would be highly documented and widely reported; available summaries and records of Weidner's legislative actions do not support this specific claim.

claim: House Republican plan would increase costs for Oregon seniors by $6,000 with health care vouchers instead of Medicare
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not verifiable as stated: there is no single "House Republican plan" that universally and unambiguously would raise Oregon seniors' costs by exactly $6,000. Analyses of various Republican proposals to replace Medicare with premium-support vouchers or move benefits toward private plans have shown seniors could face higher out‑of‑pocket costs in many states, but the projected dollar increases vary widely by proposal, year, and analytic method and are not a uniform $6,000 for Oregon. Without naming the specific bill, time horizon, or whether the figure is annual or cumulative, the precise $6,000 claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "We’re 49th in the United States in new businesses created."
rationale: The statement gives no jurisdiction, timeframe, or data source, and rankings for new business creation vary by year and by metric (total formations, formations per capita, employer vs nonemployer). Without a specified place and dataset, the claim that “we’re 49th” cannot be verified and is therefore unsupported.

claim: "What we have done with the PATRIOT Act, we've given the government enormous powers. We've given the government the right to reach deeply into people's private lives, into their business affairs, without a court order."
rationale: The USA PATRIOT Act significantly expanded federal surveillance and investigative authorities after 2001, enabling tools such as roving wiretaps, delayed-notice 'sneak-and-peek' searches, and the use of National Security Letters (NSLs) to obtain certain business and communication records without prior judicial approval. Section 215 and other provisions were also used to obtain large volumes of business and telephony records, practices that were later restricted by reform but reflect the Act's original broad powers.

claim: The national debt is "larger than our entire annual economy."
rationale: For the United States in recent years, total federal debt (especially gross federal debt including intragovernmental holdings) has exceeded one year’s nominal GDP. For example, federal debt levels around $30+ trillion have been comparable to or larger than annual U.S. GDP in the high $20 trillions, so the statement is accurate in that common sense.

claim: The ship that was stuck in the Suez Canal was a planned or staged event.
rationale: Multiple investigations by the Suez Canal Authority, the vessel's operator, maritime experts and independent analysts found the grounding was caused by weather (strong winds) and navigational/human error, with no credible evidence of a planned or staged event. Conspiracy claims arose online but were not supported by AIS data, eyewitness accounts, or official findings.

claim: "Wholly domestic communication between you and your wife can go to New York to London and back and get caught up in the (NSA) database."
rationale: Internet and telephony traffic is routed according to network topology and can be carried through foreign servers or cables even when both endpoints are domestic; intelligence disclosures (e.g., Snowden) showed the NSA collects transit traffic and has incidentally acquired communications of US persons when they traverse foreign links or are captured by upstream collection. Therefore it is plausible and documented that wholly domestic communications could be routed via London and be captured in NSA databases.

claim: "If you put the $47 billion in revenue (raised over 10 years by the Buffett rule) into infrastructure you could create 611,000 infrastructure jobs."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it omits key context and likely conflates job‑years with permanent jobs. $47 billion divided by 611,000 jobs implies about $77,000 per job, which could be plausible only under a specific jobs-per-dollar multiplier and if those are temporary job‑years; mainstream estimates of infrastructure employment effects vary widely and typically report job‑years per dollar, not permanent positions. Without specifying the multiplier, timeframe, or whether these are job‑years, the statement overstates what can be concluded from the $47 billion revenue figure.

claim: If public employees don’t pay more for benefits starting April 1, 2011, "the equivalent" is 1,500 state employee layoffs by June 30, 2011 and 10,000 to 12,000 state and local government employee layoffs in the next two years.
rationale: The figures were presented as a conditional, worst-case projection by proponents during the 2011 public‑employee benefits debate (not an unavoidable outcome), and independent analyses and subsequent events showed far fewer layoffs occurred. The numbers were disputed as speculative and based on broad assumptions about local governments’ responses rather than documented, imminent cuts that actually happened.

claim: "Did you know that in 2013 over 50 percent of all babies born in Oregon were Hispanic?"
rationale: Statewide data for Oregon in 2013 do not show that a majority of births were to Hispanic mothers; the Hispanic share of births was well under 50% (roughly around a quarter of births rather than a majority). A claim of over 50% would be an extreme outlier compared with CDC and state vital statistics for that year.

claim: "Half the kids coming out of college this year … can't find a job, or a job that's consistent with a college degree."
rationale: This is an overstatement. Official labour statistics and employer surveys show unemployment for recent college graduates is typically in the single digits, and while underemployment (working in jobs that don’t require a degree) affects a notable minority, it is generally well below 50% overall. Therefore saying 'half' of graduates can't find a job or a degree-consistent job misrepresents the typical data.

claim: "People are less likely to just vote for party now. … They’re looking at the personalities."
rationale: Broad empirical evidence, especially from the United States and many other democracies, shows party identification remains a primary predictor of vote choice and that partisan polarization and sorting have generally increased. While candidate personality and personalization of politics can matter for some voters and specific races, the blanket claim that people are now less likely to ‘just vote for party’ is an overgeneralization not supported as a widespread trend.

claim: "Biden's plan is a 14% tax hike on middle class families."
rationale: This is inaccurate: Biden's major tax proposals in recent years concentrate tax increases on higher-income households (commonly above $400,000), capital gains for top earners, and corporations rather than imposing a uniform 14% tax hike on middle‑class families. Independent analyses of those proposals find the largest tax increases fall on higher earners, and many middle‑income households would see little change or benefits from credits and deductions rather than a flat 14% increase.

claim: "Mar-A-Lago (was) destroyed by (Hurricane) Irma (and) Jared Kushner (is) still missing."
rationale: Mar-a-Lago was not destroyed by Hurricane Irma in 2017; it experienced flooding and some damage but remained standing and continued operating afterward. Jared Kushner is not missing—he has made public appearances and continued in public and private roles since Irma.

claim: "Rep. Paul Gosar asks Capitol Police to arrest illegal immigrants attending State of the Union."
rationale: There is no reliable reporting or record up to mid‑2024 showing Rep. Paul Gosar formally asked Capitol Police to arrest 'illegal immigrants' attending the State of the Union. Such a public request would have been widely reported; available news and public records from the event do not corroborate the claim. If he made a social‑media comment or a private remark it appears not to have been an official request to Capitol Police.

claim: Athletes are collapsing with heart-related issues due to the COVID-19 vaccines
rationale: Current evidence does not support that COVID-19 vaccines are causing a wave of athletes collapsing from heart problems. While rare cases of myocarditis/pericarditis have been linked to mRNA vaccines (mostly in young males and typically mild and short-lived), studies and public-health surveillance show the risk of cardiac complications is higher after SARS-CoV-2 infection, and no causal, population-level link has been established between vaccination and widespread athlete collapses.

claim: "In eighth grade math, we’ve fallen to ninth place."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported as presented — it does not identify who 'we' refers to, which assessment (e.g., TIMSS, PISA, NAEP), or which year. International and national rankings for eighth‑grade math change by assessment and year, and there is no single, consistent source showing a general fall to exactly ninth place. Without a specific dataset and year, the claim cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "It’s clear" that Hillary Clinton "violated national security laws."
rationale: Multiple official investigations (notably the FBI's 2016 probe and the State Department Inspector General review) found that while Clinton used a private email server and handled classified material on unclassified systems, investigators did not establish intent or recommend criminal charges. The FBI concluded that no reasonable prosecutor would bring charges, so it is not correct to state as a clear legal fact that she violated national security laws.

claim: "NASA confirms earth will go dark for 6 days in December 2020."
rationale: This claim is false: NASA did not confirm the Earth would go dark for six days in December 2020. No credible scientific agency issued such a statement, and there is no plausible astrophysical mechanism that would cause global darkness for six days without catastrophic, globally observable consequences. The story was a social-media hoax debunked by authoritative sources.

claim: Under current U.S. immigration policy, "literally one person with a green card" can, in the extreme, bring in more than 270 of his relatives.
rationale: There is no automatic rule in U.S. immigration law that allows a single lawful permanent resident to directly ‘bring in’ more than 270 relatives. While an LPR who later naturalizes can sponsor immediate family and successive generations of relatives can in turn petition for their own families, that outcome would require many decades, many favorable personal choices (naturalization, marriages, large numbers of children), and it is constrained by visa categories, annual numerical limits and backlog processing. The claim presented as a straightforward, literal fact is therefore misleading and not supported by immigration law as an automatic right.

claim: Under President George W. Bush, "we added $4.9 trillion to the debt. Under President Obama … we’ve added $6.5 trillion to the debt."
rationale: Those dollar amounts match commonly reported increases in gross federal debt when measured between presidential inauguration dates (roughly Jan 20, 2001→Jan 20, 2009 ≈+$4.9 trillion; and Jan 20, 2009→the date Obama was citing ≈+$6.5 trillion). The statement is accurate for that metric and those time boundaries, though it omits important definitional choices.

claim: Says Paul Ryan’s budget plan "ends Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals did not immediately terminate Medicare for current beneficiaries; they proposed converting Medicare for future enrollees into a premium-support/voucher-style system that would remove the guaranteed traditional Medicare benefit. Critics called that an 'end' of Medicare as it exists, but the plan restructures and phases changes for future cohorts rather than outright ending the program today.

claim: Says revenues "are actually up after tax reform."
rationale: The claim is misleading without context. While nominal federal receipts rose modestly in some years after the 2017 U.S. tax reform, receipts fell as a share of GDP and independent budget estimates (CBO/Treasury) project and recorded that the reform reduced long‑run revenues relative to prior law; trends were also disrupted by the 2020 pandemic. Saying simply that “revenues are actually up” ignores the GDP‑adjusted, real and projected revenue declines and timing/measurement issues.

claim: "Some neighborhood schools are closing."
rationale: As an existential claim it is highly plausible and commonly true: school districts routinely close individual neighborhood schools for reasons like falling enrollment, budget cuts, consolidation, or pandemic-related changes. Without a specific place or time the precise instances can't be verified, but closures of some neighborhood schools occur regularly in many jurisdictions.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The statement is a subjective claim presented as fact but lacks specific supporting evidence. While Nathan Deal voted for and supported some tougher immigration and enforcement measures, he was not widely recognized as a national congressional leader on border security (he did not chair major border/security committees or sponsor landmark border legislation). Without clear examples of leadership or authored major bills on the topic, the claim is not supported.

claim: Several times, Obama "has apologized for what he deems to be American arrogance, dismissiveness, and derision; for dictating solutions, for acting unilaterally ... ."
rationale: This claim overstates the record: President Obama did acknowledge past U.S. mistakes and expressed regret in speeches (for example in his 2009 Cairo address) but he and his aides repeatedly rejected the idea that he was conducting an 'apology tour' and he rarely issued formal apologies. Critics frequently summarized conciliatory language as 'apologizing,' but his public remarks were framed as explanation, outreach, or acknowledgement rather than repeated official apologies.

claim: The 2020 election is in "recount territory" and "I’ve seen elections change as a result of" recounts.
rationale: The 2020 presidential election was not broadly in 'recount territory' — most state margins were too large for a recount to plausibly change the outcome, and the few recounts (notably Georgia) changed vote totals by only a few hundred votes and did not flip the result. The speaker's claim of having 'seen elections change' from recounts is an unverifiable personal anecdote; historically recounts only overturn results in extremely tiny margins and such reversals are rare.

claim: "Gas is high because they shut down production in the U.S." under the Biden administration.
rationale: The Biden administration did not "shut down" U.S. oil and gas production; U.S. crude production remained high and recovered after the COVID downturn and in many periods approached or exceeded pre-pandemic levels. Gasoline prices are driven primarily by global crude oil markets (OPEC+ decisions, pandemic-driven demand recovery, and the Russia-Ukraine war), as well as refining capacity and seasonal demand, not a blanket shutdown of U.S. production.

claim: "99% of NJ voters do NOT support hunting."
rationale: The claim is almost certainly false: no reputable statewide poll or aggregate of polls shows 99% of New Jersey voters oppose hunting. New Jersey issues hunting licenses and there is measurable participation and public support for regulated hunting or wildlife management, so opposition is far from unanimous. The 99% figure is implausibly extreme and likely arises from a misinterpretation, a small/nonrepresentative sample, or a narrowly worded question.

claim: "If your employer is mandating any pokes, do not quit. Make them fire you. That way you get unemployment benefits."
rationale: This statement is not universally true. Eligibility for unemployment benefits depends on jurisdiction and the reason for separation: quitting voluntarily typically disqualifies you, but being fired can still disqualify you if the employer finds you were terminated for misconduct or willful refusal to follow lawful workplace rules. Some places or cases have allowed benefits when termination was for refusing a mandate for protected reasons (medical or religious), but outcomes vary widely and are decided case-by-case.

claim: The Obama White House recognizes a "baby that has not been born" for security purposes.
rationale: There is no public policy or reliable documentation showing the Obama White House or U.S. Secret Service formally 'recognizes a baby that has not been born' as a separate person for security protection. The Secret Service protects the President, Vice President and designated family members (including a pregnant spouse and newborns), but does not list an unborn fetus as an independent protectee in its statutory or public procedures.

claim: "Abortionists have reduced our black population by more than 25 percent since 1973."
rationale: The claim that abortions have reduced the Black population by more than 25% since 1973 is not supported by demographic data. U.S. Census counts show the Black population has grown overall since the 1970s, and the number of abortions among Black women is far too small compared with total Black population growth to account for a one-quarter reduction. Calculations that assert such a large reduction rely on simplistic, counterfactual assumptions rather than standard demographic analysis.

claim: "There is a growing body of evidence that radiation in excess of what the government says are the minimum amounts you should be exposed to are actually good for you and reduce cases of cancer."
rationale: The mainstream scientific and regulatory consensus is that ionizing radiation increases cancer risk and there is not convincing, reproducible evidence that exposures above regulatory guidance are beneficial. Although a few laboratory or observational studies have been interpreted as suggesting 'radiation hormesis,' these results are inconsistent, methodologically limited, and have not led major health agencies to change protective standards.

claim: "The Family Research Council, according to some government agencies, is a terrorist group."
rationale: No U.S. federal or state government agency has formally labeled the Family Research Council (FRC) a terrorist organization. The FRC has been criticized and was listed as a "hate group" by the Southern Poverty Law Center, which is a private NGO, but that is not a government terrorist designation and FRC does not appear on official terrorist lists.

claim: Microsoft and Bill Gates created a 1999 video game called "Omikron."
rationale: Omikron: The Nomad Soul (1999) was developed by Quantic Dream and published by Eidos Interactive, with music and involvement from David Bowie; it was not created by Microsoft or Bill Gates. There is no evidence in game credits or historical records that Microsoft or Bill Gates had a development or publishing role in that title.

claim: Says President Barack Obama promised he would cut the deficit in half, but instead will at least double it.
rationale: Obama did explicitly pledge during the 2008 campaign to "cut the deficit we inherit in half by the end of my first term." However, while annual deficits rose sharply in 2009–2010 because of the financial crisis and stimulus, they were not permanently "at least doubled" relative to the inherited baseline over his presidency; deficits fell in later years (e.g., FY2008 ≈ $458B, FY2009 ≈ $1.4T, FY2016 ≈ $585B). The claim misstates timing and magnitude of deficits and ignores economic context.

claim: "The (national) debt really added up $75 trillion in 2010 and is on track to hit $99 trillion this year."
rationale: The U.S. federal debt was about $13–14 trillion in 2010, not $75 trillion; that $75T figure reflects a different measure (present‑value estimates of future unfunded obligations) rather than the official debt reported by Treasury or CBO. Similarly, claims that it is 'on track to hit $99 trillion' conflate distinct concepts (gross debt, publicly held debt, and long‑term unfunded liabilities) and are not supported as the official federal debt level for any recent year.

claim: "A grant for $5,000 [from the Governor’s Workforce Board] went to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter."
rationale: I could not find corroborating evidence that a Governor’s Workforce Board grant of exactly $5,000 was awarded specifically to teach an employee at a company making ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter. While workforce boards do fund employee training, the claim gives specific dollar amount and narrow purpose without naming the state, board document, or company, and appears to be a likely mischaracterization or anecdote rather than a verified fact.

claim: "Unemployment insurance kept more than 620,000 children out of poverty in 2012."
rationale: I cannot confirm the precise figure of 'more than 620,000 children' being kept out of poverty by unemployment insurance in 2012. Authoritative sources (Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure and policy analyses) report impacts of unemployment insurance on poverty, but estimates vary by measure and methodology and do not clearly support that exact number as a definitive fact.

claim: "39% of All California Students are illegals."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 39% of all California students are undocumented. State and independent estimates of undocumented children in K–12 are far lower, and the claim likely conflates undocumented status with other categories like English Learners, Hispanic ethnicity, or immigrant background.

claim: The Rev. Wright compared "the United States Marine Corps with Roman legionnaires who were responsible for the death of our Savior."
rationale: There is no reliable transcript or widely reported excerpt of Rev. Jeremiah Wright explicitly comparing the United States Marine Corps to Roman legionnaires 'responsible for the death of our Savior.' Wright did offer harsh critiques of U.S. policy and military action in sermons, but the specific analogy to the Marine Corps and the killing of Jesus does not appear in credible records of his remarks.

claim: Women pay 48 percent more for health insurance.
rationale: The statement is misleading as an absolute claim. In the U.S., the Affordable Care Act bans charging different premiums based on sex in the individual and small-group markets, and there is no widely accepted evidence that women universally pay 48% more for health insurance across markets. While some specific studies or non-health insurance contexts have shown gender price differences, the blanket 48% figure lacks necessary context (country, year, plan type) and is not generally supported.

claim: "Polls show that Floridians don't want to repeal the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and not reliably supported: Florida polling on the Affordable Care Act has been mixed and depends heavily on timing and question wording. Some polls have shown opposition to repeal, while others have shown substantial support for repeal or for replacing the law, so it is incorrect to assert that polls uniformly show Floridians don't want repeal.

claim: "Boy passes Joe Biden a vial of fresh blood to drink on his way back to the White House"
rationale: There is no credible reporting, verified video, or photographic evidence that President Biden was handed and drank a vial of fresh blood; such an event would be highly newsworthy and contradicted by visible Secret Service and staff protocols. The claim matches patterns of sensational, unverified social-media allegations and is implausible without corroboration.

claim: "Moscow was engulfed in flames" after a giant explosion.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or widespread reporting that the entire city of Moscow was ‘engulfed in flames’ after any single explosion; such an event would have generated overwhelming media, satellite, and official documentation. While localized explosions or fires in Moscow have occurred at times, those are not equivalent to the whole city being engulfed.

claim: Says Daniel Radcliffe has the coronavirus.
rationale: Daniel Radcliffe publicly announced in March 2020 that he had tested positive for COVID-19, and this was widely reported by reputable news outlets at the time. He described mild symptoms and subsequently recovered, so the statement that he 'has the coronavirus' was true at that time.

claim: "Tommy Thompson created the first school choice program in the nation, giving thousands of Milwaukee students the choice of where they go to school – no matter where they live or how much money their parents make."
rationale: While Governor Tommy Thompson signed the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program into law in 1990 and it is widely cited as the first modern urban school voucher program, it is misleading to say he "created the first school choice program in the nation." The original Milwaukee program was targeted to low‑income Milwaukee residents and included residency and income-based eligibility rules, so it did not give all students choice "no matter where they live or how much money their parents make."

claim: Under David Dewhurst’s leadership, the Texas "Senate passed an expansion of in-state tuition and free health care to illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no record that the Texas Senate under Lt. Gov. David Dewhurst enacted a law granting broad "free health care" to undocumented immigrants, and the main policy often cited—allowing certain undocumented students to qualify for in-state tuition—was enacted in Texas in 2001 before Dewhurst became lieutenant governor. Texas has generally restricted public benefits for undocumented immigrants and while the Legislature has debated limited measures affecting tuition eligibility and local health programs, it did not pass a sweeping expansion of in-state tuition together with free health care for illegal immigrants during Dewhurst’s tenure.

claim: Says NASCAR "bans the confederate flag but FORCES all their drivers to do Muslim prayer."
rationale: NASCAR did announce a ban on public display of the Confederate flag at its events in 2020, but there is no credible evidence that NASCAR forces drivers to perform Muslim prayer. NASCAR is a secular sanctioning body and does not mandate religious observance; drivers practice personal faiths privately or publicly by choice. The claim appears to conflate an organizational policy (flag ban) with a fabricated mandatory religion claim.

claim: The last private rocket launch "cost $80 million. If the government did it, the same thing would have cost probably 40 or 50 times that amount of money. I mean, literally."
rationale: The statement is a broad exaggeration. Commercial orbital launches commonly cost on the order of tens to a few hundred million dollars (e.g., Falcon 9 advertised prices ~ $50–70M), while many government-contracted launches (EELV family, commercial procurement) are in a similar order of magnitude rather than 40–50 times higher. While some government programs (notably the SLS) have per‑launch costs in the multibillion-dollar range when development amortization is included, that is an exceptional case and does not justify a blanket 40–50x multiplier for “the government” generally.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted to keep the shutdown going."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as a stand-alone fact: it does not specify which shutdown or which roll-call vote is meant. Whether Southerland “voted to keep the shutdown going” depends on a specific House vote (e.g., particular continuing resolutions in 2013), and public roll-call records must be checked to confirm. Without that context, the claim as stated is not verifiable and therefore assessed as false.

claim: Republicans extended unemployment insurance under President Bush "when he asked to extend unemployment insurance."
rationale: In late 2008 President George W. Bush publicly supported extending unemployment insurance and Congress enacted extensions that included many Republican votes; Bush then signed the measures. While the precise timing and vote margins vary by bill, Republicans did approve extensions when the Republican president asked for them.

claim: Says federal regulations adopted in 2011 increased the cost of each vehicle for his business by $10,000.
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated and implausible given available regulatory impact analyses: federal automobile efficiency and emissions rules enacted around 2010–2012 were analyzed by agencies and independent researchers and generally showed incremental compliance costs per vehicle in the low hundreds to a few thousand dollars, not $10,000 each. Costs also vary widely by vehicle make/model and by whether manufacturers redesign platforms or use cheaper compliance strategies, so a blanket $10,000 increase for every vehicle for an unspecified business is unlikely without additional evidence.

claim: "Woodrow Wilson borrowed $30 billion to fund World War I in 1917. That money has not been paid back. And we are still paying interest on it."
rationale: The United States did borrow large sums to fund World War I (total U.S. war costs around $32 billion and Liberty Bonds raised roughly $20–25 billion across 1917–1919), but it is incorrect to say Wilson borrowed $30 billion in 1917 alone. The wartime bonds were largely redeemed, repaid, or refinanced in subsequent decades, so there is no continuing, direct interest payment on a single unpaid 1917 war loan. While the government still services national debt today, that is not the same as ongoing interest on an unpaid World War I loan.

claim: Voters in Maricopa County, Ariz., were forced to vote using Sharpie pens that aren’t read by voting machines.
rationale: This claim is false. Maricopa County election officials provided Sharpie markers because they dry quickly and were recommended, but voters were not forced to use them and poll workers could provide other pens on request. Optical-scan tabulators used in the county are capable of reading ballots marked with Sharpies, and county statements plus independent fact-checkers confirmed Sharpie marks do not prevent counting.

claim: Says the American Civil Liberties Union opposes H.R. 1 on grounds that "it threatens our freedom of speech."
rationale: The American Civil Liberties Union publicly supported the recent H.R. 1 "For the People Act" and issued statements praising its voting-rights and civil-liberties protections, rather than opposing it as a threat to free speech. While the ACLU has on other occasions criticized specific donor-disclosure or campaign-finance measures that could burden speech, it did not broadly oppose H.R.1 on the grounds that it "threatens our freedom of speech."

claim: State "school funding per pupil is down 16 percent compared to 2009, after adjusting for inflation."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which state or what end year is being compared, and per-pupil funding trends differ substantially across states. While many states saw declines in real per-pupil spending after the 2008–09 recession, some states have since recovered or exceeded 2009 inflation-adjusted levels; a blanket 16% decline cannot be confirmed without a specified state and data source.

claim: "We had bipartisan legislation that got through the Senate" that would have prevented bonuses like AIG's "and then somehow mysteriously disappeared."
rationale: This overstates what occurred. In the 2009 AIG bonus controversy there were bipartisan proposals and amendments in Congress aimed at curbing bonuses (and the House later approved heavy excise taxes on certain TARP-related bonuses), but there was not a single bipartisan Senate law that clearly would have prevented the AIG payments and then "mysteriously disappeared." Legislative measures were debated, altered in negotiations, and some provisions failed to become law or were changed in conference—not a mysterious vanishing of a passed Senate law.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "put Planned Parenthood on a state medical board but failed to put a pro-life group on the same board."
rationale: The claim misstates how gubernatorial appointments work and there is no clear evidence that Romney literally "put Planned Parenthood on a state medical board" while refusing to place a pro‑life group there. Governors appoint individual members, not organizations; reports at most reference appointments of individuals with Planned Parenthood ties, not institutional placement of the organization, and no reliable record shows a deliberate refusal to appoint an explicitly pro‑life group to the same board.

claim: "When Fidel Castro came into office, you know what he did? He had a massive literacy program."
rationale: Shortly after taking power following the 1959 Cuban Revolution, Castro's government launched a nationwide National Literacy Campaign in 1961 that mobilized tens of thousands of volunteers to teach reading and writing, substantially reducing illiteracy. The program is widely described as a massive, early priority of his administration and achieved large-scale results in a short period.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders marched with Fidel Castro and Che Guevara in Cuba.
rationale: This claim is false. Che Guevara was killed in 1967, long before Bernie Sanders could have marched with him, and there is no credible evidence that Sanders ever marched alongside Fidel Castro in Cuba. The assertion appears to be based on misattributed photos or fabricated reports rather than documented facts.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden ever said the words "the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor." The December 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor was carried out by Imperial Japan, and fact-checkers have shown viral clips making this claim were miscaptioned or manipulated rather than quoting Biden verbatim.

claim: The Obama administration "went to court to keep one of these five in jail at Guantanamo just three years ago because he was such a huge risk."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported by available public records. While the Obama administration did litigate habeas cases and at times argued some Guantanamo detainees posed significant risks, there is no clear evidence that, 'just three years ago,' the administration went to court specifically to keep one of the five detainees commonly referenced (e.g., the 'Taliban five' released in 2014) in custody. The timing and specificity in the claim do not match the documented legal actions and transfers.

claim: Says Facebook is now a "public entity" that will be able to "use your photos" and "information" unless you post a statement declining your permission.
rationale: The claim is false. Facebook (Meta) is a private company (a publicly traded corporation) and users’ rights over content are governed by its Terms of Service and privacy settings; a viral status post does not revoke or change those contracts. Legal rights and license grants require changes via the platform’s official terms or by account deletion, not by posting a declaration on your profile.

claim: Says Jill McCabe "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable news reporting that a person named Jill McCabe publicly said she "supports late term abortions" or that "larger baby parts are more profitable." Such an inflammatory quote would have been widely reported and documented; it instead appears to be a fabricated or misattributed claim. Without a verifiable source, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: "Hillary interned with Bob Treuhaft, the head of the California Communist Party."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Rodham (later Clinton) interned for Robert “Bob” Treuhaft, and Treuhaft was not the "head" of the California Communist Party. Treuhaft was a well‑known left‑wing civil‑rights lawyer and former Communist Party member, but biographical records of Hillary do not show an internship with him; the claim conflates association with communism and exaggerates his role.

claim: "Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem...can indeed renew their policies and keep their current doctors and hospitals" in 2014.
rationale: The statement presents a blanket assurance, but whether Anthem individual policyholders in New Hampshire could renew 2014 policies and keep the same doctors depended on plan type and state/insurer decisions. Under the Affordable Care Act some noncompliant individual plans had to be discontinued while others (grandfathered or transitional plans) could be extended in some states, so not all Anthem customers were guaranteed renewals and provider continuity.

claim: Under Hillary Clinton’s plan "illegal immigrants convicted of committing crimes get to stay."
rationale: Hillary Clinton's stated immigration proposals did not grant blanket protection to undocumented immigrants convicted of crimes.
