The $71 billion figure is within the range cited by these official reports.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coolmath Games was operated by a Mexican drug cartel. Coolmath Games is an educational games website run by a legitimate company, and any reports of site removal or changes have been tied to business decisions, licensing, or technical issues rather than cartel control.

claim: "Chick-fil-A now open Sunday (Blacks only)."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Chick-fil-A instituted a policy of opening on Sundays exclusively for Black customers. Chick-fil-A's corporate policy historically keeps most restaurants closed on Sundays (with limited exceptions at some non-traditional locations), and a race-based service policy would be illegal and widely reported if it existed.

claim: Says about universal basic income, "Thomas Paine was for it at our founding ... Martin Luther King, champion in the ‘60s, called it a guaranteed minimum income for all Americans… It passed the U.S. House of Representatives twice in 1971."
rationale: The statement combines accurate historical points with an incorrect legislative claim. Thomas Paine did propose an inheritance-tax–funded payment scheme in Agrarian Justice and Martin Luther King Jr. advocated a guaranteed/negative income in the 1960s, but Congress did not pass a universal basic income measure twice in 1971 — Nixon’s Family Assistance Plan (the closest major proposal) never became law and did not clear the House twice in that year.

claim: "Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus."
rationale: Jamaica confirmed its first COVID-19 cases in March 2020 and subsequently reported many additional cases and deaths through official channels. Thus the claim that Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus is incorrect.

claim: "The $5 billion website for Obamacare … never worked. Still doesn't work."
rationale: Healthcare.gov did suffer major technical failures at its October 2013 launch, but a coordinated 'tech surge' fixed many issues and the site functioned for subsequent enrollment periods with millions of people signing up. Saying it 'never worked' and 'still doesn't work' is inaccurate—while intermittent problems occurred later, the marketplace has operated and processed enrollments after the initial fixes.

claim: Says "46 percent of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me."
rationale: The claim is vague and no clear, reputable national poll is known to show exactly 46% of people believe major national news organizations 'fabricate stories about me.' Polls measure generalized trust in media or perceptions of bias, but not this precise, personalized wording for the entire population. Without identifying who 'me' is, the universe of 'people,' or the survey source and question wording, the specific numeric assertion cannot be verified.

claim: A CNN video shows "HAMMER / Scorecard Voter Software Fraud in Real Time"
rationale: There is no evidence that CNN aired a video or chyron reading "HAMMER / Scorecard Voter Software Fraud in Real Time." Independent fact-checkers reviewed the viral image/video and found it to be manipulated or misattributed; CNN's archives and broadcasts do not contain such a graphic. The claim appears to stem from a doctored screenshot circulated on social media.

claim: Quotes Thomas Homer-Dixon as saying a windmill will "never generate as much energy as was invested building it."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Thomas Homer-Dixon stated windmills will "never generate as much energy as was invested building it." Empirical life-cycle analyses show modern wind turbines produce several times the energy invested over their operational lifetimes, so the quoted absolute claim conflicts with established engineering evidence and appears to be a misattribution or out-of-context paraphrase.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Anthony Fauci served on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years; his public biography shows long-term service as director of NIAID, not as a Clinton Foundation board member. He also is not a current board member of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation—while he has collaborated with or participated in advisory activities alongside Gates-funded initiatives, that is not the same as serving on the foundation's board.

claim: "There's no evidence that white supremacists were responsible for what happened on Jan. 6. That's a lie."
rationale: The claim is false. Federal investigations, DOJ indictments and convictions, congressional and law-enforcement reports, and journalism documented that individuals with white supremacist or extremist affiliations (including members of groups like the Proud Boys and other known extremist actors) participated in and helped plan aspects of the Jan. 6 attack. While not every rioter held such views, there is clear evidence that white supremacist-aligned actors were involved.

claim: "We won. We won in a landslide. This was a landslide."
rationale: The statement asserts a "landslide" victory but gives no information about which election, when, or what jurisdiction, so it cannot be verified as true. Claims about election outcomes require official, certified results and defined vote-margin thresholds to substantiate a "landslide" characterization; absent that context the claim is unsubstantiated and treated as false.

claim: Says Sen. Rand Paul’s 2011 budget "included a big cut in the CDC."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and summaries of Sen. Rand Paul’s 2011 budget proposals do not show a specific, large line-item “big cut” targeted at the CDC; his early Senate budget rhetoric focused on broad spending caps and entitlement reductions rather than a documented large reduction to CDC funding. Without clear evidence of a major CDC line-item cut in his 2011 budget, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Says "there’s 400,000" anchor babies born in the United States a year, which are "individuals coming to our country and having their children so their children can be U.S. citizens."
rationale: Reliable estimates do not support a clean figure of 400,000 people purposely coming to the U.S. each year to give birth; research (e.g., Pew and CDC-based analyses) typically estimates births to unauthorized immigrant mothers on the order of roughly 200,000–350,000 in recent years, and many births to noncitizen mothers are to residents already living in the U.S. The claim also implies parents gain immigration benefits by having a U.S.-born child, which is misleading because birthright citizenship applies to the child and does not provide legal status to the parents or immediate immigration relief.

claim: "MSNBC announced Trump won 2020 election."
rationale: This is false. Major U.S. news organizations, including MSNBC, did not announce that Trump won the 2020 presidential election; networks and the Associated Press projected Joe Biden as the winner after key state calls in early November 2020. There is no credible record of MSNBC declaring a Trump victory in that contest.

claim: "Kasich’s budget raised taxes by billions, hitting businesses hard and the middle class even harder."
rationale: Kasich's budgets are not accurately described as wholesale tax hikes 'by billions' that hit businesses and the middle class hardest. His administration enacted notable business tax cuts (for example phasing out the tangible personal property tax and cutting income tax rates) while some revenue-raising measures and base broadenings occurred; overall Ohio's policy under Kasich tended toward net tax reductions for businesses and income tax relief for many taxpayers. Characterizing the budgets as large, targeted tax increases on businesses and the middle class is misleading.

claim: Gains in Atlanta Public Schools scores on a national standardized test lend credence to "dramatic" score increases on state tests.
rationale: There is not clear independent evidence that gains on a national standardized test definitively corroborated the "dramatic" increases reported on Georgia state tests; differences in test design, administration conditions, and who administers the national exam can limit comparability. Therefore observed gains on a district-selected national test do not necessarily lend conclusive credence to the state test increases.

claim: "Too many dead people voted" in Michigan
rationale: Official Michigan investigations, audits, and court reviews have found only isolated instances of ballots associated with voters who were deceased, typically attributable to record-timing or administrative errors, not widespread fraudulent voting by dead people. Fact-checks and state officials concluded those cases were too few to affect outcomes and did not indicate systemic impersonation of deceased voters.

claim: One Wisconsin school district "is so worried about losing state funding that it has stopped giving milk to elementary school kids during snack time."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting that a Wisconsin school district stopped giving milk at elementary snack time specifically because it feared losing state funding. The statement appears anecdotal or misattributes a local snack policy change to state funding fears without documentary evidence tying the two.

claim: 7 million people the Congressional Budget Office says won't have health insurance coverage under the Senate health care bill "don't exist."
rationale: The Congressional Budget Office's estimate that about 7 million more people would be uninsured under the Senate bill is a projection based on current enrollment and survey data, not a claim about nonexistent individuals. Saying those people 'don't exist' misrepresents the CBO's methodology and findings, though the exact number is a model-based estimate with uncertainty.

claim: Terry McAuliffe "wants to raise your taxes $1,700 to pay for his infinite promises."
rationale: The claim is a vague, partisan attack and not a documented policy commitment by Terry McAuliffe. There is no specific, verifiable proposal from McAuliffe that explicitly pledges to raise 'your taxes $1,700' to fund unspecified 'infinite promises'; the number appears to be an extrapolation or ad talking point rather than a factual statement of a enacted or proposed tax increase.

claim: "I campaigned on (the proposals in the budget repair bill for Wisconsin) all throughout the election. Anybody who says they are shocked on this has been asleep for the past two years."
rationale: The speaker overstated what was promised on the campaign trail. While the candidate campaigned on fiscal restraint, pension and benefit reforms, contemporary reporting and reactions indicate the specific provisions of Wisconsin’s 2011 budget repair bill—particularly the near-total curtailment of collective bargaining—were not clearly spelled out “all throughout the election,” and many voters and officials said they were surprised. The claim’s second sentence is a rhetorical exaggeration and not verifiable as literal fact.

claim: "Probably one out of every two households in Oklahoma has a gun."
rationale: Reliable state-level surveys of household gun ownership vary by source and year, and while Oklahoma is among higher‑ownership states it is not clearly established that exactly half of households own a gun. Estimates from organizations that model household firearm prevalence (e.g., RAND, Gallup/Pew) place Oklahoma near but often a bit below 50%, and different methodologies produce different percentages, so the blanket statement 'probably one out of every two households' is not firmly supported.

claim: Says Vice President Kamala Harris called the unvaccinated "dirty Trump people."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable news reporting that Vice President Kamala Harris ever called the unvaccinated 'dirty Trump people.' Harris has criticized vaccine refusal using public-health language, but this exact phrasing appears to be a misattribution or a distorted/edited quote.

claim: Clinton has "raised the most money from Washington lobbyists ... from the health industry, drug companies, health insurance companies (and) the defense industry."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute claim but is ambiguous about which Clinton, which election cycle, and which comparator set. While Hillary Clinton did receive large donations from health care, pharmaceutical, insurance, and defense industry donors and from individuals connected to Washington lobbying, independent analyses show she was among the top recipients in some of those sectors but not definitively the single top recipient across all categories and cycles. The unqualified claim that she "raised the most" from Washington lobbyists in each listed industry is not supported as stated.

claim: A DeKalb sewer project "will create up to 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak production, many of which will be set aside exclusively for DeKalb residents."
rationale: I could not find authoritative documentation that this DeKalb sewer project will produce 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak and that many of those jobs will be set aside exclusively for DeKalb residents. Infrastructure job claims are often reported as total 'job‑years' or include indirect/induced positions, and exclusive resident‑only hiring is generally constrained by procurement and labor law, so the phrasing appears misleading or unverified without a specific source.

claim: Says "Ron Johnson calls Social Security a Ponzi scheme and wants to privatize the program."
rationale: This claim bundles two assertions that are not fully supported together. Ron Johnson has repeatedly criticized Social Security’s long‑term financing and supported options like private retirement accounts or reforms, but there is not a clear, consistent record of him explicitly calling the entire program a “Ponzi scheme” nor advocating outright full privatization of Social Security as a single, unambiguous policy demand.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy is among seven "Tea Party freshmen" who "spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves."
rationale: I could not corroborate that Rep. Sean Duffy was specifically named among seven 'Tea Party freshmen' who collectively spent an average of $15,000 apiece on cars for personal use. While media reports have noted that some 2010 freshmen used campaign funds for vehicle purchases or leases, the claim as stated appears to conflate different reports and lacks a verifiable source tying Duffy to that group and that precise average. Without clear documentation, the specific claim is not supported.

claim: Virginia Tech swimmer Reka Gyorgy tweeted, "My finals spot was stolen by Lia Thomas, who is a biological male."
rationale: I cannot find evidence that Réka György posted that exact tweet. Media reports and her public comments show she criticized Lia Thomas and expressed that Thomas affected competitive opportunities, but the specific quoted sentence has not been verified in reliable reports and may be a paraphrase or misquote. Because the exact wording cannot be confirmed, the claim as stated is false.

claim: Quotes Winston Churchill as saying "Diplomacy is the art of telling people to go to hell in such a way that they ask for directions."
rationale: This quip is widely attributed to Winston Churchill in popular culture, but there is no reliable primary-source evidence that he ever said or wrote it. Quote researchers have found the line in later, unattributed witticisms and cannot trace it to Churchill's speeches, writings, or contemporaneous reports.

claim: Says Military Times reported that a study found "60% of sailors who had been fully vaccinated with 2-shot series vaccines are now at risk for heart disease."
rationale: No credible Military Times reporting supports the sweeping claim that a study found 60% of fully vaccinated sailors are now at risk for heart disease. Military Times coverage discussed rare myocarditis cases and small or preliminary studies with limited samples and nuanced findings, but not a 60% risk of heart disease among vaccinated sailors; the 60% figure appears to be a misinterpretation or exaggeration of small-sample imaging results of unclear clinical significance.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: The claim is too absolute: Iowa's Republican caucus has lost some determinative power in recent cycles and its winners do not automatically become the nominee, but it still matters for shaping early momentum, media coverage, fundraising, and endorsements. Therefore it does influence who becomes the party nominee even if it is not the sole or guaranteed determinant.

claim: The health care bill "cuts the deficit by over $1 trillion dollars."
rationale: Independent budget scores (CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation) for the Affordable Care Act showed a net deficit reduction measured in the low hundreds of billions over the standard 10-year scoring window, not a cut exceeding $1 trillion. The claim overstates the consensus score and omits that results vary greatly by timeframe and baseline assumptions.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: Based on Social Security Administration analyses and widely reported estimates, Social Security benefits reduce poverty for well over a million residents of Florida. Florida's large population of retirees and the SSA's state-level poverty-impact calculations support the statement that Social Security lifts more than a million Floridians out of poverty.

claim: Tax increases under Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm led to state unemployment going from 6.8 percent to 15.3 percent.
rationale: The claim wrongly asserts that state tax increases under Gov. Jennifer Granholm caused unemployment to rise from 6.8% to 15.3%. Michigan’s sharp unemployment increase occurred during the 2008–2009 Great Recession and the near-collapse of the auto industry, and while unemployment did spike in her term, attributing it primarily to state tax increases is unsupported; official series show a peak in the mid- to high-teens depending on the measure, but causation is misrepresented.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton won "health care for 8 million children."
rationale: The program that covered roughly 7–9 million children was the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), enacted by Congress in 1997 during Bill Clinton's administration. Hillary Clinton advocated for health reforms as First Lady, but she did not singlehandedly 'win' health care for 8 million children; the law was a bipartisan Congressional achievement with multiple actors involved.

claim: "Nearly 180,000 illegal immigrants with criminal records, ordered deported from our country, are tonight roaming free to threaten peaceful citizens."
rationale: Public data and independent fact-checks do not support the claim that nearly 180,000 removable illegal immigrants with criminal records are currently 'roaming free.' The figure conflates different DHS/ICE categories (e.g., people with various types of charges or convictions, people in detention, or with pending appeals), and many cited cases are not serious felonies or are already detained or under supervision. The statement therefore misrepresents the underlying data and context.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers "wants to force residents to fund Planned Parenthood abortion business."
rationale: This characterization is misleading. Governor Evers has supported publicly funded family‑planning and reproductive‑health services and defended access to Planned Parenthood, but he has not proposed a policy that would force residents to directly pay for elective abortions; federal and state rules generally prohibit public funding of most elective abortions and government funds to Planned Parenthood are typically for non‑abortion services.

claim: Says Proposition 205 "blocks market entry" for new marijuana dispensaries.
rationale: The initiative commonly referred to as Proposition 205 (Arizona, 2016) would have prioritized existing medical marijuana dispensary owners for adult-use licenses and allowed caps and local controls on retail licenses, which independent analyses and critics said would effectively exclude most new entrants. While it did not literally ban every possible new license in all circumstances, its provisions strongly restricted market entry for newcomers.

claim: "The average person who gets the minimum wage in America is 35 years old."
rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics analyses of workers paid at or below the federal minimum wage have reported a mean (average) age of about 35, and that figure has been widely cited in news and policy discussions. The statement is accurate when interpreted as the mean age in those BLS analyses.

claim: "No member of the American public has ever been killed by commercial nuclear power — a record unmatched by other fuels."
rationale: There are no confirmed cases of members of the American public being killed by commercial nuclear power operations; major U.S. commercial accidents (notably Three Mile Island in 1979) caused no direct public fatalities. Other energy sources, particularly fossil fuels, have caused numerous public deaths from accidents and air-pollution-related disease, so the safety record of U.S. commercial nuclear power in terms of public fatalities is indeed unmatched.

claim: "Forty percent of people in this country, illegally, are overstaying visas."
rationale: The statement is presented as a universal fact but gives no country, timeframe, or data source, so it cannot be verified as written. Proportions of unauthorized residents who are visa overstayers vary widely by country and over time; while some U.S. analyses have estimated figures near 40% at certain points, that is not a general truth that applies without context.

claim: "The estimated savings of this (debt ceiling) deal only pay for half of the cost of extending all of the Bush-era tax cuts for another decade."
rationale: The claim lacks a specific deal and scoring baseline, and available historical estimates show it is unlikely: CBO/OMB estimates put extending all Bush-era tax cuts for a decade at multiple trillions of dollars, while typical debt‑ceiling deal 'savings' have been in the hundreds of billions — a small fraction, not roughly half. Without a named deal and scoring methodology, the statement is not supported by general budget estimates.

claim: In Libya, "America spent $2 billion total and didn’t lose a single life."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. While U.S. combat deaths during the 2011 NATO operation in Libya were minimal, Americans were killed in Libya afterward — most notably the 2012 Benghazi attack that killed four U.S. personnel including Ambassador Chris Stevens — and U.S. government spending tied to Libya (military support, reconstruction, diplomatic and intelligence activities) exceeds a simple $2 billion figure when measured across the relevant period.

claim: By allowing brewpubs to sell beer, Georgia could become like Mexico with only a couple of manufacturers controlling all aspects of market.
rationale: Allowing brewpubs to sell beer would not plausibly produce a market like Mexico's historically concentrated beer industry. Mexico's dominance by a few large brewers arose from decades of mergers, vertical integration, and specific historical and regulatory conditions; by contrast brewpubs are small, local producers that tend to increase competition and choice rather than enable a couple of firms to control all aspects of the market.

claim: "The United States ended slavery around the world, and maybe we should get some credit for that, too."
rationale: The United States did not single-handedly end slavery around the world. While the U.S. ended slavery domestically with the Civil War and the 13th Amendment (1865) and has at times pressured other countries, many other nations abolished slavery earlier (e.g., Britain in 1833) or through their own movements and international agreements. Claiming global credit overstates the U.S. role and ignores broader international and historical processes that ended slavery in different places and eras.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
rationale: Contemporary records and later fact-checks show Orrin Hatch was among Republican senators who co-sponsored a 1993 health-reform bill that included a requirement for individuals to obtain health insurance (an individual mandate). The individual mandate concept was promoted by conservative policymakers in the late 1980s/early 1990s and Hatch’s name appears on the 1993 proposal.

claim: Says that under President Obama, there’s been a substantial increase in federal government jobs.
rationale: Reliable employment series and contemporary fact-checks show that the federal civilian workforce did not experience a substantial increase over Obama's two terms; overall federal civilian employment was roughly flat to slightly lower from 2009–2016 rather than markedly higher. While some agencies grew and temporary hiring occurred in certain years, the net change was small, not a substantial rise.

claim: California’s Central Valley and Inland Empire "are experiencing tremendous job growth."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad characterization. While parts of the Inland Empire have seen notable job gains in logistics, warehousing, and construction over the past decade, job growth across California’s Central Valley has been uneven and generally weaker, with some counties still facing high unemployment and slower wage gains. Calling both regions as a whole "experiencing tremendous job growth" is misleading.

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: This is a misleading oversimplification. The Trump-era USDA approved inspection-system changes that allow industry employees to perform some tasks formerly done by agency personnel (e.g., sorting carcasses under the New Swine Inspection System), but the federal Food Safety and Inspection Service retained regulatory authority and on-site inspectors rather than turning inspection entirely over to 'Big Ag.' Likewise, FSIS continued government pathogen testing programs (including for E. coli O157:H7 and other shiga-toxin producing E. coli) rather than a blanket halt to E. coli testing.

claim: "The governor is trying to take credit for recent actions taken by these companies. The problem is that for all three companies, the decision to move or stay in New Jersey happened before Chris Christie became governor."
rationale: The statement is specific but provides no names or dates; Chris Christie took office January 2010 and many corporate location decisions attributed to his tenure were announced after that date. Without identification of the three companies and decision dates, the blanket claim that all three decisions predated his governorship cannot be verified and is unlikely to be uniformly true.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: The general fact that Florida sees a high number of staged auto accidents is supported by law‑enforcement and insurance fraud reports, but the specific claim that three of the top five cities are in Florida and that Florida (or a Florida city) ranks No. 1 is not verifiable without a cited, time‑bound source. Rankings of 'top cities' for staged accidents vary by year and by the agency compiling the data (NICB, local prosecutors, insurers), so the blanket, unsourced rank statement cannot be confirmed as true. Given the variability and lack of a clear source, the precise numeric claim is judged false.

claim: "Since 1999, firearm deaths in Ohio have risen 58 percent."
rationale: The statement is presented without an end year or whether it refers to raw counts or per-capita rates. Official state mortality data (CDC/NCHS) show firearm deaths in Ohio have fluctuated since 1999 and the percent change varies by which end year and metric you choose; there is no clear, unambiguous basis to assert a 58% rise as a standalone fact.

claim: "Since 2007 David Jolly has given almost $30,000 to keep Democrats in Congress!"
rationale: I cannot verify that David Jolly gave nearly $30,000 specifically to support Democrats in Congress since 2007. Public campaign finance records (FEC/OpenSecrets) typically show that while he has made some contributions to candidates of both parties, the total to Democrats as described appears exaggerated and the claim conflates donations with a stated intent to "keep Democrats in Congress."

claim: "Clinton campaign official arrested by FBI on child rape/trafficking charges"
rationale: There is no credible evidence, official FBI statement, or major news reporting that any named Clinton campaign official was arrested by the FBI on child rape or trafficking charges. Claims like this have circulated as unverified rumors or conspiracy-driven hoaxes and have been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: Says Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland "voted, so the folks know, in Washington, D.C., to keep guns away from private citizens."
rationale: The statement frames Garland as having 'voted' in Washington, D.C., to bar private citizens from guns, which is misleading. Merrick Garland served as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit and participated in judicial rulings about D.C. gun regulations, but judges issue opinions in cases rather than 'voting' in a legislative sense, and the record of his votes in particular cases does not support the blanket claim as stated.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s polling numbers show that he’s "the highest with Hispanics that any Republican has ever been."
rationale: Historically, other Republicans have received higher Hispanic support than Donald Trump’s reported highs. For example, George W. Bush won about 44% of the Hispanic vote in 2004, which exceeds Trump’s national Hispanic support (roughly low 30s percent in 2020). The blanket claim that Trump is "the highest with Hispanics that any Republican has ever been" is therefore incorrect.

claim: Says in regard to providing "more tax cuts for the rich," Bill Pascrell said, "Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable reporting that Rep. Bill Pascrell praised "more tax cuts for the rich" with the quoted line. Pascrell, a Democratic congressman, is widely on record criticizing tax cuts benefiting wealthy households, so the specific quote appears to be a misattribution or fabricated.

claim: Says President Barack Obama’s "own economists say the stimulus cost $278K per job ‘created.’ "
rationale: There is no credible record of President Obama's Council of Economic Advisers or 'his own economists' claiming the stimulus cost $278,000 per job created. That $278K figure traces to a misleading arithmetic division of total ARRA outlays by a snapshot count of jobs, ignoring job-duration, counterfactuals, and standard CEA estimates. Mainstream analyses and the CEA produced much lower estimates of cost per job-year when using accepted accounting for duration and multipliers.

claim: "If you earn $100 and pay $33 income tax you’re left with $67. You then buy $67 worth of fuel and in doing so pay a 48% fuel tax (fuel tax = $32.16 + $6.70 GST). This means that the government just got $71.86 tax from your hard earned $100."
rationale: The arithmetic and tax treatment in the claim are incorrect. GST is 10% of the GST-exclusive price (so on a $67 final pump price GST would be about $6.09, not $6.70), and fuel 'tax' is often a fixed cents-per-litre excise rather than a straight 48% of the pump price; the claim mixes bases and double-counts taxes to produce the $71.86 figure. Therefore the stated total tax taken from the $100 is not accurate as presented.

claim: Medicare insurance premiums will be rising to "$120.20 per month in 2013 and $247.00 per month in 2014."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: standard Medicare monthly premiums did not jump to $120.20 in 2013 and $247.00 in 2014. Historical CMS rates show the standard Part B premium around roughly $100–$105 per month in those years, and while higher-income beneficiaries can pay larger surcharges, a general premium increase to the stated amounts did not occur.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: Multiple local public-health analyses and news reports have documented that infant mortality rates in neighborhoods within roughly a three-mile radius of Cleveland's University Circle have been unusually high and, at times, higher than the infant mortality rates reported by some low- and middle-income countries. Those comparisons were widely reported in local coverage and public-health studies, though they depend on the year and exact geographic boundaries used.

claim: "If I mail in my ballot on Sunday and show up to the polling station on Tuesday, they won’t know if I’ve already voted or not. That, my friends, is a serious concern for all of us."
rationale: In most U.S. jurisdictions election officials maintain records showing whether an absentee/mail ballot was issued or received and poll books will reflect that status. If a mailed ballot hasn't been received by Election Day, poll workers typically can see that an absentee ballot was issued and will either refuse a regular ballot or issue a provisional ballot that is counted only if the mailed ballot is not later received. Double voting is generally prevented by these tracking and verification procedures.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The claim is misleading and factually incorrect: Bill Nelson left the U.S. Senate in January 2019 and therefore could not have been part of a Senate budget passage in the last ~750 days. Moreover, federal budgets/appropriations require action by both chambers (and often the president) and simply saying '750 days since Democrats in the Senate passed a budget' omits necessary context and a clear start date.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff is "a socialist."
rationale: Jon Ossoff is a mainstream Democratic U.S. senator who has described himself as a moderate and has not advocated for core socialist policies like public ownership of major industries. His campaign platforms, voting record, and endorsements align with center-left Democratic positions rather than democratic socialism.

claim: "15 years ago, cancer drugs cost an average of $10,000 a year. Now it’s $10,000 a month."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While oncology drug prices have risen substantially and many newer cancer therapies carry monthly list prices in the tens of thousands of dollars, broad averages 15 years ago were not uniformly $10,000 per year and current average costs depend on which drugs, dosing duration, and price measure (list, launch, or net) are used — so the specific assertion is unsupported.

claim: "BIDEN: 'I'm not gonna take any questions because I think it's inappropriate.'"
rationale: I could not verify a reliable source or transcript showing President Biden uttered that exact sentence. While Biden has on occasion declined to take questions and has used similar phrasing, the specific quoted wording "I'm not gonna take any questions because I think it's inappropriate" is not corroborated by known press transcripts or credible reports.

claim: Photos show a photojournalist crying while capturing pictures of the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.
rationale: I cannot verify the claim and there is no corroborated, widely reported evidence up to mid‑2024 that a specific photojournalist was photographed crying while taking pictures at the Aqsa Mosque. Images of emotional journalists and miscaptioned photos frequently circulate during conflicts, so without an original source, date, photographer credit and metadata the assertion is unverified and likely misattributed.

claim: Florida students take "an array of standardized high stakes tests which eat up as much as 45 school days per year."
rationale: Florida’s statewide high‑stakes exams (FSA, EOCs, end‑of‑course and required make‑ups) generally occupy a small number of administration days (typically under two weeks total for most students), not 45 full school days. While districts also give additional interim, benchmark, and classroom tests that can add time, the widely quoted “up to 45 days” figure is an extreme aggregation and overstates typical statewide high‑stakes testing time.

claim: Says his budget provides "the highest state funding level in history" for education.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify and is commonly misleading: politicians often cite "highest funding" in nominal dollars while ignoring inflation, per-pupil measures, or one-time federal grants. Without specifying the state, budget year, and whether the comparison is inflation-adjusted or per-student versus total funding, the statement cannot be confirmed as accurate. Because key qualifiers are missing and such claims frequently depend on selective accounting, I judge it false as stated.

claim: "Over 73% of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and the ALS Association's own financial statements show that the viral claim is misleading: the bulk of Ice Bucket Challenge donations were routed to program services such as research and patient services, not to fundraising/overhead and executive pay. The precise breakdown varied by year and donor designation, but credible audits and Forms 990 do not support a figure that over 73% of all donated dollars went to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and 'external donations.'

claim: "We have one of the most expensive General Assemblies, per capita, in the entire country."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented because it lacks a clear referent (which state/General Assembly and which year) and no supporting budget-per-capita data were provided. Per-capita cost rankings of state legislatures vary by how costs are defined (salaries, staff, pensions, facilities) and by year, so the statement cannot be verified as true without specific, comparative fiscal data.

claim: Says that shutdowns are "ineffective" and that we now know that COVID-19 is not commonly spread "by someone going to work."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and reviews found that broad non-pharmaceutical interventions including shutdowns and stay-at-home orders reduced transmission and deaths, especially early in the pandemic, so the blanket claim that shutdowns were ineffective is incorrect. Likewise, workplace and commuting-related exposures were documented contributors to SARS-CoV-2 spread (especially in indoor, crowded, or poorly ventilated workplaces and among essential workers), so it is false to assert we now know COVID-19 is not commonly spread by someone going to work.

claim: Wagon arriving at Detroit counting center after deadline "may have been a ballot box."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the wagon shown arriving at the Detroit counting center after the deadline was a ballot box. Multiple local officials and independent fact-checks reviewed video and chain-of-custody records and concluded the cart carried supplies/election materials, not a container of uncounted ballots. The claim rests on speculation from ambiguous footage rather than verifiable proof.

claim: Attorney general candidate Brad Schimel "is in cahoots with Wisconsin Right to Life to make abortion a crime in Wisconsin."
rationale: Brad Schimel has publicly aligned with anti-abortion groups and supported enforcing restrictive Wisconsin abortion laws, but there is no documented evidence of a secret or explicit agreement that he is "in cahoots" with Wisconsin Right to Life to criminalize abortion. The claim asserts covert collusion beyond the public policy alignment, which is not substantiated by available reporting.

claim: "In fact, the data coming in from some states that have legalized marijuana is that they actually see a decrease in use over time, particularly among young people."
rationale: Multiple state- and national-level surveys and peer-reviewed analyses have found that in several U.S. states that legalized recreational cannabis (for example Colorado, Washington and others) adolescent use remained stable or declined in the years after legalization. However, results are not uniform across all states, measures (past-month vs. lifetime use), or time periods.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs."
rationale: The statement mischaracterizes federal spending under President Obama. The 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act was about $787 billion (not 'nearly a trillion') and included tax cuts, transfers, and investments; only a modest portion went to state/local aid or direct public employment, not a trillion dollars spent on 'make-work' government jobs.

claim: Says Barack Obama "put in place a board that can tell people ultimately what treatments they're going to receive."
rationale: This claim conflates advisory and cost-control bodies created under the Affordable Care Act with an authority to dictate individual care. The ACA established entities like the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) to recommend Medicare cost-saving measures and PCORI to fund research, but neither had direct power to tell individual patients which treatments they must receive; IPAB was also never implemented and was later repealed.

claim: "There are parks in Southeast Raleigh that still don’t have air conditioning in the gym"
rationale: This is a specific, local and time-sensitive assertion that I cannot verify with the available information. Determining whether particular parks in Southeast Raleigh currently lack air conditioning in their gyms requires up-to-date, site-level data from the City of Raleigh Parks & Recreation or recent on-the-ground reports; without that, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false. While older community centers sometimes lack AC, that general possibility does not validate this specific, present-tense claim.

claim: "Money raised to help (Beto) O’Rourke get elected is being used to fund migrants. This is clearly breaking campaign finance laws."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that funds raised by Beto O’Rourke’s campaign were diverted to directly fund migrants. Media fact-checks and campaign disclosures have not shown the campaign itself paying for migrant transportation or services, and allegations appear to conflate donations by supporters or separate groups with official campaign receipts. While campaign funds are restricted from personal use, the claim that campaign money is being used to fund migrants and that this is clearly a campaign finance violation is unproven and oversimplifies complex legal distinctions.

claim: Says Justice Elena Kagan recused herself in "many cases where she had little role" as solicitor general, simply because of the appearance of a conflict of interest.
rationale: After joining the Supreme Court, Justice Elena Kagan recused herself from a substantial number of cases that originated while she was Solicitor General or otherwise touched the Office of the Solicitor General. Contemporary reporting and the Court's recusal records show she sometimes recused even where her direct, hands-on involvement had been limited, citing the need to avoid the appearance of a conflict.

claim: "Illinois suffered 1,652 overdose deaths in 2014 ... of which 40 percent were associated with heroin. Illinois is ranked number one in the nation for a decline in treatment capacity between 2007 and 2012, and is now ranked the third worst in the country for state-funded treatment capacity."
rationale: I could not corroborate the specific figures and rankings as stated. Public overdose mortality reports (CDC/Illinois Dept. of Public Health) and national treatment-capacity analyses (SAMHSA and independent policy reports) do not clearly support Illinois having exactly 1,652 overdose deaths in 2014 with 40% heroin-associated, nor do they unambiguously show Illinois was #1 for decline in treatment capacity 2007–2012 and currently the third-worst for state-funded capacity.

claim: "Last week Joe Biden flashed the ‘white power’ sign. President Trump condemned white supremacists yesterday. Why hasn't Joe Biden?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden intentionally flashed a 'white power' sign; available photos and video show a common 'OK' or pointing gesture used while speaking, and interpreters and fact-checkers have treated similar claims as misleading. The 'OK' hand has been co-opted by extremists in some contexts, but that does not mean routine gestures by public figures are proof of endorsement.

claim: An anonymous e-mail says that Hillary Clinton advocates communism.
rationale: Anonymous chain e-mails and forwards alleging that Hillary Clinton advocates communism have circulated widely during past U.S. campaigns, so the existence of at least one anonymous e-mail making that claim is highly plausible. This assessment addresses the existence of such a message, not the truth of its content.

claim: Photos show celebrities reacting to Will Smith slapping Chris Rock.
rationale: Photographers and the televised Oscars broadcast captured still images of audience members immediately after Will Smith slapped Chris Rock, and those photos of celebrities' reactions were widely published by news outlets. However, some additional images circulated online were later found to be miscaptioned or taken from other events, so not every photo shared on social media is authentic.

claim: Members of Congress and their families and staff are exempt from repaying student loans.
rationale: There is no statute or standing policy that broadly exempts members of Congress, their families, or congressional staff from repaying federal student loans. They are subject to the same repayment rules as other borrowers, although individuals may qualify for existing forgiveness programs (e.g., Public Service Loan Forgiveness) or employer repayment assistance if they meet the program requirements.

claim: Claims Joe Biden said "coal is more dangerous than terrorists."
rationale: There is no credible record or reputable fact-checker that Joe Biden ever said the literal line 'coal is more dangerous than terrorists.' Biden has criticized the coal industry and framed climate change and pollution as serious threats, but that specific quotation is a misattribution or distorted paraphrase rather than a documented statement.

claim: "After World War II, we tried, convicted, and, in some cases, executed Japanese soldiers for war crimes that included charges of waterboarding."
rationale: Allied military tribunals after World War II prosecuted Japanese personnel for war crimes that included torture methods commonly described at the time as the "water cure" (forced water ingestion/simulated drowning). Several defendants were convicted of such torture-related counts and some were executed following those tribunals. The modern term "waterboarding" is anachronistic but the underlying practice was prosecuted.

claim: Says "85 percent (of immigrants) don’t show up for a scheduled court hearing or call to schedule a court hearing."
rationale: The claimed 85% no‑show rate is far higher than published analyses of immigration court outcomes. Government and independent trackers show non‑appearance/in‑absentia rates are substantially lower and vary by year, jurisdiction, and case type, so an overall 85% figure is not supported by available data.

claim: "The Border Patrol has 20,000 agents – more than twice as many as there were in 2004."
rationale: U.S. Border Patrol staffing is roughly 20,000 in recent years, but that is about double — not more than twice — the agency's size in 2004. Historical DHS/CBP staffing data show the Border Patrol had on the order of 10,000–11,000 agents in 2004, so 20,000 is approximately double rather than more than twice.

claim: "Biden’s plan will immediately let in 25,000 asylum-seekers who’d been waiting in Mexico as their cases were judged."
rationale: There is no authoritative Biden policy that would "immediately" admit 25,000 asylum-seekers from Mexico as their cases were being adjudicated. Administrations have announced parole or processing programs with caps or monthly intakes and extensive screening/vetting, and some proposals discussed numbers in the tens of thousands per month, but those would be phased, conditional, and subject to vetting and operational constraints rather than an immediate blanket admission of 25,000 pending cases.

claim: Wisconsin state lawmakers worked seven days in 2012 but got "paid for a whole year."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While critics noted that the Wisconsin Legislature held very few floor session days in parts of 2012, lawmakers legally receive an annual salary and perform many other duties (committee meetings, constituent services, interim work) beyond those few floor days. Saying they "worked seven days but got paid for a whole year" implies improper pay for no work, which ignores the broader scope of legislative responsibilities and the established salary structure.

claim: "I deployed the Texas National Guard" to the Texas-Mexico border. "And the policy worked; apprehensions at the border declined 74 percent."
rationale: Publicly available Border Patrol encounter data and contemporaneous reporting do not support a clear, causal 74% drop in apprehensions attributable to the Texas National Guard deployment. Numbers vary by sector and timeframe, and while Texas officials have highlighted localized or short-term declines, national and state-level CBP data do not show a straightforward 74% reduction caused by the Guard action. The claim conflates correlation with causation and omits specific dates and geographic scope.

claim: U.S. Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison "voted to continue Roe v. Wade."
rationale: There is no single Senate roll-call that 'votes to continue Roe v. Wade' because Roe is a Supreme Court precedent, not a federal statute. Kay Bailey Hutchison's record as a Republican senator includes votes and positions that favored restrictions on abortion and support for conservative judicial nominees, not a clear affirmative Senate vote to preserve Roe as described.

claim: "We raised the minimum wage to $15 first in city government. Now, working together with people in Albany, it's the law of the state."
rationale: The claim asserts a city government was the first to raise the minimum wage to $15 and that statewide law followed through cooperation with Albany. While many states later enacted $15 minimums, multiple U.S. cities (notably Seattle and San Francisco) adopted $15 wage ordinances in 2014, before several state-level laws. New York State did later enact a phased increase to $15, but the claim of being the first city government to do so is inaccurate without specifying a city that was uniquely first.

claim: If you know someone's name and date of birth you can change their votes on Oregon’s voting website.
rationale: Oregon’s public voter websites let you look up registration status or track ballots, but they do not allow someone to change another person’s cast ballot simply by entering name and date of birth. Oregon conducts vote-by-mail with paper ballots that are accepted based on returned ballots and signature verification, so altering a vote would require possession of the physical ballot or fraudulent signature, not merely name and DOB.

claim: "ISIS is in 32 countries."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as a definitive fact because counts of 'ISIS in X countries' vary widely depending on definition (core fighters, affiliated groups, or sympathizers) and on the date of assessment. Authoritative reports and news coverage have given different country counts at different times, and there is no consensus figure of exactly 32 countries for a general present-tense claim.

claim: "5.7 million -- that’s how many illegal immigrants might have voted" in 2008.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 5.7 million noncitizens or 'illegal immigrants' voted in the 2008 U.S. election. Claims of millions derive from misinterpreted or methodologically flawed analyses of surveys; reputable studies and official reviews find noncitizen voting is extremely rare and far below millions. Investigations and re-analyses have rejected large-scale voting by noncitizens as implausible.

claim: There is a provision in the economic stimulus plan that means that "students cannot meet together in their dorms, if that dorm has been repaired with this federal money, and have a prayer group or a Bible study."
rationale: There is no general provision in U.S. federal stimulus laws (such as ARRA or CARES) that bars students from holding private prayer meetings or Bible studies in dorm rooms that were repaired with federal money. Federal grant rules may prohibit using federal funds to directly finance religious worship or require nondiscrimination by recipients, but they do not prohibit private, student-led religious gatherings in residential spaces.

claim: Says an appointed board created under Obamacare "will have the ability to come between you and your doctor in determining the best treatment options for you!"
rationale: The statement overstates the board's authority. The Affordable Care Act created the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) to recommend Medicare cost-cutting measures, but its statutory powers were limited to Medicare payment and delivery changes and explicitly barred recommendations that would ration care, restrict benefits, or directly dictate individual doctor–patient treatment decisions. Moreover, IPAB applied to Medicare (not all patients) and was never implemented in practice and was later repealed by Congress.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton dressed up in blackface.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton dressed in blackface. Independent fact-checkers have investigated circulating images and claims and found them to be misattributed or doctored; no verified photographs, reliable reporting, or eyewitness accounts substantiate the allegation.

claim: "I had prostate cancer, five, six years ago. My chance of surviving prostate cancer, and thank God I was cured of it, in the United States, 82%. My chances of surviving prostate cancer in England, only 44% under socialized medicine."
rationale: Official cancer registry data and peer-reviewed summaries show 5-year prostate cancer survival in the United States is much higher than 82% (around the high 90s for many recent cohorts) and in England is far above 44% (typically in the mid-80s to 90s depending on period and stage). A 44% survival figure for England is inconsistent with national statistics and likely results from misinterpreting stage-specific, older, or otherwise non-comparable metrics. The claim’s attribution of the difference to 'socialized medicine' is also unsupported by these data.

claim: Says a "Local Hero" was "arrested after killing 30 pedophiles in murder spree"
rationale: A claim that someone was arrested after killing 30 people would be major news and documented by multiple reputable outlets and police statements; no credible reporting or verifiable details (name, place, date, official sources) support this story. The phrasing 'Local Hero' and lack of specifics match common sensational viral hoaxes or satirical posts rather than a verified event.

claim: Says J. David Cox, "the boss" of the jail guards "who were supposed to keep" suspected sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein alive, is also "friends with Bill and Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: J. David Cox is (or was) the president of the federal employees' union AFGE, not the employer or direct "boss" of the Metropolitan Correctional Center guards who oversaw Jeffrey Epstein. There is no credible evidence that Cox is a personal friend of Bill and Hillary Clinton; while union leaders may meet or endorse politicians, that is not proof of a personal friendship.

claim: "California lawmakers are planning to push free abortion pills on all students across the state as part of a ‘super progressive’ new policy."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that California lawmakers are planning to force or 'push' free abortion pills on every student statewide. While California has pursued laws and funding to expand voluntary access to abortion medications and services (including at clinics and through student health centers), nothing in public bills mandates distribution of pills to all students or coerces students to accept them.

claim: "[N]early one in three primary care doctors are forced to limit the number of Medicare patients they see."
rationale: There is not consistent, reliable evidence that "nearly one in three" primary care doctors are forced to limit Medicare patients; surveys of physician acceptance of Medicare and of limiting new Medicare patients have produced mixed and generally lower estimates, and the claim's wording ('forced to limit') is vague. While some clinicians report restricting Medicare intake because of reimbursement or capacity, available national data do not clearly support a stable ~33% rate for primary care.

claim: "In America, there is a father who is holding down two jobs and paying more taxes than the richest 400 families in America."
rationale: The claim is implausible: the 400 richest families in the U.S. have extremely high incomes and in absolute dollars pay very large amounts of federal and state taxes. A person working two jobs would almost certainly have far lower annual income and therefore pay far less in total taxes than those wealthy families. While tax rates vary, absolute tax payments scale with income, making the statement effectively false.

claim: "The average cost for health insurance in Florida went from about $600 a month for an individual to about $150 a month."
rationale: The claim is misleading and almost certainly false as stated: statewide average individual health insurance premiums in Florida have not fallen from about $600/month to about $150/month in any recent, broadly reported data. While subsidies and eligibility changes can reduce the net premiums some consumers pay, typical unsubsidized individual-market premiums are hundreds of dollars per month and a uniform drop to $150 would be unprecedented and unsupported.

claim: "Alexander Hamilton was an immigration hawk."
rationale: Calling Alexander Hamilton an "immigration hawk" is misleading and anachronistic. As an immigrant himself he supported policies to attract talented settlers and a uniform federal naturalization regime, but he also backed strong federal control and Federalist-era restrictions; his record is mixed and does not map cleanly onto the modern label of a strict anti-immigration "hawk."

claim: U.S. tariffs on China are "not hurting anybody" in the United States.
rationale: Broad evidence shows that U.S. tariffs on China raised costs for importers, businesses that use imported inputs, and consumers through higher prices, and provoked retaliatory tariffs that hurt U.S. exporters (notably farmers). While a few protected domestic producers benefited, the claim that tariffs are "not hurting anybody" is contradicted by widespread documented harms across multiple sectors and households.

claim: Says "in Oregon today, the average debt upon college graduation is more than $24,000."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because “today” is undefined and publicly reported Oregon averages for student debt at graduation vary by cohort and data source; recent state-level reports place the average near but not consistently above $24,000. Without a specific year or source, the claim cannot be confirmed and is misleading.

claim: In the past decade in New York State "more than 30 current and former state officeholders have been convicted, sanctioned or accused of wrongdoing — more than any other state."
rationale: I cannot verify an authoritative count showing New York had more than 30 current or former state officeholders convicted, sanctioned, or accused in the past decade and that this exceeds every other state. The claim mixes different categories (convicted, sanctioned, accused) that are counted differently by sources, and comparable spikes in allegations and convictions have occurred in other states such as Illinois, New Jersey, and California.

claim: "I have returned money every year since taking office."
rationale: The statement is too vague and lacks supporting evidence (no specifics about which funds, recipients, or years). Financial claims require documentary proof (audits, receipts, or public disclosures); absent such records, the assertion cannot be substantiated and should be treated as false.

claim: "We've got to find 2 billion gallons (of water per day) between now and 2025."
rationale: The statement gives no source or geographic scope and is not supported by widely published federal or state water-planning targets. National data (USGS) show total U.S. freshwater withdrawals are on the order of hundreds of billions of gallons per day, and official plans that quantify additional needed supply are region- and project-specific; no authoritative, general claim that we must "find 2 billion gallons per day by 2025" is documented.

claim: "Live cats have holes drilled into their skulls," posts put into their heads and coils put into their eyes, and some have had their ears cut off or are intentionally deafened or starved at UW-Madison labs that do research to improve hearing in humans.
rationale: The claim mixes accurate descriptions of common neuroscience methods (skull-mounted headposts/implants, implanted eye coils to track gaze, and experiments that can include inducing deafness) with sensational and unsubstantiated assertions (e.g., cutting off ears or routine starvation). Public reporting and scientific literature show UW–Madison auditory labs have used implants, eye coils, and procedures to study deafness under animal-care protocols, but there is no reliable evidence supporting the dramatic claim that cats routinely had their ears cut off or were deliberately starved as described.

claim: "The Red Cross sells your donated blood to hospitals for $150 and then that hospital charges you thousands for a blood transfusion."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Blood centers such as the Red Cross charge hospitals processing and service fees to recover collection, testing and distribution costs, and those fees vary (they are not a universal flat $150). Hospitals then bill patients for transfusion episodes, which can include many additional charges (crossmatching, administration, facility and professional fees) that sometimes total thousands, but that is not the same as the Red Cross "selling" one unit for $150.

claim: Says Amazon is "paying full-time employees so little that they require gov food assistance."
rationale: Multiple independent news reports and advocacy/academic studies have documented that some Amazon full-time workers enroll in government food assistance (SNAP) and other public benefits, indicating that wages and local cost of living leave portions of the workforce dependent on assistance. That said, Amazon raised its corporate minimum wage in 2018 and offers benefits, so the situation is not universal and varies by location, household size, and hours worked.

claim: "I do provide universal health care."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be verified as written—'I' is unspecified. Providing universal health care describes a system-level policy implemented by governments or states, not an individual, and most countries (including the United States) do not have fully universal government-provided health care. Without a named speaker, jurisdiction, or timeframe, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Bernie Sanders’s plan is "to raise your taxes to 90 percent."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has proposed substantially higher taxes on very high-income households and wealth (e.g., higher marginal rates, payroll/Medicare changes, and wealth/estate taxes), but there is no credible policy proposal from him to raise taxes to 90% for the general public or as a standard rate. The 90% figure is a hyperbolic characterization used by opponents and does not match his published tax plans, which target wealthy individuals and corporations rather than imposing a universal 90% tax rate.

claim: "After years of 5.5 percent average tuition increases, we now have a two-year tuition freeze for the first time in the history of the UW System."
rationale: The claim combines an unsupported average increase figure with an overstated historical assertion. While there have been periods of multi-year tuition increases in the UW System, the 5.5% average figure depends on the exact years chosen and is not a universally reported long-term average; additionally, the UW System has experienced tuition freezes or hold-the-line policies in prior years, so a two-year freeze is not clearly the first time in system history. Therefore the statement as written is misleading or incorrect.

claim: "United Nations Resolution is the single largest economic sanctions package ever on North Korea. Over one billion dollars in cost to N.K."
rationale: The claim overstates what can be attributed to a single UN resolution. While the UN has adopted multiple, progressively tougher sanctions packages on North Korea (notably in 2006–2017) described as among the toughest, authoritative estimates do not credit a single resolution alone as the "single largest" package or clearly show it imposed over $1 billion in losses; cost estimates typically aggregate effects of many UN resolutions plus national measures and vary by source.

claim: "In Chesterfield (Va.), the Southside precinct is infamous for having over 100% of the vote count…"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Chesterfield County’s “Southside” precinct legitimately recorded over 100% of the vote; assertions like this are typically the result of reporting or denominator errors, misreading partial returns, or misattributing aggregated totals. Temporary dashboard glitches or social-media posts can show percentages above 100%, but that reflects data/reporting mistakes rather than a true over‑100% turnout.

claim: "Bernie Sanders voted in favor of every war during his tenure."
rationale: This is false. Bernie Sanders has a long record of opposing major U.S. military authorizations — most notably he voted against the 2002 Iraq War authorization — so it is incorrect to say he voted in favor of every war during his tenure.

claim: "The United States is the No. 1 country in the world for energy resources. … We are the king daddy dogs when it comes to energy."
rationale: The United States is a leading producer of total energy and in recent years has been the top producer of crude oil and natural gas, but it is not unambiguously the No. 1 country for 'energy resources' broadly defined. Other countries (e.g., Venezuela, Saudi Arabia, Russia) have larger proven oil or gas reserves and China leads in many renewable capacities, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Says Jim Renacci ran against the Washington establishment in the election, but is now "hypocritically embracing it with big money, special interest fundraisers."
rationale: The statement mixes a verifiable claim (that Renacci ran as an anti-establishment candidate) with a normative accusation (that he is 'hypocritically embracing' the establishment via 'big money, special interest fundraisers'). While Renacci did position himself as an outsider in past campaigns, the claim that he is now hypocritically embracing the Washington establishment through specific big-money special-interest fundraisers is not definitively supported without concrete, dated evidence of such events or exclusive donor relationships. As written it reads as a partisan characterization rather than a strictly factual, documented claim.

claim: "Condemning violence against the police and urging support for the police" is "markedly absent" from President Barack Obama’s public remarks.
rationale: President Obama repeatedly and explicitly condemned violence against police and urged support for law enforcement in numerous public remarks (for example after shootings and attacks on officers in 2014–2016). Describing such condemnation as "markedly absent" is inaccurate given his public statements, attendance at memorials, and calls for respect and protection of police officers alongside calls for reform.

claim: U.S. Rep. John Barrow’s plan "puts the IRS in charge of your health care."
rationale: This statement is a rhetorical exaggeration. While the IRS enforces tax-related aspects of health laws (collecting penalties, administering premium tax credits and reporting), it does not operate insurance plans, set medical treatment, or directly manage health care delivery — those functions are handled by HHS/CMS, state exchanges and private insurers.

claim: "Seattle police begin gun confiscations: no laws broken, no warrant, no charges."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Seattle Police implemented a blanket policy of taking guns without warrants, charges, or any legal basis. Law enforcement in Washington generally must rely on a warrant, probable cause, court orders (e.g., extreme risk protection orders), or narrow exigent/safety exceptions and statutory seizure authorities (domestic-violence orders, involuntary mental-health holds); isolated lawful seizures could be misconstrued as a broader policy, but that does not match the claim.

claim: Says President Donald Trump this week will sign an executive order creating term limits for Congress.
rationale: There are no credible reports that President Trump announced he would sign an executive order this week that would actually create term limits for members of Congress. More importantly, an executive order cannot unilaterally impose term limits on Congress because altering members' qualifications or imposing nationwide term limits requires a constitutional amendment or legislation, not an executive action.

claim: "Measles is one of the most common causes of child blindness worldwide."
rationale: Measles can cause corneal ulceration and scarring and, particularly when combined with vitamin A deficiency, has historically been and remains a leading preventable cause of childhood blindness in many low‑income regions. Although widespread measles vaccination has reduced its contribution in some countries, measles is still one of the common causes of child blindness worldwide where immunization and vitamin A programs are weak.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim is unverified because it names no specific person or details; allegations of a federal investigation into campaign contributions are checkable facts tied to an identifiable individual and public records. Without the opponent's identity, date specifics, or referable sources, there is no substantiation to support the statement.

claim: "In seven years that (nuclear) deal will have expired, and Iran is free to go ahead and create nuclear weapons."
rationale: The 2015 JCPOA contained phased 'sunset' provisions that lift some specific limits after varying periods (commonly 10–15 years for major restrictions), not a blanket expiry after seven years. Even if some JCPOA limits lapse, the agreement never legalized weapons development and Iran remains subject to the NPT and IAEA safeguards; expiry of certain limits would make weapons breakout easier but does not automatically free Iran to build nuclear weapons.

claim: "We’re second only to Boston in college students per capita."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because 'we’re' does not identify a specific place, and rankings of college students per capita depend strongly on the geographic unit, time, and how 'college students' and population are defined. Many small college towns and specific neighborhoods can have higher student-per-capita rates than Boston, so claiming 'second only to Boston' is unlikely to be universally true without a clear dataset and definition.

claim: Democrats are "asking for a blank check book to spend as much as they want without worrying about the repercussions."
rationale: This is a broad rhetorical claim rather than an objective fact. While many Democrats support expanded federal spending on certain programs, they do not literally seek an unlimited "blank check"—Congressional budget rules, appropriations processes, oversight, and intra-party disagreements constrain and shape spending decisions. Whether a particular proposal is fiscally irresponsible should be judged on that proposal's specifics.

claim: "The government will be infiltrating" personal text messages.
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsupported prediction that a government will (generally) infiltrate personal text messages. While some governments and agencies have legal powers, targeted programs, or occasional unlawful hacks that access messages, there is no universal fact that governments will inevitably infiltrate all personal texts.

claim: Government subsidies for renewable energies such as wind and solar are 100 times greater than those given to gas and coal, and 50 times greater than what the nuclear industry enjoys.
rationale: The claim gives extreme, specific ratios (100x and 50x) without any jurisdiction, timeframe, or subsidy metric, and no reputable international analyses support such large multipliers. Major data sources (IEA, IMF, OECD) show fossil-fuel and nuclear support remain substantial in many places and that renewable subsidies are significant but not uniformly two orders of magnitude larger than gas/coal or an order of magnitude larger than nuclear. Such comparisons depend heavily on definitions (direct payments, tax expenditures, price supports, or externality valuations) and therefore the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: "Just 400 Americans -- 400 -- have more wealth than half of all Americans combined."
rationale: Multiple independent analyses and media reports comparing the combined net worth of the Forbes '400' to wealth distribution data have found that the 400 richest Americans held more wealth than the bottom 50% of Americans for much of the 2010s. The statement reflects those widely reported comparisons, though it is dependent on the year and methodology used.

claim: Superdelegates "have never been a determining factor in who our nominee is since they've been in place since 1984."
rationale: Superdelegates were introduced in the mid-1980s, but it is incorrect to claim they have 'never' been a determining factor: in multiple close Democratic contests their endorsements affected the perceived delegate math and momentum, and the party enacted 2018 rule changes specifically because superdelegates could be decisive. While they rarely overturned a clear pledged-delegate majority on a first ballot, their potential to decide or tip very close outcomes has been real and recognized by the DNC.

claim: "Barack Obama has consistently voted against tougher penalties for criminals."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and inaccurate. Barack Obama’s record on criminal penalties is mixed: he opposed certain expansions of mandatory minimums and later as president pushed for criminal justice reform (commutations, support for reduced sentencing disparities), but he also supported some crime‑control measures earlier in his career. He did not "consistently" vote against tougher penalties across all contexts.

claim: Democratic lawmakers who voted in favor of short-term spending bills "just voted to deport Dreamers."
rationale: Short-term spending bills (continuing resolutions) typically fund government operations and do not by themselves repeal DACA or order mass deportations. Voting for a CR that funds DHS or border enforcement is not the same as voting to deport Dreamers; explicit statutory changes or administrative directives would be required to terminate DACA protections. While some funding measures can include immigration-related riders that could harm Dreamers, the blanket claim that Democrats who voted for short-term spending "just voted to deport Dreamers" is misleading.

claim: Says Rick Scott "thinks employers should be able to deny women coverage for birth control."
rationale: Rick Scott has publicly opposed the ACA contraceptive mandate and in campaign and media remarks said employers should be able to decide whether to include birth-control coverage in their health plans. Multiple news reports and his own statements characterize his position as allowing employers to deny such coverage under conscience or business-choice grounds.

claim: Under the Arizona immigration law, police are required to check immigration status if someone's "lawn is overgrown" or if a dog is "barking too loudly."
rationale: Arizona's high-profile immigration statute (commonly called SB 1070) requires officers to attempt to determine immigration status only when they have reasonable suspicion that a person is unlawfully present during a lawful stop, arrest, or detention. The law does not specify trivial neighborhood conditions like an overgrown lawn or a barking dog as automatic triggers that legally require an immigration-status check. Claims that those specific minor complaints mandate status checks are inaccurate.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to replace" Obamacare "with a single-payer system."
rationale: Donald Trump has not said he wants to replace Obamacare with a single‑payer system; across his campaign and presidency he expressly opposed 'single‑payer'/'Medicare for All' and promoted market‑based alternatives, tax credits, and private insurance expansions as his replacement plans. Public statements and policy actions from his administration aimed at reducing the ACA and expanding private options rather than creating a single‑payer system.

claim: 40 percent of illegal immigrants "had a visa and then became illegal," mostly because "they changed jobs."
rationale: While some reputable analyses have found that roughly 40–45% of U.S. unauthorized immigrants were once in the country on a visa and later became undocumented (i.e., visa overstays), the assertion that this mostly occurred because they 'changed jobs' is incorrect. Most overstays involve expired tourist, student, or other temporary visas, and job-change issues affect a much smaller subset (temporary work-visa holders).

claim: "Unions don’t have to comply with Obamacare."
rationale: There is no blanket exemption in the Affordable Care Act for labor unions.
