rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that Louisiana formally declined a specific $100 million payment on the grounds that accepting it would legally require changing the state's unemployment law and thereby raise taxes on businesses. Federal unemployment-related funds sometimes carry conditions, but public records and reporting do not support the precise $100 million refusal or the claimed automatic tax increase without further legislative action.

claim: "Under Operation Warp Speed, we’ve pioneered groundbreaking therapies, reducing the fatality rate 85% since April."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes an 85% drop in ‘fatality rate’ solely to Operation Warp Speed. While COVID-19 death rates and case-fatality ratios declined after spring 2020, the reduction is variably estimated and is attributable to multiple factors (expanded testing, younger cases, improved clinical care and public-health measures), not just OWS or its therapies. There is no clear evidence that OWS alone caused an 85% reduction since April.

claim: Ed Gillespie’s "firm even lobbied for five foreign governments, including a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes."
rationale: Public lobbying-disclosure records and contemporary news coverage of Ed Gillespie’s lobbying career do show he represented foreign clients at times, but there is no well-documented evidence that his firm lobbied on behalf of five foreign governments or that it included a dictator later awaiting trial for war crimes. Major fact-checks and media reporting from Gillespie’s campaigns list specific clients and do not corroborate the specific claim as stated.

claim: "Statistics show one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years."
rationale: No reputable data support the claim that one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years. Feline biology (sexual maturity around 5–6 months, ~63-day gestation, typical litter sizes of 3–6) and real-world limits on how many females a single tom can mate with make such an outcome impossible; the figure comes from a flawed exponential-math riddle, not statistics.

claim: A second impeachment means Donald Trump loses his lifetime pension, travel allowance, Secret Service detail, and his ability to run for public office.
rationale: House impeachment alone does not strip a person of pension, travel benefits, Secret Service protection, or automatically bar them from future office. Only a Senate conviction can remove someone from office and the Senate may additionally vote to disqualify them from holding future federal office; pensions and security protections are governed by separate statutes and would not be automatically forfeited without separate legal action or legislation.

claim: Says Marilinda Garcia supports "$150 billion in new taxes."
rationale: I found no clear, documented statement or voting record showing Marilinda Garcia explicitly endorsing a policy described as $150 billion in new taxes. As a GOP politician she has generally opposed tax increases, and the $150 billion figure appears to be an unsupported or out-of-context attack line rather than a verifiable policy position she stated.

claim: "When was the last time you saw a Chevrolet in Japan? It doesn’t exist, folks."
rationale: Chevrolet vehicles do exist in Japan — the brand has been sold there historically and many Chevrolets are present today as imported, used, or enthusiast-owned cars. While General Motors has at times limited or withdrawn official Chevrolet new-car retail operations in certain markets, that does not mean Chevrolets “don’t exist” in Japan at all.

claim: A photo shows a recent White House event was actually filmed at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence provided that a recent White House event photo was filmed at Tyler Perry Studios. White House events are routinely covered by official White House photographers and a broad pool of independent media, and claims that an event was shot elsewhere usually stem from misidentification or digitally altered imagery unless supported by metadata or independent corroboration.

claim: The infant mortality rate is 15 percent higher in states with right-to-work laws.
rationale: There is no widely accepted or robust finding that states with right-to-work laws have infant mortality rates uniformly 15% higher. Empirical studies on right-to-work and health outcomes are mixed, sensitive to model specification, and often show smaller or non-robust associations once socioeconomic and healthcare access factors are controlled for. The specific 15% figure appears to be an overgeneralization not supported as a consensus estimate.

claim: The Obama administration "raised discretionary spending by 24 percent from President George W. Bush's last full-year budget and will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years."
rationale: The claim conflates inconsistent baselines and timeframes. Independent fact-checkers and government budget data show the "24%" increase depends on how discretionary spending is measured (which fiscal years and which accounts are included), and Obama-era deficits were large but did not add more federal debt by October of his second year than Bush added over eight years when using consistent OMB/Treasury measures.

claim: Says Marco Rubio believes the earth is 9,000 years old and that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction; says  Rand Paul believes the earth is 10,000 years old and God removed dinosaurs "to make space for humans."
rationale: There is no credible public record that Marco Rubio said the Earth is 9,000 years old or that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction, nor that Rand Paul said the Earth is 10,000 years old and that God removed dinosaurs 'to make space for humans.' Both have on occasion expressed skepticism about aspects of evolution or supported teaching alternatives, but the specific numeric ages and those dramatic claims are not supported by reputable reporting or documented quotes.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no U.S. Supreme Court decision that flatly ruled public schools "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law." The Court has prohibited government‑sponsored prayer or endorsement of religion (e.g., Engel v. Vitale, Abington v. Schempp) but has allowed neutral, objective academic instruction about religion as part of a secular curriculum. The claim misstates and overgeneralizes First Amendment case law.

claim: Says GOP primary opponents Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham cast a "compromise vote that cost $788 million" in higher electricity costs.
rationale: There is no publicly verifiable evidence tying a specific ‘compromise vote’ by Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham to a $788 million increase in electricity costs. Cost-attribution claims of this kind typically rely on disputed modeling and require identifying the exact bill and independent analyses; that specificity is absent here. Without a clear bill, methodology, and neutral study showing that precise dollar impact, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: The statement is too absolute. Whether a "public option" is funded only by private insurance premiums depends on the specific legislative design: many proposals intend premiums to cover plan costs, but others include taxpayer-funded subsidies, startup grants, government backstops, or use existing public revenue streams. Therefore it is incorrect to assert categorically that public options never use public money.

claim: "Now remember, property taxes went up 70 percent in the 10 years before I became governor."
rationale: The claim omits crucial details (which state, which ten-year period, and whether 'property taxes' means rates, assessed values, or total collections), so it cannot be verified as a factual statement. Without identifying the governor and jurisdiction, a blanket 70% increase in the prior decade is unsubstantiated.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: The claim that Travis Allen “refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens” is not supported by contemporaneous records and reporting. Assembly roll-call records and news coverage from the time show Republicans generally opposed the 2013 driver’s-license bill for undocumented immigrants and Allen was publicly aligned with GOP opposition, not singled out for refusing to join it.

claim: "We passed the toughest gun control law in the United States of America, the SAFE Act."
rationale: The New York SAFE Act (passed in 2013) is widely described as one of the nation's stricter state gun laws, but the categorical claim that it is "the toughest" in the United States is not verifiable. Whether a law is the "toughest" depends on specific metrics (assault‑weapon bans, magazine limits, background checks, licensing, enforcement) and other states such as California, Connecticut, and Massachusetts have comparable or stricter provisions; laws have also changed since 2013. Because the statement is an absolute comparative claim and context-dependent, it is not supportable as a fact.

claim: "At the time that (Medicare Part D) was passed (it) was actually less popular than the Affordable Care Act, according to the polls."
rationale: There is no clear, consistent poll evidence showing Medicare Part D was less popular at its enactment (2003) than the Affordable Care Act was at its enactment (2010). Poll results varied by question wording and timing, but most contemporaneous polls show Part D had at least comparable or higher net support than the ACA did when the ACA was passed, so the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: St. Pete Beach's local version of Amendment 4 resulted in "seemingly endless lawsuits (that) decimated the city's legal budget and forced the city to raise the property tax rate."
rationale: The claim asserts a direct, extreme financial impact (legal budget decimated and a forced property tax increase) tied to St. Pete Beach's local 'Amendment 4.' While local ballot measures can prompt litigation, I am not aware of reliable public records or reporting that confirm lawsuits so completely depleted the city's legal fund and directly forced a tax-rate hike. The statement appears to be an exaggerated causal claim without corroborating municipal budget and court documentation.

claim: "I’ve been against that war in Afghanistan from the very beginning."
rationale: The statement as presented is unverifiable because no speaker, date, or which phase of the Afghanistan conflict is specified. Determining whether someone was "against that war from the very beginning" requires checking that individual's contemporaneous public statements, votes, and records around the 2001 invasion and immediate aftermath; absent that evidence the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs.
rationale: Mitt Romney co‑founded and led Bain Capital, a private equity firm that invested in hundreds of companies over decades; many of those firms expanded or operated businesses that employed people. Contemporary reporting and economic analysis of Bain investments document both job gains at some portfolio companies and job losses at others, so the blanket assertion that his investments created "zero jobs" is inconsistent with the historical record.

claim: "Congress has cut funding, has slashed funding, for veterans' benefits over these last years."
rationale: Overall federal appropriations and veterans' benefit payments have trended upward in recent years; Congress has generally increased the Department of Veterans Affairs budget and mandatory benefit outlays rather than broadly "slashing" them. Although some specific line items or proposed cuts have occurred, the broad claim that Congress has cut veterans' benefits over the last years is misleading.

claim: Tim Kaine "made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row."
rationale: The claim implies an authoritative, consecutive four-year No.1 ranking attributable to Tim Kaine. While Virginia has topped some business-friendly state lists in individual years, there is no clear, single authoritative ranking showing Virginia was named "best state for business" four years in a row during Kaine’s governorship, and such rankings vary by publisher and methodology. The statement overstates both the consistency of rankings and Kaine’s sole attribution for them.

claim: Says "the mandate is 71 times that a child’s body will be injected with a disease" for immunizations.
rationale: The statement is incorrect: vaccine mandates do not result in a child being "injected with a disease" 71 times. Vaccines contain killed, inactivated, attenuated, or purified antigen components designed to provoke immunity, not to cause the full disease, and routine childhood immunization schedules involve far fewer injections or doses than 71 and do not equate to being injected with active disease each time.

claim: Says Madison and Milwaukee County both carry sanctuary status for illegal immigrants and released undocumented immigrants who have committed multiple crimes including sexual assault of a child
rationale: The claim overstates and combines different facts. While the City of Madison and Milwaukee/Milwaukee County have policies that limit local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement in some circumstances, they are not blanket "sanctuary" jurisdictions that categorically release people accused of serious crimes; routine criminal-release decisions depend on local prosecutors, judges and custodial status. There is no verifiable, general evidence that both jurisdictions systematically released undocumented immigrants who had committed multiple crimes including the sexual assault of a child as a matter of policy.

claim: "Twenty-five percent of our kids in foster care are there because their parents are involved in drugs."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute fact but lacks timeframe and jurisdiction. U.S. federal child-welfare data (AFCARS) show parental drug abuse is a common reason for foster-care entry and in some years/state samples accounts for roughly one-quarter of entries, but the percentage varies by year, state, and whether drug involvement is listed as the primary reason or a contributing factor, so a blanket "25%" claim without context is misleading.

claim: "More people without health care since George Bush took office; more children in poverty since George Bush took office."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute statement but depends on the exact timeframe and definitions used. U.S. Census and health statistics show that counts and rates of the uninsured and of children in poverty fluctuated during George W. Bush’s tenure (2001–2009), and simple “more” statements are not robustly supported without specifying start/end years and population measures. Because the evidence is mixed and sensitive to measurement choices, the blanket claim is not reliably true as stated.

claim: "PEDOPHILIA is now LEGAL in CALIFORNIA. Now a 21 year old can have sex with an 11 year old, and not be listed on the sex registry as a sex offender."
rationale: California has not legalized sexual activity between adults and children; sex between a 21‑year‑old and an 11‑year‑old would be criminal. State law (e.g., Penal Code 261.5 and 288) criminalizes sexual intercourse and lewd acts with minors, and convictions for such offenses typically trigger sex‑offender registration under Penal Code 290.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton left the country in response to any Mueller indictment; Mueller did not charge Clinton and the widely reported indictments targeted Trump associates (e.g., Manafort, Flynn, Cohen, Stone). Public reporting and her documented appearances did not show her fleeing the U.S. when indictments were announced.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that a Portland year-long composting pilot involved exactly 2,000 households and that 87% reported satisfaction. While Portland has run curbside composting pilots and surveys reporting high satisfaction, I could not confirm these exact figures from a reliable source and similar municipal summaries show varying sample sizes and satisfaction rates. Because the precise numbers are unverified, the claim as stated is judged false.

claim: The federal health care law tells "the American people precisely what type of coverage they have to have."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act sets minimum standards (minimum essential coverage and required categories of 'essential health benefits') but does not specify exactly which individual plan each American must carry. Consumers and employers choose from plans that meet those standards, and coverage details vary by plan and state; moreover the federal individual mandate penalty has been reduced to zero at the federal level since 2019.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: The claim is misleading: modern cannabis has been intensively bred and hybridized for higher THC, but it is not broadly 'genetically modified' in the sense of transgenic GMO plants. It is true that average THC potency in consumer cannabis has risen substantially since the 1970s (from roughly low single-digit percentages to averages in the double digits, with many strains and concentrates much higher).

claim: Colorado saw "increased incidents of emergency room visits by young people" and "increased incidents of driving while under the influence of marijuana" following the legalization of recreational pot.
rationale: Multiple state and federal reports and peer-reviewed studies documented increases in emergency department visits and pediatric cannabis exposures in Colorado after recreational legalization and commercialization. Similarly, law‑enforcement and traffic data showed more drivers testing positive for THC and increases in cannabis‑involved crashes or fatalities, though detection does not by itself prove impairment.

claim: "Over 81 percent of the babies that are born at LBJ Hospital right here in Houston are born of women who are not here legally."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available evidence and is implausibly high. Hospitals and birth records do not record immigration status, and demographic and public-health data for Houston show far lower shares of births to foreign-born or undocumented mothers than 81%.

claim: Says detained immigrant parents separated from their children at the border are being charged "as much as $8 a minute to call their children."
rationale: Reporting and oversight of phone services in immigrant detention show rates vary widely but do not substantiate a general claim that parents were charged "as much as $8 a minute" to call their separated children. Most documented rates for family detention and immigration facilities were far lower for domestic calls (often well under $2/min) though international or exotic collect-call arrangements and added fees can drive higher totals in rare cases.

claim: A study "from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard, and Dartmouth concluded that Medicaid’s value to its beneficiaries is significantly lower than the actual cost of the program."
rationale: I find no reputable, widely cited study jointly from MIT, Harvard, and Dartmouth that concludes Medicaid’s value to its beneficiaries is significantly lower than the program’s cost. While there are academic analyses that try to compare beneficiaries’ willingness-to-pay or measured benefits to program spending, such results are institution- and method-specific and do not support the blanket claim as stated. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute research and oversimplifies complex, contested measures of ‘value.’

claim: Says the U.S. is developing an "antivirus" that includes a chip to track your movement.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that U.S. public-health agencies or drug manufacturers are developing antiviral medicines or vaccines that contain covert location-tracking chips. Technical realities (GPS chips require power, antennas, and infrastructure; passive RFID only works at very short range) and repeated denials from regulators make the claim implausible and consistent with earlier misinformation about vaccines.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The claim is an absolute denial that no tax increases exist in 'this debt limit bill.' Major debt‑limit or omnibus agreements routinely include revenue provisions, fee changes, enforcement offsets, or expirations that affect government receipts, so an unqualified 'no tax increases. Period.' statement is not supportable without examining the full text. Blanket denials are therefore unreliable.

claim: Says "I was part of the second class to integrate Berkeley, California, public schools."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it names no person, year, or specific Berkeley school and claims a precise ordinal fact ('second class') that would require contemporaneous records. Berkeley school desegregation was a gradual, district-level process and there is no widely known documented list that would support identifying a single 'second class' to integrate. Without concrete identifiers or supporting evidence, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says President Barack Obama initially said the national health-care mandate isn't a tax, but his administration now says it is a tax.
rationale: President Obama publicly and repeatedly denied that the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate was a tax in 2009, but during the Supreme Court litigation (NFIB v. Sebelius) the Justice Department argued the payment functions as a tax and the Court upheld it under Congress's taxing power. The shift reflects the administration's legal characterization for defense of the law in court.

claim: Dr. Anthony "Fauci told us there’s nothing to worry about. That’s his quote, ‘There’s nothing to worry about.’"
rationale: There is no reliable record of Dr. Anthony Fauci uttering the exact phrase “There’s nothing to worry about.” While Fauci did make early reassurances in 2020 that the immediate risk to the general U.S. public was low and said people should not panic, those comments are not the same as the quoted categorical statement attributed here.

claim: "We don't know anything about Hillary in terms of religion. Now, she's been in the public eye for years and years, and yet there's no — there's nothing out there."
rationale: Hillary (Hillary Rodham Clinton) has a documented religious affiliation and public statements about faith: she has long been identified as a United Methodist and has discussed religion in interviews and speeches. Biographies, news coverage, and her own statements contradict the claim that 'there's nothing out there' about her religion.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: State and federal wildfire data and statements from Arizona forestry authorities consistently report that the large majority of wildfire ignitions in Arizona are caused by human activities, and public messaging often cites roughly 90% as an estimate. The exact share varies by year and by whether one counts all reported fires or only wildland/unplanned wildfires, but 'about 90%' is a commonly accurate approximation.

claim: Virginia "spends less per student today than we did in 2008."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about whether it means nominal dollars, inflation‑adjusted (real) dollars, and whether it counts state-only versus total (state+local+federal) K–12 spending. In nominal terms Virginia’s reported per‑pupil expenditures have trended up since 2008; a claim that spending is simply "less per student today than in 2008" is therefore misleading without specifying adjustments and funding sources. If someone meant inflation‑adjusted state‑only spending the statement might be contested, but as stated it is not supported.

claim: "Illegal immigration costs state taxpayers over $3 billion every year."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated: estimates of the fiscal impact of unauthorized immigrants vary widely depending on methodology, which costs (state vs. federal) are counted, and whether taxes paid are netted out. Credible analyses produce a broad range of results, and there is no consensus figure that unambiguously shows state taxpayers collectively pay 'over $3 billion every year' as a uniform fact. Some advocacy groups report multi‑billion dollar costs using specific assumptions, but those estimates are contested and often include federal or local costs or exclude tax contributions.

claim: "Tell me what Madeleine Albright’s position was on the War on Iraq. I wouldn’t be surprised if she supported it."
rationale: Madeleine Albright publicly supported removing Saddam Hussein and expressed support for the 2003 Iraq invasion at the time, saying the world was better without Saddam. She subsequently acknowledged errors in intelligence and postwar planning and voiced regret about the war's consequences.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin's record includes "opposing harsher punishments for criminals who commit violent crimes near schools."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Tammy Baldwin's record includes a general position of opposing harsher punishments specifically for people who commit violent crimes near schools. Baldwin's record emphasizes criminal‑justice reform (reducing mandatory minimums, reentry programs) and also supports child and school safety measures, but I could not find a definitive vote or public statement where she opposed enhanced penalties for violent crimes committed near schools.

claim: Says "over 40 percent of recent county bonds are for Precinct One, northeast Travis County," because he "is quick to identify projects that help make the East Side a desirable place to live."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that over 40% of recent Travis County bond proceeds were allocated to Precinct One; county bond funding is typically distributed across multiple precincts and projects, and the claim gives no timeframe or source. Without a specific bond package and allocation breakdown, the assertion is unsubstantiated and unlikely given usual county budgeting practices.

claim: Says he and President Barack Obama have the same position on gay marriage.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it does not identify who 'he' refers to, so there is no way to confirm that person's views match President Barack Obama's. Obama publicly announced support for same-sex marriage in 2012, but whether another individual holds the same position depends on that person's specific public statements or record, which are not given. Due to this missing context the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Says Democrats "have issued more subpoenas than they’ve passed bills."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: across recent congressional sessions the number of bills passed (often in the hundreds when including House or Senate actions) far exceeds the number of subpoenas issued (which are issued selectively by committees and are typically dozens at most). There is no clear evidence that Democratic lawmakers collectively issued more subpoenas than they passed bills.

claim: They passed the flu off as COVID-19, and "they’re going to do the same thing with monkeypox and shingles."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that public health authorities or other actors deliberately 'passed the flu off as COVID-19' as a systematic deception. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, monkeypox (orthopoxvirus), and shingles (varicella‑zoster) are distinct pathogens that are distinguishable by specific laboratory tests and surveillance systems, and reporting data and clinical criteria treated them separately. While testing shortages and occasional misdiagnoses occurred early in the pandemic, that is not the same as an organized effort to relabel diseases, nor is there evidence such a scheme is planned for monkeypox or shingles.

claim: "Voting in the wrong precinct led to over 14,000 registered voters statewide to lose their vote in 2008."
rationale: The claim gives a precise statewide number without naming the state and I found no corroborating, widely reported evidence that in 2008 more than 14,000 registered voters in any single state lost their vote specifically because they voted in the wrong precinct. While provisional/wrong-precinct issues did lead to some uncounted ballots in 2008, available election summaries and reporting do not substantiate this exact, large statewide figure as stated.

claim: "The 90 percent statistic of supporting background checks, that's been debunked."
rationale: Numerous reputable national polls over many years (Pew, Gallup, AP-NORC and others) have repeatedly found very high public support—often around 85–90%—for background checks on gun purchases. While critics have pointed out that support can fall when questions include trade-offs or specific policy details, those methodological critiques do not amount to a blanket debunking of the widely reported ~90% support figure.

claim: "Before the pandemic, just over 40,000 were on continuing UI claims. Now, there are well over 100,000 on state or federal UI benefits."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about jurisdiction and timing and does not match U.S. national data: before the COVID-19 pandemic continuing UI claims nationally were in the millions, not just over 40,000. While some individual states or small jurisdictions might have had ~40,000 continuing claims pre-pandemic and could currently have over 100,000 on state or federal programs, the statement as written is misleading and unverifiable without specifying which state and what dates are meant.

claim: The Paul Ryan budget proposal would "privatize Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals repeatedly called for replacing Medicare's guaranteed defined-benefit entitlement with a 'premium-support' or voucher-like system that would provide fixed federal subsidies and encourage beneficiaries to purchase private insurance. That proposal shifts much of financing and risk onto private plans and individual beneficiaries, which is commonly described as privatizing Medicare.

claim: "Pre-existing conditions are covered under my (health care) plan."
rationale: This statement is not universally true. Whether pre-existing conditions are covered depends on the specific plan and applicable laws; for example, in the U.S. most ACA-compliant marketplace and employer plans cannot deny coverage or charge more for pre-existing conditions, but some plans (such as short-term limited-duration plans or certain non-ACA plans) may not provide those protections.

claim: "President Trump marshalled the full resources of our federal government from the outset. He directed us to forge a seamless partnership with governors across America in both political parties."
rationale: Contemporaneous evidence from the early COVID-19 response shows the federal government did not immediately marshal full resources or create a seamless partnership with governors. Many governors reported shortages of PPE and ventilators, states competed with each other and with federal procurement, and critics noted delays and limited early use of federal authorities such as the Defense Production Act.

claim: "Within a few years, we will be spending more on interest payments than on national security."
rationale: The claim is too general and presented as a definite near-term outcome but lacks a specified country and precise timeframe. Interest costs have risen and in some projections for particular countries (under certain assumptions) they could approach or exceed defense/national-security budgets, but this is not a universal or guaranteed "within a few years" outcome and depends heavily on interest rates, debt levels, fiscal choices, and how "national security" is defined.

claim: "In 1972, we had a 179,000 human beings in jail in this country. Today, it's 2.3-million, and 70 percent of them are black, African-American."
rationale: The broad claim mixes accurate and inaccurate elements. It is true that the incarcerated population rose from the low hundreds of thousands in the early 1970s to roughly 2.2–2.3 million in recent years, but the 1972 figure of 179,000 is lower than common historical estimates for total prisoners, and the statement that 70% of those currently incarcerated are Black is incorrect — Black people are overrepresented but constitute roughly one-third to two-fifths of the prison population depending on the year, not 70%.

claim: "We’ve got close to 7 million Americans who have access to health care for the first time because of Medicaid expansion."
rationale: Independent enrollment and research estimates show Medicaid expansion has led to substantially more than 7 million people gaining coverage overall; most summaries put cumulative expansion enrollment in the roughly 10–12 million range depending on the year. Counts also vary by methodology and some enrollees previously had other coverage, so saying 'close to 7 million Americans who have access for the first time' understates the cumulative impact and conflates enrollment with first-time access.

claim: "Obama has proposed 442 tax hikes since taking office."
rationale: The '442 tax hikes' figure is a misleading aggregate that counts many proposed line-items, fee changes, loophole closings, and budget proposals as separate 'tax hikes,' including measures that were never enacted. Independent fact-checkers and analyses conclude Obama did propose some tax increases but not 442 distinct, implemented tax hikes as claimed.

claim: "Middle-class income rose to a record level in 2017 as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans."
rationale: This is misleading: while Census data show 2017 median household income was at a nominal high, the increase from 2016 was not statistically significant and 'middle-class income' is not precisely defined. Moreover, income gains in 2017 were uneven across households, so saying the strong economy 'lifted the fortunes of more Americans' overstates the broadness of the improvement.

claim: The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine contains an "undisclosed ingredient. … How is informed consent possible?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine contains any undisclosed ingredient; its active ingredient (mRNA) and all excipients are listed in regulatory EUA/approval fact sheets and product labels. Regulatory agencies require disclosure of ingredients and Pfizer/BioNTech have published the vaccine's ingredient list and safety data publicly, so the claim that an ingredient is undisclosed is incorrect.

claim: "Some patients who are on transplant lists for kidney or other organs are being dropped from the list simply because they are shown as a licensed card holder" for medical marijuana.
rationale: Transplant centers set eligibility rules and many consider cannabis use (including medical marijuana) when evaluating candidates; because cannabis remains federally illegal and can raise concerns about infection risk, medication interactions, and post‑transplant adherence, some programs have removed or refused to list patients who are medical cannabis card holders. Multiple news reports and case accounts document patients being denied or dropped for documented medical marijuana use or card possession.

claim: "The president came in and campaigned against me 12 times."
rationale: The claim is unverified as presented because it gives no named president, timeframe, or target, and I find no specific, corroborated record showing a president campaigned against the unnamed speaker exactly 12 times. Without identifiable parties and dates this precise numeric assertion cannot be confirmed. Given the ambiguity and lack of supporting evidence, it should be treated as not proven.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This claim is false. There is no credible evidence or official Pepsi admission that an employee contaminated products with HIV/AIDS; Pepsi has denied such stories and the allegation matches a long-running hoax. Public health experts also note HIV does not survive long outside the body and is not transmitted by canned beverages, making the claim biologically implausible.

claim: "The platform of the Republican Party says deport everybody and to hell with it."
rationale: The official Republican Party platform advocates strict immigration enforcement and removal of unlawfully present immigrants, but it does not use the crude wording 'deport everybody and to hell with it.' The claim is a vulgar, hyperbolic paraphrase rather than an accurate quotation of the party platform.

claim: The Atlanta Beltline paid nearly $3.5 million for less than a quarter-acre.
rationale: I could not find a verifiable, specific public record or reputable news report that confirms the Atlanta BeltLine paid nearly $3.5 million for a parcel smaller than a quarter-acre. While the BeltLine has made several high-profile land purchases and some small lots have drawn criticism for high prices, the exact figure and size in this claim are not corroborated by available reporting. Without a specific property, date, or source, the assertion as stated cannot be confirmed.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Multiple epidemiological and clinical studies during the emergence of Omicron showed it generally caused less severe disease, lower hospitalization rates, and lower mortality than the Delta variant; it is not supported that Omicron is five times more 'toxic' or has a higher mortality rate than Delta. The claim contradicts the bulk of published public health data, though outcomes can vary with population immunity and specific subvariants.

claim: Says that in 1770 "British parliament banned lipstick, saying it had the power to seduce men into marriage, which was classified as witchcraft."
rationale: There is no historical record of Parliament passing a law in 1770 that banned lipstick or classified it as witchcraft. British legal changes concerning witchcraft occurred earlier (notably the Witchcraft Act 1735) and while cosmetics were socially stigmatized, they were not outlawed by Parliament in 1770.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it "can't build a factory in a non-union state."
rationale: The NLRB did not tell Boeing it "can't build a factory in a non-union state." While the Board has found in past cases that Boeing engaged in unlawful anti-union motivation related to moving work (and has ordered remedies such as bargaining, notices, or make-whole relief), it does not have authority to prohibit a company from opening or operating a plant in a particular state.

claim: "Trudeau's foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics which makes mechanic lipids for Pfizer."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any ‘Trudeau’ charitable foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics. The Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation is a grant-making charity, not a corporate investor, and public information about Acuitas shows it is a privately held biotech founded by scientists and investors without any documented 40% stake held by a Trudeau-linked foundation. While Acuitas has developed lipid nanoparticle technology that has been licensed or collaborated on with vaccine makers, the specific ownership claim is unsupported.

claim: "Iowa, for good reason, for constitutional reasons, for reasons related to the Lord, should be the first caucus and primary."
rationale: The statement is a prescriptive opinion, not an objective fact, and there is no constitutional requirement that Iowa be the first caucus or primary. The order of nominating contests is set by state parties, the national party rules, and state laws, and has changed in the past. Invoking "reasons related to the Lord" as a legal basis would be a religious justification that the U.S. government cannot constitutionally adopt under the Establishment Clause.

claim: Under Hillary Clinton, State Department "officials were sending official thank-yous to people who gave to the Clinton Foundation."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and later fact-checks found State Department personnel did send official acknowledgements and thank-you messages to individuals and organizations who had given to Clinton Foundation projects while Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State. These were documented in emails and correspondence released or reported on during investigations. The existence of such thank-yous is supported by multiple news and fact-checking accounts.

claim: U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz was the lone vote in the House against an anti-human trafficking bill.
rationale: I am not aware of any authoritative roll-call where Rep. Matt Gaetz was the single lone House vote against an anti-human trafficking bill. High-profile anti-trafficking measures in recent Congresses passed overwhelmingly and news outlets have not reported Gaetz as the sole dissenter. Without a specific bill or date, the blanket claim is not supported by available voting records and media coverage.

claim: "New evidence ties COVID-19 creation to research funded by Fauci"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that Anthony Fauci funded the creation of SARS-CoV-2. Public records show NIH/NIAID provided grants for coronavirus research (e.g., to EcoHealth Alliance) focused on surveillance and basic research, and multiple fact-checks and official statements report no proof that those funds were used to engineer the virus or that Fauci funded its creation.

claim: Says David Jolly’s former firm lobbied "for hundreds of millions (of dollars) for a dictator in Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that David Jolly’s former firm undertook a lobbying effort to obtain “hundreds of millions” of dollars on behalf of any Pakistani dictator. Such work would typically show up in public lobbying/FARA filings and in news reporting; no reliable records or reputable news stories support this specific allegation tied to Jolly’s firm.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and misleading elements. Trump did win West Virginia by roughly 42 percentage points in 2016 (often described as “almost 43”), and West Virginia was among his strongest states by vote share in 2016, but whether it is the single strongest depends on the election year. The statement that "he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval" is vague and not consistently supported by state-level approval polling, which has varied over time.

claim: "Whales live as long at SeaWorld" as they do in the wild.
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and population monitoring show that killer whales (the species most commonly kept at SeaWorld) have substantially shorter average lifespans in captivity than in the wild; wild female orcas commonly live into their 50s–80s while many captive individuals die much younger. While longevity can vary by species and facility, the best available evidence contradicts the claim that whales live as long at SeaWorld as they do in the wild.

claim: According to a national survey, transit "ridership" among people age 16 to 34 increased 40 percent between 2001 and 2009.
rationale: I could not find a credible national survey that exactly supports a 40% increase in transit ridership for 16–34 year olds between 2001 and 2009. While some datasets and reports show increases in young adult transit use in certain cities or by certain metrics, the claim presents a precise nationwide percentage without a cited source and likely conflates different measures (e.g., trips, mode share, or riders).

claim: "In this country, we have a 25 percent dropout rate."
rationale: The statement is unverified and too vague: it does not specify which country, which education level (e.g., secondary or tertiary), or which timeframe and definition of ‘dropout rate’ is being used. Dropout rates vary substantially across countries and by measurement method, so asserting a 25% rate without context is unsupported.

claim: Says Donald Trump indicted Amy Coney Barrett.
rationale: This is false: a U.S. president cannot indict someone and there are no credible reports, charges, or court filings indicating Amy Coney Barrett has been indicted. Indictments are issued by prosecutors or grand juries, and public records and major news outlets show no such action involving Barrett.

claim: Says no one has died from the coronavirus in the United States.
rationale: This claim is false. The United States has recorded COVID-19 deaths since early 2020, and official sources documented hundreds of thousands to over a million deaths attributable to the coronavirus. State health departments, the CDC, and multiple peer-reviewed analyses and news reports corroborate these fatalities.

claim: "Republicans are attempting to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s Presidential Ballot in 2012."
rationale: There was no credible, party-backed Republican effort to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s 2012 presidential ballot. While isolated fringe lawsuits and 'birther' activists in several states attempted challenges to Obama’s eligibility around that time, these were not mainstream Republican Party actions and were unsuccessful.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "put out a $297 million contract to a vendor to show him how to hire Border Patrol. So, the first payment they made was $14.8 million. You know how many Border Patrol they hired with $14.8 million? Two."
rationale: I could find no credible evidence that President Trump issued a single $297 million contract to a vendor 'to show him how to hire Border Patrol' with a first payment of $14.8 million that resulted in only two hires. The specific dollar amounts and the claim that only two Border Patrol agents were hired as a result are not supported by mainstream reporting or publicly available federal contract records, and the numbers are implausible given typical government hiring and contracting practices.

claim: The ACLU didn't call for an investigation (of the Newark police department), they called for an immediate federal monitor.
rationale: Public ACLU statements concerning the Newark Police Department historically have asked for a federal civil‑rights investigation by the DOJ and, where warranted, appointment of a federal monitor; it is unlikely they expressly rejected an investigation while calling only for an immedate federal monitor. The wording in the claim omits the common dual demand for investigation plus oversight found in ACLU press releases.

claim: Say Apple’s Tim Cook "will not do business with Indiana."
rationale: Tim Cook publicly criticized Indiana's 2015 Religious Freedom Restoration Act and spoke against discrimination, but there is no reliable record of him declaring that he or Apple "will not do business with Indiana." Apple continued to operate and serve customers in the state, and Cook's statements were about opposing discriminatory laws rather than announcing a business boycott.

claim: "As chairman of the City Colleges, I cut millions in waste and we cut property taxes."
rationale: The claim mixes two different responsibilities and lacks context (no named person or dates). Governing boards of city college systems control college budgets and can cut expenses, but they do not directly set or 'cut' municipal property tax rates — those are set by elected city/county/state taxing authorities. I find no specific, verifiable evidence attributing both a multi-million-dollar waste reduction and a reduction in property taxes to a City Colleges chair as stated.

claim: Says "we brought crime rate down by 30 percent" when he was mayor of Dallas.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as stated: no specific mayor or timeframe is given, and publicly available Dallas crime data and reporting do not clearly show a uniform 30% reduction attributable to a single mayoral tenure. Without a named speaker, date range, or specified crime measure (violent crime, property crime, total index), the assertion cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: Says that according to a report, "the tech sector now drives more than one-quarter of Austin’s economy."
rationale: There is no clear, widely cited report showing the tech sector accounts for more than one-quarter of Austin’s entire economy. While technology is a major and rapidly growing part of Austin’s economy, most published measures (employment share, sector GDP) put tech below or around the low-to-mid 20% range, and some reports use different metrics (job growth, payroll) that can be misconstrued as a >25% share.

claim: "Coroner saying George Floyd died of drug overdose, not police brutality."
rationale: The Hennepin County Medical Examiner ruled George Floyd's death a homicide, listing cause as cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression. While the examiner noted the presence of fentanyl and methamphetamine, the official finding did not attribute death to a drug overdose and independent autopsy findings and trial evidence supported asphyxia from restraint as the primary factor.

claim: Says "city leadership is threatening to lay off police and emergency services personnel to balance the budget."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it names no specific city, date, or source and thus cannot be confirmed. Threats to lay off police or emergency personnel do sometimes occur in municipal budget debates, but without a cited statement, official budget document, or reputable news report this particular assertion cannot be treated as factual.

claim: "Whole of Italy goes into quarantine."
rationale: In response to the COVID-19 outbreak the Italian government issued a nationwide decree on March 9, 2020 extending lockdown/quarantine restrictions to the entire country, requiring people to stay at home except for essential reasons. Describing the situation as the "whole of Italy goes into quarantine" accurately reflects that government action and its nationwide effect at that time.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted to deport" young people known as Dreamers.
rationale: The claim is imprecise: there is no clear single roll-call where Marco Rubio cast a vote explicitly labeled 'to deport' DACA recipients. Rubio has opposed many legislative protections for Dreamers and supported stricter immigration enforcement, but that is different from a direct vote that literally ordered their deportation. Without a specific bill or vote cited, the assertion is misleading.

claim: "The New START treaty was passed despite significant concerns among some people in the State and Defense Departments."
rationale: New START was negotiated and ratified (Senate ratification in December 2010) even though a number of officials and staff in the Defense and State Departments voiced reservations about verification, impacts on missile defense and force posture. Those internal concerns were documented in public reporting and raised during congressional debate, but senior leadership nevertheless endorsed and completed the treaty process.

claim: "...the earth moves closer to the sun every year – you know the rotation of the earth. We’re moving closer to the sun."
rationale: This is incorrect: the Earth's daily rotation about its axis does not drive a steady inward spiral toward the Sun. Earth's distance from the Sun varies seasonally (perihelion/aphelion), and long-term secular changes are extremely small and governed by orbital mechanics, solar mass loss, and gravitational perturbations — overall not a yearly movement steadily closer.

claim: Obamacare premiums "have gone up 160 percent in West Virginia in 4 yrs."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported as a general statewide fact. Public analyses and fact-checks have found that changes in Obamacare premiums depend on the specific plan, metal tier, and benchmark chosen and that no consistent statewide benchmark premium in West Virginia increased by 160% over a recent four-year span; large percentage increases have been reported for some individual plans but are not representative of overall premiums or consumer costs once subsidies are considered.

claim: "Some of the men serving in the (Afghan) armed forces have never driven a vehicle before."
rationale: Multiple credible reports and assessments of the Afghan armed forces over the past two decades note that many recruits came from rural areas with limited exposure to civilian vehicles and low literacy, and that formal driver training was not universal; as a result, some servicemen had never driven a vehicle. The claim is plausible and supported by consistent reporting about skill gaps in the Afghan security forces.

claim: President Obama has "the worst ratings of any president at the end of his first year."
rationale: This is incorrect. Historical presidential approval polling shows several presidents finished their first year with lower approval ratings than Barack Obama did at the end of his first year. Therefore Obama did not have the worst first-year ratings on record.

claim: "TSA WILL ACCEPT DRIVERS PRIV CARDS FOR ID AT THE AIRPORT"
rationale: Most "driver's privilege" or nonstandard driver cards issued for individuals not eligible for regular driver's licenses are not REAL ID–compliant and are explicitly marked "NOT FOR FEDERAL IDENTIFICATION," so they are generally not accepted by TSA as proof of identity for boarding commercial flights. Only state IDs that meet REAL ID standards (or other accepted federal documents like a passport) are accepted by TSA for domestic air travel when enforcement is in effect.

claim: "It costs a hell of a lot more money to put somebody in jail than send them to the University of Virginia."
rationale: The claim is vague and hyperbolic. While many U.S. jurisdictions do spend tens of thousands of dollars per incarcerated person per year and those annual incarceration costs can exceed a single year of in‑state tuition and room at public universities, whether it is "a hell of a lot more" than sending someone to the University of Virginia depends on what costs and timeframe are compared (annual incarceration cost vs annual tuition vs total degree cost, and in‑state vs out‑of‑state tuition). Without a clear metric the blanket statement is not reliably true.

claim: Says Bill Clinton "spent $3 billion and got nothing. And (North Korea) started making nuclear weapons a day later."
rationale: This misstates the 1994 Agreed Framework. The Clinton administration negotiated a deal that froze North Korea's plutonium program and involved multilateral commitments (including construction of light-water reactors and energy assistance) with cost estimates that vary and were not a single $3 billion US outlay. North Korea did not "start making nuclear weapons a day later" — DPRK nuclear activities resumed years later after the collapse of the agreement in the early 2000s.

claim: Obama "says he'll raise taxes on electricity."
rationale: There is no clear contemporaneous record of President Barack Obama explicitly saying he would 'raise taxes on electricity.' He supported climate and energy policies (e.g., cap-and-trade discussions, emissions regulations) that critics argued would raise electricity prices, but claiming he said he would directly tax electricity misrepresents those proposals.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme: it is a government-run social insurance program financed primarily by payroll taxes and statutory trust funds, with benefits defined by law and administered transparently. A Ponzi scheme involves fraudulent promises of high returns, concealment, and private enrichment; Social Security has no secret operator diverting funds and is backed by Congressional taxing authority. While the system is pay‑as‑you‑go and faces long‑term financing challenges, those fiscal issues do not make it a fraud.

claim: "Ted Cruz defended a Chinese company that stole an invention from an American inventor."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Ted Cruz personally defended a Chinese company accused of stealing an American inventor's invention. While Cruz practiced law before his Senate career, public records and reporting do not document him taking on such a defense, and no high-profile case tying him directly to that allegation has been substantiated.

claim: "CA inmate pregnant after being forced to share prison with transgender ‘woman.’"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting or official confirmation that a California inmate became pregnant after being forced to share a cell with a transgender woman. Similar viral claims have been investigated and debunked, and California Department of Corrections housing decisions are handled case-by-case rather than by blanket forced placements; a high-profile incident of this kind would have corroborating news or official records.

claim: "It’s been proven over and over again Medicaid has the worst outcomes in the industrialized world as far as the quality of health care."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad assertion not supported by the evidence. Research on Medicaid shows mixed results: for some measures and conditions Medicaid enrollees have similar outcomes to privately insured patients, while for others they experience worse access or outcomes, but there is no consensus or repeated proof that Medicaid produces the worst quality outcomes among all industrialized countries. Cross-country comparisons are also inappropriate without adjusting for population differences and social determinants of health.

claim: Jason Carter supports using Georgia tax dollars to promote Obamacare
rationale: During his 2014 campaign for Georgia governor Jason Carter publicly said he would use state resources to help enroll Georgians in the Affordable Care Act marketplace and to support Medicaid expansion, statements opponents summarized as using tax dollars to "promote Obamacare." Those campaign remarks and debate answers make clear he backed state-funded outreach/enrollment assistance related to the ACA.

claim: "We didn't go out and take" information from the Hillary Clinton campaign.
rationale: The statement as presented is too vague to verify — it omits who 'we' refers to, when this occurred, and what 'take' means (copy, hack, acquire legally, etc.). Because the claim lacks necessary context and there is no clear evidence confirming a universal denial across all actors, I classify it as false as stated. Specific investigations of 2016-era campaigns showed various data acquisitions and transfers, so an unqualified denial is not verifiable.

claim: "The president and vice president can't be from the same state."
rationale: The Constitution does not categorically prohibit the president and vice president from being from the same state. The Twelfth Amendment requires that electors cast at least one of their votes for someone who is not an inhabitant of the elector’s state, which can create practical electoral issues but is not an absolute ban on same-state tickets.

claim: "Our children do not spend any time in school learning about our own U.S. Constitution."
rationale: Public school curricula in the United States routinely include instruction on the U.S. Constitution as part of history and civics courses; many states mandate civics or U.S. history standards that explicitly cover the Constitution. While depth and timing vary by grade and district, the blanket statement that children spend no time learning about the Constitution is contradicted by standard K–12 curricula.

claim: "John McCain said...in December he was surprised there was a subprime mortgage problem."
rationale: I could not find corroborating evidence that John McCain made a statement along the lines of being surprised there was a subprime mortgage problem 'in December.' McCain did comment on the housing and credit problems during 2007–2008, but the specific quoted claim appears to be a vague or misattributed paraphrase without a reliable contemporaneous source. Given the lack of a verifiable transcript or news report of that exact remark, the claim is likely false or misleading.

claim: European allies "pay us $2.5 billion a year to keep our forces there. It would cost us more money to bring the troops home than to keep them in Europe."
rationale: The claim mixes misleading accounting and an unproven cost comparison. NATO allies do provide some host‑nation support and reimbursements for specific expenses, but they do not collectively 'pay us $2.5 billion a year' as a direct fee to keep U.S. forces in Europe, and the U.S. pays the lion's share of basing and personnel costs. The assertion that returning troops would cost more than staying is speculative and not supported by publicly available, detailed Pentagon cost estimates comparing full withdrawal versus continued basing.

claim: "Corrupt political bosses. Money laundering. Fraud. It’s just another day at the office for Vin Gopal."
rationale: There is no public record of Vin Gopal being convicted of money laundering, fraud, or operating as a corrupt political boss. The statement reads like a broad, unproven political charge rather than a factual summary of proven criminal conduct. Without criminal convictions or credible, substantiated findings, labeling routine behavior as organized corruption is not supported by available evidence.

claim: During his time as House speaker, "unemployment came down from 5.6 percent to under 4 (percent)."
rationale: The claim, as stated, is not verifiable because it fails to identify which House speaker or the exact date range. Different speakers presided over periods with different unemployment trajectories; while under one speaker (Paul Ryan, 2015–2019) unemployment did fall from roughly mid-5% to below 4% by 2018, the precise start/end months and rates matter. Without that context the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "Moderna patent uncovers horror nanocensor contained in bioweapon."
rationale: The claim conflates a patent filing with proof of a deployed "horror nanocensor" bioweapon. Moderna's patents publicly describe mRNA technology and delivery systems (e.g., lipid nanoparticles); there is no credible evidence in patent texts or from independent experts that they disclose or confirm a covert nanoscale bioweapon device.

claim: There were no American flags at the first Democratic presidential debate.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which year’s “first Democratic presidential debate” is meant, but as a blanket statement it is incorrect: major U.S. primary debates typically include American flags in the venue or onstage, and photographic media coverage of recent first Democratic debates (for example the 2019 primary debates) show U.S. flags present. Without a specific date, asserting there were no flags is not supported by general evidence.

claim: "No one beta-tested" healthcare.gov.
rationale: The absolute statement is false because the healthcare.gov system underwent multiple rounds of testing by contractors and government teams (including unit, integration, and some load/end-to-end tests) prior to launch. However those tests were incomplete, limited in scope, and there was no wide public 'beta' with large-scale real user trials, which contributed to the high-profile failures at rollout.

claim: Georgia has "a dropout rate that’s higher" than Alabama's.
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as an ongoing fact because high-school dropout rates vary by year and by measurement source. Recent state and federal data do not show a consistent pattern where Georgia's dropout rate is reliably higher than Alabama's; in some years Alabama's rate has been equal or higher. Without a specified year or data source the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative confirmation for the specific figures given. While ACA medical-loss-ratio (MLR) rebates are regularly paid to enrollees nationwide, recent CMS and industry reports show different totals, recipient counts, and per-person averages than the claim's 13 million + 8.5 million and about $100 each. The claim lacks a cited year or source and appears to overstate or misstate commonly reported MLR rebate figures.

claim: Says she couldn't take stimulus money because it required "universal building codes."
rationale: There is no evidence that federal stimulus packages (e.g., CARES Act, American Rescue Plan) imposed a blanket requirement that recipients adopt a single "universal building code." While some federal grants and disaster-recovery funds include conditions or require compliance with certain construction or resilience standards, they do not typically force jurisdictions to adopt a single nationwide building code. The claim as stated is misleading without naming a specific program with verifiable conditions.

claim: "Estimates say individuals who escaped these high tax states have taken with them around $2 trillion in adjusted gross income."
rationale: The statement is unverified and too vague — it gives no timeframe or identify which “high tax states” are meant. Public IRS migration and policy analyses do document net shifts in adjusted gross income between states, but I am not aware of a credible, widely cited estimate that unambiguously totals “around $2 trillion” moved by departing individuals without additional qualifiers. Because the claim lacks source, period, and definition, it cannot be treated as a factual, supported number.

claim: "The fact is" the Clinton Foundation has "got about 80 percent in overhead and 20 percent of the money is actually getting into the places it should."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and the foundation's own tax filings show the Clinton Foundation's program expenses are far greater than 20% in most years, so the claim that 80% is overhead is inaccurate. The 80/20 figure stems from a misreading of accounting categories and one-off transfers, not the foundation's audited program vs. overhead ratios.

claim: Obama "suggested bombing Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Obama publicly suggesting that the United States should 'bomb Pakistan' as a sovereign nation. As president he authorized targeted counterterrorism operations in Pakistani territory (drone strikes against militants and the 2011 Abbottabad raid to kill Osama bin Laden), but those were framed as actions against terrorist targets, not a proposal to bomb Pakistan itself.

claim: Barack Obama is the "First President to terminate America’s ability to put a man in space."
rationale: This is false: presidents before Obama presided over terminations of U.S. crewed-launch programs that left the country unable to launch astronauts for periods (for example, after the mid-1970s end of Apollo/Skylab/Apollo–Soyuz the U.S. had no domestic crewed-launch capability until the Space Shuttle in 1981). Obama did oversee retirement of the Space Shuttle in 2011, which temporarily ended U.S. domestic crewed-launches until commercial crew flights resumed in 2020, but he was not the first president to preside over such a gap.

claim: The new health care law "will cut $500 billion from Medicare. That will hurt the quality of our care."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did include roughly $500 billion in net Medicare savings over about a decade, primarily from reduced payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans, but it did not cut standard Medicare beneficiary benefits. The follow-on claim that those savings 'will hurt the quality of our care' is speculative and not supported by the budget analyses, which identified payment and efficiency changes rather than direct benefit reductions.

claim: A space shuttle the National Museum of the United States Air Force near Dayton would be "within a day's drive of 60 percent of the U.S. population."
rationale: The statement is unlikely to be true because 'a day's drive' is ambiguous but normally means on the order of 6–8 hours (roughly 400–500 miles), and a large share of the U.S. population lives on the West Coast and in parts of the Mountain and Southwest states well beyond that range from Dayton. While Dayton is centrally located relative to the eastern half of the country, pushing the reachable population up, it is unlikely to encompass as much as 60% of the U.S. under typical driving-day assumptions.

claim: Chinese workers made "90,000 banners" for Trump’s 2020 re-election campaign and the president chose to hire "Chinese workers instead of American workers"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that the Trump 2020 campaign specifically commissioned exactly 90,000 banners made by Chinese workers or that the president deliberately chose Chinese labor instead of American workers. Reporting on campaign merchandise shows varied supply chains with some items sourced overseas, but the precise figure and the categorical claim about choosing Chinese over American labor are unsubstantiated.

claim: "This year, a majority of states are seeing premiums and costs double" under Obamacare.
rationale: Available federal and nonpartisan analyses do not show premiums and overall costs doubling in a majority of states in any recent enrollment year. While some states or specific markets have seen large premium spikes, most states experienced modest changes and many consumers receive tax-credit offsets, so a nationwide majority doubling would have been widely reported but is not supported by the data.

claim: Untaxed corporate earnings used to be "$2.5 trillion … I guess it’s $5 trillion now. Whatever it is, it’s a lot more. So we have anywhere from 4 (trillion) to 5 or even more trillions of dollars sitting offshore."
rationale: The claim mixes figures and lacks necessary context. Official U.S. estimates before the 2017 tax reform put accumulated unrepatriated foreign earnings of U.S. multinationals at roughly $2.5–$3 trillion, and the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act changed tax treatment and prompted repatriation; there is no clear, authoritative basis to say untaxed corporate earnings currently total $4–5+ trillion offshore as stated. Different sources and definitions (U.S. vs global, 'deferred' vs permanently untaxed) produce widely varying numbers, so the blanket $4–5 trillion assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says he "helped to draft parts of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform bill."
rationale: The claim is underspecified because it does not identify who “he” is, so it cannot be verified as stated. Without a named individual and supporting evidence (contemporaneous records, staff acknowledgments, or media reporting) there is no basis to confirm that the person actually helped draft parts of Dodd-Frank. Absent such verification, the statement should be treated as unproven and thus not established as factual.

claim: Trade deals are negotiated in "secret" and, unlike corporate interests, politicians never invite "the leaders of the AFL-CIO or steelworkers or the mine workers to come in and sit down in these meetings."
rationale: While many trade negotiations are conducted under confidentiality and drafts are restricted, it is not true that politicians 'never' invite labor leaders. Labor organizations (for example, AFL-CIO and other unions) have formal channels for input—such as labor advisory committees and direct consultations with trade negotiators—and have been invited to meetings and briefings, even if access is more limited than that enjoyed by corporate interests. The claim’s absolute wording ('never') is therefore incorrect.

claim: Zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago.
rationale: There are no credible reports that zoo animals were released during recent protests in Chicago; the Lincoln Park Zoo and city officials reported the facility was secured and closed to the public. Multiple contemporary fact-checks debunked viral social-media claims that animals had escaped or been released during protests.

claim: Says Joe Biden repeatedly told Americans he's going to raise their taxes.
rationale: Joe Biden repeatedly promised during his campaign and in office that he would not raise federal taxes on households earning under $400,000 per year, and he framed proposed tax increases as targeted at corporations and high-income earners. Although he has proposed raising taxes on wealthy individuals, capital gains, and corporations, he did not repeatedly tell the broad public that he would raise their taxes.

claim: "On average, one person dies by suicide every 22 hours in West Virginia."
rationale: Saying "one person dies by suicide every 22 hours in West Virginia" implies about 398 suicides per year. Recent publicly reported state-level vital statistics show annual suicide counts in West Virginia typically vary in the low-to-mid hundreds, so the 22-hour figure may be approximately true for some years but is not a reliably accurate or consistently supported average without a specified year and data source.

claim: Says swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is a "safe, easy way" to remove them from skin.
rationale: Public-health authorities do not endorse swabbing ticks with soapy cotton as a ‘safe, easy’ removal method; using substances or irritants can cause a tick to regurgitate its gut contents and increase risk of pathogen transmission. The recommended method is to use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin and pull straight out, then clean the bite site and monitor for symptoms.

claim: Bing Energy said it decided to move to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax."
rationale: There is no reliable public record or company statement showing Bing Energy explicitly said it moved to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s “plan to eliminate the corporate tax.” While Rick Scott has promoted pro-business tax policies, reporters and company releases typically cite a mix of incentives, logistics, and workforce factors for relocations, and I found no corroborating quotation attributing the move to that specific plan.

claim: "Because of my policies, Black Unemployment has just been reported to be at the LOWEST RATE EVER RECORDED!"
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions: that Black unemployment is at the "lowest rate ever recorded" and that this is "because of my policies." Without a specific date or BLS citation the first part is not verifiable here (historical low points for Black unemployment have occurred at different times), and the causal claim is unsupported because unemployment rates reflect many factors beyond a single actor's policies. Therefore the blanket statement as written is not reliable.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted against the bipartisan Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: In 2013 Senator Marco Rubio voted against the Senate's bipartisan reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which passed the Senate by a wide margin. He cited objections to provisions expanding protections to same-sex couples and undocumented immigrants when explaining his 'no' vote.

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: There is no evidence that Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio personally “set” Florida’s delegate rules to make the primary winner-take-all to block a particular candidate. Delegate allocation rules are established by the state Republican Party (and sometimes state law) well before a given campaign and are not unilaterally set by individual candidates. While Florida’s GOP rules have at times awarded delegates on a winner-take-all basis, that was a formal party rule, not demonstrably the product of Bush and Rubio conspiring to deny someone delegates.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: El Paso's population is about 680,000–700,000 and has long been among the safest large U.S. cities; some individual years did record very few homicides (as low as five). Media and police reports put El Paso's roughly 10-year annual homicide average near the high teens, and the August 2019 Walmart attack killed 22 people — more than that 10-year average in a single day.

claim: "On average, 65% of gun deaths in America are from suicides."
rationale: Federal mortality data show that suicides make up the majority of U.S. firearm deaths, but the share is typically closer to about 50–60% in recent years rather than 65%. While the percentage fluctuates by year and age group, 65% overstates the usual annual proportion.

claim: "Trump Management was charged with discriminating against African-Americans and breaking federal law."
rationale: In 1973 the U.S. Department of Justice sued Trump Management, Inc. (part of the Trump organization) alleging it discriminated against African-American prospective tenants in violation of federal civil rights/fair housing laws. The case was resolved with a 1975 consent decree addressing discriminatory practices; the company settled but did not admit wrongdoing.

claim: "We have the lowest beer tax in the nation."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not specify who "we" refers to (which state, locality, or time). In the U.S. several states and localities have very low beer excise taxes, so a blanket claim of having "the lowest" is unlikely to be true without precise jurisdiction and a date.

claim: Say Ohio Reps. Marcia Fudge, Marcy Kaptur and Dennis Kucinich are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: None of the three are known to have publicly identified themselves as socialists or been members of major socialist organizations. They are (or were) elected Democrats—Kaptur is a long-time Democratic Representative, Fudge was a Democratic Representative who left Congress to join the Biden cabinet, and Kucinich was a progressive Democratic Representative but not an openly self-described socialist—so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: The statement is an overly broad generalization about the entire American public. Polling shows mixed views: many Americans oppose across-the-board tax hikes but commonly support raising taxes on high earners or corporations or to fund specific programs, and responses vary with question wording and timing.
