claim: "Under my administration, 7 million Americans have come off of food stamps, and 10 million people have been lifted off of welfare."
rationale: Official program enrollment data do not support the claimed totals. SNAP (food stamp) participation declined modestly in the pre‑pandemic years of the administration but by fewer than 7 million people, and the main cash 'welfare' program (TANF) has a caseload far smaller than 10 million and did not fall by that amount under the administration. The claim therefore overstates and mixes different programs and time periods.

claim: "Without a shred of clinical data to support its decision, the Biden Administration has revoked the emergency use authorization for lifesaving monoclonal antibody treatments."
rationale: Regulators did not revoke EUAs "without a shred of clinical data." The FDA and HHS cited laboratory neutralization studies showing that specific monoclonal antibodies lost activity against emergent SARS‑CoV‑2 variants and used genomic surveillance/variant prevalence and real‑world effectiveness reports to conclude the treatments would no longer be effective. While there were not always new randomized trials for each variant, decisions were based on multiple lines of scientific evidence.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The statement is an absolute, categorical claim that is contradicted by available evidence. Calls to impeach President Obama were concentrated among conservative Republicans but were not literally all white, all older, or exclusively in the far-right wing; supporters included people of varying ages and political positions and there are documented exceptions to each element of the claim.

claim: "Beachgoers trash Florida beaches with 13,000 pounds of litter after beaches reopen."
rationale: I cannot confirm a statewide figure of exactly 13,000 pounds of litter dumped by beachgoers immediately after Florida beaches reopened. While media and local authorities reported increased trash at some beaches when they reopened, the precise 13,000-pound claim appears to be unverified or misattributed without a clear timeframe or official inventory.

claim: "American coronavirus vaccine killed five Ukrainians."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an “American coronavirus vaccine” killed five Ukrainians; major health authorities and independent fact-checkers have not verified a causal link between COVID-19 vaccines and such a specific cluster of deaths. While deaths have occasionally occurred after vaccination, investigations typically find no causal connection or attribute causes to underlying conditions rather than the vaccine itself.

claim: Muslims "attempted to establish the first Islamic Sharia court inside the United States in the town of Irving, Texas."
rationale: This claim overstates and misframes events. While there was media controversy in 2007 about discussions in Irving, Texas regarding an Islamic arbitration panel or proposals by some local leaders, there is no evidence Muslims sought to create a government-recognized “Sharia court” there as a novel first-of-its-kind; private religious arbitration (including by Muslim communities) has existed and any arbitration must operate under U.S. law. The reporting conflated informal or proposed mediation mechanisms with establishing an official Sharia court.

claim: "No one has died of cancer or heart disease since the COVID-19 thing started."
rationale: This claim is false. National and global vital statistics from 2020 onward show continuing deaths from cancer and heart disease — in fact they have remained among the leading causes of death each year since the COVID-19 pandemic began. Medical systems and mortality reporting did not stop recording non-COVID causes of death.

claim: "In ‘Resident Evil’ the Umbrella Corporation releases a virus that infects the people of Raccoon City. A biological research lab with the exact same logo as the Umbrella Corporation can be found in the city where the coronavirus outbreak originated."
rationale: The first part (Resident Evil’s Umbrella Corporation releasing a virus that infects Raccoon City) accurately describes the fictional plot. The second part is false: there is no reliable evidence that a real-world biological research lab in the city where the COVID-19 outbreak began uses the exact same Umbrella Corporation logo; this claim arose from social-media comparisons and misinterpretations, and independent fact-checks show the logos differ or are coincidental.

claim: "McCain opposes repeal of the death tax."
rationale: The statement is misleading: Senator John McCain has generally supported reducing or eliminating the federal estate tax (commonly called the 'death tax') in various proposals, often carving out exemptions for small businesses and farms. He did not broadly 'oppose repeal' of the estate tax in his public policy positions during his presidential campaigns and Senate career.

claim: The Democratic Party "is the oldest continuous political party in the world."
rationale: The U.S. Democratic Party has roots in the Jeffersonian Democratic-Republicans of the 1790s and was organized under the Democratic name by 1828, but it is not unambiguously the oldest continuous political party in the world. Other parties (notably the British Tory/Conservative tradition whose origins go back to the 17th–18th centuries) and differing standards for what counts as unbroken continuity mean the global claim is inaccurate or at best disputed.

claim: "McCain opposes a woman's right to choose."
rationale: Senator John McCain long identified as pro‑life and supported significant restrictions on abortion; during his Senate career and 2008 presidential campaign he opposed legal abortion as a matter of policy and criticized Roe v. Wade. While he did endorse limited exceptions (rape, incest, life of the mother), his stated positions and voting record indicate opposition to a broad 'right to choose.'

claim: Says John Cornyn dodged the draft during the Vietnam War.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that John Cornyn illegally dodged the Vietnam draft. Public biographical information and contemporary reporting indicate he was a college student during the draft era and used lawful deferments; journalists and official records have not documented criminal draft evasion by him.

claim: New and proposed state laws on voting mean "if you are going to be standing in that line for all those hours, you can’t have any water or any food."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. While some recent and proposed state voting laws include restrictions on third parties distributing items near polling places and have been criticized for potentially preventing handing out food or water to voters in line, the statutes differ by state and often include exemptions (voters’ own items, poll workers, or certain nonpartisan relief). They do not uniformly or categorically prohibit voters from having any food or water while waiting.

claim: "George Floyd’s ‘murder’ filmed before COVID-19."
rationale: George Floyd was killed and the widely circulated bystander video was recorded on May 25, 2020, which is after COVID-19 was widely circulating and after the WHO declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020. Therefore the filming did not occur before COVID-19.

claim: Says Rick Scott cut education by over a billion dollars, meaning thousands of teachers "lost their jobs" and "class sizes went up."
rationale: This claim mixes factual elements with overreach. Rick Scott supported and signed budgets in his early term that reduced K–12 spending by roughly around a billion dollars in that budget cycle, but independent fact-checkers and budget records show the assertion that "thousands of teachers lost their jobs" and that class sizes universally "went up" as a direct, single result of a >$1B cut is misleading—teacher staffing and class sizes varied by district and were affected by multiple factors, not a single statewide mass firing caused directly by one cut.

claim: Amanda Murphy has "two vacation homes around the world."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which Amanda Murphy it refers to and I find no reputable reporting or public asset disclosure indicating that any politician named Amanda Murphy owns “two vacation homes around the world.” Because there is no corroborating evidence or source provided, the assertion is unverified and likely false.

claim: A majority of Americans have voted for a party that … wants a world in which you cannot call your parents mom and dad."
rationale: There is no evidence that a major U.S. political party officially advocates banning people from calling their parents 'mom' and 'dad.' Party platforms and mainstream policy proposals do not include such prohibitions; isolated calls for inclusive language in some schools or statements by individuals have been exaggerated into a false claim about party policy.

claim: "Virginia papers called (Scott) Rigell’s campaign ‘Mostly False.’"
rationale: There is no evidence that multiple Virginia newspapers collectively labeled Scott Rigell’s entire campaign 'Mostly False.' The phrase 'Mostly False' is a specific fact-checker rating (e.g., PolitiFact) rather than typical newspaper copy, and claims using that wording should cite a particular fact-check or publication. Without named papers or a specific fact-checked claim, the broad statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year.
rationale: Multiple reliable sources (Guttmacher Institute and CDC/state health reports) show Texas had well under 80,000 abortions per year in recent years—typically in the tens of thousands (roughly 40,000–60,000) and declining further after 2021 restrictions. The claim that Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year is not supported by those data.

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: The broad claim that vaccines will directly kill 'some people' and cause a large number of people to develop autoimmune diseases is not supported by evidence. Clinical trials and large-scale safety monitoring show that serious adverse events and deaths causally linked to vaccines are exceedingly rare, and while rare immune-mediated reactions (for example Guillain-Barré or myocarditis in specific contexts) have been observed, they do not occur at the large scale asserted. Overall, benefits of approved vaccines substantially outweigh the small risks and there is no evidence of an impending wave of widespread autoimmune disease caused by vaccines.

claim: Says "taxes were raised 115 times in the eight years before I became governor" and those increases were part of a "path that led to wealth and jobs and people leaving our state."
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely false as presented because no state, governor, or precise time frame is given to confirm 115 separate tax increases in the prior eight years. Counts of 'tax increases' vary widely depending on definitions (rate changes, new fees, or legislative budget actions), and the causal claim that those increases produced wealth and jobs losses and out‑migration is speculative and would require economic analysis and evidence. Without specific supporting documentation, the combined numerical and causal assertions cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says "Snoop Dogg arrested for conspiracy after talking about his ‘murder Trump’ video."
rationale: There are no credible reports that Snoop Dogg was arrested for conspiracy over a 'murder Trump' video. While he has posted provocative or politically charged videos in the past, such content has drawn criticism but not an arrest for conspiracy. U.S. authorities have not publicized any such charge against him.

claim: Says President Barack Obama broke his promise to keep a Wisconsin GM plant from closing.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable pledge by President Obama to personally keep a specific Wisconsin GM plant open; he campaigned in places like Janesville promising to fight for auto jobs, but plant closures resulted from GM's bankruptcy and restructuring decisions, not a unilateral presidential commitment he could enforce. Framing this as Obama having 'broken his promise' misstates both what he said and the limits of presidential power over private companies.

claim: "60 percent of the jobs lost in the 2008 recession were living-wage jobs. Of the jobs we’ve gotten back, only 40 percent are living-wage."
rationale: The claim gives precise percentages but does not cite a definitional threshold, data source, or time window; estimates of how many lost or recovered jobs are "living-wage" vary substantially with the wage cutoff and period considered. Official BLS data and academic analyses show that middle- and higher-wage sectors lost many jobs in 2008–09 and that recovery included a disproportionate share of lower-wage positions, but the specific 60% lost / 40% recovered living-wage figures are not a well-established, reproducible statistic. Without a clear definition and source the statement is misleading.

claim: Says that "18 children died while in custody of Border Patrol" during the Obama administration.
rationale: The statement misstates the official record and conflates different categories of custody. Independent fact-checks and government data show that while multiple migrant children died in U.S. immigration-related custody or after encounters during the Obama years, far fewer died while physically held by Border Patrol specifically; some deaths occurred after transfer to other agencies or outside continuous Border Patrol custody, and counts depend on definitions and timeframes.

claim: "Of all cities in the United States with more than 100,000 people, Providence is the 183rd safest."
rationale: The claim gives a very specific rank without naming a source or year. National city-safety rankings vary by methodology and year (FBI crime data, WalletHub, SafeWise, etc.), and Providence is not consistently reported as exactly 183rd among U.S. cities over 100,000. Without a cited dataset and year the precise numeric claim cannot be verified and is likely incorrect.

claim: Requesting a chargeback is "a better way to get back at" GoFundMe.
rationale: Framing chargebacks as a way to "get back at" GoFundMe is misleading: chargebacks are a consumer protection mechanism for unauthorized, fraudulent, or improperly processed transactions, not a tool for retaliation against a platform. Banks and card networks investigate disputes and may deny or reverse chargebacks if there is legitimate activity or if platform-level dispute processes apply, and abusing chargebacks can be treated as fraud.

claim: Says to Hillary Clinton, "You heard what I said about (the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal), and all of a sudden you were against it."
rationale: There is no clear, attributable record of an individual saying exactly this line to Hillary Clinton; while opponents (notably Donald Trump) frequently criticized Clinton for changing her position on the Trans-Pacific Partnership, the precise quoted sentence cannot be verified as an actual, sourced utterance. The claim appears to conflate general criticism of Clinton's TPP position with a specific direct quote that lacks documentary support.

claim: "Japan says goodbye Moderna, hello ivermectin."
rationale: There is no evidence Japan has adopted a policy replacing Moderna COVID-19 vaccines with ivermectin. Japan's health authorities have not approved ivermectin as a substitute for COVID-19 vaccination, and Moderna (and other mRNA vaccines) continue to be used and recommended for COVID-19 prevention and boosters. Ivermectin is an antiparasitic that major health agencies do not endorse as an effective COVID-19 treatment.

claim: The Foundation for Government Accountability, which supported a Florida law requiring drug testing of welfare recipients, is a "Koch brothers affiliated group."
rationale: The Foundation for Government Accountability (FGA) is a conservative policy shop that promoted drug-testing rules in Florida, but it is not documented as a Koch brothers–affiliated organization. Reporting and organizational records identify it as an independent think tank; while it shares policy goals with Koch network groups and may overlap in donors or coordination, there is no clear evidence that it is formally a Koch-affiliated entity.

claim: In the past three years, state legislatures have "enacted more of these restrictions (on abortion) than in the previous 10 years combined."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits definitions, timeframe, and a source; available public trackers show that while many new abortion bans and restrictions were enacted after the 2022 Dobbs decision, the prior decade also saw a large number of incremental restrictions across states. Without a clear counting methodology (what counts as a ‘restriction’, which three-year and ten-year windows), the assertion that the past three years produced more restrictions than the previous ten combined cannot be substantiated. Given the ambiguity and mixed data, the claim as stated is not reliably supported.

claim: "Obama settled 43,000 Somalian refugees in Minnesota. As of 2016, there were around 80,000. No wonder Ilhan Omar was elected. It was planned."
rationale: The claim mixes inaccurate numbers and an unfounded conspiracy. Federal refugee resettlement to Minnesota from Somalia during the Obama years was far lower than 43,000, and mid‑2010s estimates of Minnesota's total Somali population vary but do not support a claim that Obama resettled 43,000 Somalis there; moreover there is no credible evidence that refugee placements were part of a plan to elect Ilhan Omar, whose victory resulted from ordinary campaigning and community support.

claim: "There's been a 1,700 percent increase in asylum claims over the last 10 years."
rationale: The statement is unqualified and implausible as a global figure: UNHCR and national statistics show asylum claims have risen and fallen in different places over the past decade, but there is no clear global or major-country trend of a 1,700% increase over ten years. Some individual countries or short multi-year windows have seen very large percentage rises from small baselines, but presenting a single 1,700% figure without specifying country, baseline, or exact timeframe is misleading.

claim: Japan's "interest on its own debt" is "25 percent of its national budget"
rationale: Japan's interest payments on its national debt are far smaller than 25% of the national budget. Despite very high debt-to-GDP, extremely low interest rates have kept annual interest costs to only a small single-digit percentage of central government spending in recent years, not one-quarter of the budget.

claim: Illegal immigration on the U.S.-Mexico border is "the lowest in 17 years."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it gives no time window and contradicts publicly reported CBP encounter trends: encounters fell dramatically during the 2020 pandemic year and have fluctuated since, so recent counts are not clearly the lowest in 17 years. Official border statistics show years with lower totals than some recent months/years, making a blanket 'lowest in 17 years' statement misleading without specifying the metric and period.

claim: McCain's attacks on Obama are 'not true,' 'false,' 'baloney,' according to media outlets.
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. While specific McCain attacks on Obama were fact-checked and labeled false or misleading by some outlets and fact-checkers during the 2008 campaign, there is no basis to claim media outlets broadly or uniformly described his attacks as ‘not true,’ ‘false,’ or ‘baloney’ without specifying which claims or which outlets.

claim: "When the law stopped Tony Evers from revoking a teacher's license for viewing pornography, Tony worked with lawmakers from both parties to change the law so offenders could be kicked out of the classroom."
rationale: There is no clear, contemporaneous evidence that a specific law definitively 'stopped' Governor Tony Evers from revoking a teacher's license for viewing pornography and that he then worked with lawmakers from both parties to pass a bipartisan fix to remove offenders from classrooms. While Evers has publicly pushed for tighter standards and disciplinary authority after misconduct incidents, the details and partisan makeup of any legislative action do not match the categorical sequence described in the claim.

claim: "Never in American history has so much been spent at one time. Never in American history will so many taxes be raised and so much borrowing be needed to pay for this reckless spending."
rationale: This statement is false because U.S. history contains prior episodes—most notably World War II—when federal spending and borrowing surged to levels far larger relative to the economy, and substantial tax increases were enacted to finance the war. Recent large nominal-dollar spending (for example during COVID-19) may be the largest in raw dollars, but not the largest relative to GDP, and the absolute future claim that "never will" so many taxes be raised is speculative and unprovable.

claim: "Hillary ignored multiple requests for security, didn’t respond for 13 hours, & let 4 Americans die in Benghazi. Trump rushed in reinforcements, threatened to destroy Iran, & made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad."
rationale: The statement bundles several inaccurate or unsupported assertions. Official reviews (State Department Accountability Review Board and multiple congressional investigations) found security lapses and leadership failures around the 2012 Benghazi attack but did not find that Hillary Clinton personally ignored repeated requests or sat silent for 13 hours or intentionally 'let' the four Americans die. While President Trump publicly issued harsh threats toward Iran and authorized lethal strikes (including the 2020 Baghdad strike that killed Qasem Soleimani), the claim that he 'rushed in reinforcements' and thereby 'made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad' is misleading and not supported by public records.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton once "wanted a wall" on the Mexican border.
rationale: Hillary Clinton has at times publicly supported building physical barriers on parts of the U.S.–Mexico border. As a U.S. senator and during immigration debates she backed measures favoring border fencing and used language indicating she wanted barriers in some areas, though her wording and emphasis shifted over time toward comprehensive reform.

claim: Says Michael Kors said, "I’m tired of pretending I like blacks."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that fashion designer Michael Kors uttered that quote; reputable news outlets and fact-checkers do not document a verified source or recording of him saying, “I’m tired of pretending I like blacks.” The line appears to be a viral misattribution or fabrication rather than a documented public statement by Kors.

claim: "Since President (Donald Trump’s) election, 36,000 jobs have been created in WI."
rationale: The claim gives no clear cutoff date or data source and therefore cannot be verified as stated. Official state employment series (from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and Wisconsin labor reports) show different job-change totals for Wisconsin depending on the measure (nonfarm payrolls, household survey, private jobs) and time window after the November 2016 election, so a flat figure of 36,000 is not reliably supported. Because the statement lacks context and does not match published BLS-series totals for common windows, it is misleading.

claim: "Connecticut's take on slot machines is 25 cents on the dollar. And the state's take on table games:  zero."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Connecticut’s payments from tribal casinos are governed by negotiated compacts and have varied over time and by revenue type — they are not a simple, universal ‘25 cents on the dollar’ for slots and ‘zero’ for table games. In many compacts the state received a percentage or negotiated payments tied to slot revenue and later agreements and renewals included payments tied to table games, sports betting, and other revenue streams.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: Official labor statistics and surveys show unemployment among recent college graduates is far lower than 50%; while some graduates experience short-term unemployment or underemployment, the claim that one in two cannot find any job is not supported. The headline 50% figure would greatly exceed typical reported unemployment or joblessness for new college graduates.

claim: Says Joe Biden was asleep and snoring during a TV interview.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that President Joe Biden fell asleep and was snoring during a televised interview; viral clips claiming this are either edited, taken out of context, or show brief eye closures rather than sustained sleep. Fact-checkers and reputable news organizations have not substantiated a genuine instance of him sleeping and snoring on-air during an interview.

claim: "The states that are locked down are increasing at twice the rate we are" in Florida
rationale: The statement asserts a precise comparative growth rate (that 'locked down' states are increasing at twice Florida's rate) without providing a timeframe, metric, or source. Publicly available COVID-19 trends show state-by-state growth varied over time, and there is no consistent evidence that locked-down states uniformly increased at exactly twice Florida's rate. Thus the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: This blanket claim is inaccurate: over the past two decades France has repeatedly cooperated with the United States on major foreign-policy actions (e.g., NATO operations in Afghanistan, leading role with the US/UK in Libya 2011, participation in the anti-ISIS coalition, and joint sanctions and support for Ukraine after Russia's 2014 and 2022 actions). While there have been notable public disagreements and bilateral rows (for example AUKUS in 2021 and periodic tensions under different US administrations), those exceptions do not mean France has not ‘stood by’ the US on many key issues.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: State reports and media coverage in 2013 did note roughly 20,000 Kansans received cancellation or nonrenewal notices when certain individual-market plans failed to meet Affordable Care Act requirements, but that does not prove 20,000 people actually ‘lost’ coverage. Many affected policyholders obtained replacement plans, temporary extensions, or enrolled through the exchanges, so the claim as stated is misleading and unproven.

claim: Says "Florida is a model" for successful pretrial release programs.
rationale: There is no clear consensus that Florida is broadly "a model" for successful pretrial release programs. While some Florida counties have implemented risk-assessment tools and supervised release pilots, the state's approaches are patchwork, results are mixed, and other states (notably New Jersey and Kentucky) are more widely cited as national models for pretrial reform. The claim overgeneralizes and lacks supporting evidence.

claim: "Replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts does not alter state or federal benefits."
rationale: Federal benefits and many federal legal rights are explicitly tied to the legal status of “marriage,” so replacing state marriage licenses with privately or differently named domestic-union contracts would generally change access to federal programs (tax filing status, Social Security spousal/survivor benefits, immigration sponsorship, veterans’ benefits, etc.). States can design domestic-union schemes to replicate some state-level benefits, but without statutory federal recognition those federal benefits would not automatically follow. Historically, differences in recognition (e.g., pre-Obergefell and DOMA-era effects) show that name and legal recognition matter for federal entitlements.

claim: Says "Canada has one-tenth of our population—yet it issues far more high-skilled visas (more than 150,000) yearly than we do (65,000)."
rationale: The statement mixes an approximate population ratio (Canada ≈1/9–1/10 of the U.S.), which is roughly correct, with an inaccurate and misleading comparison of visa counts. The U.S. issues many more high-skilled temporary and employment-based visas overall once all categories (H‑1B including the 20k advanced-degree exemption, L, O, TN, employment‑based green cards, etc.) are counted, and Canada’s figures cited ("more than 150,000") appear to conflate different permit categories and timeframes. Because "high-skilled visas" and the baseline country (“we”) are undefined, the specific numeric claim is unreliable and false as stated.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The claim as phrased is unverifiable and therefore unreliable because it does not specify which country or time period 'we' refers to and which mortality metric is being used. COVID-19 mortality varies widely by country and over time, and differences in testing, reporting, and whether one means case fatality rate, infection fatality rate, or deaths per capita materially change rankings. Without those details the blanket statement cannot be supported.

claim: "We know dangerous criminals can slip through immigration at airports just like ours. Yet Joe Donnelly stood right here with the radical left against all efforts to secure our most vulnerable entry points."
rationale: The statement is a broad, partisan claim that mixes a plausible general concern (that criminals sometimes enter at airports) with an unsupported and exaggerated accusation that Joe Donnelly 'stood... with the radical left against all efforts' to secure entry points. Donnelly is a moderate Democrat with a mixed voting record and has supported some immigration and enforcement measures, so it is inaccurate to say he opposed 'all efforts' or uniformly sided with a 'radical left' agenda.

claim: "Inspections of abortion centers around Virginia have found multiple violations of parental consent laws … but Gov. Terry McAuliffe and his administration have done nothing."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions — that inspections found multiple parental-consent violations and that Gov. McAuliffe did nothing — but public records and reporting do not unambiguously support both. Virginia state agencies have authority to inspect and have in past conducted reviews and taken regulatory or corrective steps in response to complaints at clinics; there is no clear, documented record that the governor entirely ignored multiple confirmed violations. The statement overstates the case and omits important context about timing, specific findings, and enforcement actions.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid will worsen health care options for the most vulnerable among us in Texas."
rationale: Empirical evidence from U.S. Medicaid expansions shows that expansion reduces uninsured rates, increases use of primary and preventive care, lowers uncompensated hospital care, and improves financial security for low-income people. While local effects can vary and provider supply constraints or reimbursement issues can create challenges in some areas, the balance of research indicates expansion improves — not worsens — health care options for vulnerable populations.

claim: Keystone XL allows "Canada to pump their oil, send it through our land, down to the Gulf, where it will be sold everywhere else."
rationale: Keystone XL was proposed to carry crude from Alberta through the U.S. to Gulf Coast refineries and terminals, which would make it easier for Canadian oil producers to reach Gulf markets and for that oil to be refined or exported globally. The phrasing is imprecise — the pipeline provides transportation capacity rather than "allowing Canada to pump" — but the core claim about routing Canadian crude through U.S. land to the Gulf for sale elsewhere is accurate.

claim: "Under (Obamacare), you can’t reward a person for better behavior. You can’t have incentives to be healthier."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did not categorically ban rewarding healthier behavior; it explicitly preserved and clarified rules allowing nondiscriminatory workplace and insurer wellness programs that offer financial incentives or reduced cost-sharing. There are legal limits and protections (e.g., community rating/guaranteed issue for premiums, and caps on incentive size), but incentives for wellness are permitted under the law.

claim: Says George Floyd died "because he had a system full of fentanyl and meth," and "beat women and held guns to their pregnant bellies."
rationale: Medical evidence shows George Floyd's death was ruled a homicide attributed to cardiopulmonary arrest from law enforcement restraint and neck compression; toxicology did detect fentanyl and methamphetamine but these were listed as contributing factors, not the sole cause. The additional claim that he 'beat women and held guns to their pregnant bellies' is not substantiated by reliable public records and appears to be an unproven, sensational allegation.

claim: "Our jobless rate, our unemployment rate, is the lowest of all of the big cities in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated because it gives no city name or date; unemployment rankings among New Jersey's large cities change over time and require specific, recent labor-force data to verify. Without a defined time period and the specific city referred to by "our," the statement cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false as a general assertion.

claim: Joe Biden "wants to get rid of something called ‘stepped up basis’" that reduces inheritance taxes.
rationale: President Biden has proposed eliminating or substantially limiting the 'stepped-up basis' treatment so that heirs would owe capital gains tax on appreciated assets at death above a set exemption (roughly $1 million per individual in proposals). That proposal is aimed at reducing the tax advantage of inheriting unrealized gains and raising revenue.

claim: "They're saying that 40 percent of the traffic that goes over [the Sakonnet River Bridge is from] out of state."
rationale: There is no widely reported or readily documented evidence that exactly 40% of traffic over the Sakonnet River Bridge is from out of state. Typical traffic studies for regional bridges in Rhode Island show a majority of trips are local or in-state commuters, so the specific 40% figure appears unsupported without citation. The claim may be a rough estimate or refer to a specific season or measurement method rather than a general fact.

claim: Says President Barack Obama said when "we got bin Laden, terrorism problem solved."
rationale: There is no credible transcript, recording, or contemporaneous news report showing President Obama saying "when we got bin Laden, terrorism problem solved." In his public remarks after Osama bin Laden's death he described it as a major achievement and said justice had been done, but he also warned that terrorism remained a threat and did not claim the problem was solved.

claim: "Your chances of throwing it are actually a little bit better in that situation."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify because it does not define what 'it' refers to or specify the situation. Probabilistic claims require concrete definitions and data; without them the assertion is untestable. Therefore it cannot be judged true and is treated as false for lack of evidence.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: There is no public record or credible reporting that former President Barack Obama was ordered by any court to pay $400 million in restitution. Such an unprecedented judgment against a former president would have been widely reported; the claim appears to confuse or conflate it with a separate, contested $400 million transfer/settlement involving Iran under the Obama administration, which was not a court-ordered personal restitution.

claim: Says New Jersey Rep. Leonard Lance voted repeatedly "to let insurance companies charge more to people aged 50 and over."
rationale: The claim says Lance voted repeatedly to let insurers charge more for people 50 and over. While some Republican health bills (notably the 2017 AHCA) included provisions that could allow larger age-based premium differences, there is no clear evidence that Lance cast multiple distinct votes specifically and repeatedly authorizing higher charges for people over 50; describing his record as repeated votes to do so overstates the available public voting record.

claim: Says Sam Houston opposed slavery and as governor said Texas should not leave the union over slavery.
rationale: The claim is misleading: Sam Houston did oppose Texas's secession and, as governor in 1861, refused to take an oath to the Confederacy and argued Texas should not leave the Union. However, he was not an opponent of slavery as an institution—he owned slaves and supported slavery's legality—so the statement that he 'opposed slavery' is incorrect.

claim: "There have been some estimates that if you deported everybody who is in Texas illegally," it "would create an economic recession for the state."
rationale: Multiple economic studies and analyses have modeled the effects of removing undocumented immigrants from Texas and concluded that large-scale deportation would cause substantial declines in employment, output, and state tax revenue, outcomes that analysts say could be large enough to trigger a recession. The claim only asserts that such estimates exist, which is supported by published modeling from economists and policy groups.

claim: Images that show a 90-year-old UK woman receiving the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine appeared online in a CNN news story in October.
rationale: The widely reported 90-year-old was Margaret Keenan, who received the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine on December 8, 2020, and images of that event were published on and after that date. Independent fact-checks and publication timelines show no credible evidence that CNN ran those images in October, so the claim that they appeared in a CNN story in October is incorrect.

claim: Jim Marshall "votes liberal in Washington ... and we aren't fooled."
rationale: The claim is a vague political attack rather than a specific factual statement — "votes liberal" is subjective and depends on which bills and which timeframe are meant. Jim Marshall (the former Georgia congressman) was widely described as a Blue Dog/centrist Democrat with a mixed voting record, so the blanket assertion that he "votes liberal" in Washington is not verifiably true as an absolute.

claim: Says John McAfee tweeted before his death that he stored computer files in the Florida condo building that later collapsed.
rationale: There is no verifiable record of John McAfee tweeting that he had stored computer files in the Florida condo building that later collapsed. Independent fact-checkers and searches of his public/archived posts found no such tweet; the claim appears to have circulated as a post-collapse conspiracy without evidence.

claim: As Florida secretary of state, Kurt Browning "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register in Florida."
rationale: Contemporary news reports and state statements documented that a relatively small number of noncitizen registrations in Florida were flagged and traced to DMV/data errors or mistaken self-attestation, not to an intentional action by Secretary of State Kurt Browning. There is no reliable evidence that Browning 'allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register' as an intentional or direct act, and reported counts and causes have varied in follow-up reviews.

claim: Refugees are throwing rocks and trying "to kill you."
rationale: The claim is a broad, categorical assertion about all refugees that is unsupported. While isolated incidents involving some migrants or asylum-seekers throwing rocks at authorities have been reported in specific contexts, there is no evidence that refugees as a group are generally throwing rocks or trying to kill people.

claim: David Perdue did not support the 2014 farm bill that U.S. Sens. Isakson and Chambliss did.
rationale: Senators Johnny Isakson and Saxby Chambliss voted in favor of the Agricultural Act of 2014. David Perdue was not a U.S. senator until January 2015 (and thus did not vote for that bill) and publicly distanced himself from that farm bill during his 2014 Senate campaign, so he did not support the same enacted 2014 bill in the way those senators did.

claim: Says "J.B. Pritzker’s tax plan" includes a "new tax per mile you drive with government tracking device."
rationale: The claim misrepresents public proposals. While Illinois and other jurisdictions have studied or sought grants for voluntary mileage-based pilot programs and there have been discussions about replacing fuel taxes with per-mile charges, J.B. Pritzker’s tax plans did not enact a statewide mandatory per-mile tax that requires a government tracking device. Reporting indicates any mileage programs discussed were studies or optional pilots, not an implemented compulsory tracking tax.

claim: Richmond is "the most vegan-friendly city."
rationale: The claim is a universal comparative statement without a specified metric or city context and is not supported by widely cited rankings of vegan-friendly cities. Major recurring rankings and general consensus typically list cities like Portland, Los Angeles, London, and Berlin as among the most vegan-friendly rather than any Richmond. While some Richmonds may have growing vegan scenes, calling Richmond 'the most vegan-friendly city' is unsupported and overly broad.

claim: If you work 40 hours a week at the proposed minimum wage of $10.10 an hour, "you get out of poverty."
rationale: A $10.10 hourly wage at 40 hours/week yields about $21,008 per year before taxes. Whether that 'gets you out of poverty' depends on household size and the official poverty threshold: it would lift a single person (and in many years a two- or three-person household) above the U.S. federal poverty line but would be below the poverty line for larger households and may be insufficient in high-cost areas or after taxes and expenses. The original claim is therefore overly broad and misleading.

claim: "I was the most bipartisan senator in the United States Senate."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented because it gives no identity, timeframe, or metric for "most bipartisan." Bipartisanship rankings vary by measure (e.g., co-sponsorship, roll-call votes) and by year, so the blanket claim cannot be verified and is therefore not supported.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh’s mother presided over foreclosure case against Christine Blasey Ford’s parents, which fueled motivation for sexual assault accusation.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Brett Kavanaugh’s mother presided over a foreclosure case involving Christine Blasey Ford’s parents. Contemporary fact-checks and court records do not show her serving as a judge in such a proceeding, and reporting that attempted to tie a foreclosure to Kavanaugh’s family was debunked. The suggested motive for Ford’s allegation therefore lacks factual support.

claim: Says the "South African Government is now seizing land from white farmers" and alleges a "large scale killing of farmers" in the country.
rationale: While South Africa has an active land reform debate (including proposals for expropriation without compensation), there is no credible evidence that the government is conducting a widescale, racially targeted seizure of land from white farmers. Similarly, farm murders and violent attacks do occur and are a serious problem, but independent crime data and research do not support the claim of a government-backed or countrywide 'large-scale killing' campaign specifically targeting white farmers.

claim: "Attorney General McCollum, Speaker-Designate Cannon, Senate President-Designate Haridopolos and I stood up to Governor Crist and worked to remove Jim Greer as Chairman because of his mismanagement of the party."
rationale: While Jim Greer was removed as Florida Republican Party chairman amid internal disputes and later faced criminal charges, there is no clear evidence that Attorney General Bill McCollum, Speaker‑designate Dean Cannon, Senate President‑designate Mike Haridopolos and the speaker‑claimant jointly 'stood up to Governor Crist' and worked as a coordinated group to remove Greer specifically for mismanagement. The claim ties a specific coalition and motive together without corroborating public records or contemporaneous reporting naming all those individuals as a unified effort against Governor Crist to oust Greer.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines contain nanoparticles that enable location tracking via 5G. Authorized mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles as biocompatible carriers for RNA, not electronic or radio-emitting devices, and injected particles cannot act as transmitters for cellular networks. Locating someone by 5G would require an active powered transmitter or a linked device, which these formulations do not contain.

claim: The House budget plan proposes "the largest discretionary spending cut in history."
rationale: Calling the House budget plan "the largest discretionary spending cut in history" is misleading. Whether a proposed cut is the largest depends on how you measure (nominal dollars vs. inflation-adjusted dollars, percentage of GDP, or discretionary as a share of the budget) and on which historical baseline you use; prior budgets and austerity moves have produced larger cuts by some measures. Public analyses and budget historians note that the claim lacks the necessary context to be accurate as an unqualified statement.

claim: Figures for September 2014’s job growth in Wisconsin mark the "largest private-sector job creation we've had in the month of September in more than a decade"
rationale: State and federal monthly employment series for Wisconsin show that although September 2014 recorded solid private‑sector job gains, the increase was not unprecedented for the month of September over the prior decade. Historical BLS/Wisconsin Labor data indicate other Septembers in the previous ten–fifteen years produced comparable or larger private‑sector gains, so the quoted superlative is unsupported without additional qualification.

claim: Says Texas ranks 44th nationally in education funding per pupil.
rationale: The claim gives no year or data source, and per-pupil funding rankings change by year and methodology. While Texas has historically ranked in the low-40s in some datasets, asserting it 'ranks 44th nationally' as a standalone fact cannot be verified without a specific year and metric.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits the specific two-year period and the detailed fundraising breakdowns for super PACs vary significantly by election cycle. Public FEC and reporting data show that while a small number of wealthy donors often supply a large share of super PAC funds and corporations/companies do contribute, the precise figures (>$180 million total, ~50% from <200 people, ~20% from corporations) are not a consistently documented, verifiable statement without a specified timeframe.

claim: When President Barack Obama said ISIS, or ISIL, was contained, he "was responding very specifically to the geographic expansion of ISIL in Iraq and Syria."
rationale: When President Obama used language about ISIL/ISIS being "contained," he was speaking in the context of U.S. policy to stop the group's territorial expansion in Iraq and Syria. His public remarks and the administration's strategy focused on preventing further geographic gains and rolling back control of territory rather than claiming the organization was eliminated entirely.

claim: About 800 people refused to get a drug screening because they are "out there on drugs."
rationale: I cannot find credible evidence or authoritative reporting that around 800 people refused drug screening claiming they were "out there on drugs." The statement provides no time, place, or source and the specific large number is not corroborated by available public records or news coverage, making the claim unverified and likely false.

claim: "New Jersey has the largest transit system in the entire country."
rationale: New Jersey Transit is a large statewide agency but it is not the largest transit system in the United States. The New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) is widely recognized as the nation's largest by ridership and network size, and other major agencies (e.g., Chicago CTA, Los Angeles Metro) also exceed NJ Transit on common metrics. The claim fails because it does not specify a metric and is incorrect as stated.

claim: The United States is "#1 in oil consumption" in the world.
rationale: As of recent international energy statistics (through the early 2020s), the United States consumes more petroleum and liquid fuels than any other single country, typically around 19–20 million barrels per day, ahead of China. Major energy agencies’ annual data consistently list the U.S. as the top national oil consumer in that period.

claim: "The nuclear test conducted in our nation this time is the Earth's 2,054th nuclear test. The five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council have conducted 99.99 percent of the total nuclear tests."
rationale: The exact total number of nuclear tests historically is roughly in the low 2,000s (commonly cited totals around 2,050–2,055 depending on counting rules), so calling a given test the 'Earth's 2,054th' is uncertain and depends on definitions and timing. The assertion that the five permanent U.N. Security Council members conducted 99.99% of tests is incorrect: several non‑P5 states (notably India, Pakistan, North Korea and South Africa) conducted multiple tests, so the P5 share is far below 99.99%.

claim: Says over 1,000 mail in ballots were found in a dumpster in California.
rationale: Major fact-checks and contemporaneous news reporting found no verified case of over 1,000 completed mail-in ballots being recovered from a California dumpster; viral claims were traced to exaggerations, misidentified materials (such as ballot applications or county-handled envelopes), or far smaller numbers. Verified incidents that did occur involved at most dozens or were items collected by election officials, not evidence of thousands of discarded ballots.

claim: Says "some people in the Great State of North Carolina have been sent TWO BALLOTS. RIGGED ELECTION in waiting!"
rationale: While isolated incidents have occurred where a small number of North Carolina voters were mailed duplicate ballots due to administrative errors, the leap to a ‘RIGGED ELECTION’ is unsupported. State and local election officials and standard election safeguards (ballot tracking, signature checks, and cancellation procedures) mitigate double-voting, and there is no credible evidence of a coordinated, systemic rigging scheme.

claim: "At the moment, energy companies spend 0.25 percent on R&D."
rationale: The claim states a single current figure but is overly broad and unsupported: R&D intensity in the energy sector varies significantly by subsector, company and accounting definition, and there is no single universal value of 0.25 percent. Many firms report R&D spending that is both below and above 0.25% depending on whether the percent is of revenue, capital spending, or another base and which year is measured.

claim: "The Florida Legislature has not filed a lawsuit to fight Amendments 5 and 6."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but provides no timeframe or year for 'Amendments 5 and 6.' Whether the Florida Legislature filed suit depends on the specific amendments and year, and I have no definitive evidence confirming a complete absence of any legislative lawsuit. Because the assertion is unverifiable as stated and likely false without supporting details, I mark it FALSE.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "been very clear where she stands on trade."
rationale: Characterizing Hillary Clinton as having "been very clear where she stands on trade" is misleading. Her public record shows shifting positions — for example she voiced support for the Trans‑Pacific Partnership and later opposed it during the 2016 campaign — and she has made mixed statements about trade policy over time, which critics and reporters described as inconsistent.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The statement is broadly correct: Florida law can treat buying/possession of marijuana as a felony in certain circumstances (e.g., amounts over statutory thresholds or intent to distribute), tampering with an odometer is a felony when done with intent to defraud, and interfering with lobster/fish traps can trigger felony wildlife or property charges depending on the conduct. The punchline "So basically spring break" is an exaggeration but the underlying claim that such acts can be felonies in Florida is accurate.

claim: "Voting machines found in bus in Arizona."
rationale: There is no verified evidence that secret or illicit voting machines were 'found in a bus' in Arizona. Investigations and contemporaneous reporting after viral videos showed election equipment being moved concluded the items were part of routine transport or storage and not evidence of a covert operation.

claim: "President Trump has lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont, overseeing a 11,742 decline of Vermont residents on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: there is no clear evidence that President Trump personally “lifted the prospect of voters” or directly caused an exact 11,742 decline in Vermont residents on food stamps. SNAP enrollment is administered by USDA and state agencies and fluctuates with economic conditions, eligibility rules, and pandemic-era policy changes, so attributing a precise drop to a single presidential action without a cited timeframe or source is unverified.

claim: Says Scott Walker is proposing to add 485 employees "in the category of supervisor and management" to his Department of Administration.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Scott Walker proposed creating 485 new employees specifically classified as "supervisor and management" in the Wisconsin Department of Administration. Reporting around Walker's budgets showed proposals that involved reclassifications, transfers, or statewide position authorizations, but not a discrete addition of 485 new DOA supervisors/management. The claim appears to conflate different counts or types of position changes into a single misleading number.

claim: A photograph shows Joe Biden with a Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan.
rationale: There is no verified, credible photograph showing Joe Biden pictured with a Ku Klux Klan Grand Wizard. Viral images making that claim have been debunked as doctored or misattributed; Biden did pose with some former politicians who had past KKK connections (notably Robert Byrd) but no authenticated photo shows him with a Grand Wizard.

claim: "Our income, our GDP per capita, is almost 50 percent higher than (it is for) the average European."
rationale: The statement is too vague and cannot be verified as presented because it does not identify which country, which year, or whether GDP per capita is measured in nominal terms or PPP. GDP per capita differences with an ‘average European’ vary substantially by country and by measurement choice: some countries are well below, others (e.g., the United States by some measures/years) may exceed 50%, but a blanket claim of ‘almost 50 percent higher’ is not generally supportable without context. Because of this missing context the assertion is unreliable.

claim: "The senior senator from Arizona (John McCain) said he couldn't support repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' because of the economy."
rationale: John McCain did oppose repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' at the time, but his publicly stated reasons focused on military readiness, unit cohesion, and the effect on the armed forces — not the economy. There is no reputable record of McCain saying he couldn't support repeal because of economic concerns.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court decided in 1982 that non-citizen children must get free K-12 education.
rationale: In Plyler v. Doe (1982) the U.S. Supreme Court held that states may not deny free public K–12 education to children based on their immigration status, finding such exclusion violated the Equal Protection Clause. The ruling obligates public primary and secondary schools to educate non-citizen (including undocumented) children, though it does not govern higher education or other benefits.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: As Vermont's governor, Phil Scott is not a member of the U.S. House and therefore cannot cast a vote to impeach a president; impeachment votes are taken by the U.S. House of Representatives. There is no record of Scott having 'voted to impeach' President Trump—he may have expressed opinions or state bodies could pass symbolic resolutions, but the governor does not vote in federal impeachment proceedings.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: Recent data from sources that track child uninsured rates (e.g., American Community Survey / KIDS COUNT) show Missouri's rate of uninsured children is around or below the national average and does not rank among the very highest states. States such as Texas, Oklahoma, Nevada and Florida have consistently reported higher child uninsured rates than Missouri.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: The claim is extremely unlikely: electricity generation mixes are typically diverse and measured at utility or state levels rather than by congressional district boundaries. Power plants and grid flows cross district lines, and even coal-heavy regions usually include some natural gas, hydro, renewables, or imported power rather than 100% coal generation.

claim: "Biden invested the entire family fortune in Ukraine gas and oil. Then shuts down Keystone pipeline. Starting to get the picture."
rationale: The claim mixes a truthful action with a false blanket assertion: Joe Biden did revoke the Keystone XL permit in January 2021, and Hunter Biden had paid ties to a Ukrainian energy firm (Burisma). However, there is no credible evidence that Biden or his family 'invested the entire family fortune in Ukraine gas and oil.' That sweeping financial claim is unsupported and misleading.

claim: "If they made no changes whatsoever, the [state employees pension] plan still had enough money to go forward for approximately the next 16 years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which state plan, which valuation date, or which actuarial assumptions underpin the 16‑year figure. Projections of pension solvency vary widely based on assumed investment returns, contribution policy, demographic assumptions and the baseline funding status; without those specifics the blanket 16‑year claim cannot be confirmed. Therefore I treat the unsupported assertion as false.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: John McCain at times denied supporting the privatization of Social Security, yet archived campaign footage and public statements from earlier periods show he endorsed allowing workers to invest some payroll taxes in private personal accounts. Multiple contemporary fact-checkers and news reports documented those past statements, demonstrating the apparent contradiction between his denials and the video record.

claim: "So Trump comes to Nashville to oversee damage from the tornado. He flies into the area in a helicopter to get there without further traffic problems in the city. He writes PERSONAL checks to those in need, with his personal accountant in tow."
rationale: There are no credible reports that President Trump flew by helicopter into Nashville to personally oversee tornado damage or that he handed out personal checks to victims with his personal accountant present. Media coverage and official accounts of the Nashville tornado response describe federal/state/FEMA involvement and do not document such on-the-spot private cash distributions by the president.

claim: "Youth usage of marijuana has actually gone down in states that have fully legalized."
rationale: Empirical evidence is mixed rather than uniformly showing declines: some fully legal states have reported decreases in certain youth-use measures while others show no change or small increases. Major national surveys and systematic reviews conclude there is no consistent, across-the-board decline in youth marijuana use that can be attributed to full legalization.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republican leadership, the number of people collecting food stamps has declined by more than two million."
rationale: While SNAP participation did fall by several million in the late 2010s (so a decline of more than two million occurred across some years), attributing that drop solely to "President Trump and Republican leadership" is misleading. The decline reflected broader factors including an improving economy after the Great Recession, administrative and eligibility changes that predated or were implemented by multiple administrations, and enrollment trends that began before Trump and reversed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: Under Republican-backed state budget, the state education agency estimates expansion of Wisconsin’s school voucher program "could cost nearly $2 billion annually"
rationale: Multiple news reports and the Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction’s analysis tied to the Republican-backed budget indicated that a large expansion of the state’s school voucher program could cost up to nearly $2 billion per year, depending on the scope and phase-in. The estimate was presented as a potential maximum impact rather than a guaranteed immediate outlay.

claim: A proposed San Antonio ordinance will allow men into women’s restrooms in the city.
rationale: Municipal nondiscrimination proposals discussed in San Antonio have aimed to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex or gender identity, which would allow transgender women to use women’s restrooms consistent with their gender identity. That is not the same as broadly allowing any man to enter women’s restrooms; the ordinances regulate discrimination, not create a general right for unrelated men to enter single-sex spaces.

claim: Says his administration balanced "two budgets with over $13 billion in deficits without raising taxes."
rationale: The claim as written is not verifiable because it uses an unspecified pronoun (“his administration”) and gives no time period or jurisdiction. Broadly, assertions that an administration ‘‘balanced’’ multi-year budgets totalling $13B+ in deficits without raising taxes are commonly achieved through one-time transfers, accounting shifts, federal aid, or spending cuts rather than true recurring balance; without specifics this cannot be confirmed. Given the ambiguity and lack of evidence, the claim is treated as false.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While Ayotte supported GOP budget resolutions that proposed major changes to higher-education funding and some Republican budgets projected big reductions in student-aid spending over a decade, there is no direct Senate vote by Ayotte for a budget explicitly and solely cutting Pell Grants by $90 billion. The $90 billion figure conflates projected reductions across multiple student-aid programs or long-term budget projection assumptions rather than a clear, enacted $90 billion Pell cut vote by Ayotte.

claim: "We are within the margin of error."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify: 'within the margin of error' depends on a specific estimate, its reported margin of error, and the comparison being made. Without information on the measured quantity, sample size, confidence level, and the numerical margin, the claim cannot be confirmed and therefore cannot be treated as true.

claim: "The deficit was on track to top $1 trillion the year I took office."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits who "I" refers to and which fiscal year is meant; without that context it cannot be confirmed. US federal deficits have varied by year and administration—some years were projected or recorded above $1 trillion (e.g., FY2009, COVID-era FY2020–21) while others were not—so the blanket claim is misleading without speaker and date.

claim: Allen West called Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" and said "this country's got to get on sound footing by destroying it."
rationale: Allen West did publicly call Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in past remarks, but there is no reliable record of him saying the specific line quoted—"this country's got to get on sound footing by destroying it." The claim combines a true characterization with an apparent misquote or embellishment of his position.

claim: States with voter ID laws have seen "zero decrease" in participation. "Most have seen an increase."
rationale: The claim is an overstatement: empirical research on voter ID laws is mixed, and several rigorous studies have found declines in turnout in some states or among particular groups (young, minority, low-income voters), while other states showed no effect or increases likely driven by other factors. Saying there has been "zero decrease" and that "most have seen an increase" ignores heterogeneity across states, law strictness, election year, and confounding variables, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: The claim gives a precise statistic ("over 70 percent") about Kathryn Starkey's voting/seconding behavior but no verifiable vote records or a defined time period were provided. I cannot confirm that specific percentage from the information given, so absent public roll-call records or meeting minutes supporting it, the claim cannot be verified and is treated as false.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: Extensive contemporary records and Barack Obama’s own memoirs identify his biological father as Barack Obama Sr., a Kenyan economist. Frank Marshall Davis was a left-leaning journalist and occasional mentor figure to Obama’s family in Hawaii, but there is no credible evidence—no birth, legal, or genetic documentation—that Davis was Obama’s father. The claim stems from long-debunked conspiracy theories rather than verifiable facts.

claim: "Richard Nixon was the last president to be impeached."
rationale: Nixon resigned in August 1974 before the full House voted on articles of impeachment; the House Judiciary Committee had approved articles but the House never formally impeached him. The most recent president(s) actually impeached by the House are Donald Trump (impeached in 2019 and again in 2021).

claim: U.S. debt is "now equal to 100 percent of the GDP."
rationale: The claim is misleading. U.S. federal debt measures vary: gross (total) federal debt has been above 100% of GDP in recent years, while 'debt held by the public' has been close to but not exactly 100% and changes with the quarter and data source. Saying it is "now equal to 100 percent of the GDP" as a blanket statement is inaccurate without specifying which debt measure and which date.

claim: The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and claimed Israeli forces killed her during its recent war with Hamas.
rationale: I cannot find verified evidence that The New York Times knowingly published an old stock photo of a young girl and explicitly claimed Israeli forces killed her in the recent Israel–Hamas war. Major news organizations, including the NYT, have on occasion published images with incorrect captions and issued corrections, but the broad claim as stated (that NYT published an old stock photo and asserted Israeli forces killed the pictured girl) is unverified and lacks corroboration from reliable reporting.

claim: Says West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction."
rationale: This specific claim is unsupported. West Virginia does have relatively low employment and elevated rates of opioid addiction and incarceration, but official employment-to-population and labor-force-participation figures are not uniformly 'around 50%' for all adults and researchers attribute low participation to multiple causes (aging population, disability, economic decline), not solely addiction or convictions. There is no authoritative evidence that roughly half of adults are out of work specifically because of addiction or criminal convictions.

claim: Putin beheaded bioweapon engineers in Ukraine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that President Vladimir Putin personally beheaded anyone, nor that Russian forces carried out documented beheadings of 'bioweapon engineers' in Ukraine. Such an extreme claim would have been widely documented by independent journalists, international investigators, and human rights organizations, but no corroborated reports exist. The allegation appears to originate from unverified or propagandistic sources and mirrors debunked disinformation about 'bioweapons' in Ukraine.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: Public roll-call records show that neither Senator Cruz nor Senator Rubio has missed the majority of Senate votes. Both have missed some votes at times (e.g., due to campaigning or travel), but their absences constitute a minority, not a 'vast majority', of roll-call votes.

claim: "Calling for the assassination of the president is a federal crime."
rationale: Under U.S. federal law, making threats against the President (18 U.S.C. § 871) is a federal crime, and related statutes criminalize interstate threats, solicitation, or conspiracy to kill a federal official. However, purely abstract or political advocacy can implicate First Amendment protections; speech becomes criminal when it constitutes a true threat or incitement to imminent lawless action.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: The claim presents a blanket, routine practice that South Korean police regularly spray rioters with dye to identify and arrest them later. There is no evidence of a nationwide, standard policy to do this; while law enforcement in various countries sometimes use colored dye or marking agents in specific incidents, that is not documented as a regular or official practice across South Korea.

claim: AIDS was transmitted to humans because "one guy" had sex with "a monkey" and then started "having sex with men."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. HIV/AIDS arose from multiple zoonotic transmissions of simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) into humans—HIV‑1 from chimpanzees and HIV‑2 from sooty mangabeys—most plausibly via exposure to infected blood during hunting/butchering and other contacts, not from a single man having sex with a monkey. After zoonosis, human-to-human spread (including sexual transmission) distributed the virus more widely.

claim: Says 2010 video clip showing coffins in a field proves "COVID was planned."
rationale: A video from 2010 appearing to show coffins cannot by itself prove that COVID-19 was planned because the pandemic began in late 2019; an earlier clip is unrelated temporal evidence. Such footage can be misattributed or show unrelated events (e.g., stockpiles, burials, funerary displays, drills), and using it as proof of foreknowledge or orchestration is a logical fallacy without corroborating provenance and direct evidence.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The claim conflates a luxury fashion brand (Saint Laurent) with government-issued personal protective equipment. Governments procure standardized, functional hazmat suits from specialized suppliers, not high-fashion houses, and a photo alone does not prove official issuance. Absent documentation of procurement or authoritative labeling, the statement is implausible and likely a mischaracterization or joke.

claim: Undocumented immigrants "pay $12 billion a year into Social Security."
rationale: Multiple official analyses and academic studies have estimated that unauthorized (undocumented) immigrants contribute on the order of $10–13 billion annually in payroll taxes to Social Security, and $12 billion per year is a commonly cited, supported approximate figure. The exact amount varies by year and methodology, but the claim matches mainstream estimates of payroll-tax contributions by undocumented workers.

claim: In Texas, "sexting is a felony sex offense for teenagers — that can mean up to 10 years in prison."
rationale: This is misleading. Texas law historically allowed teen sexting to be prosecuted under child‑pornography statutes, but that was not a blanket rule and reforms and prosecutorial practice have generally treated consensual teen‑to‑teen sexting as a juvenile matter or a misdemeanor rather than an automatic felony. Felony sentences (which can reach years in prison) generally apply when adults are involved or for more serious child‑pornography distribution offenses, not uniformly for teenagers who exchange images consensually.

claim: The man in a mugshot is "responsible for lighting 32 of the wildfires" on the West Coast.
rationale: No credible law-enforcement report or major-news coverage confirms that a single individual pictured in a mugshot was responsible for lighting 32 separate West Coast wildfires. Wildfire cause investigations typically identify lightning, equipment, accidents, or isolated arson incidents, and a claim that one person started so many fires would be extraordinary and widely documented but is not supported by reliable sources.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks verifiable specifics (who 'he' is, which jurisdiction, and which Attorney General guidance). Public-release rules for internal affairs records vary by state and country, and while some attorneys general issue guidelines about confidentiality, those guidelines do not universally prohibit release and often depend on local law or pending investigations. Without a named person and jurisdiction, the assertion that AG guidelines categorically protect the record cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Oregon, once again, remains among the top five hungriest states in the nation."
rationale: National food-insecurity/hunger rankings from major sources (e.g., USDA and Feeding America) consistently show the highest rates concentrated in several Southern states; Oregon typically does not appear in the top five. Without a specified year or metric, there is no evidence supporting the claim that Oregon is once again among the five hungriest states.

claim: U.S. military involvement in Libya "allowed thousands of surface-to-air missiles to fall into the hands of radical Islamists."
rationale: While NATO/US intervention and the 2011 collapse of Libyan state control did lead to widespread looting of weapons and some man‑portable air‑defense systems (MANPADS) went missing, there is no reliable evidence that "thousands of surface‑to‑air missiles" specifically fell into the hands of radical Islamist groups. Investigations and expert reports documented proliferation of small arms and some SAMs but gave far lower or uncertain counts and showed weapons dispersed among many militias and traffickers rather than being concentrated in extremist hands.

claim: "You couldn’t buy a cannon when, in fact, the Second Amendment passed."
rationale: The claim that you couldn’t buy a cannon when the Second Amendment passed overstates the case. Cannons were expensive and uncommon for private individuals in the 1790s, but they were manufactured and supplied by foundries and used by state militias and some private actors; there was no universal legal impossibility preventing purchase across the new United States.

claim: Says Google Earth blocked people from seeing the Suez Canal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Google Earth intentionally 'blocked' the Suez Canal from public view; the canal is normally visible on Google Maps/Earth. Temporary issues such as low-resolution imagery, outdated images, provider licensing, or processing delays can make areas appear unclear, but these are not the same as deliberate blocking.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: State tax data and prior fact-checks show that a large majority of New York State personal income tax receipts come from New York City together with the downstate suburbs (Westchester, Nassau and Suffolk). Aggregated audits of recent tax-year data put the share in the high-60s to about 70 percent, so the rounded claim is accurate.

claim: Photo shows "Myrtle Beach 30 minutes ago."
rationale: There is no evidence provided to confirm the photo was taken at Myrtle Beach '30 minutes ago.' Without original file metadata, a verifiable source, or corroborating live feeds, the claim is unsupported and could reflect an older or misattributed image.

claim: "President Trump just saved Christmas for 13 million retirees."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported by public reporting: there is no verifiable, widely reported executive action by President Trump that specifically 'saved Christmas' for exactly 13 million retirees. Major benefit changes or emergency interventions affecting millions of retirees would require legislation or clear administrative orders and would have been widely documented; no such corroborating evidence matches this precise claim.

claim: "Trump wins the award Obama never could."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify because it does not name any specific award.
