There is no clear evidence that Donald Trump won a particular award that Barack Obama was categorically unable to win, and Obama has won major honors himself (notably the Nobel Peace Prize), so as stated the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "99 percent of the time police officers aren't charged when they kill young people of color."
rationale: The specific claim that officers are not charged 99% of the time for killing young people of color is not supported by available evidence. Research and public incident databases show that while criminal charges against officers in fatal encounters are relatively rare, the frequency varies by dataset, time period, and definition (charged vs. indicted vs. convicted) and is not uniformly as low as 1% across all cases.

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and likely inaccurate as stated. While Ted Cruz has a substantial national donor network and raised large sums from outside Texas during his 2016 presidential run, campaign receipts vary by cycle and are not predominantly sourced from 'Washington' specifically; many contributions come from across the country and from within Texas as well. Absent a defined timeframe or data source, asserting that 'most' of his money comes from Washington is unsupported.

claim: "A golf course closes somewhere in America every 48 hours."
rationale: The claim is a recurring sound bite from the recession era but is imprecise and not supported by current industry data. While there were periods when many courses closed annually, recent years show far fewer net closures and the rate fluctuates; saying a course closes somewhere in America every 48 hours as a steady, factual statement is misleading.

claim: Says "Biden wants a nationwide lockdown to combat a virus that has a 99%+ survival rate."
rationale: The claim conflates two misleading points: President Biden did not call for an across-the-board nationwide lockdown as policy; he advocated a national strategy of testing, masking, and targeted restrictions rather than a blanket lockdown. The stated '99%+ survival rate' is an oversimplification — COVID-19 survival/IFR varies substantially by age, health status, and time period, so presenting a single >99% survival figure as justification is misleading.

claim: North Carolina has "the strictest anti-gerrymandering standards in the entire country."
rationale: North Carolina has adopted limits on partisan gerrymandering in recent amendments and statutes, but it is not objectively established as having the "strictest" standards nationwide. Several states (for example Arizona, California, Iowa and others) use independent redistricting commissions or have clearer, more structural bans on partisan mapping, and court rulings have repeatedly found NC maps problematic. "Strictest" is therefore not supportable as a factual claim.

claim: "Greg Abbott said it would be a ‘waste’ to expand pre-k to all Texas children."
rationale: I could not verify a reliable record of Governor Greg Abbott quoting the exact phrase that expanding pre‑K to all Texas children would be “a ‘waste’.” While Abbott has publicly opposed universal pre‑K expansion and argued the state should target early‑childhood programs to those most in need, the specific quoted wording appears to be a paraphrase rather than a documented verbatim statement.

claim: "Due to ... tax cuts and lower (property) values, 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 property taxes."
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because it lacks any jurisdiction or data source; property tax totals vary by locality and many jurisdictions did not see a $3 billion drop between 2007 and 2009. While recessions and tax changes can reduce property tax revenue, assessments, timing of reassessments, and local rate changes often blunt year-to-year swings, so the unsupported blanket figure is not verifiable.

claim: "Jim Renacci cheated on his income taxes" and is a "deadbeat citizen."
rationale: There is no verified evidence that Jim Renacci was criminally convicted of cheating on his income taxes; media coverage around him referenced tax disputes and political attacks alleging unpaid or late taxes but did not substantiate a criminal tax-evasion finding. Calling him a “deadbeat citizen” is a partisan characterization rather than a documented legal status.

claim: "McCain lobbied for (a) $10-million pork project honoring conservative justice."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Senator John McCain lobbied for a specific $10‑million earmark described as a “pork project honoring [a] conservative justice.” McCain was widely known for opposing earmarks and pork-barrel spending, and major media and congressional records do not document a high-profile $10M project of that description tied to him.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: No Lancet peer‑reviewed study reports uniform vaccine efficacies as tiny percentages like 1.3%, 1.2% or 0.84% for AstraZeneca, Moderna, J&J and Pfizer. Randomized clinical trials and many peer‑reviewed analyses reported large relative risk reductions (about 94–95% for the mRNA vaccines in initial trials; lower but substantial efficacy for AstraZeneca and J&J), and the quoted tiny numbers appear to be a misrepresentation or misuse of absolute risk reduction or other metrics, not a confirmed finding in The Lancet.

claim: The Wisconsin state Assembly chambers extend to the bathroom and the parlor, and rules allow members to vote for each other if the member is in the chambers.
rationale: The Assembly "chamber" refers to the designated legislative floor, not bathrooms or parlors, and Wisconsin Assembly rules require members to be physically present on the floor to cast a vote. Wisconsin does not permit members to routinely cast votes on behalf of absent colleagues (no general proxy voting), so the claim that the chamber "extends" into private rooms and allows members to vote for each other under that definition is incorrect.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and news reporting found no evidence that the clip shows a lone individual wearing explicitly 'Muslim garb' or that the person was identified as a suspect; the footage is ambiguous and the cathedral fire was investigated as accidental with no credible link to a person of the type claimed. The claim relies on visual inference from low-resolution video and unverified commentary rather than verified identification.

claim: "Breaking: Santa Fe killer expresses his love for Obama."
rationale: There is no credible reporting that the Santa Fe shooter publicly 'expressed his love for Obama.' Major news coverage of the Santa Fe shooting did not record such a statement and the claim appears to be a social‑media rumor without evidence. Given the absence of verifiable sources, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: This is false. Iceland's laws protect freedom of religion and there is no Icelandic law or official declaration that labels all religions as mental disorders. Classifying mental disorders is a medical matter handled by health authorities (e.g., WHO/ICD), not by declaring belief systems illegal or medical conditions.

claim: ICE está en Uvalde, Texas, "entonces los padres indocumentados tienen que temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos están vivos".
rationale: Contemporary news reports and eyewitness accounts from Uvalde documented the presence of ICE/DHS personnel at family reunification and identification sites after the school shooting, and immigrant advocates and some parents reported that the agents' presence caused fear of detention or deportation. ICE publicly stated agents were assisting the federal response and not conducting immigration arrests, but that distinction did not eliminate documented fear among undocumented families trying to check on children.

claim: "BREAKING: Pennsylvania initiated a FULL audit of the RIGGED ELECTION"
rationale: There was no state-initiated, statewide "full audit" in Pennsylvania that confirmed a "rigged" election. Pennsylvania certified its results and multiple recounts and court challenges found no evidence of widespread fraud; while some county-level or partisan reviews have occurred, they were not a statewide audit that overturned results.

claim: Says "CNN host Fareed Zakaria calls for jihad rape of white women."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that Fareed Zakaria, a CNN host and commentator, ever called for 'jihad rape of white women.' The allegation appears to be a fabricated, defamatory claim with no support in transcripts, videos, or reputable news coverage of his statements.

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: The video does show President Biden repeating the phrase after it is spoken, but analysis of the inauguration footage shows the words were audible from a nearby staffer giving directions off-camera, not transmitted through a hidden earpiece. Multiple news fact-checks reviewed the clip and found no evidence of an earpiece or other audio feed to Biden.

claim: "What I have done -- and this is unprecedented ... is I've said to each agency ... 'look at regulations that are already on the books and if they don't make sense, let's get rid of them.'"
rationale: Telling agencies to review existing regulations and remove those that "don't make sense" is something presidents have done before, so the claim that this is "unprecedented" is incorrect. While an officeholder may indeed have directed agencies to audit and cut regulations, regulatory review and deregulatory orders have long precedent in multiple administrations and through OMB/OIRA processes.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The statement presented as an absolute fact is incorrect because approval/trust ratings for "the media" and for Congress vary by poll, time period, and how each is defined. In some polls and years the media polls lower, while in many others Congressional approval is as low or lower; there is no consistent universal ranking that supports the categorical claim.

claim: "The number of SWAT raids have gone up by 1,400 percent since the 1980s."
rationale: The broad trend — a large rise in SWAT deployments since the 1980s — is well documented, but the specific figure of a 1,400% increase is not a consistently supported, verifiable statistic. Different reputable studies and news analyses report widely varying increases (from several hundred percent to over two thousand percent) depending on the exact start/end years, definitions of SWAT actions, and data sources, so the precise 1,400% claim is misleading.

claim: Says Sen. Thad Cochran "voted to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on ... the Bridge to Nowhere in Alaska instead of shifting the money to repair a bridge damaged by Hurricane Katrina."
rationale: The claim implies a direct vote choosing to fund the Alaskan 'Bridge to Nowhere' instead of repairing a Katrina-damaged bridge. In reality, the Alaska earmark (roughly $200–300 million) was included in earlier transportation legislation and later efforts to rescind or redirect earmarks after Katrina failed; there was no single clean vote that swapped those funds for Katrina bridge repairs. Presentations that say Cochran 'voted to spend' that money instead of shifting it are therefore misleading about the timing and choices on the Senate floor.

claim: "A gallon (of gasoline) delivered to the front lines for our troops in Afghanistan cost more than $400."
rationale: Multiple Pentagon and media reports documented that the marginal cost to deliver fuel to remote forward operating bases in Afghanistan—when flown in by helicopter or sent with heavily guarded convoys—reached or exceeded roughly $300–$400 per gallon, and figures over $400 per gallon were reported for some locations and periods. This refers to delivered logistical cost, not the retail pump price for gasoline in the United States.

claim: "The U.S. has now spent more on reconstructing Afghanistan than was spent on the Marshall Plan and the reconstruction of Europe."
rationale: The claim is misleading. U.S. spending on Afghanistan reconstruction is often cited around $140–150 billion (per SIGAR totals), while the Marshall Plan appropriation was about $12.4 billion in 1948 dollars (which converts to roughly $100–150 billion depending on inflation measure). Comparisons hinge on which inflation index, time frame, and which reconstruction costs are counted; moreover the Marshall Plan was only one component of postwar European recovery, so a simple greater/less-than claim lacks necessary context.

claim: Says the names of CNN anchors Chris Cuomo, Brian Stelter and Jake Tapper were on the flight logs of Jeffrey Epstein’s private plane.
rationale: Publicly released Epstein flight logs and reporting by independent fact-checkers do not show Chris Cuomo, Brian Stelter, or Jake Tapper listed as passengers. CNN and multiple fact-check organizations have stated there is no credible evidence those anchors were on Epstein’s plane, and online lists that purported to show their names were unverified or contained common-name ambiguities.

claim: Says he is the "ranking member" of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
rationale: The House January 6 select committee did not have an officially recognized Republican 'ranking member.' House Democrats appointed the committee membership, and Speaker Pelosi did not seat the GOP leader's nominees; while some Republicans (for example Rep. Jim Banks) later styled themselves as the committee's 'ranking member' in statements, that title was not formally recognized by the committee or the House.

claim: Says Mark Kelly wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Mark Kelly has publicly said he does not support 'defund the police' and has criticized the slogan while expressing support for law enforcement and for reforms and investments in mental-health and crisis response. News coverage and his own statements show he opposes cutting police funding rather than advocating it.

claim: Under Gov. Scott Walker, "unemployment is increasing in Wisconsin at twice the rate it is nationally."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or metric and is not supported by broad labor market data from Gov. Walker's tenure. Bureau of Labor Statistics state and national series show Wisconsin's unemployment rate generally moved in line with or below the national rate and fell over most of Walker's term; there is no sustained period where Wisconsin's unemployment rose at twice the national rate. Short monthly swings can differ, but they do not substantiate the categorical statement.

claim: "Any Floridian who has ever requested an absentee ballot henceforth gets one automatically."
rationale: Florida does not automatically send future absentee ballots to every person who has ever requested one. Voters who want ballots sent to them for all future elections must be placed on a permanent vote-by-mail list (or renew requests where required); a single past request does not universally entitle someone to automatic future mail ballots. Local election rules and changes in state law can also affect how requests are handled.

claim: Video shows Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pouring shots for a group of people "days before testing positive" for COVID-19.
rationale: Known fact-checks show the circulating video of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pouring shots was filmed well before she ever tested positive for COVID-19; it does not depict an event 'days before' a positive test. Claim conflates an unrelated earlier clip with her later positive test, creating a misleading timeline.

claim: Says Ronald Reagan "was behind in the polls in 1980 going into the debate with Jimmy Carter and then turned around 10 days later and won 40 states."
rationale: It is true Reagan gained momentum after the Oct. 28, 1980 debate (some polls showed him trailing beforehand), but the claim’s specifics are wrong: the election was one week after the debate (Nov. 4), not 10 days, and Reagan carried 44 states in the landslide, not 40. Those factual errors make the statement inaccurate.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: Public warnings from the UN and major humanitarian agencies in early 2017 stated that more than 20 million people across four countries—Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northeastern Nigeria—were at risk of dying of starvation within months if emergency assistance was not scaled up. The UN phrasing and media reporting used timeframes on the order of months (often cited as six months).

claim: "Close to half of the folks in this country illegally entered legally (but) overstayed (their ) visas."
rationale: Reliable estimates from DHS and research organizations show that a substantial share of the U.S. unauthorized population are visa overstays, typically around 40%–50%, so saying "close to half" is a fair characterization. The exact share varies by year and methodology, but multiple analyses (including Pew and DHS) have reported figures near that range.

claim: Says only seven percent of 2009’s stimulus bill went toward transportation projects, yet they created over one-third of the bill’s total jobs.
rationale: This claim misstates the distribution and job impacts of the 2009 ARRA. Transportation-related spending was a modest but larger share than a simple 7% characterization once broader infrastructure categories are considered, and authoritative post‑ARRA accounting (OMB/GAO and Recovery.gov summaries) does not support that transportation projects alone produced over one‑third of the bill’s total jobs; jobs were spread across tax relief, health, education, and state fiscal relief as well. Additionally, ARRA job effects were reported in terms of estimated 'job‑years' and are not directly comparable to a single snapshot headcount.

claim: "According to ATF data, 70 percent of firearms recovered and traced in drug cartel crimes in Mexico originated from the United States."
rationale: ATF trace data for various multi-year periods has shown that a large majority—often around 70 percent (and in some analyses higher)—of firearms recovered and traced in Mexico and linked to drug trafficking were originally sold in the United States. However, ATF and analysts note this statistic applies to the subset of weapons that were submitted for and successfully completed traces, not to all firearms recovered.

claim: Says after Hurricane Sandy, New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg "refused to allow the National Guard into the city to restore civil order because Guardsmen carry guns!"
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Mayor Bloomberg did not "refuse to allow" the National Guard into New York City after Hurricane Sandy. The New York National Guard was activated by the governor and thousands of Guard members were deployed to assist with relief and security; the mayor does not have unilateral authority to block state-controlled Guard deployments. The assertion that Bloomberg's motive was that "Guardsmen carry guns" is unsupported and contradicted by contemporaneous reporting and official actions.

claim: Wisconsin ranks 48th out of all 50 states in venture capital investment.
rationale: The claim presents an absolute statewide rank without specifying year or metric; venture capital rankings vary by year and by measure (total dollars, deals, per-capita). Wisconsin often ranks low nationally in VC but its exact position fluctuates across reports and is not consistently 48th. Without a specific dataset or year, the blanket statement is not reliably supported.

claim: The home-mortgage deduction is widely thought to be "a middle-class benefit. It's not -- 73 percent of it goes to people making a quarter-million dollars or more a year."
rationale: The mortgage interest deduction is indeed concentrated among higher-income households who itemize, but reputable analyses (IRS, Tax Policy Center, CBO) show the share of the deduction received by households with incomes of $250,000+ is substantially lower than 73% and varies by year and measurement. The quoted 73% figure is not supported by standard distributional estimates and likely misstates or misattributes the underlying statistic.

claim: Alison Alter "has exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars to fund her campaign."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating, specific evidence that Alison Alter 'exploited a campaign finance loophole' to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars. While candidates in some jurisdictions can receive public matching or grant dollars if they meet program rules, calling that an 'exploit' requires proof of rule-breaking or loophole manipulation which is not documented in available general sources. Without jurisdictional details or records showing misconduct, the claim is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Says many public-employee unions falsely told their Wisconsin members his budget-repair bill sought 12 percent to 13 percent of their incomes for health insurance premiums.
rationale: The claim overstates and simplifies a complex dispute. Wisconsin’s 2011 budget-repair law required public employees to begin contributing toward pensions and to pay a share of health insurance premiums, but it did not uniformly require that workers pay 12–13% of their incomes for health coverage. Some union communications used an illustrative 12–13% figure (or combined pension and health contributions) in ways that were misleading for some employees, but the actual obligation varied by plan, coverage level, and salary.

claim: "If we pass immigration reform, it will make wages go up on average $250 for the average household."
rationale: The statement asserts a precise $250 average household wage gain from an unspecified 'immigration reform,' but economic effects depend strongly on the specific policy, timeframe, and modeling assumptions. Scholarly and government analyses generally find small aggregate gains or mixed distributional effects, not a single agreed-upon $250 per household increase.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The statement gives no dates or source and thus is not verifiable as a current fact. Official confirmation requires checking the BLS monthly private nonfarm payroll series for the specific 30-month window; different 30‑month periods produce different totals, so the blanket claim cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Sanctioning a country's central bank can severely disrupt its ability to conduct international payments, access foreign reserves, and stabilize its currency, but it does not inevitably or immediately "shut down" the entire economy. Historical precedent (e.g., sanctions on Iran's central bank in the 2010s) shows large economic contraction, higher inflation, and hardship, yet the economy continued to function through domestic activity, barter, regional banking channels, and other workarounds. The ultimate impact depends on the scope, enforcement, and duration of sanctions and on humanitarian exemptions and alternative arrangements.

claim: "Ohio has lost more population than every other state in the country except for two."
rationale: The claim is too broad and misleading because it gives no timeframe or metric. Across different periods and measures (decennial census, annual estimates, or net domestic migration) multiple states — for example New York, Illinois, West Virginia and at times California — have lost as much or more population than Ohio; Ohio’s losses are not consistently the third‑largest. Without a specified period or whether this is absolute or percentage loss, the statement is not supported.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine "want to shut down shale, and shut down natural gas."
rationale: Neither Hillary Clinton nor Tim Kaine advocated an outright policy to "shut down" shale or eliminate natural gas production. Clinton's 2016 platform called for stronger regulation of fossil fuels and limits on fracking in certain areas while supporting a transition to cleaner energy, not an immediate shut-down of natural gas; Kaine likewise did not call for eliminating natural gas and has supported a role for it as part of an energy mix or transition. Characterizing their positions as wanting to "shut down" shale/natural gas is a misleading overstatement.

claim: Says Fox News gave Republican senators twice the air time as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State.
rationale: The assertion is specific (Republican senators received twice the airtime as Democrats) but provides no citation or identifiable hearing to verify. I am not aware of a widely reported, verifiable media monitoring study showing Fox News gave GOP senators exactly double the airtime during any specific Islamic State hearing; without a named hearing, date, or analysis, the precise numeric claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Kanye West got 40,000 votes in the presidential election in Kentucky.
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Kanye West did not receive 40,000 votes in Kentucky in the recent presidential election. Publicly reported 2020 presidential returns show West had limited ballot access and a nationwide total of roughly 60,000 votes, with his state-level totals far below 40,000; Kentucky returns list only a small number of votes for him. The claim significantly overstates his Kentucky vote count.

claim: "Corporate income has increased as a share of" gross domestic product.
rationale: The statement is presented as a general, timeless fact but is not universally true: corporate income (profits) as a share of GDP has varied over time and across countries rather than monotonically increasing. In the U.S. and other economies corporate profit shares rose in some periods (e.g., post-1980s/2000s) but fell in others, and results depend on definitions (pre‑tax vs after‑tax profits).

claim: "Car thefts (are) increasing in 8 of the 10 most populous (Wisconsin) counties."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated because no timeframe or data source is given, and my training data does not confirm that car thefts were increasing in exactly 8 of the 10 most populous Wisconsin counties. Vehicle-theft trends vary by county and year and require county-level FBI (UCR/NIBRS) or Wisconsin DOJ statistics to substantiate. Without a cited dataset and period, the claim is not supported.

claim: Obama served on a board with former Weather Underground member William Ayers and "that relationship with Mr. Ayers on this board continued after 9/11."
rationale: Barack Obama and William Ayers both served on the board of the Woods Fund of Chicago and their board service overlapped. Public records and contemporary reporting show both were board members around 1999–2001 (Obama’s term extended into 2002), meaning their board relationship did continue at the time of and immediately after the September 2001 attacks.

claim: Congressman Jeff Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported."
rationale: The claim presents an absolute position that Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported." His record shows support for stronger immigration enforcement but also involvement in bipartisan talks and support for protections for certain groups (such as DREAMers), so he has not unequivocally endorsed mass detention/arrest/deportation of all undocumented immigrants. The statement overgeneralizes and misrepresents his nuanced positions.

claim: "We could cut unemployment in half simply by reclaiming the jobs taken by illegal workers."
rationale: This is misleading and unlikely to be true. The number of unauthorized workers is not large enough, relative to unemployed people, in many periods to cut unemployment by half, and jobs are not perfectly interchangeable — skill, geographic, wage, and legal barriers mean unemployed residents often would not or could not immediately fill those positions.

claim: "There have been more than 300 mass shootings in the United States this year – more than any other country in the world."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it fails to specify which year and which definition of 'mass shooting' is being used. Depending on the definition (e.g., 4+ people shot vs. 4+ killed) U.S. tallies from sources like the Gun Violence Archive have recorded well over 300 incidents in recent years and the U.S. typically has more such incidents than other countries, but the unspecified year and varying definitions prevent a definitive true/false determination.

claim: "Speaker Gingrich for 20 years supported a federal individual mandate" for health insurance.
rationale: While Newt Gingrich has at times praised the concept of an individual mandate and even said he had supported such ideas for years, his record is not a clear 20-year continuous endorsement of a federal individual mandate. Much of his prior support was framed as state-level or market-based approaches, and he publicly opposed the federal mandate in the Affordable Care Act during his 2012 campaign.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: The claim is presented without any source, date, or identification of which Bill White is meant, so it cannot be confirmed. Without corroborating reporting or a direct statement showing that a specific Bill White refused to debate, the assertion is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: "The United States was paying for anywhere from 70 to 90 percent of (NATO), depending on the way you calculate."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it conflates different measures. The U.S. does not pay 70–90% of NATO’s common budgets (the U.S. share is roughly about 20–25%); depending on year and calculation the U.S. accounts for roughly 60–75% of total NATO members’ combined defence spending, but not as high as 90%. Saying the U.S. was paying '70 to 90 percent of NATO' without specifying the metric is inaccurate.

claim: President Obama was "raised Muslim."
rationale: This is false. While Barack Obama’s father was Muslim and he spent part of his childhood in predominantly Muslim Indonesia, he was primarily raised by his non-Muslim mother, attended a Catholic school and a public school there, and has said he was not raised in the Muslim faith and later identified as Christian. He was not brought up practicing Islam.

claim: "24 of every 100 kids in school today speak Spanish."
rationale: The claim is imprecise about location and timeframe. Interpreting it for the United States, government surveys show Spanish is the largest non-English language among children but the share is roughly in the low-20% range (about 20–22%), not a precise 24 of every 100; numbers also vary by state and year, so the blanket statement is unsupported.
